items: Scientific knowledge is built from observations and evidence, and everyday words such as "theory" and "law" have a much more precise meaning in science. Learning the exact meanings lets you describe how science works.
Observation: information gathered with the senses or with instruments. It is qualitative (a description, such as a colour change) or quantitative (a measurement with a number and a unit).
Hypothesis: a testable, tentative explanation or prediction. It is tentative (not yet confirmed) because evidence from an experiment can support it or contradict it.

Theory: a well-tested explanation of a wide range of observations, supported by a large body of evidence from many investigations. Examples are the kinetic theory of matter (matter is made of moving particles) and collision theory (reactions happen when particles collide).

Law: a statement, often mathematical, that describes what always happens under stated conditions. Examples are the law of conservation of mass (the total mass stays the same during a reaction) and Boyle's law (a law linking the pressure and volume of a gas).
A law describes what happens; a theory explains why it happens. This is why a theory never turns into a law: they do different jobs, and a law is not a "proven theory".

Evidence: data from observation and experiment that are used to support or reject a hypothesis or theory. Scientific knowledge rests on evidence, not on authority or opinion, so a claim is only as good as the data behind it.
Scientists follow a recognisable sequence of steps, from first noticing something to sharing what they found. Each step exists so that the final conclusion rests on evidence that others can check.
1. Make observations and ask a question about what you have noticed.
2. Research what is already known, so that you do not repeat work or ignore existing evidence.
3. Form a hypothesis (a tentative explanation) and use it to make a prediction of what should happen if it is right.
4. Test the prediction with a fair, controlled experiment, in which only one factor is changed and the others are kept the same.
5. Analyse the data and draw a conclusion.
6. Accept, modify or reject the hypothesis, depending on whether the data support it.
7. Communicate the results so that others can check them.
In practice the steps above are not completed once and then left behind. Real investigations loop back, and they need imagination as well as method.
Scientists repeat, redesign and troubleshoot (find and fix faults in) experiments, so the cycle is iterative, meaning it is repeated and each pass improves on the last.
Unexpected results often lead to new questions and new hypotheses, so a surprising result can open a new line of investigation.
Creativity and imagination, as well as logic, are used to propose hypotheses and to design experiments and models, because no rule produces a good idea automatically.
One reliable, reproducible result (one that others can obtain again) that contradicts a hypothesis can be enough to reject it, whereas agreeing results never prove a hypothesis absolutely.
Scientific ideas are not fixed for ever. They change in a particular way, and that way is what makes science reliable.
Scientific knowledge is tentative (provisional): it is the best explanation of the evidence available now, and it can change when new evidence appears.
Ideas change when new observations do not fit the existing explanation, because an explanation has to account for everything observed.
Ideas change when new technology or instruments allow measurements that were not possible before.
Ideas change when a better explanation is proposed and tested against the evidence.
A theory is refined or replaced only when the new idea explains all the old evidence as well as the new evidence; this is how science progresses.
Long-standing, well-tested theories are durable. They are rarely discarded completely; they are modified or have their limits identified.

The atom shows how ideas change. Each model of the atom was replaced or refined when new evidence did not fit the earlier one. A model here means a picture of the atom that explains what has been observed.

Dalton (early 1800s): matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms (atoms that cannot be split), and atoms of the same element are identical. This was supported by the laws of chemical combination (rules for the masses in which elements combine).

Thomson (1897) discovered the electron, a negatively charged particle, which showed that atoms are not indivisible. He proposed the plum pudding model, with negative electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge.

Rutherford (1911): his gold-foil experiment, carried out by Geiger and Marsden, showed that most of the atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus (the central core). This is the nuclear model.
Bohr (1913) proposed that electrons move in fixed energy levels around the nucleus, which explained line emission spectra (the separate coloured lines of light that an element gives out when heated).

The current orbital model describes electrons in orbitals, which are regions with a high probability of finding an electron. There is more on this in "Atomic structure: the nuclear model" and "The orbital model and electronic structure".
Scientists are people, and people can unknowingly tilt results. Bias is a tendency, deliberate or not, to collect, interpret or present information so as to favour one outcome.
Confirmation bias: expecting a particular result and then seeing it in the data.
Selecting only the data that support a hypothesis, or using small or unrepresentative samples, introduces bias, because the results then do not reflect the whole picture.
Funding or commercial interests, and personal or political beliefs, can introduce bias, for example when a result would benefit whoever paid for the study.

Scientists reduce bias with fair tests that use controls (a comparison with nothing changed), repeats and random sampling (choosing subjects by chance), and with blind trials (where those taking part do not know which treatment they receive) where possible.

Scientists also publish all results, including negative ones (results that do not support the hypothesis), declare funding and conflicts of interest, and invite independent checks by other scientists. There is more on this in "Science as a global enterprise and researching an issue".

Much of chemistry is about things too small to see, such as atoms and molecules. Scientists use models to think about them. A model is a representation of an object, system, process or idea that helps us understand, explain or predict something we cannot see or handle directly.
Physical models include ball-and-stick and space-filling molecular models, which are three-dimensional builds of a molecule that show how its atoms are arranged.
Diagrams used as models include dot-and-cross diagrams (showing the electrons in bonds), energy-level diagrams and energy profile diagrams (showing how energy changes during a reaction).
Mathematical models are equations, such as PV = nRT, which links the pressure, volume, amount and temperature of a gas.
Symbolic models are chemical formulae and equations, which use symbols to stand for substances and reactions.
Computer or digital simulations show particles and processes moving and changing, which a fixed diagram cannot do.
A theory can also act as a model: the kinetic theory models matter as moving particles, and collision theory models how reactions happen.
Models are used because they do things that direct observation cannot. They give us a way to picture, explain and test ideas.
Models make the very small, the very large and the invisible understandable; a molecular model shows the shape of a molecule that is far too small to see.
Models explain observations: the particle model (matter as tiny moving particles) explains why gases can be compressed but liquids cannot be compressed much.

Models allow predictions that can be tested: the ideal gas equation predicts the volume of a gas at a new temperature and pressure, and VSEPR theory (which treats electron pairs around an atom as repelling one another) predicts molecular shapes.
Models help scientists communicate ideas to each other and to the public, because a shared picture is easier to discuss than an unseen object.
A model is useful but never complete. Knowing where a model stops working is as important as knowing what it explains.
Every model is a simplification: it leaves out detail and rests on assumptions, so it is never a perfect copy of reality.
A model works only within a range of conditions; the ideal gas model fails at high pressure and low temperature, where real gases deviate from it.
Ball-and-stick models show atoms as hard coloured balls and bonds as rigid sticks, and they show the wrong relative sizes and distances, so they can mislead.
Different models of the same thing may each explain some observations but not others, so chemists choose the model that suits the question.
The Bohr model (electrons in fixed energy levels) explains flame colours and line spectra but not the shapes of orbitals.
Models are tested against evidence and are modified or replaced when they fail to explain new observations.
Science is not done by lone individuals. It is a worldwide effort in which results are shared, so that every scientist can build on what others have found.
Scientists work in universities, industry and government laboratories around the world, sharing results and building on each other's work, so new research starts from what is already known.
Large problems such as climate change, new medicines and clean energy are tackled by international collaborations, because countries working together can share data, equipment and funding.

Scientists publish in journals (magazines that print research reports) and present at conferences (meetings where scientists talk about their work) so that results are available to everyone and can be checked.
A scientific claim is only worth believing if others can look at the evidence behind it. This is why science depends on reports that are complete and clear.
Scientific claims must be supported by evidence that others can examine, so data, methods and conclusions are published together and a reader can judge whether the conclusion follows.
A report must describe the method in enough detail for another scientist to repeat it exactly, because a result can only be checked if the experiment can be redone.

Clear communication uses precise scientific terms, SI units (the international system of units), correct significant figures (the number of meaningful digits in a measurement), labelled tables and graphs, and cited sources (credited references), so the reader cannot misread the results.
Conventions are agreed rules that all scientists use, so that results mean the same everywhere. Without them, a chemist in one country could not be sure what a chemist in another country meant.

IUPAC (the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) sets the rules for naming compounds, so that each compound has one systematic name (a name built by the agreed rules), e.g. but-1-ene, and it agrees chemical symbols and atomic masses.
The SI (Système International) system of units has base units (the basic units from which others are built), including the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K) and mole (mol).
The SI base units also include the ampere (A) and the candela (cd).

Other shared conventions are chemical symbols and formulae, standard conditions for measurements, and international hazard symbols (pictograms, small warning pictures) on chemicals, so that a danger is recognised in any country.
Before research is published, other experts check it. This step, called peer review, is one of the main ways science keeps its standards high.
Peer review is the evaluation of a scientist's work by other independent experts in the same field (peers) before it is published.
1. The scientist submits a paper (a written report of the research) to a journal.
2. The editor, who runs the journal, sends the paper to reviewers.
3. The reviewers check the method, data, analysis and conclusions for errors and originality (whether the work is new), and whether the conclusions are justified by the data.
4. The paper is accepted, returned for changes, or rejected.
Peer review filters out poor or flawed work, reduces bias (unfair leaning towards one result) and gives readers confidence in published results.
Peer review does not guarantee that a result is correct; results are checked by others repeating the work.
Two similar words describe two different tests of whether a result can be trusted. The difference is who repeats the experiment and how.
Repeatable: the same experimenter, using the same method and equipment, gets the same or very similar results when the experiment is repeated.
Reproducible: a different experimenter, using different equipment or a different method, gets the same results.
A claim is accepted only when its results are reproducible, because results that no one else can reproduce are not accepted.
Researching an issue works best when you plan it. A clear question and a record of where your information came from make the final work easy to check.
Start with a focused research question about the issue, e.g. “What are the environmental effects of lithium mining?”, so you know exactly what you are looking for.
Identify keywords (the important search words) and search systematically rather than reading whatever appears first.
Record every source used: author, title, date, publisher or website, and the date accessed, so others can find and check it.
Take notes in your own words and keep a research log (a running record of what you searched and found).
Data used in a research project come from two places: your own measurements, or someone else's. Knowing which is which matters when you judge how far to trust them.
Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator, e.g. by experiment or measurement.
Secondary data are collected by someone else, e.g. published results, government statistics, databases or the results of other class groups.
Secondary data are used to compare with primary data, to check or support conclusions, or where an experiment cannot be done in school.
Sources differ in how much you can trust them. Knowing the kind of source gives you a first idea of how reliable it is likely to be.
Peer-reviewed journal articles (reports checked by other experts before publication) are the most reliable sources but are often technical.
Books and textbooks, and reports from government agencies and scientific bodies, are further kinds of source.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is Ireland's environmental regulator (the body that monitors and enforces environmental rules).
The EPA publishes reports and data on air and water quality.
News media, websites, blogs and social media are accessible but of variable reliability; they may simplify, sensationalise (make more dramatic than the facts) or omit detail.
Company or campaign-group material may be written to sell a product or promote a view, so it may present only what suits that aim.
Once you have found a source, you must judge how far to rely on it. Asking the same set of questions of every source lets you compare them fairly.
Authority: who wrote the source, and are they qualified and named?
Accuracy and evidence: are the claims supported by data and references, and can they be checked against other sources?
Currency: is the source up to date?
Purpose and bias: is it trying to inform, persuade or sell; who funded it; does it present only one side?

Detail: does it explain methods, sample sizes (how many were measured) and uncertainties (how far the values might be off), or does it give only conclusions? A source may lack the detail needed to judge it.
Corroboration (independent confirmation): a claim supported by several independent, reliable sources is more trustworthy than a claim from one source.
Every investigation starts with a question, but not every question can be settled in a laboratory. A scientific question is one that evidence can answer.
A scientific question can be answered by collecting evidence through observation (careful looking and recording) or experiment (changing something and measuring the effect).

A good question is specific and focused and names measurable quantities, so you know exactly what to measure. For example: “How does the concentration of hydrochloric acid affect the rate of its reaction with calcium carbonate?”
Questions of value, opinion or ethics, such as “Are plastics bad?”, cannot be answered by scientific investigation, because no measurement can decide what is good or bad.
A vague question, or one that cannot be tested with the available methods, is unsuitable. A vague question can often be refined into a testable one by naming the quantities to be measured.
A variable is any factor in an experiment that can change. Sorting variables into three types is how you make a test fair and know what you are really testing.
The independent variable is the one the investigator deliberately changes, for example the concentration of acid.
The dependent variable is the one that is measured, and it may change as a result of changing the independent variable, for example the rate of reaction.

Controlled variables are all the other factors that could affect the result. They are kept the same so that the test is fair, because then any change in the result can only be due to the independent variable.
A hypothesis is based on existing scientific theory rather than on a guess. It turns a question into a statement that an experiment can test.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that leads to a testable prediction, so it is a statement, not a question.

A good hypothesis states the expected relationship between the independent and dependent variables and gives the reason. For example: “Increasing the concentration of acid increases the rate of reaction, because there are more acid particles per unit volume and so more frequent effective collisions”.
That reason is drawn from collision theory (the theory that reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy).
A hypothesis must be falsifiable, which means an experiment could show it to be wrong. A statement that no result could ever contradict cannot be tested.
A prediction is the specific result expected if the hypothesis is correct, for example “doubling the concentration will roughly halve the time taken”.
There is usually more than one way to collect evidence for the same hypothesis. Choosing between them means weighing each against a set of criteria.
A hypothesis can often be tested in more than one way. For example, the rate of a reaction that gives off gas can be found in three ways.
Measure the volume of gas collected in a gas syringe (a calibrated syringe that the gas pushes out), the mass lost on a balance, or the time taken for a solid to disappear.

Strategies are compared by validity (does it measure what it should?), the accuracy and precision of the measurements, how easily other variables can be controlled, safety, cost and time, and the range and number of data points.
The strategy chosen should give the most reliable and valid evidence with acceptable safety, and the choice must be justified, meaning you give reasons using the criteria above.
A good plan lets someone else carry out your investigation exactly as you intended. It also shows that you have thought about the whole process before starting.
A plan states the aim or hypothesis, the variables, the equipment and chemicals, a step-by-step method, the measurements to be taken and how often, and the number of repeats.
A plan also includes a risk assessment (a check of what could go wrong and how to prevent it) and states how the data will be recorded and analysed.
Choose a suitable range and number of values for the independent variable, so that a trend can be seen. At least five values across a sensible range is a suggested minimum.
Include a control where appropriate: a set-up in which the factor being tested is absent, for comparison. For example, hydrogen peroxide with no catalyst shows how it behaves without the catalyst.
Examiners use these words to judge how well an investigation was designed. Each one has a distinct meaning, so keep them separate.
Fairness (a fair test): only the independent variable is changed, and all other variables are controlled.
Validity: the investigation actually tests the hypothesis and measures what it claims to measure. It requires a fair test and suitable measurements.
Reliability: results can be trusted because they are consistent when the investigation is repeated.
Reliability is improved by repeating each measurement at least three times, calculating a mean (the average of the repeats), and comparing the results with those of other groups.

Accuracy and precision (how close a result is to the true value, and how close repeats are to each other) are improved by choosing suitable equipment and good technique. There is more on this in Measurement, error and data.
Error: likely sources of error are identified in advance and the design is changed to reduce them. For example, a burette rather than a measuring cylinder is used for accurate volumes.
Integrity: all results are recorded honestly, including unexpected ones. Data are not invented, altered or selectively deleted, and others' work is acknowledged.
The right piece of equipment depends on what is being measured and how exactly it must be measured. Resolution is the smallest change the instrument can show.
A pipette or burette is used for accurate volumes of solution, because they are made to deliver exact volumes.
A volumetric flask is used to make up a solution to an exact volume.
A measuring cylinder is used only where an approximate volume is enough, because it is less accurate than a pipette or burette.
A balance with a suitable resolution, for example 0.01 g, is used for small masses.
A thermometer or temperature probe with an appropriate range is used to measure temperature.
A gas syringe is used to measure gas volumes.
Data-loggers and sensors for pH, temperature and pressure give continuous readings, meaning the values are recorded automatically as the reaction proceeds.
Each choice of equipment is justified in terms of accuracy, precision and safety.
Chemicals and equipment can cause burns, poisoning or fires, so safe habits are part of every investigation. These rules apply whatever the experiment.
Wear eye protection (safety glasses or goggles) and a lab coat, and tie back long hair, so that splashes and flames cannot reach the eyes, skin or hair.
Do not eat or drink in the laboratory, and wash hands after practical work, so that no chemical is swallowed.
Use a fume cupboard (a ventilated cabinet that draws fumes away) for toxic or harmful gases and for volatile (easily evaporating), flammable or harmful liquids.
Heat flammable liquids such as ethanol with a water bath or electric heater, never with a naked flame, because their vapour could catch fire.
When diluting concentrated acids, add the acid to water, never water to acid.
Use a pipette filler (a rubber bulb or device that draws liquid up); never pipette by mouth.
Know the location of the eyewash, fire blanket, extinguisher and first aid; report spills and breakages; dispose of chemicals as instructed.
A risk assessment is a planned check of what could cause harm in an experiment and how to prevent it. It depends on telling a hazard apart from a risk.
A hazard is anything that could cause harm, such as a corrosive acid (one that damages skin and materials).
A risk is the likelihood that harm will happen and how serious it would be.
1. Identify each hazard from labels, hazard pictograms (warning symbols) and safety data sheets (documents giving a chemical's hazards and handling advice).
2. Assess the risk of each hazard.
3. Decide on control measures that reduce the risk.
4. Know what to do in an emergency.

The GHS (Globally Harmonized System) uses nine hazard pictograms, each with a red diamond border: corrosive, flammable, toxic, harmful or irritant (exclamation mark), oxidising, health hazard, environmental hazard, explosive and compressed gas.

Example: concentrated sodium hydroxide is corrosive, so there is a risk of skin and eye burns. Controls are goggles, gloves, small volumes and dilute solutions where possible; if it touches the skin, wash it with plenty of water.

Chemistry measurements only make sense when everyone uses the same units. SI (the international system of units) gives one agreed set, and you often have to convert between it and the smaller units used in the lab.

The SI base units used in chemistry are the metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance. Derived units are built from these, such as m³ for volume and the pascal (Pa) for pressure.
Volume: 1 dm³ (a cubic decimetre, a cube 10 cm along each edge) = 1 L = 1000 cm³ = 1000 mL. Also 1 m³ = 1000 dm³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g, and 1 g = 1000 mg (milligrams), so a quantity in grams is turned into milligrams by multiplying by 1000.

Temperature: T (K) = θ (°C) + 273.15, often rounded to 273, where θ is the Celsius temperature. For example 25 °C = 298 K. Use kelvin in gas calculations because the kelvin scale starts at 0 K, with no negative values.

Pressure: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa. The IUPAC (the international chemistry organisation) standard pressure is 100 kPa (1 × 10⁵ Pa), and 1 atm (one atmosphere, the average air pressure at sea level) = 101 325 Pa.
Convert by multiplying or dividing by the conversion factor (the number linking the two units) and writing the unit at each step, so mistakes show up. For example 250 cm³ = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 L.
Two words that sound alike describe how good a measurement is: accuracy and precision. They mean different things, and every instrument also has limits on how well it can measure.
Accuracy is how close a measurement, or a mean (the average of repeated readings), is to the true or accepted value.
Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other, meaning their spread.
Precision is also used for the smallest division an instrument can read, which is its resolution. A scale marked in 0.1 cm³ steps has a finer resolution than one marked in 1 cm³ steps.
Results can be precise but not accurate, such as closely grouped readings that are all off the true value because a balance has not been zeroed (set to read 0 g with nothing on it).
Results can be accurate on average but not precise, with readings scattered on either side of the true value so that the mean lands close to it.
Every instrument has an uncertainty, the amount by which a reading could be out.
Typical school values are ±0.06 cm³ for a 25 cm³ pipette, ±0.05 cm³ per reading for a 50 cm³ burette, ±0.3 cm³ for a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and about ±1 cm³ for a 100 cm³ measuring cylinder.

Volumetric glassware (pipettes, burettes and volumetric flasks, made to deliver or hold one exact volume) is far more accurate than a measuring cylinder, which is why a pipette is used for accurate volumes.

Significant figures (assumed knowledge): answers are reported to the same number of significant figures (the meaningful digits in a number) as the least precise measurement used, so the answer does not look more exact than the data. This is usually three in titration calculations.
No measurement is perfect. Errors fall into two types that behave differently, and knowing which type you have tells you how to reduce it.
Random error is unpredictable variation that scatters readings above and below the true value. It is reduced by repeating and averaging, because the highs and lows cancel out.

Examples of random error are misjudging the end point of a titration (the moment the indicator changes colour), reading a meniscus (the curved surface of a liquid in glassware) and temperature fluctuations.
Systematic error is a consistent error that shifts all readings in the same direction.

Examples of systematic error are a balance that has not been zeroed, a thermometer that reads 1 °C high, heat lost to the surroundings in a calorimetry experiment (one that measures heat changes), and parallax always from the same angle.

Repeating does not reduce systematic error, because every repeat is wrong in the same way. It is reduced by calibrating the equipment (checking it against a known standard and adjusting it) or by improving the method.
Parallax error occurs when a scale is read from an angle, which makes the liquid level appear to sit at a different mark. Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Anomalous results (outliers, readings that do not fit the rest) caused by mistakes are identified and either repeated or excluded with a reason.
Percentage error = (experimental value − accepted value) ÷ accepted value × 100.
Data are the observations and measurements collected in an experiment. They come in two kinds, and you choose which to record according to what the question asks.
Qualitative data are descriptions without numbers, such as a colour change, effervescence (fizzing as a gas is given off) or a precipitate (an insoluble solid) forming.
Quantitative data are measurements with numbers and units, such as a mass in g or a volume in cm³.
Select the data that answer the question. Record the raw data (the readings exactly as measured) first, then the processed data, such as means and rates, which are worked out from the raw data.
A results table organises raw data so it can be read and graphed. A set layout means a reader can see at once what was changed and what was measured.

The independent variable (the quantity you change) goes in the first column. The dependent variable (the quantity you measure in response) and its repeats go in the following columns, with a mean column.
Each column heading gives the quantity and its unit, e.g. “Time / s”, so units are not written in the body of the table.
All readings are recorded to the same number of decimal places, matching the resolution of the instrument (the smallest division it can read).
A graph turns a table of results into a picture of the pattern, and it lets you read off values or find a rate.
The independent variable is plotted on the x-axis (horizontal) and the dependent variable on the y-axis (vertical). Both axes are labelled with the quantity and its unit.
Scales are chosen so that the points fill more than half of the grid, with even and sensible intervals.
Points are plotted accurately as small crosses, which show the exact position of each reading.
A line or smooth curve of best fit is drawn through the general trend, because the line shows the underlying pattern. The points are not joined dot to dot.
The line is not forced through the origin unless the origin is a real data point.
A line graph is used when both variables are continuous (can take any value in a range, such as time and volume); a bar chart is used for categories.
Once the data are plotted, you describe the pattern, measure it and use it to predict. These skills are used to read off values, find rates and draw conclusions.

Describe the pattern: the values increase, decrease, level off, are directly proportional (a straight line through the origin, so doubling one variable doubles the other) or are inversely proportional (one variable goes up as the other goes down).
The gradient (steepness) of a straight line is the change in y divided by the change in x.
For a curve, the gradient at a point is found from a tangent (a straight line touching the curve at that point only) drawn at that point; this gives a rate.
Interpolation reads a value within the range of the data; extrapolation extends the line beyond it and is less reliable, because the pattern may not continue outside the range measured.
Both interpolation and extrapolation are predictions.
Trends in a table or a series of compounds allow predictions, e.g. the boiling point of the next alkane (the next hydrocarbon in the series) can be predicted from the trend in the series.

Mathematical representations (equations linking quantities) are rearranged and used, e.g. PV = nRT, the gas equation linking pressure, volume, amount in moles and temperature. Means, percentages and rates are calculated.
Chemistry uses very large and very small numbers, such as the number of particles in a mole. Scientific notation writes them compactly.
Scientific notation (standard form) writes a number as A × 10ⁿ, where A is between 1 and 10 and n is a whole number (the power of ten).
The Avogadro constant (the number of particles in one mole) is 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
0.00050 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴: the decimal point moves four places to the right, so the power of ten is −4.

The last steps of analysis are to deal with any result that does not fit and then to state what the data show. A good conclusion is tied to the data and to the hypothesis (the prediction being tested).
An anomalous result does not fit the pattern of the other results. It is identified on the graph or in the table, and a reason is suggested, such as a misreading.
An anomalous result is left out of the mean and of the line of best fit, and this is stated, so the reader knows the data were treated openly.
A conclusion states the relationship shown by the data and says whether it supports the hypothesis.
A conclusion explains the relationship using scientific theory or a model, e.g. collision theory (the model that reactions happen when particles collide).
The conclusion is justified by reference to the data and states its limits: the range tested, the amount of data and the size of the errors.
Correlation (a link between two variables) does not prove causation (that one causes the other): the link may be due to a third factor.

A log is a portfolio of experimental and research data, kept while the work is done rather than written up afterwards. It is the raw record that everything else in an investigation, from evaluation to the final report, is built from.
A log (laboratory notebook or portfolio) is a dated, ongoing record of all experimental and research work, kept as the work happens, so nothing has to be remembered later.
The log records the aim (what you are trying to find out) and the plan, and any changes made to the plan and why.
It also records the raw data (the actual measurements, before any calculation) and observations, including unexpected ones, plus calculations, sources consulted, problems met and reflections.
The log provides evidence of what was done, so it supports honesty and integrity: anyone can check that the results came from the work.
The log allows the work to be repeated or written up later, because the plan, changes and data are all written down. The Chemistry in Practice Investigation brief asks students to keep one.
An evaluation judges the strengths and weaknesses of the method and the data; it is not a summary of what was done. Each judgement should lead to a specific improvement.
Evaluate the method: was the test fair and valid (did it really test what it set out to test), and which variables (things that could change the result) were hard to control?

Evaluate the data: was there enough of it, over a wide enough range; how much did the repeats vary (a big spread means low reliability); were there anomalous results (ones that do not fit the pattern)?

Identify the main sources of error and their likely effect, stating whether each makes the result larger or smaller than the true value. For example, heat lost to the surroundings makes a measured temperature rise smaller than the true value.

Human error on its own is not an acceptable source of error because it names no specific cause; name the specific mistake, such as misreading a meniscus (the curved surface of a liquid in a measuring cylinder or burette).

Suggest specific improvements, each matched to an error, e.g. collecting a gas in a gas syringe instead of over water, using a data-logger (an electronic sensor that records readings automatically), or insulating a calorimeter (the container in which heat changes are measured) to cut heat loss.
Suggest further investigations that would test the conclusion more fully.
Judge how confident you can be in the conclusion, based on the strengths and weaknesses of the method and the data.
Evaluation looks at the experiment; reflection looks at you as an investigator. It asks how well your own planning and thinking worked.
Reflection asks what went well, what did not, what would be done differently, and what was learned about investigating.
Reflection is honest about difficulties, because a problem that is hidden cannot be learned from.
An investigation is valuable for the process it teaches, not only for getting a right answer, so a result that did not work out still has something to reflect on.
The skills built in practical work are not tied to one experiment. They can be reused when a problem looks completely new.
Skills transfer: the same method of planning, controlling variables and analysing data applies to new problems, because the thinking is the same even when the chemistry differs.
In an unfamiliar problem, identify what is being asked, the chemistry it depends on, and the data given.
Set out a step-by-step approach to the problem, so that each step can be checked.
Check that the answer is sensible, for example that its size and units are reasonable for the situation.
A scientific report follows a fixed order so that any reader can find what they need and judge the work. It is written in enough detail for someone else to repeat the investigation.
A report has a title, followed by an introduction giving the background research and the research question, and then the hypothesis (a testable prediction of the result).
The method gives the equipment, a step-by-step procedure and the safety precautions, in enough detail for the work to be repeated.
The results are presented as tables and graphs, and the analysis gives the calculations and the patterns in the data.
The report ends with a conclusion (what the results show about the hypothesis), an evaluation and references (the list of sources used).
The report is written in the past tense, because the work is already done, and in an impersonal style, with no 'I' or 'we'.
Chemistry has its own precise vocabulary and its own ways of showing information. Using them correctly makes a report exact and unambiguous.
Precise terms are used, e.g. 'dissolves', not 'melts', for a solid going into solution, and 'effervescence' for bubbles of gas, because each word names one particular process.
Correct SI units (the international standard units of measurement) and IUPAC names (the internationally agreed systematic names of compounds) are used throughout.

Representations include balanced chemical equations with state symbols, structural formulae (showing how atoms are bonded), labelled diagrams of apparatus, tables, graphs and energy profile diagrams (which show how energy changes during a reaction).
The same findings have to be presented differently depending on who will read them. What a specialist needs is not what a class or the public needs.
Scientists need full technical detail, the data and references, as in a journal paper or a conference poster, so that they can check and build on the work.
The public, policy-makers or a class need plain language, the key findings stated first, simple graphics, and technical terms explained, because they do not have the specialist background.
The same findings may be communicated as a report, poster, presentation, infographic (a picture-based summary) or article.
The format is chosen for the purpose and the audience.
A scientific opinion has to be backed up, and the evidence behind it has to be traceable. Citing sources lets readers check the evidence and credits the people who produced it.
An argument states a claim, supports it with evidence and reasoning, and considers counter-arguments (points against the claim).
Each source is cited in the text and listed in full in the references, so that readers can check it.
Copying someone else's work without acknowledgement is plagiarism.
When evaluating someone else's argument, check its evidence, reasoning and sources before agreeing or disagreeing, so that your opinion rests on more than a first impression.
Chemistry has been shaped by individual scientists whose discoveries changed how people live. For each one, know what they did, when, and what the impact on society was, including any downside.
Robert Boyle (born 25 January 1627 at Lismore Castle, Co. Waterford) pioneered experimental chemistry and argued that knowledge should come from experiment, not just from argument or authority.
Boyle's law, published in 1662, relates the pressure and volume of a gas, so it gave chemists a measured, testable rule about how gases behave.
Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table (a chart that arranges the elements in order) in 1869, and he left gaps in it for elements not yet discovered.
Mendeleev predicted the properties of those undiscovered elements, which showed the table was more than a list; the periodic table now organises all of chemistry.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic (a medicine that kills bacteria), in 1928; he shared the Nobel Prize (a major international award) in 1945 with Florey and Chain.
Penicillin was mass-produced from the 1940s, so it became widely available, and antibiotics have since saved very many lives.
Fritz Haber developed the ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen (Nobel Prize 1918), and Carl Bosch scaled it up industrially in the early 1900s, so it could be run in large factories.

Ammonia-based fertilisers (chemicals added to soil to help crops grow) help feed much of the world's population, but the same chemistry was used to make explosives: a discovery can have both positive and negative impacts.

John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino developed the lithium-ion battery (a rechargeable battery), for which they received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; it powers phones, laptops and electric vehicles.
Chemistry matters at three levels: to each person's daily life, to society as a whole, and to the planet. Each level has its own examples.
Personal: chemistry provides medicines, clean water, food, cleaning products, cosmetics, and materials for clothing and phones.
Personal: understanding chemical labels and hazards helps people make safe choices, for example when storing or using household products.
Social: chemistry supports public health through water treatment, vaccines (preparations that train the body to fight a disease) and medicines.

Social: chemistry supports agriculture through fertilisers and pesticides (chemicals that kill pests that damage crops), and provides jobs in the chemical and pharmaceutical (medicine-making) industry.
Ireland has a large pharmaceutical industry, so chemistry provides jobs here in particular.
Global: chemistry helps tackle climate change (the warming of the Earth) through cleaner fuels, batteries and carbon capture (trapping carbon dioxide before it enters the air).
Global: chemistry helps tackle pollution, food security (everyone having enough food) and the use of resources.
Science does not happen in isolation. The society around scientists affects which questions get studied and which methods are allowed.
Funding: governments, companies and charities decide what research is funded, often according to social needs or profit, so money steers which problems get studied.
Public concern and urgent problems drive research, for example the search for vaccines during a pandemic (a disease outbreak spreading across the world), or for alternatives to fossil fuels.
Laws and regulations, for example on chemical safety, emissions (gases released into the air) and animal testing, limit or direct research.
The ethical values of society (its beliefs about right and wrong) decide what research is acceptable.
When chemistry is applied to a real issue, the science is not the only consideration. Four kinds of factor influence whether and how it is used, and people can also act on them personally.
Economic factors include the cost of development, production and disposal, jobs and profit, because a process that is too expensive may never be used.
Social factors include effects on health, safety, communities and quality of life.
Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future generations, through the use of renewable resources and energy (ones that are not used up) and the management of waste.
Ethical factors include whether an application is right, for example fairness, risks to people or the environment, and informed consent (people agreeing only after being told the risks).
Being personally effective means making informed choices, for example about recycling, energy use and product claims, and taking part in public debate using evidence.
The specification links all its topics through a few big ideas. These help you connect individual pieces of chemistry to the world outside the lab.
The specification's three cross-cutting themes are Health, Sustainability and Technology.
The themes are lenses (ways of looking) for studying how chemistry applies to real life, and the written examination includes questions on them.
News, advertising and social media often report science second-hand rather than as the original research. It is therefore important to check what they say before believing it.
News, advertising and social media may simplify, exaggerate or sensationalise (make more dramatic than the facts justify) science.
They may report a single study as settled fact, or leave out uncertainty and context, so a tentative result sounds like proof.
Headlines are written to attract attention, so they may not match the findings of the study.
A checklist of questions lets you test any claim, whether it is a news report or an advertisement. Each one looks at a different weakness a claim might have.
What exactly is being claimed, and is it a scientific claim, meaning one that can be tested with evidence?
Where does the claim come from: is the original study named, peer-reviewed (checked by independent experts before publication) and available to read?

How strong is the evidence: what is the sample size (how many were tested), were there controls (a comparison group), have the results been reproduced (repeated by others), and was the study done in people, animals or cells?
Is cause being confused with correlation? Two things happening together (correlation) does not prove that one causes the other.
Who benefits: is the source selling a product or promoting a view, and who funded the research?
Do other independent experts and sources agree?
Are scientific words used correctly, or misused to sound convincing, for example “chemical-free” or “natural means safe”?
Once a claim has been checked, you need to discuss it fairly. Good discussion keeps facts and opinions apart.
Separate evidence from opinion, and base conclusions on the weight of the evidence, meaning how much good evidence there is on each side.
Acknowledge uncertainty and the limits of current knowledge, because science can say what the evidence shows so far but cannot always give a final answer.
Consider different perspectives, economic, social, ethical and environmental, while keeping the scientific evidence separate from them.
Some claims appear again and again in advertising and online. Each can be answered with a fact from chemistry.
“Chemical-free”: everything, including water and food, is made of chemicals, so nothing can truly be chemical-free.
“Natural is always safe; synthetic (man-made) is dangerous”: toxicity (how poisonous something is) depends on the substance and the dose, not on whether it is natural.
Some natural substances are highly toxic, and a synthetic substance can be identical to a natural one, so the origin does not change the chemistry.
Alkaline-water and detox claims: the body controls its own pH (the scale that measures how acidic or alkaline a liquid is), and drinking alkaline water does not change blood pH.
Human blood pH is kept between about 7.35 and 7.45.
Stomach acid has a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5, so it is strongly acidic and would quickly neutralise any alkaline water swallowed.
Chemistry describes the same event in three different ways: what you can see, what the particles are doing, and how we write it down. Good answers link all three.

The macroscopic (observable) level is what we see, measure and handle, for example ice melting, a solution changing colour, or gas bubbles forming. You need no special equipment to notice these changes.

The sub-microscopic (particulate) level is made up of atoms, ions (charged particles), molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and electrons, and how they move and rearrange. These particles cannot be seen with a light microscope, which is why the level is called sub-microscopic.
The sub-microscopic level explains the observations at the macroscopic level: what we see happens because of what the particles do.
The symbolic level uses formulae, equations, diagrams and graphs to represent the particles and the changes, so that a change can be written down in a short, exact form.
Chemists move between the three levels: an explanation links what is seen to what the particles do, and writes it symbolically.
Each example runs from the observation, to the particle explanation, to the symbolic equation. These two show the full three-level pattern.
Ice melting, observed: a solid becomes a liquid at 0 °C at standard pressure (the agreed reference pressure for quoting melting points).

Ice melting, particles: water molecules gain energy and partly overcome hydrogen bonds (attractions between neighbouring water molecules), so they move past one another and the solid becomes a liquid.
Magnesium in hydrochloric acid, observed: the solution fizzes and the magnesium disappears.

Magnesium in hydrochloric acid, particles: magnesium atoms lose electrons to form Mg²⁺ ions, and hydrogen ions gain electrons to form H₂ molecules. The H₂ is the gas that causes the fizzing, and the Mg²⁺ ions dissolve, so the metal disappears.
Magnesium in hydrochloric acid, symbolic: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).
Two more examples show how a simple observation is explained by the behaviour of electrons or ions.
A sodium salt in a flame, observed: a yellow-orange colour.

A sodium salt in a flame, particles: electrons in sodium atoms are excited (raised) to higher energy levels, and emit light of a specific energy as they fall back. That specific energy is what gives the colour.
A salt dissolving in water, observed: the solid disappears.
A salt dissolving in water, particles: water molecules surround and separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (the charged particles that make up sodium chloride), so the solid breaks up and seems to vanish.
A salt dissolving in water, symbolic: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
Particles are far too small to see, so chemists depend on pictures and models to understand them. Visualisation is a key part of understanding core concepts.
Chemists visualise particles they cannot see using drawings, physical models, animations and computer simulations.
Generating a model has steps: 1. Propose a representation that fits the observations.
2. Use the model to make a prediction.
4. After testing, keep, modify or discard the model, depending on whether the test supports it.
Models are simplified representations of complex systems or phenomena; the three properties below apply to every model.

Simplified, with underlying assumptions: the kinetic theory (the model of gases as moving particles) assumes that gas particles have negligible volume and no forces between them. Real gases are more complicated, but the assumptions keep the model usable.

Modified as more data become available: the Bohr model of electrons in fixed energy levels was modified to the orbital model when it could not account for the spectra (patterns of light emitted) of atoms with more than one electron.

Predictive: VSEPR theory (a model of how electron pairs arrange themselves around an atom) predicts the bond angle in a molecule before it is measured, and the ideal gas equation predicts the volume of a gas.
Leaving Certificate Chemistry is assessed in two parts, so the investigation counts for a large share of the final grade.
Leaving Certificate Chemistry has two assessment components, both set and marked by the State Examinations Commission (SEC).
The written examination is worth 60% and is taken at Higher or Ordinary level, so students choose the level that suits them.

The Chemistry in Practice Investigation is worth 40%, or 200 marks. One common brief (the same task) is set for Higher and Ordinary level, and the investigation is assessed at the level at which the written paper is taken.
Grades are H1 to H8 at Higher level and O1 to O8 at Ordinary level, in bands of 10% from 30% to 100%; below 30% is grade 8.

The written examination uses a range of question types and assesses all four contextual strands (the main areas of the course), the unifying strand, and the application of chemistry to the cross-cutting themes of sustainability, health and technology.
The investigation starts from a brief, a document that tells students what the task is and gives them a context to work in.
The SEC publishes an Investigation Brief each year in term two of Year 1 (fifth year); the brief for the 2027 examination was issued in January 2026.
The 2027 brief asks students to investigate how the rate of a chemical reaction (how fast it happens) can be controlled, investigating one or more aspects of that topic.
The brief sets out the requirements and includes stimulus material (supplied information) that sets a context.
The brief allows students to develop their own ideas related to that context, and helps teachers and students to plan, so everyone knows what is expected before the work starts.
Students keep an investigative log (a running record of their work) that they draw on to write the report.
The work has two strands, research and experiment, which together build an evidence-based argument in a final report.

Scientific research: students gather, process and evaluate information from secondary sources (existing published material, not their own results) on an issue related to the brief; this may inform the experimental work, for example by suggesting a hypothesis to test.
Experiment: students generate a hypothesis (a testable prediction) for an issue related to the brief, then plan and design the experiment.
Experiment: students carry out laboratory work to gather primary data (their own measurements), then analyse the data and form conclusions.
Students develop an evidence-based argument in response to the brief and submit a report in Year 2 (sixth year), in a format prescribed by the SEC.
The specification envisages up to 20 hours of work; a separate document, “Guidelines to support the Chemistry in Practice Investigation”, covers organisation.

Students give an authentic account of how the work unfolded, discuss the outcomes and say how they might revise the process. Engaging with the process matters more than a perfect answer, so an honest account of what went wrong is worth giving.
Experimental design is covered in more detail in “Questions, hypotheses and designing investigations”.
The SEC brief allocates the 200 marks in four blocks of 50, one for each criterion (a standard the report is judged against).
Criterion A, 50 marks: title and introduction, background research and references.
Criterion B, 50 marks: designing and planning, and conducting the experiment, including safety, fairness, accuracy and choice of equipment.
Criterion C, 50 marks: data and data analysis, and conclusions, because the conclusions must follow from the data.

Criterion D, 50 marks: scientific literacy (communication, coherence, relevance and a reflective approach), judged across the whole report rather than in one section, because these qualities run through every part of it.
The SEC also fixes the headings, limits and layout of the report, so students need to follow the format exactly.

The report uses seven numbered headings, each on a new page, so every section is easy to find: Title and Introduction; Background Research; Designing and Planning; Conducting the Experiment; Data and Data Analysis; Conclusions; References.
The report body is no more than 1,500 words (references, data tables, formulae, equations and labels are not counted), with no more than 20 images and no video.
Text is Arial and black, with 14-point bold headings and 12-point body text at 1.5 line spacing, portrait pages, 20 mm margins with nothing in them, and page numbers at the bottom centre.

The experiment and primary data collection are carried out under the direct supervision of the chemistry teacher, and every source, including any use of AI, is referenced, so the report shows where each idea came from.

The completed SEC cover page goes first; the report is converted to PDF, printed and proof-read, then given to the teacher by Friday 23 April 2027 with Authentication Form P.2 signed by the student, teacher and principal.

The NCCA descriptors of quality describe high and lower achievement in four areas: knowledge and understanding; investigative skills in design and method; investigative skills in analysis and conclusions; and relation to the work of scientists in society.
High achievement in knowledge and understanding shows considerable understanding of the brief, a clearly described purpose, and relevant research that evaluates a wide range of appropriate sources.
High achievement in knowledge and understanding also shows thorough engagement with the chemical concepts, explaining the phenomena clearly and accurately.
High achievement in design and method has a probing research question and a testable hypothesis underpinned by chemical concepts, so the experiment can genuinely support or reject the hypothesis.
High achievement in design and method has a thorough investigative design, with appropriate methods collecting high-quality primary data.
The remaining two areas are analysis and conclusions, and relation to the work of scientists in society. The block ends with what lower achievement looks like.

High achievement in analysis and conclusions has clear, appropriate data and analysis, and valid conclusions justified by the data, so each conclusion rests on evidence, and related to the hypotheses.

High achievement in analysis and conclusions has a thorough evaluation that acknowledges limitations in the research, design and data gathering, because naming weaknesses shows the student understands how reliable the results are.
High achievement in analysis and conclusions has a summary of key areas and a coherent, consistent report with supporting references and reflections.
High achievement in relation to the work of scientists in society has a considered reflection that locates the outcomes within broader societal and scientific issues relating to the brief.
Lower achievement shows limited understanding of the brief, an unclear purpose, little research and a simple design, which means the work does little to answer the brief.
Lower achievement shows conclusions not linked to the data, no limitations identified, and few references or reflections.
A model of the atom is a picture scientists use to explain the evidence they have. These two early models are background to the nuclear model: each was accepted in its time and then replaced.
Dalton's atomic theory (John Dalton, 1803–1808): all matter is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms, which means that atoms cannot be split into anything smaller.
Dalton's atoms of the same element are identical, atoms of different elements differ in mass, and atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
Dalton's atoms are not created or destroyed in chemical reactions, so a reaction only rearranges the atoms that were already there.

Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 using cathode rays (beams of particles given off in a glass tube from which the air has been removed). The electron is a negatively charged particle much lighter than an atom and present in all atoms, so atoms are divisible.
Thomson's plum pudding model: the atom is a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding, so the atom is neutral overall because the charges cancel.

The nuclear model came from a scattering experiment, in which a beam of particles is fired at a target and the paths of the deflected particles are studied. The results could not be explained by the plum pudding model.

Gold-foil experiment (1909): Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, directed by Rutherford, fired a beam of alpha particles, which are small, fast, positively charged particles, at a very thin sheet of gold foil.
A fluorescent screen (a screen that gives off a flash of light where a particle hits it) was placed around the foil and showed where the particles went after they hit the foil.
Observation: most particles passed straight through the foil, so most of the atom is empty space.
Observation: some particles were deflected through large angles, so there is a concentrated region of positive charge that repels them, because like charges repel.
Observation: a very few particles bounced straight back, so this positive region is very small and very dense, containing almost all of the atom's mass.

This positive region is the nucleus. Rutherford published the nuclear model in 1911: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom, with electrons moving around it in the mostly empty space outside.

Later work found that the nucleus contains protons (positively charged particles) and neutrons (particles with no charge): Rutherford identified the proton, and Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

Diagram: the gold-foil set-up, labelled with the alpha particle source, the beam, the gold foil and the fluorescent screen, and the paths of particles past the nuclei: straight through, deflected, and bounced back.
Niels Bohr proposed energy levels in 1913 to explain why atoms emit light only at certain frequencies. His model keeps the nucleus but gives the electrons a definite arrangement around it.
Electrons move around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits called energy levels (shells), each with a fixed energy.
An electron in a given energy level does not lose energy, so it stays in that level rather than spiralling inwards.
An electron can move to a higher energy level by absorbing a definite amount of energy.
When the electron falls back to a lower level, it emits light of a definite energy. This explains the lines in emission spectra (the separate coloured lines an element gives out when heated).
Energy levels are numbered n = 1, 2, 3…, with n = 1 closest to the nucleus and lowest in energy.
The energy levels hold up to 2, 8, 18… electrons.
The orbital model is the current model. It describes where electrons are likely to be found, not the path they follow.
Electrons do not follow fixed paths; they occupy orbitals, which are regions of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron.

Main energy levels are divided into sublevels, labelled s, p, d and f; each sublevel is made of orbitals, and each orbital holds up to two electrons. There is more on this in the later subsection on the orbital model.
The model developed from evidence that electrons behave as waves as well as particles, which a fixed circular path cannot describe.
It also rests on the principle that the exact position and the exact path of an electron cannot be known at the same time, which is why only probabilities can be given.
Each model rested on an assumption, and each had a limitation: evidence it could not explain. The first two models fail because the atom has parts and a structure they did not allow for.
Dalton: assumed that atoms are indivisible and that all atoms of an element are identical.
Dalton: limited because subatomic particles (particles smaller than the atom) exist, and because isotopes show that atoms of the same element can differ in mass.
Plum pudding model: assumed that positive charge is spread through the atom.
Plum pudding model: limited because it cannot explain the large deflections and the particles that bounced back in the gold-foil experiment, which need a small, dense positive centre.
The nuclear model fixed the problem of the positive charge but said little about the electrons.
Nuclear model: assumed that electrons orbit the nucleus like planets.
Nuclear model: limited because it does not say how electrons are arranged in the space around the nucleus.
Nuclear model: limited because a charged electron moving in a circle would be expected to lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would not be stable.
Nuclear model: limited because it cannot explain line spectra (the separate lines of light an element emits).
The Bohr model fixed the nuclear model's problems for hydrogen but not for other atoms. The orbital model is the best fit for the evidence, but it has its own limitation.
Bohr model: assumed that electrons move in fixed circular orbits with fixed energies.
Bohr model: explains the spectrum of hydrogen, which has one electron, but not the spectra of atoms with more than one electron.
Bohr model: does not account for sublevels or for the wave nature of electrons.
Bohr model: treats the electron's exact path as known, but the exact position and path of an electron cannot be known at the same time.
Orbital model: the best fit for the evidence available, but its limitation is that it is mathematical and abstract.
Orbital model: gives probabilities of where an electron is found, not exact positions, and is hard to picture.
Scientists judge a model by how well it explains the evidence. Replaced models are not useless, because they still work for the things they explain well.
Each model was accepted because it explained the evidence of its time, and was replaced or refined when new evidence did not fit.
The Bohr model is still enough to explain flame colours and simple line spectra.
The Bohr model's arrangement of electrons in shells, such as 2, 8, 8, is still used to predict bonding.
The nuclear model still explains why atoms are mostly empty space.
An atom is made of protons, neutrons and electrons. Their masses and charges are given relative to the proton (that is, as comparisons with it), because the real values are very small numbers.
Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1, found in the nucleus.
Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0 (no charge), found in the nucleus.
Electron: relative mass about 1/1840 of a proton, so negligible though not zero; relative charge −1; found outside the nucleus, in energy levels (orbitals).
The relative values hide the real sizes. The actual masses show how tiny the particles are and how much lighter the electron is.
Actual masses: proton 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; neutron 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; electron 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
The proton and neutron have almost the same mass, which is why each is given a relative mass of 1.
The charge on a proton is equal in size and opposite in sign to the charge on an electron, so equal numbers of each cancel out.
The particles are not spread evenly. The nucleus is tiny, yet it holds almost all the mass, and the rest of the atom is mostly empty.
Protons and neutrons, collectively called nucleons, make up the nucleus, which holds almost all of the atom's mass because electrons are so light.
The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom: an atom is about 10⁵ (100 000) times the diameter of its nucleus, so most of the atom is empty space.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the positive and negative charges cancel.
The number of protons identifies the element: every atom with 6 protons, for example, is carbon.

Exams ask you to state the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion. An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it carries a charge. The number of protons never changes in an ion.
Number of protons = atomic number (the number of protons in the nucleus).
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number, where the mass number is the total of protons and neutrons.
In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons.
A positive ion has lost electrons, so number of electrons = number of protons − charge, e.g. Na⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons.
A negative ion has gained electrons, so number of electrons = number of protons + charge, e.g. Cl⁻ (chlorine-35) has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons; O²⁻ has 8 protons and 10 electrons.
The three particles were found one at a time. The order of discovery follows how easy each is to detect.
The electron was discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897.
The proton was identified by Rutherford about 1917–1919.
The neutron was discovered by Chadwick in 1932.
The neutron was found last because it has no charge, which makes it hard to detect.
Two whole numbers describe the nucleus of an atom. Together they give the number of each particle and are written beside the element's symbol.
Atomic number (Z): the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element.
Each element has its own atomic number, and the periodic table is arranged in order of atomic number.
Mass number (A): the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number (A − Z).
Nuclear notation writes the mass number at the top left and the atomic number at the bottom left of the element symbol, e.g. ²³₁₁Na has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and (as an atom) 11 electrons.
Atoms of one element are not all identical. They can have different numbers of neutrons, and such atoms are called isotopes.
Isotopes have the same atomic number, so the same number of protons, but different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons.
Hydrogen-1 (¹H) has no neutrons; hydrogen-2 (²H), called deuterium, has one neutron; hydrogen-3 (³H), called tritium, has two.
Chlorine-35 (³⁵Cl) has 18 neutrons and chlorine-37 (³⁷Cl) has 20 neutrons.
Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon.
Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons and the same electron arrangement, and electrons control how an atom reacts.
Isotopes have slightly different physical properties that depend on mass, such as density and rate of diffusion (how fast a gas spreads out).
Isotopes are written by name and mass number, e.g. chlorine-35, or in nuclear notation, e.g. ³⁵₁₇Cl.
Because an element's isotopes have different masses, one atom's mass number does not describe the element as a whole. Relative atomic mass is an average over its isotopes.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): the average mass of the atoms of an element, taking account of the abundance of its isotopes, relative to one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
Carbon-12 is the standard: an atom of carbon-12 is defined as having a mass of exactly 12 units.
Ar has no units, because it compares masses.
The mass number of a single isotope is always a whole number; Ar is a weighted average of the isotopes present, so it is usually not whole.

Chlorine is about 75.8% chlorine-35 and 24.2% chlorine-37, giving Ar(Cl) = 35.45 (quoted as 35.5 in school tables). There is more on calculating Ar from isotopic abundance in the later subsection on the mole.

The current model of the atom has a tiny nucleus at the centre and electrons arranged around it in energy levels and orbitals. Knowing these four ideas, nucleus, energy level, orbital and capacity, lets you describe any atom.

The nucleus is a tiny, dense, positively charged centre of the atom, containing protons (positive particles) and neutrons (particles with no charge). There is more on this in Atomic structure: the nuclear model.
Electrons (the negatively charged particles) surround the nucleus and are arranged in main energy levels, numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4…
The main energy levels increase in energy, and in average distance from the nucleus, as n increases, so an electron in n = 3 has more energy and is on average further out than one in n = 1.
Within a main energy level, electrons occupy orbitals, which are the smaller regions that make up the level.
An orbital is a region of space around the nucleus in which there is a high probability of finding an electron.
Each orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons, so an orbital that is full is holding a pair.
The maximum number of electrons in main energy level n is 2n²: 2 in n = 1, 8 in n = 2, 18 in n = 3 and 32 in n = 4.
Each main energy level is divided into sublevels (smaller groups of orbitals within the level), made of orbitals; the sublevels and how they fill are covered later in this subsection.
The Bohr model, an older picture of the atom, drew electrons orbiting like planets. The orbital model keeps part of that idea but changes how we describe where an electron is.
The Bohr model gives electrons fixed circular paths at fixed distances from the nucleus.
The orbital model gives no exact path or position for an electron, only the probability of it being found in each region.
The orbital model keeps the Bohr idea of fixed energy levels, so electrons can only have certain energies.
Electrons behave both as particles and as waves, so their exact position and motion cannot both be known; the orbital model therefore describes probability instead of a path.

Diagram: the nucleus at the centre, with fuzzy regions (electron clouds) around it; label the nucleus (protons, neutrons) and the orbitals (electron density). Beside it, draw a Bohr diagram of circular shells for comparison.

In hydrogen, the single electron cannot have just any energy. This is the idea behind the hydrogen spectrum, and it gives two terms, ground state and excited state, that you must be able to distinguish.
The electron in a hydrogen atom can exist only in certain allowed energy levels, n = 1, 2, 3…, so its energy is quantised: it can take only certain fixed values.
The ground state is the lowest energy level available to an electron, which is n = 1 for hydrogen.
An excited state is any higher energy level, reached when the atom absorbs energy, for example from heat or an electric discharge (a current passed through a gas).
Excited states are unstable, so the electron soon falls back to a lower level.

When an excited electron drops to a lower level, the atom has to get rid of the energy difference. It does so as light, and the equation Em − En = hf links the size of the drop to the light given out.
An electron transition is a jump of an electron from one energy level to another.
When an electron falls from a higher level (energy Em) to a lower level (energy En), the energy difference is emitted as a photon, a packet of light energy.
The photon's energy is related to its frequency (the number of wave cycles per second) by Em − En = hf, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, and f is the frequency in hertz (s⁻¹).
Light is emitted when electrons fall to lower levels; when electrons jump up to higher levels they absorb energy instead.
Because the energy levels are fixed, each transition has one definite energy difference, so it emits light of one definite frequency, seen as one line of one colour.
A larger energy gap gives light of higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
An emission spectrum is the pattern of light an element gives out when its atoms are excited. Hydrogen's pattern is separate lines, and that is direct evidence for fixed energy levels.

An emission spectrum is produced by passing an electric discharge through hydrogen gas at low pressure and viewing the light through a spectroscope (an instrument that splits light into its colours) or diffraction grating.
It is a line spectrum: separate bright coloured lines on a dark background, not the continuous band of colours produced by white light.
Each line corresponds to one transition from a higher energy level to a lower one.
A continuous spectrum would be seen if the electron could have any energy, so the line spectrum is evidence that energy levels are fixed.
The lines of hydrogen fall into groups called series, named by the level the electrons fall to. The visible lines are the Balmer series, and each colour comes from a different starting level.
The visible lines form the Balmer series, made by electrons falling to n = 2.
Red line, 656 nm: the electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2.
Blue-green line, 486 nm: the electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2.
Blue-violet line, 434 nm: the electron falls from n = 5 to n = 2.
Violet line, 410 nm: the electron falls from n = 6 to n = 2.
Falls to levels other than n = 2 give lines outside the visible region. The spacing of the lines also reflects how the levels are spaced.
Transitions down to n = 1 form the Lyman series, which lies in the ultraviolet (light of higher energy than visible light).
Transitions down to n = 3 form the Paschen series, which lies in the infrared (light of lower energy than visible light).
The lines get closer together at higher energy, because the energy levels themselves get closer together further from the nucleus.

Diagram: an energy-level diagram with levels n = 1 to 6, spaced more closely going up; downward arrows to n = 2 labelled with the four visible lines, plus arrows to n = 1 (ultraviolet) and n = 3 (infrared).
Diagram: beside it, sketch the line spectrum with the four visible lines labelled.
Hydrogen's lines come from electrons changing level. The same thing happens in every element, which is why heating a compound in a flame makes a colour you can use to identify it.
Heating an atom in a flame gives energy to its electrons, which move up to higher energy levels.
The electrons fall back to lower levels and give out the energy as light.
Each element has its own set of energy levels, so it gives out its own colours of light, which identifies the element.
A flame test identifies a metal from the colour its salt gives to a flame. A fair test needs the right equipment, and everything except the metal kept the same.
Aim: to identify the metal in a salt from the colour it gives to a flame.

Equipment: Bunsen burner; platinum or nichrome wire loop (or wooden splints soaked overnight in deionised water); watch glasses; concentrated hydrochloric acid; samples of the chlorides of the six metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, copper, barium and strontium); deionised water.
Independent variable (the one you change): the metal in the salt being tested.
Dependent variable (the one you observe): the colour of the flame.
Controlled variables: the same flame, the same amount of salt on the wire, and the same cleaning procedure before every test.
Control: a clean wire with no salt on it, held in the flame, gives no colour, so any colour seen with a salt comes from the salt.
The method is four steps, repeated for each salt. The cleaning step matters most, because leftover salt from a previous test would colour the flame and give a wrong result.
1. Clean the wire by dipping it in concentrated hydrochloric acid and holding it in the hottest part of a non-luminous (blue) Bunsen flame, with the air hole open, until it gives no colour.
2. Dip the wire in the acid again, then into the salt so that a little sticks to it; chlorides are used because they are volatile (they vaporise easily in the flame).
