3. Hold the wire at the edge of the non-luminous flame and note the colour.
4. Clean the wire again before testing the next salt; if splints are used, use a different splint for each salt.
Repeats: repeat each test to confirm the colour observed.
Viewing potassium through cobalt-blue glass filters out the yellow light from any sodium impurity, so the lilac colour can be seen.
The chemicals and the hot wire are hazards, and the result only means something when it is compared with known colours. Each piece of apparatus also needs a labelled diagram.
Safety: wear goggles, so that no splash or spark reaches the eyes.
Safety: concentrated hydrochloric acid is corrosive, so wear gloves and use a small volume.
Safety: barium salts are toxic, so wash hands after handling them and do not ingest them.
Safety: keep the hot wire away from the skin, because it can burn.
Conclusion: a flame colour that matches a reference colour in the list of flame colours below identifies the metal in the salt.
Diagram: a Bunsen burner with a non-luminous (blue) flame, and a wire loop holding the salt at the edge of the flame; label the air hole, the non-luminous flame and the wire loop.
Diagram: a wooden splint loaded with salt, held at the edge of the flame; label the splint and the salt.
Diagram: cobalt-blue glass held between the eye and the flame; label the cobalt-blue glass.
Each of the six metals gives its own flame colour. Learn the colour for each, and note the one pair that look alike.
Lithium: crimson red, which is why it is easily confused with strontium.
Sodium: bright yellow-orange; the colour is persistent (it lasts and is strong).
Lithium and strontium are both red and are hard to tell apart by eye, so their line spectra are used to distinguish them.
A flame colour is a mix of light of several wavelengths. Splitting the light with a spectroscope separates it into lines, which gives a more precise way to identify an element.
A spectroscope splits the light from a flame or electric discharge into its separate colours.
Each element gives a line emission spectrum: a pattern of bright lines at specific wavelengths on a dark background, unique to that element like a fingerprint.

To identify an element, compare the lines from an unknown sample, obtained as primary data (your own measurements) from a spectroscope or as secondary data (from another source) such as a published spectrum, with reference spectra of known elements.
A match of all the lines identifies the element.
The syllabus names three elements whose line spectra you must be able to use. Their lines explain the flame colours seen, and the same idea is applied in stars and fireworks.
Sodium: two very close bright yellow lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm (the sodium D lines), which give its yellow flame.
Strontium: several lines, strongest in the red, so its flame looks red.
Copper: lines mainly in the green, giving its blue-green flame.
Line spectra are used to identify elements in samples and in stars.
Fireworks use metal salts for their colours: strontium for red, barium for green, sodium for yellow and copper for blue-green.
For the first 20 elements, you can write an atom's electrons as a list of numbers, one for each main energy level. The electrons fill from the inside out.
Electrons fill the lowest energy levels available first, because that is the most stable arrangement.
For elements 1 to 20, the first main energy level holds up to 2 electrons, the second up to 8 and the third up to 8; the fourth level starts to fill at potassium.
The outer-shell (valence) electrons, those in the outermost occupied level, determine the chemical properties of an element.
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, which is why they have similar properties.
Write the number of electrons in each main energy level, from the inside out, separated by commas. These ten examples show the pattern.
Potassium and calcium show the fourth level beginning to fill, and a shell diagram is a way to draw an arrangement.
Diagram: a Bohr-style shell diagram for sodium; label the nucleus as 11 protons and 12 neutrons, and label the shells holding 2, 8 and 1 electrons.
Atoms with a full outer energy level are stable. Many atoms reach one by losing or gaining electrons, which turns them into ions (charged particles).
A stable electronic configuration has a full outer energy level, as in the noble gases (the very unreactive elements in group 18): helium 2, neon 2,8 and argon 2,8,8.
Atoms usually reach a full outer level of eight electrons (an octet), or two for the first level.
Metals in groups 1, 2 and 13 lose electrons to form positive ions with a noble-gas configuration: Na⁺ 2,8; Mg²⁺ 2,8; Al³⁺ 2,8.
Potassium and calcium ions also have noble-gas configurations: K⁺ 2,8,8; Ca²⁺ 2,8,8.
Non-metals in groups 15, 16 and 17 gain electrons to form negative ions with a noble-gas configuration: N³⁻ 2,8; O²⁻ 2,8; F⁻ 2,8.
Sulfide and chloride ions have noble-gas configurations: S²⁻ 2,8,8; Cl⁻ 2,8,8.
Ions with the same electron arrangement as each other are isoelectronic; for example Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ and Ne all have the arrangement 2,8.
A main energy level is split into sublevels, and each sublevel is made of orbitals. The type of sublevel decides how many orbitals it has and so how many electrons it holds.
A sublevel is a subdivision of a main energy level, made of orbitals of equal energy; the sublevels are s, p, d and f.
An s sublevel has 1 orbital, holding 2 electrons, because each orbital holds 2.
A p sublevel has 3 orbitals, holding 6 electrons, because each orbital holds 2.
A d sublevel has 5 orbitals, holding 10 electrons, because 5 × 2 = 10.
The higher the main energy level, the more types of sublevel it contains. The sublevels fill in order of increasing energy, and this order has a surprise at 4s and 3d.
Level 1 contains 1s only, so it holds just 2 electrons.
Level 2 contains 2s and 2p, so it holds 2 + 6 = 8 electrons.
The order of filling, from lowest to highest energy, is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p.
The 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first.
Three rules decide how electrons are placed in orbitals. Together they let you draw an orbital (box) diagram and count unpaired electrons.
Aufbau principle: the filling rule above, applied to orbitals; electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbital available first.
Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (a property of the electron, like turning in opposite directions), shown as ↑↓.
Hund's rule: when filling orbitals of equal energy, such as the three 2p orbitals, electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins before any pairing occurs.
Orbital (box) diagrams show one box per orbital, with arrows for electrons.
Nitrogen: 1s ↑↓; 2s ↑↓; 2p ↑ ↑ ↑, giving three unpaired electrons (electrons alone in an orbital).
Oxygen: 1s ↑↓; 2s ↑↓; 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑, giving two unpaired electrons, because its fourth 2p electron has to pair up with one already in an orbital.
The s, p, d notation writes each sublevel followed by its number of electrons as a superscript. Up to calcium the sublevels simply fill in the order given above.
Notation writes each sublevel followed by its number of electrons as a superscript: sodium 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.
Calcium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s², with 4s filling before 3d because 4s is lower in energy.
Once 3d starts to fill, the configurations get longer. The 4s sublevel fills before 3d, but the configuration is written with the levels in order.
Iron: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s², written in level order rather than filling order.
Noble-gas shorthand replaces the configuration of the previous noble gas with its symbol in square brackets: potassium [Ar] 4s¹; iron [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s².
Two elements do not follow the filling order exactly. One electron moves from 4s into 3d, because a half-full or full d sublevel is more stable.
The chromium and copper exceptions occur because a half-full or full d sublevel is especially stable.
To write an ion, take the atom's configuration and remove or add electrons at the outermost sublevel. The result is usually a stable configuration, with full sublevels.
Ions, excluding transition metal ions, are written by removing or adding electrons from the outermost sublevel: Na⁺ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.
Stable configurations at this level are full sublevels (s², p⁶) and the noble-gas configuration ns² np⁶.
An orbital's shape shows where the electron is most likely to be found. You need only the s and p shapes.
An s orbital is spherical and centred on the nucleus.
The 2s orbital is larger than the 1s orbital, because it belongs to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus.
A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, with two lobes on either side of the nucleus.
The three p orbitals in a sublevel, px, py and pz, lie at right angles to each other along the x, y and z axes, and have equal energy.
Diagram: a sphere labelled s, and three dumbbells along the x, y and z axes labelled px, py and pz.

By the mid-1800s over 60 elements were known, and chemists looked for relationships among their properties. Two early attempts at a pattern, Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves, led towards the periodic table.

An element is a substance that cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means, so each of the 60-plus known elements was a basic building block that chemists tried to sort by its properties.

Johann Döbereiner (1829) noticed triads: groups of three elements with similar properties in which the atomic weight (the old term for relative atomic mass, the mass of an atom compared with other atoms) of the middle element is about the average of the other two.

Döbereiner's triads included lithium, sodium and potassium; calcium, strontium and barium; and chlorine, bromine and iodine. In each, the three elements behave alike and the middle one sits between the others in atomic weight.

John Newlands (1864–1865) proposed the law of octaves: when the elements were arranged by atomic weight, every eighth element had properties similar to the first, like the eighth note repeating in a musical scale.
Newlands' law worked for the lighter elements but broke down for the heavier ones, and he left no gaps in his table, so there was no room for elements that had not yet been discovered.
Dmitri Mendeleev produced a table that chemists came to accept as correct. His success came from trusting a pattern enough to leave gaps and make predictions that were later confirmed.
Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass), placing elements with similar properties in the same vertical column, called a group.
Mendeleev's periodic law: the properties of the elements vary periodically with their atomic weights, which means similar properties recur at regular intervals as atomic weight increases.
He left gaps for elements not yet discovered and predicted their properties, rather than forcing the known elements to fit with no spaces as Newlands had done.
His predicted elements eka-aluminium and eka-silicon were matched by gallium (discovered 1875) and germanium (discovered 1886); scandium (discovered 1879) matched eka-boron.
The discovery of elements with the predicted properties convinced chemists that the table was correct, because a prediction that comes true is strong evidence for the pattern behind it.

Where atomic weight order placed an element in the wrong group, he reversed the order of the pair: tellurium (relative atomic mass 127.6) is placed before iodine (relative atomic mass 126.9) so that iodine sits with the other halogens (the reactive non-metals chlorine, bromine and so on).
The table organised all the known elements, showed relationships between them, made predictions that were confirmed, and became the basis of the modern table.
Mendeleev's table was later improved by new discoveries. These explained why his pattern worked and removed the need for his reversed pairs.
The noble gases helium, neon, argon, krypton and xenon were discovered in the 1890s (William Ramsay and others) and were added as a new group, now group 18.
Henry Moseley (1913) showed by experiment that each element has a whole-number atomic number, equal to the number of protons (positively charged particles) in its nucleus (the atom's centre).
The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number, so tellurium (atomic number 52) naturally comes before iodine (atomic number 53) and Mendeleev's reversal is unnecessary.
Modern periodic law: the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers, meaning the properties repeat in a regular pattern as atomic number increases.

The repeating pattern is explained by electron arrangement: elements in the same group have the same outer-electron arrangement (the same number of electrons in the outermost energy level), so they behave alike.
The modern table keeps Mendeleev's idea of groups of similar elements but differs from his in five ways.
Order: Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic weight; the modern table orders them by atomic number.
Gaps: Mendeleev's table had gaps for undiscovered elements; the modern table has none, because all the elements up to 118 are now known.
Noble gases: absent from Mendeleev's table, which was drawn up before they were discovered; present in the modern table as group 18.
Number of elements: Mendeleev's table contained fewer elements, while the modern table contains 118.
Blocks: Mendeleev's table had no separate blocks of elements (sets of columns grouped by the type of sublevel being filled); the modern table is divided into blocks.
The table is arranged so that elements with the same outer electrons fall in the same column. This is why the elements in a column behave alike.
A group is a vertical column of elements; using IUPAC numbering (the internationally agreed system) there are 18 groups, numbered 1 to 18.
Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer energy level (the outermost shell of electrons), so they have similar chemical properties.
For groups 1 and 2, the group number equals the number of outer electrons, so group 2 elements have 2 outer electrons.
For groups 13 to 18, the number of outer electrons is the group number minus 10, so group 17 has 7 outer electrons; helium, in group 18, is the exception with 2 outer electrons.
Group 1 elements are the alkali metals and group 2 elements are the alkaline earth metals.
Group 17 elements are the halogens and group 18 elements are the noble gases.
While a group is a column of similar elements, a period is a row, and its number tells you how many energy levels the atoms use.
A period is a horizontal row of elements; there are 7 periods.
The period number equals the number of occupied main energy levels (shells holding electrons); sodium, with electron arrangement 2,8,1, has three occupied levels, so it is in period 3.
Across a period, one proton and one electron are added at each step, and the elements change from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.
Period 1 has 2 elements (hydrogen and helium); periods 2 and 3 have 8 each; period 4 has 18.
The elements fall into three types according to where they sit on the table. A staircase line marks the boundary between metals and non-metals.
About three-quarters of the elements are metals, found on the left and in the centre of the table.
Non-metals are found on the right of the table; hydrogen is also a non-metal, even though it sits at the top left.
A staircase line running from boron to astatine separates metals from non-metals.
Metalloids (semi-metals) lie next to the staircase line, including boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium; they have some properties of metals and some of non-metals.
Metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires), and form positive ions (charged atoms).
Non-metals are dull, poor conductors of electricity (graphite is an exception), brittle as solids, and often form negative ions or share electrons.

A block is the set of elements whose highest-energy electron enters the same type of sublevel (a subdivision of an energy level, labelled s, p, d or f). The blocks explain the overall shape of the table.
The s-block is groups 1 and 2, together with helium; its highest-energy electron is in an s sublevel.
The p-block is groups 13 to 18, except helium; its highest-energy electron is in a p sublevel.
The d-block is groups 3 to 12, in the middle of periods 4 to 7; its electrons fill a d sublevel.
The f-block is the lanthanides and actinides, usually shown below the main table; its electrons fill an f sublevel.

The shape of the table follows from sublevel capacities: 2 columns for s, 6 for p, 10 for d and 14 for f, because an s sublevel holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14. This is why the d-block is ten elements wide.
Diagram: an outline of the periodic table with the s, p, d and f blocks shaded and labelled, and group and period numbers marked.
Each element's box and position give information about its atoms and its behaviour, so the table works as a quick reference.
Each box gives the symbol, atomic number and relative atomic mass of an element.
The atomic number gives the number of protons and, in a neutral atom, the number of electrons, because the positive and negative charges must balance.
The group gives the element's outer-electron arrangement.
The period gives the number of occupied energy levels.
The element's position relative to the staircase line shows whether it is a metal, non-metal or metalloid.
Elements in the same group share an outer-electron arrangement, so they behave in similar ways. This lets you predict reactions and ion charges from the group alone.

Reactions can be predicted from a group: sodium reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, so potassium, in the same group, will react with water in the same way, giving potassium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Group 1 elements form 1⁺ ions, group 2 elements form 2⁺ ions and group 13 elements form 3⁺ ions, because each loses its outer electrons (1, 2 and 3 respectively).
Group 15 elements form 3⁻ ions, group 16 elements form 2⁻ ions and group 17 elements form 1⁻ ions, because each gains the electrons needed to fill its outer level.
Noble gases (group 18) have full outer energy levels and are very unreactive, so they have no tendency to form ions.
The formula of a compound follows from the charges of its ions, which must balance to give no overall charge. The group of each element gives you its ion's charge.
Magnesium (group 2) forms Mg²⁺ and chlorine (group 17) forms Cl⁻, so two chloride ions balance one magnesium ion and the formula is MgCl₂.
Aluminium (group 13) forms Al³⁺ and oxygen (group 16) forms O²⁻, so two aluminium ions balance three oxide ions and the formula is Al₂O₃.
Trends in the table allow properties of unfamiliar elements to be estimated from their neighbours. The trends themselves are taught in full elsewhere.
Properties change gradually and predictably down a group and across a period, so an unknown property can be estimated from neighbouring elements.
Astatine (At, atomic number 85) lies at the bottom of group 17; from the trend in the halogens it is predicted to be a dark solid that is less reactive than iodine.
Mendeleev used the same approach to predict the properties of undiscovered elements.

Every trend is explained by electron arrangement: the number of outer electrons, the number of occupied energy levels and the nuclear charge (the positive charge of the nucleus, equal to the number of protons).
Most atoms are not stable on their own. They join to other atoms because the joined arrangement has less energy, and the force that holds them together is called a chemical bond.
A chemical bond is a force of attraction that holds atoms or ions (atoms that have gained or lost electrons and so carry a charge) together in an element or compound.

Atoms bond to reach a more stable arrangement of electrons, usually a full outer energy level (the outermost shell of electrons) like the nearest noble gas (the unreactive group 18 elements); this is the octet rule, and bonding lowers their energy.

Only the outer (valence) electrons take part in bonding, because the inner electrons are held close to the nucleus (the atom's positively charged centre) and are not available to be lost, gained or shared.
In ionic bonding one atom hands electrons over to another, leaving two oppositely charged particles that attract each other.
An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction (the attraction between opposite charges) between oppositely charged ions.
It forms when electrons are transferred from one atom, usually a metal that forms a positive ion, to another atom, usually a non-metal that forms a negative ion.
Example: sodium (2,8,1) gives one electron to chlorine (2,8,7): Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ and Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. The numbers show the electrons in each energy level.
Both ions have the electron arrangement of a noble gas, which is why the transfer happens: each atom ends up with a full outer energy level.
Ionic compounds form a giant lattice (a huge regular repeating array) of ions, not molecules (separate small groups of atoms).
In sodium chloride each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions, and each Cl⁻ ion by six Na⁺ ions.
The formula NaCl gives only the ratio of the ions, one Na⁺ to one Cl⁻, because there is no single unit to count.
Diagram: a section of the sodium chloride lattice, drawn as a cube, showing alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
Non-metal atoms usually cannot give electrons away easily, so they share them instead. The shared electrons hold the atoms together.
A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms, usually two non-metals; both nuclei are attracted to the shared pair, which is what holds the atoms together.
A single bond is one shared pair, such as in H–H and Cl–Cl.
A double bond is two shared pairs, as in O=O and C=O in CO₂.
A triple bond is three shared pairs, as in N≡N.
Covalently bonded atoms form molecules (separate small groups of atoms), e.g. H₂O, CH₄ and NH₃.
A few substances have giant covalent structures, in which atoms are linked by covalent bonds throughout instead of forming separate molecules, e.g. diamond.
Not every shared pair is shared fairly. Whether the sharing is equal or unequal depends on how strongly each atom attracts the electrons.
A pure (non-polar) covalent bond shares electrons equally, because both atoms attract them equally, as in H–H and Cl–Cl.
The C–H bond is nearly non-polar.
A polar covalent bond shares electrons unequally, because one atom attracts them more strongly, as in H–Cl and O–H.

The atom that attracts the shared electrons more strongly gets a partial negative charge (δ−), and the other atom gets a partial positive charge (δ+), e.g. Hδ+–Clδ−. The charges are only partial because the electrons are shifted, not fully transferred.
Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of a scale, not two separate boxes. Real bonds sit at different points along it, depending on how the electrons are shared.
Bonds are not simply ionic or covalent; they lie on a continuum (a smooth scale) from pure covalent, through polar covalent, to ionic.
At one end, pure covalent bonds share electrons equally, because both atoms attract them equally.
In the middle, polar covalent bonds share electrons unequally, because one atom pulls harder.
At the other end, ionic bonds involve complete transfer of electrons, so ions form.
Examples along the continuum: Cl–Cl (pure covalent), H–Cl (polar covalent), Na⁺Cl⁻ (ionic).
Most bonds have some ionic and some covalent character, so they sit between the ends, not exactly at them.

The difference in electronegativity (how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a bond) between the atoms decides where a bond lies. There is more on this in Bond type and intermolecular forces.

Diagram: a horizontal line labelled pure covalent – polar covalent – ionic, with the electron pair drawn shared equally at the left end, shifted towards one atom in the middle, and fully transferred at the right end.
Setting ionic and covalent bonding side by side shows what each does to the electrons and what kind of structure results. Metals have a third type of bonding.
Ionic bonding transfers electrons and forms ions; covalent bonding shares electrons and forms molecules (mostly).
Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal; covalent bonding occurs mostly between two non-metals.
Ionic compounds are giant lattices; covalent bonds are polar or non-polar depending on the atoms involved.

Metallic bonding (assumed): positive metal ions are held together by a sea of delocalised outer electrons (electrons free to move through the whole metal), which explains why metals conduct electricity.
To predict a formula you need to know how many electrons an atom is likely to lose, gain or share. This number is its valency, and the octet rule explains it.
Valency is the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares when it bonds; it is the combining power of an element.
The octet rule: atoms tend to lose, gain or share electrons to reach eight electrons in their outer energy level.
Hydrogen follows a different rule: it needs two electrons in its outer level, matching helium (the noble gas with two electrons).
Elements in group 1 and group 17 have a valency of 1, because they lose one electron (group 1) or gain one (group 17) to reach an octet.
Elements in group 2 and group 16 have a valency of 2, because they lose two electrons (group 2) or gain two (group 16).
Elements in group 13 and group 15 have a valency of 3, because they lose three electrons (group 13) or gain three (group 15).
Elements in group 14 have a valency of 4, because they share four electrons to reach an octet.
An ionic compound has no overall charge, so the positive and negative charges must cancel. This gives a simple method for writing any ionic formula.
Step 1: Write the charge on each ion, e.g. Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻.
Step 2: Combine the ions so that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻) give CaCl₂, as one Ca²⁺ balances two Cl⁻.
Aluminium ions (Al³⁺) and oxide ions (O²⁻) give Al₂O₃, as two Al³⁺ balance three O²⁻.
Magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) and nitride ions (N³⁻) give Mg₃N₂, as three Mg²⁺ balance two N³⁻.
Some ions are made of several atoms bonded together that carry one overall charge. They behave as a single unit when you write formulae, so you need to know them.
Negative compound ions: hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, hydrogencarbonate HCO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, sulfite SO₃²⁻ and phosphate PO₄³⁻.
Positive compound ion: ammonium NH₄⁺. It is given only as an ion to use in formulae.
Brackets are used round a compound ion when more than one is needed, so that the subscript applies to the whole ion, e.g. Ca(OH)₂ and (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Covalent formulae follow from valency too. Atoms share electron pairs until each has a complete outer level.
Covalent formulae: atoms share enough electron pairs to complete each octet.
Hydrogen (valency 1) and oxygen (valency 2) form H₂O, because two hydrogens are needed to supply the two bonds oxygen can make.
Nitrogen (valency 3) and hydrogen form NH₃, with three hydrogens for nitrogen's three bonds.
Carbon (valency 4) and hydrogen form CH₄, with four hydrogens for carbon's four bonds.
Carbon and oxygen form CO₂, with two double bonds.
A Lewis diagram is a way of drawing bonding that tracks every outer electron. It shows which electrons are transferred, shared or left unused.
A Lewis diagram shows the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses; the different symbols let you see which atom each electron came from.
Shared pairs of electrons are drawn between the atoms they join, so you can count the bonds.
Lone pairs are pairs of outer electrons that are not used in bonding.
Ionic compounds: show each ion in square brackets with its charge, e.g. [Na]⁺ [Cl]⁻, with eight electrons around the chloride ion.
Magnesium oxide, an ionic example, is drawn as [Mg]²⁺ [O]²⁻.
Covalent examples to draw: H₂, Cl₂, HCl and H₂O, where water has two lone pairs on oxygen.
Ammonia, NH₃, has one lone pair on nitrogen, because nitrogen has five outer electrons and uses only three in bonds.
O₂ has a double bond, N₂ has a triple bond, and CO₂ has two double bonds.
Diagram: dot-and-cross diagrams of sodium chloride, water and nitrogen, with lone pairs labelled.
Orbitals are the regions of space around a nucleus where an electron is most likely to be found. Covalent bonding can be described as these regions merging.
A covalent bond forms when an orbital of one atom, holding one electron, overlaps an orbital of another atom holding one electron.
The shared pair occupies the overlap region between the two nuclei, which is where both nuclei can attract it.
The way two orbitals overlap decides the type of bond. Overlap can be head-on or sideways, which gives sigma and pi bonds.
A sigma (σ) bond is formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the line joining the two nuclei.
Sigma bonds are formed by s–s overlap in H₂, s–p overlap in HCl, and end-on p–p overlap in Cl₂.
A pi (π) bond is formed by sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals, above and below the line joining the nuclei.
Every single bond is a σ bond, so H–H is one σ bond.
A double bond is one σ bond and one π bond; a triple bond is one σ bond and two π bonds, as in N₂.
π bonds are weaker than σ bonds because sideways overlap is less effective.
π bonds prevent rotation about a double bond.
Diagram: head-on overlap of two s orbitals and of two p orbitals (σ); sideways overlap of two p orbitals, showing electron density above and below the axis (π).
Sometimes a bonding pair cannot be pinned between just two atoms. Benzene is the key example, where electrons spread round a whole ring.
In delocalised bonding, electrons are spread over several atoms rather than confined between two.
In benzene (C₆H₆), each carbon uses one p orbital, and the six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring.
This forms a ring of delocalised π electrons above and below the plane of the ring.

All six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are identical, with lengths between those of single and double bonds, because the electrons are shared evenly round the ring. There is more on this in Allotropes of Carbon. Hydrocarbons.
Higher Level students apply the same valency rules past calcium, to the main-group elements up to krypton (element 36).
The same rules apply to elements 21–36 in the main groups.
Potassium bromide is K⁺Br⁻, because group 1 and group 17 both have a valency of 1.
Calcium bromide is CaBr₂, because Ca²⁺ needs two Br⁻ to balance.
Gallium (group 13) forms Ga³⁺ ions, since group 13 has a valency of 3.
Arsenic (group 15) and hydrogen form AsH₃, since group 15 has a valency of 3.
Selenium (group 16) and hydrogen form H₂Se, since group 16 has a valency of 2.
The octet rule and Lewis diagrams are useful but not perfect. Some real molecules break the rule, and the models leave out several properties.
Some molecules are stable with fewer than eight outer electrons on the central atom, e.g. BF₃, with six around boron.
Elements in period 3 and beyond (the third row of the periodic table and below) can have more than eight outer electrons, e.g. PCl₅, with ten around phosphorus.
SF₆ has twelve electrons around sulfur.
The octet rule and Lewis diagrams do not predict the shape of a molecule, how polar a bond is, or bond strength.
They cannot show delocalised bonding, as in benzene.
Predictions from valency assume purely ionic or purely covalent bonding, but real bonds lie on a continuum.
The shape of a molecule follows from a simple idea: electron pairs carry negative charge, so they push each other away. VSEPR turns that idea into a rule for predicting shape.
VSEPR stands for valence shell electron pair repulsion.
The theory applies to molecules of the form ABn (a central atom A bonded to n atoms B), with up to four pairs of electrons around a central atom and single bonds only.
Electron pairs in the outer (valence) shell of the central atom repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible, which fixes the shape of the molecule.
Both bonding pairs and lone pairs count, because both are regions of negative charge that repel.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs: lone pair–lone pair repulsion is greater than lone pair–bond pair repulsion, which is greater than bond pair–bond pair repulsion.
Lone pairs therefore squeeze the bond angles smaller.
The shape is described by the positions of the atoms only, not the lone pairs, so NH₃ (three bonded atoms plus one lone pair) is called pyramidal.
Predicting a shape is a short routine that starts from the Lewis diagram. Follow the same three steps for every molecule.
Step 1: Draw the Lewis (dot-and-cross) diagram of the molecule.
Step 2: Count the electron pairs around the central atom, and how many of them are bonding pairs and how many are lone pairs.
Step 3: Arrange the pairs as far apart as possible, and name the shape from the positions of the atoms, adjusting the angle for lone pairs.
With up to four pairs around the central atom, these five shapes are the ones you need to know. Each depends on how many pairs are bonding and how many are lone.
Two bonding pairs and no lone pairs: linear (a straight line), 180°, e.g. BeCl₂ (gas).
Three bonding pairs and no lone pairs: trigonal planar (three atoms in one flat plane round the centre), 120°, e.g. BF₃.
Four bonding pairs and no lone pairs: tetrahedral (four atoms pointing to the corners of a pyramid-like solid), 109.5°, e.g. CH₄, CCl₄ and SiH₄.
Three bonding pairs and one lone pair: pyramidal (trigonal pyramidal), about 107°, e.g. NH₃. PH₃ is also pyramidal, but its measured angle is much smaller, about 93.5°.
Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs: V-shaped (bent), about 104.5°, e.g. H₂O.
H₂S is also V-shaped, but its measured bond angle is much smaller than water's, about 92°.
Ammonia and water have the same number of electron pairs as methane, yet their bond angles are smaller. Lone pairs are the reason.
NH₃ and H₂O have four electron pairs arranged roughly tetrahedrally, as in CH₄.
The lone pairs push the bonds closer together, because they repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so the bond angle falls as the number of lone pairs rises from 0 to 2: from CH₄ to NH₃ to H₂O.
Molecules are three-dimensional, so a flat drawing needs a convention to show depth. Models let you see the shape directly.
Diagram: 3D shapes drawn with wedges for bonds towards the viewer and dashed lines for bonds away from the viewer, with any lone pairs shown on the central atom.
3D models: ball-and-stick kits show bond angles, so you can see the shape directly.
Digital models, from molecular-modelling software or apps, can be rotated on screen.
Diagram: the five shapes, each with its example, bond angle and any lone pairs labelled.
Every salt is built from two kinds of ion, and each kind is identified by a different test. Before you meet the individual tests, you need the ground rules that make them reliable.
A salt contains a cation (a positive ion, usually a metal) and an anion (a negative ion), so a full identification needs one test for each.
The anion tests are carried out on a solution of the salt in deionised water (water with its dissolved ions removed), because the tests rely on ions moving freely in solution.
Tests work only above a certain minimum concentration of the ion, so very dilute solutions may give no visible result even when the ion is present.
Use deionised water and clean test tubes, so that ions from tap water or other samples don't give false results.
Test a blank of deionised water as a control (a test run with no sample, to show what the reagent does by itself).
A precipitate is an insoluble solid that forms when two solutions are mixed, which is why it appears as cloudiness or a coloured solid in the liquid.
Effervescence is fizzing as a gas is given off.
The cation in a salt is identified by a flame test, in which a sample of the salt is heated in a flame and the colour of the flame is observed. Each of the cations below gives its own colour.
Flame tests identify six cations: sodium, potassium, copper, lithium, barium and strontium, each giving its own flame colour. There is more on this in The orbital model and electronic structure.
Chloride ions are detected by making insoluble silver chloride. The test is simple, but the acid used matters.
Add a few drops of silver nitrate solution, acidified with dilute nitric acid (nitric acid is added to make the mixture acidic).
A white precipitate of silver chloride forms: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
Confirm the precipitate by showing that it dissolves in dilute ammonia solution.
Use nitric acid, not hydrochloric acid, because hydrochloric acid would add chloride ions of its own and give a false positive.
Nitric acid is added first to remove carbonate ions, which would also give a precipitate with silver nitrate.
Sulfate and sulfite ions both react with barium ions to give a white precipitate, so a second step with acid is needed to tell them apart.
Add barium chloride solution: sulfate and sulfite both give a white precipitate, so this step alone cannot distinguish them.
Then add dilute hydrochloric acid: barium sulfate does not dissolve, but barium sulfite dissolves, and this difference identifies which ion was present.
Barium sulfite reacts with the acid, which is why it dissolves: BaSO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → BaCl₂(aq) + SO₂(g) + H₂O(l).
Safety: sulfur dioxide is a toxic, choking gas, so use small amounts in good ventilation.
Both ions release carbon dioxide when acid is added, so a second test with magnesium sulfate is needed to tell them apart. Carbonate has the formula CO₃²⁻ and hydrogencarbonate HCO₃⁻.
Add dilute hydrochloric acid to the solid: both give effervescence of carbon dioxide.
Confirm the gas as carbon dioxide: it turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms, Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l).
To tell them apart, add magnesium sulfate solution: a carbonate gives a white precipitate immediately in the cold, Mg²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → MgCO₃(s).
A hydrogencarbonate gives no precipitate with magnesium sulfate solution until the mixture is heated.
On heating: Mg²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻ → MgCO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l).
Nitrate ions are detected with the brown ring test. Iron(II) ions convert nitrate into a gas that forms a brown coloured compound, and the layering of the liquids makes the colour appear as a ring.
Add freshly made iron(II) sulfate solution to the test solution in a test tube.
Hold the tube at an angle and carefully run concentrated sulfuric acid down the side, so that it forms a dense layer at the bottom; don't shake.
A brown ring forms where the two layers meet, showing nitrate.
Iron(II) reduces nitrate (gives electrons to it) to nitrogen monoxide: 3Fe²⁺ + NO₃⁻ + 4H⁺ → 3Fe³⁺ + NO + 2H₂O.
Nitrogen monoxide forms a brown complex (an ion in which a molecule is attached to a metal ion) with more iron(II): Fe²⁺ + NO → [FeNO]²⁺.
Safety: concentrated sulfuric acid is very corrosive; wear goggles and gloves, and add it slowly.
Phosphate ions are detected by making a yellow precipitate with ammonium molybdate in strongly acidic conditions.
Add a few drops of concentrated nitric acid, then ammonium molybdate solution, and warm gently.
A yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate shows phosphate.
Safety: concentrated nitric acid is corrosive and an oxidising agent (it can make other substances burn or react vigorously); use a fume cupboard (a ventilated enclosure that draws fumes away).
The ions in these tests are the ones that matter in water supplies, where they come from natural and human sources and affect water quality.
Chlorides come from sea water and road salt, such as that spread on roads in winter; chlorination of water also gives chloride.
Nitrates and phosphates come from fertilisers, animal slurry, sewage and detergents.
Nitrates and phosphates contaminate water and cause eutrophication (excess nutrients that cause algae to overgrow in water). There is more on this in the environmental chemistry chapter.
Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, so it forms scum with soap.
Calcium and magnesium ions with hydrogencarbonate ions cause temporary hardness, which is removed by boiling.
Calcium and magnesium ions with sulfate or chloride ions cause permanent hardness.
Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates come from water flowing over limestone, which is calcium carbonate.
Here the tests are combined to identify both ions in an unknown salt. A logical order and proper controls make the conclusion reliable.
Aim: to identify the cation and the anion in an unknown salt, using primary data (results you observe yourself in the experiment).
Step 1: Carry out a flame test on the solid to identify the cation, because the flame colour depends on the cation.
Step 2: Add dilute hydrochloric acid to a little of the solid to test for carbonate and hydrogencarbonate, then dissolve a little of the salt in deionised water.
Step 3: Carry out the other anion tests on separate portions of the solution in a logical order, recording the reagent, observation and conclusion in a table.

Step 4: Run each test on a known sample of the ion alongside, as a positive control (to show the test works), and on deionised water as a negative control (to show the reagents give no result on their own).
Step 5: Conclude the identity of the salt and write its formula, e.g. a lilac flame and a white precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in ammonia indicate potassium chloride, KCl.
Diagram: the brown ring test tube, showing the lower layer of concentrated sulfuric acid, the upper aqueous layer and the brown ring at the boundary.

When two atoms share a pair of electrons in a covalent bond (a bond formed by sharing electrons), the pair is not always shared equally. Electronegativity tells you which atom pulls harder on it. There is more on the continuum from ionic to non-polar covalent bonding in “Types of chemical bonding”.
Electronegativity is the relative attraction that an atom in a molecule has for the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond. The higher the value, the harder the atom pulls on the pair.
It is measured on the Pauling scale, on which fluorine, the most electronegative element, has the highest value of 3.98 (about 4). Pauling values are relative, so they have no units.
Non-metals have high electronegativities and metals have low ones, so a non-metal bonded to a metal pulls the electrons strongly towards itself.

Electronegativity follows a pattern in the periodic table. Both halves of the pattern are explained by how close the bonding electrons are to the nucleus (the positive centre of the atom) and how much positive charge pulls on them.
Across a period (a row of the periodic table, left to right) electronegativity increases, for example from Na 0.93 to Cl 3.16.

Across a period the nuclear charge (the positive charge of the nucleus) increases while electrons are added to the same main energy level (shell), so the atomic radius (the size of the atom) decreases.
Because the atomic radius decreases across a period, the bonding electrons are closer to a more highly charged nucleus, so the nucleus attracts them more strongly.
Down a group (a column of the periodic table) electronegativity decreases, for example from F 3.98 to I 2.66.
Down a group each element has an extra energy level, so the atomic radius increases and the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus.
Inner electrons screen (shield) the outer electrons from the nucleus. The bonding electrons are therefore further away and less strongly attracted, even though the nuclear charge is greater.
Noble gases are usually given no electronegativity value because they rarely form bonds, so there is no shared pair to attract.

The difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms predicts the bond type: the larger the difference, the more ionic the bond. The cut-offs below are guides, not sharp boundaries, because bonding is a continuum (a smooth range from ionic to non-polar covalent).
Step 1: Look up the Pauling electronegativity of each atom.
Step 2: Subtract the smaller value from the larger to find the difference.
Step 3: Compare the difference with the cut-offs below.
A difference greater than 1.7 gives a mainly ionic bond (electrons largely transferred from one atom to the other), for example NaCl: 3.16 − 0.93 = 2.23.
A difference between about 0.4 and 1.7 gives a polar covalent bond (a bond in which the shared pair is pulled unequally), for example H–Cl: 3.16 − 2.20 = 0.96; O–H: 3.44 − 2.20 = 1.24.
A difference less than about 0.4 gives a non-polar (pure) covalent bond, in which the pair is shared almost equally, for example C–H: 2.55 − 2.20 = 0.35.
A bond between identical atoms has a difference of zero, so the pair is shared equally and the bond is non-polar, for example Cl–Cl: 3.16 − 3.16 = 0.
In a polar bond the more electronegative atom carries the partial negative charge (δ−) and the less electronegative atom carries the partial positive charge (δ+).

Ionic compounds are made of oppositely charged ions packed in a lattice (a regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement). Their properties follow from the strong attraction between those ions and from whether the ions can move.
Ionic compounds are solids at room temperature, for example sodium chloride and magnesium oxide.
Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C and boils at 1413 °C.

The melting and boiling points are high because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic attractions (attractions between opposite charges) between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity, because the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot carry charge.
Molten ionic compounds, and ionic compounds dissolved in water, conduct electricity, because the ions are free to move and carry charge.
Many ionic compounds are soluble in water, because polar water molecules (molecules with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end) attract and surround the ions.
Ionic compounds are insoluble in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, because non-polar molecules have no charged ends to attract the ions.
Covalent compounds are made of separate molecules. Because of this, melting or boiling them only has to separate one molecule from the next, which takes far less energy than melting an ionic lattice.
Many covalent compounds are gases or liquids at room temperature, for example methane, carbon dioxide and water.
Some covalent compounds are solids with low melting points, for example iodine and sugar.
Iodine sublimes (turns straight from solid to gas) on gentle heating and melts at 114 °C.
Covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points, because only the weak forces between molecules have to be overcome.
The covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break when a covalent substance melts or boils: methane boils at −162 °C.
Whether a covalent compound conducts or dissolves depends on whether it has charged particles and on whether its molecules are polar (have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end).
Covalent compounds do not conduct electricity, because there are no ions or free electrons to carry charge.
Some covalent compounds, such as hydrogen chloride, form ions when they dissolve in water and then conduct.
Non-polar molecules such as methane and iodine are insoluble or only slightly soluble in water, but dissolve in non-polar solvents.
Polar molecules such as ethanol, sugar and ammonia dissolve in water, because they can form hydrogen bonds with it. There is more on this in “Intermolecular forces and physical properties”.
“Like dissolves like” sums up covalent solubility: polar molecules dissolve in water and non-polar molecules dissolve in non-polar solvents.

Putting the two types side by side shows four paired differences, and each has its own reason: melting and boiling points depend on whether strong ionic attractions or only weak forces between molecules must be overcome, and conductivity depends on whether ions are free to move.
Melting and boiling points: ionic compounds are high; covalent compounds are low.
Electrical conductivity: ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved; covalent compounds generally do not conduct.
Solubility: ionic compounds are usually soluble in water; covalent compounds are usually soluble in non-polar solvents.
State at room temperature: ionic compounds are solids; covalent compounds are often gases or liquids.

Exception: giant covalent substances such as diamond and graphite have very high melting points, because strong covalent bonds must be broken. There is more on this in “Allotropes of Carbon. Hydrocarbons”.
A simple conductivity test shows whether a substance contains ions that are free to move. Ionic compounds pass the test when molten or dissolved.
Step 1: Melt the substance, or dissolve it in water.
Step 2: Dip two carbon electrodes (the rods that carry current into the liquid) into it, connected to a battery and a bulb (or an ammeter, which measures current).
Step 3: A lit bulb, or a current on the ammeter, shows that ions are present and free to carry charge.
Diagram: a conductivity circuit with a battery, a bulb and two carbon electrodes dipping into a beaker of solution; label the battery, bulb, electrodes and beaker.

Two different kinds of attraction operate in a molecular substance: bonds inside each molecule and forces between molecules. Keeping them apart explains why melting and boiling are easy compared with breaking a molecule.
Intramolecular bonding is the strong covalent bonding within a molecule, holding its atoms together.
Intermolecular forces are the weaker forces of attraction between separate molecules.
Intermolecular forces are much weaker than covalent bonds: boiling water overcomes the forces between H₂O molecules but does not break the O–H bonds.
Van der Waals forces are the collective name for the intermolecular forces: London dispersion forces and permanent dipole–dipole forces (including hydrogen bonding).
Diagram: two water molecules, with the O–H covalent bonds labelled “intramolecular” and the attraction between an H of one molecule and the O of the other labelled “intermolecular (hydrogen bond)”.
Even a molecule with no permanent charged ends still attracts its neighbours weakly. London dispersion forces are the intermolecular force that every molecule has.
London dispersion forces act between all molecules, and are the only intermolecular forces between non-polar molecules, for example H₂, Cl₂, CH₄ and noble gas atoms.

They arise because electrons are always moving: at any instant the electron cloud may be unevenly spread, giving a temporary (instantaneous) dipole (one side slightly negative, the other slightly positive).
The temporary dipole induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule (pushes its electrons to one side), and the two attract.

London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces for small molecules, but they get stronger as molecules get larger and have more electrons, because a bigger electron cloud is easier to distort.
Polar molecules have charged ends all the time, not just for an instant. This gives them an extra attraction on top of London dispersion forces.
A polar molecule has a permanent dipole: a δ+ end and a δ− end, which arises from polar bonds. There is more on this in “Electronegativity and bond type”.
Dipole–dipole forces are attractions between the δ+ end of one polar molecule and the δ− end of a neighbouring one, for example between HCl molecules (Hδ+–Clδ−).
Dipole–dipole forces are stronger than London dispersion forces between molecules of similar size, because the charged ends are permanent.
Hydrogen bonding is the strongest of the intermolecular forces. It needs a hydrogen atom attached to one of three very electronegative atoms, F, O or N.

A hydrogen bond is a particularly strong dipole–dipole attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a small, very electronegative atom (F, O or N) in one molecule and a lone pair on an F, O or N atom of a neighbouring molecule.
A lone pair is a pair of outer electrons on an atom that is not used in bonding, so it can attract the δ+ hydrogen of a neighbouring molecule.
It is strong because the H–F, O–H and N–H bonds are very polar, leaving the small hydrogen atom strongly δ+.
A hydrogen bond is between molecules, not a covalent bond to hydrogen.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F: there is no hydrogen bonding between CH₄ molecules or in HCl.
Examples: water (H₂O), ammonia (NH₃), hydrogen fluoride (HF), alcohols such as ethanol, and carboxylic acids.
Hydrogen bonds are the strongest intermolecular forces.
Diagram: water molecules with δ+ and δ− labelled, and hydrogen bonds drawn as dashed lines from H to the lone pair on O of the next molecule.

When an ionic compound dissolves in water, the ions are pulled out of the lattice by the polar water molecules. The attraction between a full charge and a partial charge is called an ion–dipole force.
An ion–dipole force is the attraction between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule.
When sodium chloride dissolves in water, the δ− oxygen ends of water molecules are attracted to Na⁺ ions and the δ+ hydrogen ends to Cl⁻ ions.
The ions become surrounded by water molecules (hydrated).
Ion–dipole forces are stronger than dipole–dipole forces; they explain why ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents such as water.
Diagram: a Na⁺ ion surrounded by water molecules with their O atoms pointing towards it, and a Cl⁻ ion surrounded by water molecules with their H atoms pointing towards it.
Putting the forces in order lets you predict which substance holds its molecules together most strongly, for molecules of similar size.
For molecules of similar size, London dispersion forces are weaker than dipole–dipole forces, which are weaker than hydrogen bonds.
All intermolecular forces are much weaker than covalent and ionic bonds, which is why melting or boiling a molecular substance leaves its molecules intact.

Melting and boiling are about the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. Intermolecular forces (the attractions between separate molecules) decide how much energy a molecular substance needs to change state.
To melt or boil a molecular substance (one made of separate small molecules), energy must be supplied to overcome the intermolecular forces, so the molecules can move apart.
The stronger the intermolecular forces, the higher the melting and boiling points, because more energy is needed to pull the molecules apart.

Substances with only London dispersion forces (weak attractions caused by temporary uneven electron distribution) between small molecules are gases at room temperature, because the forces are too weak to hold them together. Methane is an example: it boils at −162 °C.
Group 14 hydrides (compounds of hydrogen with the group 14 elements) rise steadily in boiling point: CH₄ < SiH₄ < GeH₄ < SnH₄.

Hydrogen bonding (a strong intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen) gives unusually high boiling points. Water boils at 100 °C, but hydrogen sulfide, a heavier molecule with no hydrogen bonding, boils at −60 °C.
Whether one substance dissolves in another depends on the attractions between their particles. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving and the solute is the substance that dissolves.
A substance dissolves when the attractions between solvent and solute particles are similar to or stronger than the attractions they replace. This is summed up as “like dissolves like”.

Polar substances (those whose molecules have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end) and hydrogen-bonding substances such as ethanol, ammonia and sugar dissolve in water, because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
Non-polar substances such as iodine, hexane and oils do not dissolve in water. They dissolve in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, where the London forces are similar to those they replace.
Hexane and water do not mix, which means they form two layers.
Water is a very small molecule, yet it behaves unlike other small molecules. The reason is hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
Water has a high boiling point and a high melting point for such a small molecule, because the hydrogen bonds between molecules take a lot of energy to overcome.
Ice is less dense than liquid water: hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice (a regular arrangement with gaps between molecules), so ice floats.
Water is a good solvent for ionic and polar substances, because it can form attractions with them.
Secondary data means results taken from tables or graphs rather than measured yourself. The boiling points below (bp) are the sample data you may be asked to interpret.
Noble gas boiling points (the noble gases are the group 18 elements): He −269 °C; Ne −246 °C; Ar −186 °C; Kr −153 °C; Xe −108 °C.
Halogens (the group 17 elements) at room temperature: fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
Alkane (hydrocarbon) boiling points: methane −162 °C; ethane −89 °C; propane −42 °C; butane −1 °C; pentane 36 °C; hexane 69 °C.
Group 16 hydride boiling points: H₂O 100 °C; H₂S −60 °C; H₂Se −41 °C; H₂Te −2 °C.
Group 15 and 17 hydride boiling points: NH₃ −33 °C vs PH₃ −88 °C; HF 20 °C vs HCl −85 °C.
Compounds of similar mass: ethanol (bp 78 °C, hydrogen bonding) vs propane (bp −42 °C, London forces only).

At Higher Level you must explain why the boiling points in the data follow their patterns. Two ideas do all the work: London forces grow with molecule size, and hydrogen bonding lifts a boiling point far above the trend.
Down group 18, down group 17 and along the alkane series, boiling points rise because the molecules have more electrons and larger electron clouds, so London dispersion forces get stronger.
In the group 16 hydrides, boiling point rises from H₂S to H₂Te as London forces increase with size. Water is far higher than the trend predicts because of hydrogen bonding.
The same anomaly (a value far out of line with the trend) appears for NH₃ in group 15 and HF in group 17, which both form hydrogen bonds.

Molecules of similar mass have higher boiling points if they are polar (attracted by dipole–dipole forces, the attractions between opposite ends of polar molecules), and much higher ones if they hydrogen bond, e.g. ethanol compared with propane.
Diagram: a graph of boiling point against period for the hydrides of groups 14, 15, 16 and 17, showing the high values of H₂O, HF and NH₃ and the steady rise from CH₄ to SnH₄.

Some bonds share electrons unequally, but that does not always make the whole molecule polar. Whether it does depends on the shape. The shapes named here are given; see “VSEPR theory” for how shapes are predicted.
A polar bond has an uneven share of electrons, giving a slightly positive end (δ+) and a slightly negative end (δ−).
A polar molecule has an overall uneven distribution of charge, with a δ+ end and a δ− end.
Whether a molecule is polar depends on both its bonds and its shape: polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel out, so the molecule has no δ+ or δ− end.
A dipole is the pair of δ+ and δ− ends of a polar bond. In a symmetrical molecule the dipoles pull in opposite directions and cancel, while in an unsymmetrical molecule they add up.
Carbon dioxide: each C=O bond is polar, but the molecule is linear (O=C=O, in a straight line), so the two bond polarities point in opposite directions and cancel; CO₂ is non-polar.
Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄): four polar C–Cl bonds arranged tetrahedrally (pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron) cancel; CCl₄ is non-polar.
Boron trifluoride (BF₃): three polar B–F bonds at 120° in a trigonal plane (flat, evenly spaced) cancel; BF₃ is non-polar.
Water: two polar O–H bonds in a V-shaped (bent) molecule do not cancel, so water is polar, with δ− on oxygen.
Ammonia: three polar N–H bonds in a pyramidal molecule (a shape like a pyramid, with nitrogen at the top) do not cancel, so NH₃ is polar.
Trichloromethane (CHCl₃): the C–H bond differs from the three C–Cl bonds, so the tetrahedral molecule is unsymmetrical and polar.
Diagram: CO₂, CCl₄, H₂O and NH₃, with arrows (or δ+ and δ− labels) on each bond showing whether the polarities cancel; label each molecule polar or non-polar.
Polarity decides which intermolecular forces act between molecules. Those forces then set the boiling point and the solubility.

Polar molecules attract each other by permanent dipole–dipole forces (or hydrogen bonds) as well as London dispersion forces, so they have stronger intermolecular forces than non-polar molecules of similar size.

Non-polar molecules, including symmetrical ones with polar bonds, have only London dispersion forces between them. For example, carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature, and tetrachloromethane is immiscible with water (does not mix with it).
A symmetrical molecule usually has a lower boiling point and lower solubility in water than an unsymmetrical one of similar size, because its forces between molecules are weaker.
Tetrachloromethane is immiscible with water, while trichloromethane is slightly soluble; both dissolve in non-polar solvents.
A molecule can contain polar bonds and still be non-polar overall. What matters is the shape. These shapes are stated, not derived.
A molecule with polar bonds is polar overall only if its shape is unsymmetrical, so that its charge is unevenly spread.
Water is V-shaped (bent), so it is polar.
Ammonia is pyramidal, so it is polar.
Carbon dioxide is linear and methane is tetrahedral: both are non-polar.
Once you know a molecule's shape and polarity, you can predict its boiling point and what it dissolves in.
Polar molecules have stronger forces between them than non-polar molecules of similar size, so they have higher boiling points.
Polar molecules tend to dissolve in polar solvents such as water; non-polar molecules dissolve in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane.
Water is a liquid at room temperature and dissolves salts, because it is polar and forms hydrogen bonds; methane is a non-polar gas and is almost insoluble in water.
Ammonia, which is polar, is very soluble in water; carbon dioxide, which is non-polar, is only slightly soluble.
Polar molecules respond to an electric charge and non-polar ones do not. A charged rod held beside a thin stream of liquid shows which kind a liquid is made of.
Aim: to show whether a liquid is made of polar molecules.
Apparatus: a burette (a long graduated tube with a tap) clamped above a beaker, a polythene (or acetate) rod, a cloth, and liquids such as water and cyclohexane.
Diagram: a burette clamped above a beaker, releasing a thin stream of liquid; label the burette, the beaker and the stream.
Diagram: a charged polythene rod held beside the stream, with the stream bending towards it; label the rod, the stream and the direction of deflection (the sideways bend).
Independent variable (the one you change): the liquid tested.
Dependent variable (the one you observe): whether the stream is deflected.
Controlled variables (kept the same): the same rod and cloth, with the rod recharged before each test, so that every liquid meets a charged rod.
The method is the same for each liquid, and comparing the two streams gives the conclusion.
Step 1: Charge the rod by rubbing it with the cloth.
Step 2: Let a thin stream of the liquid run from the burette, and hold the rod close to the stream without touching it.
Step 3: Repeat with the other liquid, recharging the rod each time.
Result: the stream of water is deflected (attracted) towards the rod; the stream of cyclohexane is not deflected.
The water stream is attracted to the rod whether the rod is charged positively or negatively, because the molecules rotate.
Explanation: polar molecules turn so that their oppositely charged end faces the rod and are attracted to it; non-polar molecules are not attracted.
Safety: cyclohexane is flammable and harmful, so use no flames, small volumes and good ventilation, and collect it for disposal.
An element's position in the periodic table tells you how its atoms behave. Columns are called groups, and the groups on the left and right edges are the ones you need to know.
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons (the electrons in the highest occupied energy level), so they undergo similar reactions.
Going down a group, atoms have more energy levels (the shells that hold electrons around the nucleus), which explains the trends in reactivity within each group.
Groups 1 and 2 are on the left of the periodic table; they are metals that lose electrons to form positive ions (charged particles).
Groups 17 and 18 are on the right; the halogens (group 17) are non-metals that gain electrons, and the noble gases (group 18) neither gain nor lose electrons.
Hydrogen appears in group 1 in some tables but is not an alkali metal.
Group 1 is the first column of the periodic table. Its metals are named alkali metals because they form alkaline solutions with water, and each has a single outer electron that it loses very easily.
Members: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium; each atom has one outer electron.
State and conductivity: soft, shiny solids when freshly cut, with low densities and low melting points for metals; good conductors of heat and electricity.
Reactivity: very reactive, so they tarnish quickly in air (the shiny surface goes dull as it reacts) and are stored under oil to keep air and moisture away.
Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded (inner electrons block some of the nucleus's pull), so it is lost more easily.
They form 1+ ions (Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺) because each atom loses its one outer electron, and they make ionic compounds such as sodium chloride.
Safety: use only small pieces, behind a safety screen and wearing goggles, because the reactions are vigorous; never touch them with bare hands.
All the alkali metals react with water to give an alkaline solution and hydrogen gas. What you see changes with the metal, and the observations show the trend in reactivity.
With water they form an alkaline hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g).
Lithium floats and fizzes steadily on the water, the gentlest of the three.
Sodium melts into a silvery ball that darts about on the surface.
Potassium reacts violently, and the hydrogen it gives off burns with a lilac flame.
The solution formed turns universal indicator (a mixture of dyes that shows pH by colour) purple, showing that it is alkaline.
Group 2 sits next to group 1. These metals are also reactive, but each atom has two outer electrons to lose, which makes them a little less reactive than their group 1 neighbours.
Members: beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium; each atom has two outer electrons.
State and conductivity: solid metals, harder and denser than group 1 metals; good conductors.
Reactivity: reactive, but less so than group 1 metals in the same period (the same row), because two electrons must be lost.
Calcium reacts steadily with cold water: Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g).
Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but burns in air with a bright white flame: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
Reactivity increases down the group, for the same reason as group 1: the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded.
They form 2+ ions (Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺) because each atom loses its two outer electrons.
The halogens are the reactive non-metals in group 17. Each atom is one electron short of a full outer level, so it readily gains one electron.
Members: fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine (astatine); each atom has seven outer electrons.
The halogens exist as diatomic molecules (two atoms joined together): F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.
Fluorine is a pale yellow gas at room temperature, and chlorine is a yellow-green gas.
Bromine is a red-brown liquid at room temperature. Iodine is a grey-black solid that forms a purple vapour when heated.
Conductivity: halogens are non-metals and do not conduct electricity.
Reactivity: very reactive non-metals that gain one electron to form 1− halide ions (negative ions of a halogen): F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻.
They react with metals to form salts, e.g. 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s).
Reactivity decreases down the group because larger atoms attract an extra electron less strongly, as it is further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Because reactivity falls down group 17, a more reactive halogen can push a less reactive one out of a solution of its salt. This is called displacement, and the colour change shows it has happened.
Displacement: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its salt.
Chlorine and potassium bromide: Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq); the colourless solution turns orange-brown as bromine forms.
Chlorine and potassium iodide: Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq); the solution turns brown as iodine forms.
Bromine displaces iodine from a solution of its salt but does not displace chlorine, because bromine is less reactive than chlorine.
Safety: halogens are toxic and corrosive, so they are used in a fume cupboard (an enclosure that draws fumes away from the user).
The noble gases are the last column of the periodic table. Their atoms already have a full outer energy level, so they have almost no tendency to react, and their uses depend on that.
Members: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon.
State: colourless, odourless gases made of single atoms (monatomic).
Reactivity: very unreactive (inert) because they have full outer energy levels, a stable arrangement: helium has 2 outer electrons and the others have 8.
Helium is used in balloons and airships because it is unreactive and has a low density.
Argon is used in filament light bulbs and as a shield gas in welding, where its lack of reactivity protects the hot metal and the filament.
Neon is used in advertising signs, where it glows red in an electric discharge.

The periodic table lists elements in order of atomic number (the number of protons in an atom). Relative atomic mass (the average mass of an atom of the element, compared with carbon-12) follows a looser pattern.
Atomic number increases by one from each element to the next.
Relative atomic mass generally increases with atomic number.
Relative atomic mass falls in a few places: argon (39.95) comes before potassium (39.10), and tellurium (127.6) comes before iodine (126.9).
These exceptions come from the mix of isotopes (atoms of the same element with different masses) of each element, not from mistakes in the table.
The way outer electrons change across and down the table explains why elements are arranged in periods (rows) and groups (columns).
Across a period, the number of outer electrons increases by one at each step, all in the same main energy level, which is why a period is one row.
Down a group, the number of outer electrons stays the same, so the elements react similarly, but a new main energy level is added each time, so the outer electrons are further out.
The repeating pattern of outer-electron arrangements causes periodicity (the regular repeating of properties down the table): elements with the same outer arrangement fall in the same group.
Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract bonding electrons towards itself. Values are on the Pauling scale.
Electronegativity increases across a period, e.g. sodium 0.93 to chlorine 3.16 in period 3.
Electronegativity decreases down a group, e.g. fluorine 3.98 to iodine 2.66 in group 17.
The explanation for these values is in "Bond type and intermolecular forces".
Atoms react because they are more stable with a full outer level. This explains why reactivity rises and falls in a pattern across and down the table.
Atoms react to reach a full outer level of eight electrons (the octet rule), by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.
Metals react by losing electrons: reactivity increases down group 1 and group 2, because the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Across a period, metal reactivity decreases from group 1 to group 2 to group 13.
Non-metals react by gaining electrons: reactivity decreases down group 17, because larger atoms attract an extra electron less strongly.
Across a period, non-metal reactivity generally increases towards group 17.
Noble gases already have a full outer level, so they have no need to gain or lose electrons and are unreactive.
Period 3 runs from sodium to argon. Across it the elements change from metals to non-metals, and the physical properties change with them.
Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are shiny metals and good conductors.
Silicon is a metalloid (an element with properties between those of a metal and a non-metal) and a semiconductor (it conducts only slightly).
Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon are non-metals and non-conductors.
Melting points rise across period 3 to a maximum at silicon (1414 °C), which has a giant covalent structure (a huge network of atoms joined by covalent bonds).
Beyond silicon, melting points fall sharply for the molecular non-metals and for argon.
Down group 1, melting points decrease: lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C, potassium 63 °C.
Down group 17, melting and boiling points increase, so the halogens change from gases to a liquid to a solid.
These trends are Higher Level only. Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom, and atomic radius is the size of the atom.
Atomic (covalent) radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.
First ionisation energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Successive ionisation energies of an element always increase.
Higher Level trends extend to the first 36 elements, to krypton; Ordinary level uses the first 20, to calcium.
How strongly an atom holds its outer electrons depends on three factors. They explain every trend in atomic radius and ionisation energy that follows.
Effective nuclear charge: the more protons in the nucleus, the stronger the pull on the outer electrons.
Distance: the further the outer electrons are from the nucleus (more energy levels), the weaker the pull on them.
Screening (shielding): inner electrons shield the outer electrons from the full nuclear charge; electrons in the same energy level shield each other very little.
Atomic radius measures the size of an atom. Its trends follow from the nuclear charge, the number of energy levels and the screening.
Atomic (covalent) radius: half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms of the same element joined by a single covalent bond.
Across a period it decreases: nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same main energy level, with little extra screening, so the outer electrons are pulled closer.
Down a group it increases: each element has an extra energy level, and the extra inner electrons screen the outer electrons, outweighing the increase in nuclear charge.
Noble gases are not given a covalent radius because they don't form bonds.

First ionisation energy measures how tightly an atom holds its outermost electron. The data below show the trends, and a few elements break the pattern because of sublevel stability and electron pairing.

First ionisation energy: the minimum energy needed to completely remove the most loosely bound electron from a neutral gaseous atom in its ground state (lowest energy state): X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. Its unit is kJ mol⁻¹.
Period 2 first ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): Li 520, Be 899, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314, F 1681, Ne 2081.
Period 3 first ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 787, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1521.
Values are standard data book figures, rounded.

Across a period the value generally increases, because nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so the outer electron is held more tightly. Noble gases have the highest first ionisation energy in each period.
Down a group the value decreases, because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more screened, despite the larger nuclear charge.
Group 1 metals have the lowest values in each period, which is why they lose electrons easily and are so reactive; the value falls down the group to potassium at 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

The rise across a period is not perfectly smooth, because a few elements have a lower value than the one before. The cause is the stability of particular sublevels (subdivisions of an energy level, such as 2s and 2p) and electron pairing.
Beryllium is higher than boron (899 against 801 kJ mol⁻¹) because beryllium's 2s sublevel is full (1s² 2s²), a stable arrangement.
Boron's outer electron is alone in a 2p orbital (1s² 2s² 2p¹), which is slightly higher in energy and more screened, so it is removed more easily.
Nitrogen is higher than oxygen (1402 against 1314 kJ mol⁻¹) because nitrogen's 2p sublevel is half full, with one electron in each orbital (2p³), a stable arrangement.
In oxygen (2p⁴) one 2p orbital holds a pair of electrons, and repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove.
The same pattern occurs in period 3: magnesium (738) is higher than aluminium (578), and phosphorus (1012) is higher than sulfur (1000).
Diagram: a graph of first ionisation energy against atomic number for elements 1 to 20, showing peaks at the noble gases, troughs at the alkali metals and small dips after Be, N, Mg and P.
After the first electron is removed, more can be taken away one at a time. The sizes of the successive energies reveal how an atom's electrons are arranged in energy levels.
Second ionisation energy: the energy needed to remove an electron from a 1+ ion, not a second electron from the neutral atom: X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻; the third and later follow the same pattern.
Successive ionisation energies always increase, because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion, so the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons more tightly.
A very large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a new, inner energy level, which is closer to the nucleus and less screened.
Magnesium: 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ mol⁻¹; the big jump between the second and third shows two outer electrons, so magnesium is in group 2.
Sodium: 496 then 4562 kJ mol⁻¹; the big jump after the first shows one outer electron, so sodium is in group 1.
A graph of the log of successive ionisation energies against electron number for potassium shows jumps that group its electrons into 2, 8, 8 and 1, which is evidence for main energy levels.
Atoms are far too small to count, so chemists count them by weighing. The mole links a mass that can be weighed to a number of particles.
The mole (symbol mol) is the SI unit (the internationally agreed system of units) of amount of substance, so it measures how much of a substance there is by counting its particles.
One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions or electrons); this number is the Avogadro constant, NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Before 2019 the mole was defined through carbon-12 (the carbon atom with 6 protons and 6 neutrons): the Avogadro constant was the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.
Since the 2019 SI redefinition the value of the Avogadro constant is exact by definition.
