Always state the particle, because a mole of different particles contains different numbers of atoms: one mole of oxygen atoms (O) contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.
One mole of oxygen molecules (O₂) contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and 1.204 × 10²⁴ atoms, because each O₂ molecule is made of two atoms.
This shows the scale of the mole: one mole of water is only 18 g (about 18 cm³, since water has a density of about 1.00 g cm⁻³) but contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules.
To weigh out a mole you need to know what one mole of the substance weighs. That comes from the relative atomic masses of its atoms, and density links mass to volume for liquids and solids.

Relative molecular mass (Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses (Ar, the mass of an atom compared with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom) of all the atoms in a molecule (or formula unit, the simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound); it has no units.
Relative atomic masses used in these calculations: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, S 32, Cl 35.5, Ca 40.
Example: Mr(H₂O) = 2(1) + 16 = 18, because water has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Example: Mr(H₂SO₄) = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98, because there are two H, one S and four O.
Example: Mr(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100, because there is one Ca, one C and three O.
Molar mass (M) is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole (g mol⁻¹); it is numerically equal to Ar or Mr, so the molar mass of water is 18 g mol⁻¹.
Density is mass per unit volume (how much mass is packed into a given space): ρ = m ÷ V, in g cm⁻³ or kg m⁻³.
Every mole calculation uses the same few relationships. Each one is a single step, and you can chain them together.
Moles from mass: n = m ÷ M, with m in g and M in g mol⁻¹. Example: 8.8 g of CO₂ (M = 44 g mol⁻¹): n = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.20 mol.
Mass from moles: m = n × M, which is the same relationship turned round. Example: 0.25 mol of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹): m = 0.25 × 58.5 = 14.6 g.
Number of particles from moles: N = n × NA, because each mole holds 6.02 × 10²³ particles. Example: 0.20 mol of CO₂: N = 0.20 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²³ molecules.
Moles from number of particles: n = N ÷ NA, which reverses the previous step.
Number of atoms: multiply the number of molecules by the number of atoms in each molecule, because each molecule contains that many atoms.
Example: 0.20 mol of CO₂ contains 0.20 × 3 = 0.60 mol of atoms, so 0.60 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.61 × 10²³ atoms.
Gases are usually measured by volume and liquids by volume and density, so these also have to be converted to moles. Moles are the middle step in every conversion.

Gas volume from moles: V = n × molar volume (the volume of one mole of gas), using 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP (standard temperature and pressure, the agreed reference conditions for gases: 0 °C and 101.3 kPa).
Mass from volume and density: m = ρ × V, then convert the mass to moles with n = m ÷ M.
Example: 10.0 cm³ of ethanol (density 0.789 g cm⁻³): m = 10.0 × 0.789 = 7.89 g.
Continuing the ethanol example (M = 46 g mol⁻¹): n = 7.89 ÷ 46 = 0.172 mol.
Conversion route: mass ⇄ moles ⇄ number of particles, and moles ⇄ gas volume; always go through moles.
Not all atoms of an element have the same mass, so the relative atomic mass in the data tables is an average. That average rests on two ideas: isotopes and mass number.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different mass numbers, because they have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The mass number of an isotope is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus (the central core of the atom).

Relative atomic mass (Ar) is the weighted average of the isotope masses, using their percentage abundances (the percentage of the element's atoms that are that isotope), relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Each isotope contributes to the average in proportion to how abundant it is. Common isotopes count for more than rare ones.
Step 1: multiply each isotope's mass number by its percentage abundance.
Step 2: add the products together, to get the total mass contributed by 100 atoms.
Step 3: divide the total by 100, because the abundances are percentages, so Ar = Σ(mass number × % abundance) ÷ 100.
Quick check: the answer must lie between the lightest and heaviest isotope mass numbers, nearer to the more abundant isotope.
Here the three-step method is applied to chlorine, boron and magnesium, the last with three isotopes.
Chlorine example (75% ³⁵Cl, 25% ³⁷Cl): the products are 35 × 75 = 2625 and 37 × 25 = 925.
Adding the products gives 2625 + 925 = 3550, and 3550 ÷ 100 = 35.5, so Ar(Cl) = 35.5, nearer 35 because ³⁵Cl is three times as abundant as ³⁷Cl.
Boron example (19.9% ¹⁰B, 80.1% ¹¹B): the products are 10 × 19.9 = 199 and 11 × 80.1 = 881.1.
Adding the products gives 199 + 881.1 = 1080.1, and 1080.1 ÷ 100 = 10.8, so Ar(B) = 10.8.
Magnesium example, three isotopes (79.0% ²⁴Mg, 10.0% ²⁵Mg, 11.0% ²⁶Mg): the products are 24 × 79.0 = 1896, 25 × 10.0 = 250 and 26 × 11.0 = 286.
Adding the products gives 1896 + 250 + 286 = 2432, and 2432 ÷ 100 = 24.3, so Ar(Mg) = 24.3.
The method also runs backwards: if you are given the relative atomic mass and the isotopes, you can find how much of each there is, using algebra.
For two isotopes, let the abundance of one isotope be x%; the other is then (100 − x)%, because the two abundances add up to 100%.
Set up Ar = [mass₁ × x + mass₂ × (100 − x)] ÷ 100 and solve for x.
Boron example (Ar = 10.8; isotopes ¹⁰B and ¹¹B): 10x + 11(100 − x) = 1080.
Expanding gives 10x + 1100 − 11x = 1080, so 1100 − x = 1080 and x = 20.
The abundances are therefore about 20% boron-10 and 80% boron-11, matching the 19.9% and 80.1% used in the Ar calculation.
Using whole mass numbers is an approximation, because real isotope masses are not exact whole numbers; data-book isotope masses give more accurate abundances.
Gas volumes can be compared directly, with no need to weigh. Avogadro's law says why: the volume of a gas depends only on how many molecules it holds.
Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules.
So at fixed temperature and pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles: V ∝ n (double the moles and the volume doubles).
Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes: gases react in volumes that are in simple whole-number ratios to one another and to the volumes of any gaseous products, at the same temperature and pressure.
Example of combining volumes: 2 volumes of hydrogen react with 1 volume of oxygen.
Avogadro's law explains Gay-Lussac's law: the volume ratio equals the mole ratio in the balanced equation, because equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules.
Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) reads as 1 volume of nitrogen + 3 volumes of hydrogen → 2 volumes of ammonia.
Gas volumes change with temperature and pressure, so a volume is only useful if the conditions are stated. Chemists agree a standard set of conditions, STP, and quote the molar volume under them.
Standard temperature and pressure (STP) is 0 °C (273 K) and 101.3 kPa (1 atmosphere, 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa).
Temperature in gas calculations must be in kelvin (the absolute temperature scale, where 0 °C is 273 K).
Molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at a stated temperature and pressure.
At STP the molar volume is 22.4 L mol⁻¹ (22 400 cm³).
At room temperature (about 20 °C) and pressure, the molar volume is about 24.0 L mol⁻¹, larger than at STP because the gas is warmer.
IUPAC (the international chemistry body) now uses a standard pressure of 100 kPa, at which the molar volume at 273.15 K is 22.7 L mol⁻¹.
Leaving Certificate calculations use 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP unless told otherwise.
Molar volume applies to gases only, not to liquids or solids.
The value 22.4 L mol⁻¹ can be calculated from the ideal gas equation, and it can be found by experiment.

From the ideal gas equation PV = nRT (P pressure, V volume, n moles, R the gas constant, T temperature in kelvin), the volume of n moles is V = nRT ÷ P. There is more on this in Gas laws and the ideal gas equation.
For 1 mol at 273 K and 101 325 Pa, with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: V = 1 × 8.314 × 273 ÷ 101 325.
This gives V = 0.0224 m³ = 22.4 L, the molar volume at STP.
Experimentally, weigh a gas cylinder (for example, of oxygen) before and after releasing a known volume of gas into a gas syringe (a calibrated syringe that collects and measures gas volume).
Find the number of moles of gas released from the mass lost, using n = m ÷ M.
Scale the volume to one mole and correct it to STP to obtain the molar volume.
Diagram: a gas cylinder on a balance, connected by tubing to a gas syringe; label the cylinder, the balance, the tubing and the scale of the gas syringe.
At STP every mole of gas occupies 22.4 L, so converting between volume and moles takes one step. Mass and volume are linked through moles.
Moles from gas volume at STP: n = V ÷ 22.4, with V in L. Example: 5.6 L of CO₂ at STP: n = 5.6 ÷ 22.4 = 0.25 mol.
Volume from moles at STP: V = n × 22.4 L. Example: 0.50 mol of O₂ occupies 0.50 × 22.4 = 11.2 L at STP.
Mass to volume goes through moles, because 22.4 L is the volume of a mole: first n = m ÷ M.
Example: 8.0 g of methane (M = 16 g mol⁻¹): n = 8.0 ÷ 16 = 0.50 mol.
Because volume ratios equal mole ratios, the balanced equation tells you the gas volumes directly, with no need to convert to moles.
Example of reacting gases: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
The volumes of methane and oxygen are in the ratio 50 cm³ : 100 cm³, which is 1 : 2 as in the equation, so all the reactants are used up.
So 50 cm³ of CO₂ is formed, measured at the same temperature and pressure, because the equation gives 1 mole of CO₂ for every 1 mole of methane.

Aim: to determine the relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid by turning a measured mass of it into vapour. The vapour fills a flask of known volume, so its moles can be found from the gas equation.
A volatile liquid evaporates easily, i.e. it has a low boiling point, so it can be turned completely into vapour at 100 °C. Propanone (CH₃COCH₃, boiling point 56 °C) is used.
If the mass (m), volume (V), temperature (T) and pressure (P) of the vapour are measured, the number of moles is n = PV ÷ RT, where R is the gas constant.
Relative molecular mass is then Mr = m ÷ n, giving the molar mass in g mol⁻¹.
The vapour is assumed to behave as an ideal gas (a gas that obeys the gas equation exactly).
The flask holds the vapour, the boiling water bath heats it, and the balance and barometer supply the measurements needed for the calculation.
A clean, dry conical flask (about 250 cm³), a small square of aluminium foil held by a rubber band, and a pin.
A large beaker of boiling water (the water bath) on a hotplate, with a thermometer in the water.
A top-pan balance reading to 0.01 g, a barometer (to measure atmospheric pressure), a graduated (measuring) cylinder, and a dropper of the volatile liquid (propanone).
Diagram: the conical flask with its foil cap, rubber band and pinhole, clamped in a beaker of boiling water on a hotplate; label the water bath and the thermometer.
Diagram: a top-pan balance with the flask on the pan, and a barometer; label the pan and the display or scale.
Diagram: a graduated (measuring) cylinder, read at eye level with the bottom of the meniscus (the curved surface of the water) on the scale.
The aim of the first steps is to fill the flask with pure propanone vapour at a known temperature.
1. Weigh the dry conical flask with the foil cap and rubber band.
2. Add about 2–3 cm³ of propanone, replace the foil cap and pierce one small pinhole in it.
3. Clamp the flask in the boiling water bath so that as much of it as possible is immersed.
4. Leave it until all the liquid has vaporised; the vapour pushes the air out of the flask through the pinhole and excess vapour escapes.
The flask is then left full of propanone vapour at the temperature of the boiling water.
5. Record the temperature of the water bath and the atmospheric pressure from the barometer.
Once the flask has been filled with vapour, you measure the mass of vapour and the volume it occupied.
6. Remove the flask and cool it, so the vapour condenses.
Dry the outside of the flask thoroughly and reweigh it; the increase in mass is the mass of vapour that filled the flask.
7. Find the volume of the flask by filling it completely with water and measuring the water with a graduated cylinder.
The numbers below are sample data for illustration. Every quantity must be in SI units before it goes into the equation.
Sample data: mass of vapour 0.51 g; volume of flask 270 cm³ = 2.70 × 10⁻⁴ m³; temperature 100 °C = 373 K; pressure 101 000 Pa.
Units: P in Pa, V in m³ and T in K; 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³.
Moles: n = PV ÷ RT, with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Relative molecular mass: Mr = m ÷ n = 0.51 ÷ (8.79 × 10⁻³) = 58.0.
The accepted Mr of propanone (CH₃COCH₃) is 58, so the result agrees with it.
Propanone is flammable and its vapour is harmful to breathe, and the apparatus is hot.
Propanone is highly flammable: use no naked flames, and heat the water bath with a hotplate or electric heater.
Propanone vapour is an irritant: work in a well-ventilated room.
Take care with boiling water and hot glassware, because they can cause burns.
The result depends on measuring the mass of vapour, so anything that changes the measured mass, or makes the vapour differ from the ideal, gives an error.
If not all the liquid vaporises, or the flask is removed too early, the liquid left in it makes the mass too high and so Mr too high.
Wait until no liquid is visible in the flask before removing it from the bath, so that all the liquid has become vapour.
Water left on the outside of the flask when it is reweighed makes the mass too high; dry it carefully.
A pinhole that is too large lets air re-enter as the flask cools, or lets vapour escape before weighing, which affects the measured mass.
Part of the flask is above the water, so the vapour there is cooler than 373 K.
The vapour is not a perfect ideal gas, especially close to its boiling point.
The mass of vapour is small compared with the flask, so a balance reading to 0.01 g (or better) is needed.
Repeat the experiment and average the results, because this reduces the effect of random errors in a single run.
Much of chemistry happens in solution, so you need exact words for the parts of one. Every later idea in this subsection, from concentration to dilution, is built on them.
A solution is a uniform (homogeneous) mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Uniform means it looks and behaves the same throughout, with no layers or visible particles.
The solute is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent is the substance it dissolves in. When the solvent is water the solution is called an aqueous solution.
A solvent can only hold so much solute at a given temperature. The names unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated describe how close a solution is to that limit, or beyond it.
An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute at that temperature, so extra solute added to it simply dissolves.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature, with undissolved solid present. Any more solute added just sits at the bottom.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution holds at that temperature. It is unstable, which means it is easily upset and will not stay as it is.
A supersaturated solution is made by cooling a hot saturated solution carefully. A solid is usually more soluble when hot, so the cooled solution is left holding more than it normally could.

Adding a small seed crystal (a tiny crystal of the solute) to a supersaturated solution makes the excess solute crystallise suddenly, because the crystal gives the dissolved solute a surface to grow on.
Examples of solutes that form supersaturated solutions: sodium thiosulfate and sodium ethanoate.
Saying a solution is strong or weak is not precise enough for chemistry. Concentration gives the amount of solute in a fixed volume, so it can be calculated with and compared.
Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, usually in mol L⁻¹ (molarity, M, meaning moles of solute per litre) or g L⁻¹ (grams of solute per litre).
Concentration (mol L⁻¹) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres, so c = n ÷ V and n = c × V. Remember that the volume is that of the whole solution, not just the solvent.

Model: the same number of solute particles in a smaller volume gives a higher concentration, because the particles are packed more closely. Diluting spreads the same particles through a larger volume.
A standard solution is a solution whose concentration is accurately known. It is the starting point for finding the concentrations of other solutions.

Here are two calculations. One finds the concentration from a mass of solute, and the other works backwards from a concentration to the mass to weigh out. Convert cm³ to litres first by dividing by 1000.
Finding a concentration: 5.30 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃, M = 106 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved. Anhydrous means it has no water of crystallisation. Moles: n = 5.30 ÷ 106 = 0.0500 mol.
The 0.0500 mol is made up to 500 cm³ (0.500 L). Then c = 0.0500 ÷ 0.500 = 0.100 mol L⁻¹.
Finding a mass needed: for 250 cm³ of 0.100 M sodium hydroxide (M = 40 g mol⁻¹), first find the moles from n = c × V = 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol.
Then change moles to mass by multiplying by the molar mass (the mass of one mole): m = 0.0250 × 40 = 1.00 g.

To make a standard solution by weighing, you must trust the mass on the balance to be the true amount of the substance. Only certain substances are reliable enough, and they are called primary standards.
A primary standard is a substance that can be weighed out accurately to make a standard solution directly.
A primary standard is available in a very pure state, so the mass weighed is all the substance and not impurities.
A primary standard is stable in air: it does not absorb water or carbon dioxide, or react with oxygen. If it did, its mass would change while being weighed.
A primary standard has a known formula, so its molar mass and the moles weighed out can be calculated, and it dissolves readily in water.
A primary standard preferably has a high molar mass, which reduces weighing errors. A larger mass is needed for each mole, so a small error on the balance is a smaller fraction of the whole.

Which substance you choose depends on the type of titration (a method that reacts measured volumes of two solutions to find an unknown concentration). Some familiar laboratory chemicals fail the tests for a primary standard.
Anhydrous sodium carbonate is a primary standard used in acid–base titrations (reactions between an acid and a base).
Ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O, dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid, is a primary standard for redox titrations (reactions involving the transfer of electrons).
Sodium hydroxide is not a primary standard because it absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so its mass is not the true mass of sodium hydroxide.
Hydrochloric acid is not a primary standard because its concentration changes as HCl evaporates.
Solutions of sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid are standardised, meaning their exact concentration is found, by titration against a primary standard.

Making a standard solution from a weighed primary standard is an investigation with a fixed method. The aim is a solution of accurately known concentration, here 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask (a flask with a single mark showing an exact volume).
1. Weigh accurately (to 0.01 g or better) the calculated mass of the primary standard on a clock glass or weighing boat.
2. Transfer the solid to a beaker, and rinse the clock glass into the beaker with deionised water from a wash bottle, so that none of the weighed solid is left behind.
3. Dissolve the solid in a small volume of deionised water, stirring with a glass rod.
4. Pour the solution through a funnel into a volumetric flask of the required volume, e.g. 250 cm³.
5. Rinse the beaker, glass rod and funnel into the flask with deionised water so that no solute is lost.

6. Add deionised water until the flask is near the mark, then add the last drops with a dropper until the bottom of the meniscus (the curved surface of the liquid) sits on the graduation mark, viewed at eye level.
7. Stopper the flask and invert it about 20 times so the solution is uniform.
The choice of glassware decides how accurate the final concentration is. The diagrams below show the apparatus used in the method.
Precision and accuracy: the volumetric flask holds an accurately known volume, whereas a beaker or measuring cylinder is not accurate enough.
Diagram: a volumetric flask with its graduation mark, and the meniscus shown at eye level.
Diagram: a funnel in the neck of the volumetric flask during the transfer.
Diagram: a beaker with a glass rod stirring the dissolving solid.
A concentrated solution can be turned into a weaker one by adding solvent. The solute is not changed, only spread through more volume, which gives a simple equation to use.
Diluting adds solvent, so the number of moles of solute stays the same. This gives c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, where c₁ and V₁ are the original solution and c₂ and V₂ the diluted one.
Example: to make 250 cm³ of 0.10 M HCl from 1.0 M HCl, V₁ = (0.10 × 250) ÷ 1.0 = 25 cm³.
Pipette 25 cm³ of the 1.0 M acid into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and make up to the mark with water.
Use a pipette (a glass tube that measures one exact volume), with a pipette filler to draw up the liquid, for the volume of the original solution, and a volumetric flask for the final volume.
Diagram: a pipette with a pipette filler, filled to the graduation mark.
Sometimes a whole range of concentrations is needed, such as for a set of test solutions. Rather than diluting from the stock solution every time, you dilute step by step.
Serial dilution is a series of dilutions, each using the previous solution, usually by the same factor.
Example: starting from 1.0 M, take 10 cm³ and make it up to 100 cm³ to give 0.10 M. Repeating from that solution gives 0.010 M and then 0.0010 M.
Serial dilution is used to make a range of concentrations accurately.
Concentration can be expressed in several ways depending on the substance and the use. Each unit says how much solute is present in a fixed amount of solution or mixture.
mol L⁻¹ (molarity, M): moles of solute per litre of solution.
g L⁻¹: grams of solute per litre of solution.
%w/v (weight per volume): grams of solute per 100 cm³ of solution. For example, 5% w/v glucose contains 5 g per 100 cm³.
%v/v (volume per volume): cm³ of solute per 100 cm³ of solution, used for a liquid dissolved in a liquid. For example, wine labelled 12% v/v contains 12 cm³ of ethanol in every 100 cm³.
%w/w (weight per weight): grams of solute per 100 g of the whole mixture, used for solids and creams. For example, 1% w/w hydrocortisone cream has 1 g in every 100 g.
The molar mass links moles to grams, and the fact that 100 cm³ is one-tenth of a litre links g L⁻¹ to %w/v. Between them you can move from any one of these units to any other.
mol L⁻¹ to g L⁻¹: multiply by the molar mass. Example: 0.10 M NaOH × 40 g mol⁻¹ = 4.0 g L⁻¹.
g L⁻¹ to mol L⁻¹: divide by the molar mass. Example: 9.8 g L⁻¹ of H₂SO₄ ÷ 98 g mol⁻¹ = 0.10 mol L⁻¹.
g L⁻¹ to %w/v: divide by 10, since 100 cm³ is one-tenth of a litre. Example: 4.0 g L⁻¹ = 0.40% w/v.
To reverse the step, multiply %w/v by 10 to get g L⁻¹.
%w/v to mol L⁻¹: multiply by 10 to get g L⁻¹, then divide by the molar mass. Example: 0.9% w/v physiological saline (NaCl, M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹): 0.9 × 10 = 9.0 g L⁻¹.
Then 9.0 g L⁻¹ ÷ 58.5 g mol⁻¹ = 0.15 mol L⁻¹.
Percentages for liquids and creams tell you how much of the active substance is in a given amount of the product. These calculations turn the percentage back into an actual volume or mass.
%v/v to volume: volume of solute = volume of solution × %v/v ÷ 100.
Example: ethanol in 750 cm³ of 12% v/v wine = 750 × 12 ÷ 100 = 90 cm³.
%v/v to mass, using density (the mass of each cm³ of the substance): mass = volume × density.
Example: 90 cm³ of ethanol × 0.789 g cm⁻³ = 71 g.
%w/w to mass: mass of solute = mass of mixture × %w/w ÷ 100.
Example: 30 g of a 1% w/w cream contains 30 × 1 ÷ 100 = 0.30 g of the active ingredient.
Some solutions are so dilute that mol L⁻¹ gives very tiny numbers. Parts per million is a convenient unit for these, and it is used for pollutants and similar substances.
p.p.m. (parts per million) is the number of parts of solute in one million parts of solution or mixture. It is used for very dilute solutions, such as pollutants and dissolved substances in water.
For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 p.p.m. = 1 mg of solute per litre of solution (1 mg L⁻¹). This holds because 1 L of water has a mass of about 1 kg, which is 10⁶ mg.
For solids, 1 p.p.m. = 1 mg per kg.
Example: 0.0050 g of a substance in 2.5 L of water. First 0.0050 g = 5.0 mg. Then 5.0 mg ÷ 2.5 L = 2.0 p.p.m.
Example: 1.0 mg L⁻¹ of fluoride is 1.0 p.p.m. Fluoridated water in Ireland is about 0.6–0.8 p.p.m. (mg L⁻¹).
p.p.m. to mol L⁻¹: convert to g L⁻¹ first, e.g. 2.0 p.p.m. = 2.0 mg L⁻¹ = 0.0020 g L⁻¹, then divide by the molar mass.

Everything around you, from air to iron, is matter. Chemistry starts from one idea: matter is built from particles too small to see, and how those particles are arranged decides whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules or ions) that are constantly moving, with spaces between them.
Solid: the particles are packed closely in a fixed, regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions, so a solid keeps its shape.
Liquid: the particles are close together but can move past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Gas: the particles are far apart and move rapidly and randomly in all directions, so a gas spreads out to fill any space.
Diagram: three boxes showing the particle arrangement in a solid, a liquid and a gas.
A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle, so it has fixed properties. There are two kinds of pure substance: elements and compounds.
A pure substance contains only one kind of particle (one element or one compound) and has fixed properties, such as a sharp melting point and boiling point (a single exact temperature, not a range).
An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom; it cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means (that is, by a chemical reaction), e.g. iron (Fe) and oxygen (O₂).
A compound is a substance made of two or more different elements chemically combined (joined by bonds) in a fixed ratio, e.g. water (H₂O) and sodium chloride (NaCl).
A compound has properties that differ from those of its elements, because the elements are bonded together, so it can be separated into them only by a chemical reaction.
A molecule (a group of atoms joined together) can be of an element (O₂, N₂, Cl₂), where all the atoms are the same, or of a compound (H₂O, CO₂), where the atoms are different.
A mixture is two or more substances that are not chemically combined, so each keeps its own properties. Mixtures are grouped by whether they look the same all the way through.
A mixture can have a variable composition (the amounts of each substance can change), and its components keep their own properties.

A mixture can be separated by physical methods (ones that need no chemical reaction), and it has no sharp melting or boiling point: it melts or boils over a range of temperatures. There is more on this in Using the kinetic theory: separation techniques.
A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout and a single phase (one visible part), e.g. salt solution, air and an alloy (a mixture of metals).
A heterogeneous mixture is non-uniform, with visibly different parts or phases, e.g. sand and water, oil and water, and granite.
Because a pure substance has a fixed melting point and a mixture does not, melting point can be used to check whether a sample is pure.
A pure substance has a sharp melting point that matches the data-book value (the accepted figure listed in reference tables).
Impurities lower the melting point and make the substance melt over a range of temperatures, so a low or spread-out melting point shows the sample is not pure.
Compounds and mixtures both contain more than one element, so they are easy to confuse. The difference is whether the substances are chemically combined.
A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture has a variable composition.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined; the substances in a mixture are not.
A compound has new properties because its elements are chemically combined; a mixture's components keep their own properties because they are not.
A compound can be separated only chemically, because its elements are bonded; a mixture can be separated physically, because nothing is bonded.
Energy is usually taken in or given out when a compound forms, whereas there is little energy change when a mixture is made.

Diagram: particle diagrams of an element (single atoms and diatomic molecules, which are molecules of two atoms), a compound (identical molecules, each made of two kinds of atom) and a mixture (two kinds of particle mixed together).
The kinetic theory states that matter is particles in motion. We cannot see the particles, so the theory rests on effects we can see.
The kinetic theory of matter states that all matter is made of particles that are in constant, random motion.
The particles have kinetic energy (energy of movement), so the higher the temperature, the faster they move.

The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the temperature in kelvin (the temperature scale that starts at absolute zero), so doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the average kinetic energy.
The evidence for the theory comes from effects we can see that are caused by particles we cannot see.
Brownian motion is the continuous, random, zig-zag movement of small visible particles suspended in a gas or liquid. It shows that the invisible particles around them are moving.
Robert Brown, a botanist (a scientist who studies plants), first observed Brownian motion in 1827, using pollen grains in water.
Aim: to observe the motion of smoke particles in air as evidence for the kinetic theory.
Step 1: Fill a small glass cell with smoke and cover it.
Step 2: Light the cell from the side, so the smoke particles scatter light and show up.
Step 3: View the cell through a microscope.
Observation: the smoke particles appear as bright specks that jiggle about randomly and never stop.
The jiggling of the smoke is the evidence. It can be explained only if the air around the smoke is made of moving particles.
Explanation: the smoke particles are bombarded unevenly from all sides by fast-moving, invisible air molecules; at any instant more molecules hit one side than the other, so the particle moves.
The smoke particles are visible solid particles, not air molecules; they are moved by the invisible air molecules.
Conclusion: the air is made of particles in constant, random motion, and the motion becomes more vigorous when the temperature is raised.
Diagram: a smoke cell lit from the side under a microscope, and the zig-zag path of one smoke particle.

Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration, until they are evenly mixed, as a result of their random motion. Gases show it clearly.
Diffusion needs no stirring or currents, because it results from the random motion of the particles alone.
Bromine experiment: a few drops of liquid bromine are placed in a gas jar, giving brown vapour that spreads upwards through a second jar of air placed on top.
The bromine jars are evenly coloured when the vapour has diffused through both jars, which shows the particles have spread out until evenly mixed.
Safety for bromine: bromine is toxic and corrosive, so use a fume cupboard (a ventilated cabinet that removes fumes) and gloves.
This experiment shows that gases diffuse and that lighter gas particles diffuse faster than heavier ones. Two gases start at opposite ends of a tube and meet where they react.
Method: cotton-wool plugs soaked in concentrated ammonia and concentrated hydrochloric acid are placed at opposite ends of a long glass tube, which is sealed with stoppers.
Observation: after a few minutes a white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube where the two gases meet: NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s).
The ring forms nearer the hydrochloric acid end of the tube, because the lighter ammonia travels further.

Explanation: ammonia molecules (Mr 17, relative molecular mass) are lighter than hydrogen chloride molecules (Mr 36.5), so at the same temperature they diffuse faster and travel further before they meet.
Safety: concentrated ammonia and hydrochloric acid give off irritant, corrosive fumes, so use a fume cupboard, goggles, gloves and tongs to handle the plugs.
Diagram: the long tube with the ammonia plug at one end, the hydrochloric acid plug at the other, and the white ring closer to the hydrochloric acid end.
Diffusion is not limited to gases. It also happens in liquids, but far more slowly.
Diffusion also happens in liquids, e.g. a crystal of potassium manganate(VII) slowly colours still water purple.
Diffusion is much slower in liquids than in gases, because the particles are closer together and collide more often.

The kinetic theory says matter is made of particles that are always moving. How close the particles are, how strongly they attract one another and how they move explain why solids, liquids and gases behave so differently.

Solids have a fixed shape and volume and cannot be compressed (squeezed into a smaller volume), because the particles are held tightly in fixed positions by strong forces and only vibrate on the spot.
Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container and flow, because the particles are close together but can slide past one another.

Gases fill their container and are easily compressed, because the particles are far apart, with weak forces between them, and move rapidly and randomly. The empty space between them is what lets them be pushed closer.
Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of the container. Many fast collisions every second add up to a steady push on the walls.

Each change of state is explained by the energy of the particles and the forces between them. Heating gives particles energy to break free of those forces, and cooling takes energy away so the forces win again.

Melting (solid to liquid): heating makes the particles vibrate more until they have enough energy to overcome some of the forces holding them in place and begin to move past one another. This happens at the melting point.
Freezing (liquid to solid): cooling removes energy, the particles slow down, and the forces pull them back into fixed positions.
Evaporation (liquid to gas, below the boiling point): the fastest-moving particles at the surface escape, and because the fastest (highest-energy) particles leave, the remaining liquid cools.

Boiling (liquid to gas at the boiling point): particles throughout the liquid have enough energy to overcome the forces between them, so bubbles of vapour (the substance as a gas) form within the liquid.
Condensation (gas to liquid): cooling slows the particles so that the attractive forces pull them close together.
Sublimation (solid to gas directly, without melting), e.g. iodine, and solid carbon dioxide (“dry ice”), which sublimes at atmospheric pressure at −78 °C.
Deposition (gas to solid directly) is the reverse of sublimation, e.g. iodine vapour forming crystals on a cold surface.
Diagram: a triangle of the three states with arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporation and boiling, condensation, sublimation and deposition.
A heating curve plots temperature against time as a pure substance is heated at a steady rate. The flat sections show the changes of state, and they show where the supplied energy goes.
When a pure solid is heated at a steady rate, its temperature rises until it reaches the melting point, then stays constant until it has all melted.

During a change of state the energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to increase their kinetic energy (the energy of their movement), so the temperature does not rise even though heat is being supplied.
The temperature then rises again until the boiling point, where it stays constant until all the liquid has boiled.
The boiling plateau (flat section) is longer than the melting plateau because far more energy is needed to separate the particles completely than to loosen them.

Diagram: a heating curve for water (temperature against time) from ice below 0 °C to steam above 100 °C, with the two flat sections labelled melting at 0 °C and boiling at 100 °C. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at standard pressure.

The kinetic theory is a model, a simplified picture of reality. Its assumptions and limitations show when it explains behaviour well and when it does not. The assumptions below are what the model takes to be true about particles.
Assumption: the particles are tiny spheres in constant, random motion.
Assumption: the higher the temperature, the greater the average kinetic energy (energy of movement) of the particles.
Assumption: collisions between particles are perfectly elastic, which means no kinetic energy is lost when they collide.
Assumption: in a gas the volume of the particles themselves is negligible (so small it can be ignored), and there are no forces between the particles except during collisions.
A model is useful only if you know where it fails. The first two limitations come from what the simple model leaves out about the forces between particles.

Limitation: real particles are not hard spheres, and they do attract one another. These forces between particles (intermolecular forces) are what make liquids and solids exist and decide melting and boiling points, which the simple gas model ignores.

Limitation: the model treats all particles as identical, so it does not explain why different substances have different melting and boiling points. That needs the types of bonding and intermolecular forces. There is more on this in Polarity, shape and physical properties.
The model also says nothing about what is inside particles, and it works best only for gases under certain conditions.
Limitation: the model does not describe the structure inside particles or what happens to bonds, and it is qualitative (it describes behaviour in words), giving no values.

Limitation: in real gases at high pressure or low temperature the particles' volume and attractions matter, because the particles are then squeezed close together or moving slowly, so gases deviate from the model. There is more on this in Gas laws and the ideal gas equation.

A mixture is separated by using a physical property in which its components differ. So the first step is always to work out how the components differ, then choose the technique that uses that difference.

Particle size and solubility (whether a substance dissolves) separate by filtration; solubility and volatility (how easily a substance turns to vapour) by evaporation and crystallisation; boiling point by distillation.
Solubility in a solvent and attraction to paper separate by chromatography; immiscibility (the liquids do not mix) and density by a separating funnel.

Heterogeneous mixtures (the components can be seen as separate parts), such as an insoluble solid in a liquid or two immiscible liquids, are separated by filtration, decanting (carefully pouring off the liquid) or a separating funnel.
Homogeneous mixtures (uniform throughout), such as solutions and miscible liquids (liquids that mix completely), need evaporation, crystallisation, distillation or chromatography.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid (one that does not dissolve) from a liquid. The paper has holes small enough to hold back the solid particles but large enough to let the liquid through.
Example: sand is separated from salt solution by filtration, because sand is insoluble and the salt is dissolved in the water.
Step 1: Fold filter paper into a cone and place it in a funnel.
Step 2: Pour the mixture through the filter paper; the solid (residue) stays on the paper and the liquid (filtrate) passes through.
Diagram: filter funnel with filter paper over a conical flask, labelled residue and filtrate.

When a solid is dissolved in a liquid, filtering will not work because the dissolved solid passes through the paper. Instead you remove the solvent (the liquid that does the dissolving) by heating, either completely (evaporation) or only partly (crystallisation).
Evaporation recovers a dissolved solid by heating the solution until all the solvent has gone, e.g. salt from salt water. It is used when the solid does not decompose (break down) on heating.
Step 1 of crystallisation: Heat the solution to evaporate some solvent until it is saturated (cannot dissolve any more solid). A drop on a cold glass rod forms crystals when it is saturated.
Step 2 of crystallisation: Leave the solution to cool slowly so that crystals form, e.g. copper(II) sulfate crystals.
Step 3 of crystallisation: Filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold solvent and dry them.
Crystallisation gives purer, larger crystals than evaporating to dryness, because soluble impurities stay in the solution.

Distillation separates a liquid from a solution, or two liquids with different boiling points, by boiling and condensing the vapour. The liquid with the lower boiling point boils off first and is collected separately.
Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution, or two liquids with very different boiling points, e.g. pure water from salt water.
Step 1: Heat the mixture in a flask containing anti-bumping granules (small pieces that make boiling smooth and stop violent bursts of bubbling).
Step 2: The liquid with the lower boiling point boils, and its vapour passes into a water-cooled condenser (a tube that cools the vapour back to liquid).
Step 3: The vapour condenses in the condenser, which has water in at the bottom and out at the top.
Step 4: The distillate (the liquid that has condensed) is collected in a receiving flask.
Step 5: A thermometer at the side arm reads the boiling point of the liquid that is distilling.

Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points, using a fractionating column (a tall column that gives repeated condensing and re-boiling), e.g. ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from water (boiling point 100 °C).
Crude oil is separated into fractions (groups of compounds with similar boiling points) by fractional distillation.
Distillation heats liquids that may be flammable and produces vapour, so the apparatus and heat source matter as well as the method.
Safety: flammable liquids are heated with a heating mantle or water bath, not a naked flame, so the vapour cannot ignite.
Safety: a closed system is never heated, because the pressure would build up as the vapour expands.

Diagram: a distillation set-up with a round-bottomed flask and granules, the thermometer bulb at the side arm, a Liebig condenser (a straight condenser cooled by a water jacket) with water flow, and a receiving flask.

Paper chromatography separates and identifies small amounts of soluble substances, such as the dyes in an ink or food colouring, or a mixture of indicators. Each substance is carried up the paper by a solvent at its own speed.
Step 1: Draw a pencil line near the bottom of the chromatography paper; use pencil, because ink would run.
Step 2: Put small spots of the mixture and of known substances on the line.
Step 3: Stand the paper in a little solvent in a covered container, with the solvent level below the spots, so the spots are not washed into the solvent.
Step 4: Let the solvent rise up the paper, then remove the paper and mark the solvent front (the highest point the solvent reached).
Principle: components that are more soluble in the solvent (the mobile phase, which moves) and less attracted to the paper (the stationary phase, which stays still) travel further.
Retention factor (Rf) is the distance moved by the spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent.
Components are identified by matching their spots and Rf values with those of known substances.
Diagram: a chromatogram with the pencil start line, the spots, the solvent front and the separated spots.
A separating funnel separates two immiscible liquids of different density. Immiscible liquids settle into two layers, with the denser liquid underneath.
Examples: oil and water, or an organic layer from an aqueous layer (a water-based layer), which is used to purify an ester.
Step 1: Pour the mixture into the separating funnel and let the layers settle.
Step 2: Remove the stopper and run off the lower, denser layer through the tap.
Step 3: Collect the upper layer separately.
Diagram: a separating funnel with two layers, the stopper and the tap labelled.

Gas pressure is the force of the particles hitting the container walls, per unit area. For a fixed mass of gas (a set amount, with none added or lost) at constant temperature, pressure and volume are linked by Boyle's law.
Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (when one doubles, the other halves): P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
The law was stated by Robert Boyle in 1662, and Charles's law is named after Jacques Charles.
Particle explanation: in a smaller volume the particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises.
Example: 200 cm³ of gas at 100 kPa (kilopascals, a unit of pressure) is compressed to 50 cm³ at the same temperature.
Step 1: Rearrange P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ to P₂ = P₁V₁ ÷ V₂, because P₂ is the unknown.
Step 2: P₂ = 100 kPa × 200 cm³ ÷ 50 cm³ = 400 kPa. The volume fell to a quarter, so the pressure rose four times.
Heating a gas makes it expand if its pressure is held constant. For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, volume and temperature are linked by Charles's law.
Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its temperature in kelvin (K, the absolute temperature scale): V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
Particle explanation: hotter particles move faster and hit the walls harder, so the gas expands to keep the pressure the same.
Example: 300 cm³ of gas at 27 °C (300 K) is heated to 127 °C (400 K) at constant pressure.
Step 1: Rearrange V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ to V₂ = V₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁, because V₂ is the unknown.
Step 2: V₂ = 300 cm³ × 400 K ÷ 300 K = 400 cm³.
A third pair of properties completes the set: pressure and temperature at constant volume. The combined gas law then joins all three relationships into one.
Pressure law (Gay-Lussac's law): at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its temperature in kelvin: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂.
Particle explanation: faster particles hit the walls more often and harder, so the pressure rises.
Combined gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, for a fixed mass of gas. It is useful when pressure, volume and temperature all change together.
The gas laws only work on a temperature scale that starts at the lowest possible temperature. That scale is the kelvin scale.
Temperatures in the gas laws must be in kelvin (K), not in °C; using °C gives wrong answers, because a gas at 0 °C does not have zero volume or pressure.
Absolute zero (0 K = −273 °C) is the temperature at which, in theory, an ideal gas would have zero volume.
At absolute zero the particles would stop moving.
Plotting the relationships shows them as straight lines, which is the easiest way to see what proportional means.

Diagram: a graph of V against 1/P, which is a straight line through the origin for Boyle's law, and a graph of V against T in K, which is a straight line through the origin for Charles's law. Label the axes with their quantities and units.
The ideal gas is a model that allows analysis and prediction of how gases behave. It is a simplified picture of a gas, built on a set of assumptions.
An ideal gas is a gas that obeys the gas laws, and PV = nRT, exactly under all conditions.
The ideal gas model assumes that the gas particles are in constant random motion, so they keep colliding with the walls and each other.
The ideal gas model assumes that the volume of the particles themselves is negligible (so small it can be ignored) compared with the volume of the container.
The ideal gas model assumes that there are no attractive or repulsive forces between the particles.
The ideal gas model assumes that collisions are perfectly elastic, which means no kinetic energy (energy of movement) is lost in a collision.
The ideal gas model assumes that the average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature.
No real gas is ideal, but most gases behave nearly ideally at room temperature and pressure, so the model allows useful predictions.
Real gases break the ideal assumptions about particle volume and attractive forces. They deviate most in conditions where those assumptions fail.
Real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, and behave most ideally at low pressure and high temperature.
At high pressure the particles are squeezed close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
At low temperature the particles move slowly, so the attractive forces between them become significant; this is close to the point where the gas condenses (turns into a liquid).
Small, non-polar particles (with no charged ends) and weak intermolecular forces (forces between molecules), such as helium and hydrogen, behave most ideally.
Polar molecules with strong attractions, especially those that hydrogen bond, such as ammonia and water vapour, deviate most.
The ideal gas equation combines the gas laws into one relationship between pressure, volume, amount and temperature.
PV = nRT, where P is pressure in pascals (Pa), V is volume in cubic metres (m³), n is the number of moles (the amount of gas), and T is temperature in kelvin (K).
R is the gas constant, 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. It is the same for every gas, and its units match pascals, cubic metres, moles and kelvin.
The equation combines Boyle's law, Charles's law, the pressure law and Avogadro's law (equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules) into one equation.
The equation applies exactly only to an ideal gas, but it gives good results for real gases at ordinary conditions.
PV = nRT only works when every quantity is in the units that R uses. Mixed units are the commonest error, so convert every quantity before substituting.
Pressure: kPa × 1000 = Pa, so 101 kPa = 101 000 Pa.
Volume: cm³ × 10⁻⁶ = m³, so 250 cm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
When the moles, temperature and pressure are known, rearrange the equation to find the volume. Convert units first.
Given: 0.50 mol of nitrogen at 27 °C and 100 kPa.
Step 2: Convert the pressure: 100 kPa = 100 000 Pa.
Step 3: Rearrange the equation to V = nRT ÷ P, because V is the unknown.
Step 5: Convert to litres: 0.0125 m³ × 1000 = 12.5 L.
If the volume, pressure and temperature are measured, the equation gives the amount of gas in moles.
Given: 600 cm³ of oxygen at 20 °C and 101 kPa.
Step 1: Convert the volume: 600 cm³ = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³; the temperature is 20 °C + 273 = 293 K.
Step 2: Rearrange the equation to n = PV ÷ RT, because n is the unknown.
Measuring the mass of a gas as well as its volume, pressure and temperature lets you work out its molar mass, which identifies the gas.
Since n = m ÷ M (moles = mass ÷ molar mass), the molar mass is M = mRT ÷ PV.
Given: 1.60 g of a gas occupies 1.20 L at 27 °C and 101 kPa (sample data).
Step 1: Convert the volume to m³: 1.20 L = 1.20 × 10⁻³ m³; the temperature is 27 °C + 273 = 300 K.
Step 3: M = m ÷ n = 1.60 g ÷ 0.0486 mol = 32.9 g mol⁻¹.
The answer is close to 32, the Mr of oxygen, so the gas could be oxygen (sample data).
A fixed amount of gas in a container of known volume exerts a pressure that depends on its temperature. The equation gives that pressure.
Given: 0.10 mol of gas in a 2.0 L container at 25 °C.
Step 1: Convert the volume to m³: 2.0 L = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³; the temperature is 25 °C + 273 = 298 K.
Step 2: Rearrange the equation to P = nRT ÷ V, because P is the unknown.
A quick check catches most arithmetic and unit slips before you hand in the answer.
Check the units of the answer, and check whether the answer is sensible.
A mole of gas at room conditions occupies about 24 L, so a volume far from this for one mole signals an error.
The equation can be verified by comparing a measured gas volume with the volume it predicts. Magnesium reacting with acid gives a known amount of hydrogen gas to test it with.
Aim: to verify the ideal gas equation by comparing a measured gas volume with the volume it predicts.

Step 1: React a weighed piece of magnesium ribbon, e.g. 0.048 g, with excess dilute hydrochloric acid (so all the magnesium reacts) in a flask connected to a gas syringe (a syringe that collects and measures gas volume): Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).
Step 2: When the reaction stops and the apparatus has cooled to room temperature, record the volume of hydrogen, the room temperature and the atmospheric pressure.
Step 3: Moles of hydrogen = moles of magnesium, because the equation shows a 1 : 1 ratio: 0.048 g ÷ 24 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0020 mol, using Ar(Mg) = 24.
Step 4: Predicted volume V = nRT ÷ P = 0.0020 × 8.314 × 293 ÷ 101 000 = 4.82 × 10⁻⁵ m³ = 48.2 cm³ (sample data).
Step 5: Compare the measured volume with the predicted volume; close agreement verifies the equation for a gas behaving nearly ideally.
Diagram: a conical flask containing acid, with the magnesium added, connected by a delivery tube to a gas syringe. Label the flask, acid, magnesium, delivery tube and gas syringe.
The equation can also be checked by testing one relationship at a time, holding the other quantities constant.
A gas syringe connected to a pressure sensor shows that PV is constant at constant temperature.
A sealed flask in a water bath shows that P/T is constant, because the volume stays fixed while the temperature is changed.

Every substance can be described by what it looks like and does on its own, and by how it behaves when it reacts. Chemists split these descriptions into physical properties and chemical properties, and this split is the basis for telling the two kinds of change apart.
A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the substance into a new substance, so you can test it and still have the same material afterwards.

Physical properties include colour, state (solid, liquid or gas), density (mass per unit volume), melting point, boiling point, solubility (how well it dissolves), electrical conductivity (whether it carries a current) and hardness.
A chemical property describes how a substance reacts to form new substances, so it can only be found out by reacting the substance.

Chemical properties include flammability (whether it burns), reactivity with water, oxygen or acids, whether a substance is acidic or basic, and how it decomposes (breaks down into simpler substances) on heating.
In a physical change the substance looks or behaves differently but is still the same substance. Only how its particles are arranged or spaced has altered.
A physical change is one in which no new substance is formed; the particles are not changed, only their arrangement or spacing.
A physical change is usually easily reversed and involves only a small energy change, because no new substance forms; only the arrangement or spacing of the particles changes.
A change of state is always a physical change: melting, boiling, freezing and condensing only move the same particles further apart or closer together.
Examples of physical change: melting ice, boiling water, dissolving sugar or salt in water, sublimation of iodine (solid turning straight to gas), crushing a solid and magnetising iron.
The mass is unchanged in a physical change, because the same particles are present before and after.
In a chemical change the substances you start with are used up and different substances are made. This happens by rearranging atoms, so the product has properties of its own.
A chemical change, or chemical reaction, is one in which one or more new substances are formed, with different properties from the starting substances.
In a chemical change bonds are broken and new bonds are made, so the atoms are rearranged into new particles.
A chemical change is usually difficult to reverse, because the new substances have to be turned back into the originals by another reaction.
A chemical change usually involves a noticeable energy change, with heat or light given out or taken in, because breaking and making bonds changes the energy stored in the substances.
Total mass is conserved in a chemical change too, if nothing escapes, because the atoms are only rearranged. There is more on this in the investigation on conservation of mass below.
Because a chemical change makes new substances, it often produces something you can see, hear, feel or smell. These are the signs to look for, but they are clues rather than proof.
A gas is given off (effervescence, which is fizzing or bubbling), showing a new gas has been made.
A precipitate forms, meaning an insoluble solid appears in a solution.
A permanent colour change occurs, since the new substance has a different colour from the old one.
The temperature changes, because the reaction gives out or takes in heat.
A colour change alone is not proof of a chemical change: dissolving copper sulfate in water gives a blue solution, which is a physical change.
These are the reactions to quote when asked to classify a change or give an example of a chemical change. In each one a new substance is formed.
Burning magnesium forms white magnesium oxide, a new substance with light and heat given out.
Magnesium fizzing in hydrochloric acid, where the fizzing is gas being given off.
Heating copper(II) carbonate decomposes it: the green solid forms black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide.
Neutralisation of an acid by a base is also a chemical change; the equations are given in the section on balancing equations.
Put side by side, the two kinds of change differ on four points. The test is always whether a new substance has been made.
No new substance is formed in a physical change, but a new substance is formed in a chemical change.
A physical change is easily reversed; a chemical change is usually difficult to reverse.
A physical change involves a small energy change; a chemical change usually involves a large energy change.
Particles are unchanged in a physical change, but atoms are rearranged into new particles in a chemical change.
Borderline case: dissolving salt in water is a physical change, because evaporating the water recovers the salt unchanged, even though its ions (charged particles) are separated.
Weighing reactions carefully showed that nothing is lost or gained in the total mass. This is one of the two laws behind all physical and chemical changes.

Law of conservation of mass: in a chemical reaction or physical change, matter is neither created nor destroyed, so the total mass of the products (substances made) equals the total mass of the reactants (substances that react).
Antoine Lavoisier established the law in the late 1700s (published 1789) by careful weighing of reactions in sealed vessels, so that no gas could escape unnoticed.
The number of moles (the amount of substance, counted in particles) or molecules may change in a reaction, but the mass does not.
Energy follows a similar rule to mass. It can change form during a reaction, but the total stays the same.
Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
When a fuel burns, chemical energy (energy stored in the bonds of the fuel) is changed to heat and light.
The total energy of a reaction and its surroundings stays the same, so any energy lost by the reacting substances appears in the surroundings.
The two laws are not just facts to state; they explain two things chemists do every day.
Both laws underpin all physical and chemical changes.
Conservation of atoms, and so of mass, is why chemical equations must be balanced: there must be the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.
Conservation of energy is why energy changes in reactions can be measured: the heat given out or taken in is accounted for in the surroundings.
This experiment tests the law of conservation of mass using your own measurements (primary data). The idea is to weigh a reaction without letting anything escape.
Aim: to verify, using primary data, that mass is conserved in a chemical reaction.
Hypothesis: the total mass before and after the reaction will be the same, because atoms are only rearranged.
Measured variable: the total mass of the stoppered apparatus before and after the reaction; no variable is changed on purpose.
Two solutions that react to form a precipitate are kept apart inside a stoppered flask until the flask is tilted. Because the flask is sealed, any change in mass would show up on the balance.
Apparatus: conical flask, small test tube, stopper, electronic balance (0.01 g), sodium chloride solution and silver nitrate solution.

Diagram: a stoppered conical flask on a balance, containing sodium chloride solution, with a small test tube of silver nitrate solution standing upright inside; label the flask, stopper, test tube and both solutions.
Step 1: Pour some sodium chloride solution into the conical flask.
Step 2: Half-fill the small test tube with silver nitrate solution and lower it carefully, upright, into the flask so the solutions don't mix.
Step 3: Stopper the flask and weigh the whole apparatus.
Step 4: Tilt the flask so the solutions mix; a white precipitate of silver chloride forms: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq).
Step 5: Reweigh the stoppered flask, and repeat the investigation three times.
The reweighed flask gives the result, and the precautions come from the chemicals used.
Results: the mass before and after the reaction is the same, within the precision of the balance (0.01 g), so mass is conserved.
Safety: silver nitrate stains the skin and is an irritant, so wear gloves and goggles.
Lead nitrate is not used in this method because it is toxic.
Mass can seem to be lost if a gas is made and escapes. Comparing an open flask with a sealed one shows that the law still holds.
In an open flask, marble chips (calcium carbonate) reacting with hydrochloric acid make the mass on the balance decrease: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
The carbon dioxide escapes, so the apparent loss of mass is gas leaving the flask, not mass being destroyed.
If the same reaction is done in a sealed flask, or with a balloon over the neck to trap the gas, the mass stays the same.
When magnesium burns in air, the product is heavier than the magnesium, because oxygen from the air has combined with it: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Models let us explain why mass is conserved. All three below show the same idea: the same atoms are present before and after, just arranged differently.
Particle model: in a reaction the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form the products; no atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same.
A balanced equation is a symbolic model of conservation: the silver nitrate equation has 1 Ag, 1 N, 3 O, 1 Na and 1 Cl on each side.
A physical model, such as molecular model kits, shows the same idea: building the reactant molecules, taking them apart and rebuilding the product molecules uses exactly the same pieces.
Diagram: particle diagrams of 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, showing four H atoms and two O atoms before the reaction and after it.

A formula can tell you two different things about a compound: the simplest ratio of its atoms, or the exact number of atoms in one molecule. Keeping the two apart is the key to every formula calculation that follows.

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound, e.g. CH₂O, which says only that there are two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom for every carbon atom.
The molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule (a group of atoms bonded together), e.g. C₆H₁₂O₆ for glucose.
The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so C₆H₁₂O₆ is six times CH₂O.

For ionic compounds (compounds built from a lattice of positive and negative ions, not separate molecules) the formula is always the empirical formula, e.g. NaCl and MgO, because the formula only gives the simplest ratio of ions.

Percentage composition tells you what fraction of a compound's mass is made up by one element, or by one part such as water. It uses the relative atomic mass (Ar, the mass of an atom of the element compared with other atoms) and the relative molecular mass (Mr, the sum of the Ar values of all the atoms in the formula).
Relative atomic masses used in these calculations: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Mg 24, S 32, Cu 63.5.
Percentage by mass of an element = (number of atoms of the element × Ar ÷ Mr) × 100. You multiply Ar by the number of atoms because each atom in the formula contributes its mass.
Example: nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (Mr = 80): (2 × 14 ÷ 80) × 100 = 35.0%.
Example: water in hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O (Mr = 249.5): (5 × 18 ÷ 249.5) × 100 = 36.1%. Here the 5 water molecules are treated as one part, each with a mass of 18.

Experiments measure masses or percentages, not atoms, so to get a formula you convert each element to moles (the chemist's counting unit, which lets you compare numbers of atoms) and then find the simplest ratio.
1. Write the mass (or percentage) of each element.
2. Divide each by its relative atomic mass to get the number of moles, which turns masses into amounts that can be compared atom for atom.
3. Divide each by the smallest number of moles to get the ratio, so that the element present in the smallest amount becomes 1.
4. If the ratio is not whole (e.g. 1.5 or 1.33), multiply all values by 2 or 3 to get whole numbers.
Do not round a ratio such as 1.5 to 2; multiply all the values up instead, because rounding changes the ratio of atoms and gives the wrong formula.
Dividing by the smallest value, 3.33, gives H 6.7 ÷ 3.33 = 2.0, so the ratio is 1 : 2 : 1 and the empirical formula is CH₂O.

When a reaction gives the masses of the elements rather than percentages, the method is the same. Sometimes one mass has to be found by subtraction first, as in this example of magnesium burning in oxygen to form magnesium oxide.
Example from masses (sample data): 2.40 g of magnesium burns to give 4.00 g of magnesium oxide.
The mass of oxygen is the mass of oxide minus the mass of metal: 4.00 − 2.40 = 1.60 g, because the extra mass is the oxygen that combined with the magnesium.
Mg 2.40 ÷ 24 = 0.100 mol and O 1.60 ÷ 16 = 0.100 mol, so equal numbers of moles of each element combined.
The ratio Mg : O is 1 : 1, so the formula is MgO.
The empirical formula gives only the simplest ratio. If you also know the relative molecular mass (Mr), you can work out how many empirical units are in one real molecule.
1. Divide the relative molecular mass (Mr) by the mass of the empirical formula unit (the sum of the Ar values in the empirical formula).
2. Multiply every number in the empirical formula by that result.
Example: empirical formula CH₂O (mass 30) and Mr = 180: 180 ÷ 30 = 6, so the molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆.
Example: a hydrocarbon (a compound of only carbon and hydrogen) of 85.7% C and 14.3% H, with Mr 56: C 85.7 ÷ 12 = 7.14 and H 14.3 ÷ 1 = 14.3.
Dividing by 7.14 gives the ratio 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (mass 14).
56 ÷ 14 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.
You can find the formula of magnesium oxide by burning a known mass of magnesium and weighing the product. The gain in mass is the oxygen that combined, which gives the mole ratio.
1. Weigh a clean crucible (a small heat-proof dish) and lid, add a coiled length of clean magnesium ribbon and reweigh.
2. Heat strongly, lifting the lid slightly from time to time to let air in (magnesium needs oxygen to burn) while keeping white smoke (magnesium oxide) from escaping.
3. When the magnesium no longer glows, remove the lid and heat strongly for a few more minutes.
4. Cool and reweigh, then heat, cool and reweigh again until the mass is constant (it stops changing, which shows the reaction is complete).
5. Calculate the masses of magnesium and of oxygen that combined, then their moles and ratio, as in the mass example for empirical formulae.
Safety: do not look directly at burning magnesium, which is very bright; the crucible is very hot, so use tongs and a heat-proof mat.

Diagram: a crucible with its lid on a pipeclay triangle (a wire frame with clay-covered sides that holds the crucible), on a tripod over a Bunsen burner; label the crucible, lid, pipeclay triangle, tripod and Bunsen burner.

Some salts hold water inside their crystals. This water is part of the formula, and heating a sample and measuring the mass lost lets you find how many water molecules there are for each unit of the salt.
Water of crystallisation is water chemically held in a fixed ratio within the crystals of some salts, shown after a dot in the formula, e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O and Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
Heating to constant mass drives off the water of crystallisation; for example, blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate turns white, becoming anhydrous (without water).
Example (sample data): 2.50 g of CuSO₄·xH₂O gives 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ (Mr 159.5) when heated to constant mass.
Mass of water lost: 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g, because the water is the only thing driven off on heating.
Moles of water: 0.90 ÷ 18 = 0.050 mol (Mr of H₂O = 18).
Ratio of water to CuSO₄ = 0.050 : 0.0100 = 5 : 1, so x = 5 and the formula is CuSO₄·5H₂O.
A chemical equation is a short way of describing a reaction. It must follow the law of conservation of mass: atoms are neither made nor destroyed, so the equation has to balance.
A chemical equation shows the reactants (the substances that react, on the left) and the products (the substances formed, on the right), written as formulae.
A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, because atoms are conserved (law of conservation of mass).
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous, meaning dissolved in water.
The coefficients, the large numbers in front of formulae, give the ratio of moles, or molecules, that react.
For example, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means 2 mol of hydrogen react with 1 mol of oxygen to give 2 mol of water.
Balancing is done by trial and adjustment, but following the same four steps each time keeps it reliable. The only things you may change are the coefficients.
1. Write the correct formula of every reactant and product.
Never change a formula (the small subscript numbers) to balance an equation; change only the coefficients, because changing a subscript makes a different substance.
2. Count the atoms of each element on each side, so you can see which elements are unbalanced.
3. Balance by putting coefficients in front of formulae, starting with an element that appears in only one substance on each side.
Leave hydrogen, oxygen and any element on its own until last, because changing their coefficients disturbs the other elements least at that point.
4. Check every element again and make sure the coefficients are the smallest whole numbers.
Add state symbols to every formula, so the equation shows whether each substance is a solid, liquid, gas or in solution.
Hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are diatomic (their molecules have two atoms) and are written as H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.
Combustion means burning in oxygen. These four equations show how to balance a metal and three fuels, including one that needs a fraction doubled.
Ethane burning, with the fractional coefficient 3½ for O₂ doubled to give whole numbers: 2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l).
These equations show a metal reacting with an acid, neutralisation (an acid reacting with a base), decomposition (one substance breaking down) and a metal reacting with water.
Aluminium and hydrochloric acid (metal and acid): 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g).
Calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
In a solution, ionic compounds are split into separate ions. An ionic equation leaves out the ions that do nothing, so it shows only what really changes.
An ionic equation shows only the ions that take part in the reaction, leaving out spectator ions (ions that are unchanged in solution).
Example: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) becomes Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
In that reaction Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions, because they are in solution before and after the reaction.
Neutralisation of any strong acid by a strong base is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), because only the hydrogen and hydroxide ions react.
An ionic equation must balance in charge as well as in atoms, because charge is also conserved, e.g. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ cancel to give neutral AgCl.
The coefficients in a balanced equation are mole ratios, so the equation tells you how much of one substance reacts with or makes another.
The balanced equation gives the mole ratio of any two substances in the reaction.
In propane burning, 1 mol of propane needs 5 mol of oxygen and produces 3 mol of carbon dioxide.
This mole ratio is the starting point for calculating masses of reactants and products. There is more on this in the chapter Stoichiometry: Limiting Reactants and Percentage Yield.
Acids show a common set of properties that can be observed in the laboratory and at home. These shared properties are how we decide whether a substance counts as an acid.
Acids taste sour, but laboratory chemicals must never be tasted because many are corrosive or poisonous.
Acids turn blue litmus (a dye that changes colour in acids and bases) red, and they have a pH below 7 (pH is a number that describes how acidic or basic a solution is).
Acids react with reactive metals such as magnesium and zinc to give hydrogen gas, so bubbles form on the metal.
Acids react with carbonates (compounds containing the CO₃²⁻ ion, such as chalk) to give carbon dioxide, seen as fizzing.
Acids neutralise bases, which means they react with them so that both lose their acidic or basic character.
Examples: hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), nitric acid (HNO₃), ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH, in vinegar) and citric acid (in citrus fruits).
Bases are the chemical opposites of acids. Their properties mirror those of acids, and some of them dissolve in water to form alkalis.
Bases taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery, because they react with the oils on the skin.
Bases turn red litmus blue and have a pH above 7.
Bases neutralise acids, so an acid and a base each cancel out the other's properties.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, e.g. sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH) and aqueous ammonia (NH₃), which is ammonia dissolved in water.
Many bases are insoluble in water, e.g. copper(II) oxide and magnesium hydroxide, so they are not alkalis.

Concentrated alkalis (those with a lot of dissolved base in a small volume of water) are corrosive, meaning they damage skin and other materials: sodium hydroxide is the main ingredient of oven cleaners and drain cleaners.

You cannot tell whether a clear solution is acidic or basic by looking at it, so chemists add an indicator. An indicator is a substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in an acidic or a basic solution.
Litmus is red in acid and blue in base, so it is the simplest test for which kind of solution you have.
Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; it changes colour between pH 8.3 and pH 10.
Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base; it changes colour between pH 3.1 and pH 4.4.
Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators, so it gives a range of colours across the pH scale: red in strong acid, through orange, yellow and green at pH 7, to blue and purple in strong base.
Natural indicators, such as red cabbage extract, also change colour between acidic and basic solutions.
Common substances are classed as acids or bases according to the properties they show. For each one, the category is justified by a property you can observe or a substance it contains.
Vinegar is an acid: it contains ethanoic acid, tastes sour, turns blue litmus red and fizzes with baking soda.
Citric juices are acids: lemon juice contains citric acid, tastes sour and has a pH of about 2–3; orange juice has a pH of about 3–4.
Antacids (medicines for excess stomach acid) are bases: they contain magnesium hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide, calcium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate, and neutralise excess stomach acid.
Toothpaste is mildly basic, so it neutralises the acids that bacteria in plaque (the film of bacteria on teeth) produce, which would otherwise attack tooth enamel (the hard outer layer of the tooth).
Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) is a weak base.
Oven cleaner (sodium hydroxide) is a strong alkali, which is why it is corrosive and must be handled with care.
Lemonade and cola are acids because they contain citric, carbonic or phosphoric acid.

Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water; the acid and base cancel out each other's properties. This is useful whenever something is too acidic and needs to be corrected.

Lime in agriculture: crops grow poorly in acidic soil, so farmers spread lime (calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide) or ground limestone (calcium carbonate) to neutralise the acid and raise the soil pH.
Ground limestone in soil: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂. Here H⁺ stands for the acid in the soil.
Acid indigestion: the stomach contains hydrochloric acid, and excess acid causes indigestion and heartburn, so a base is taken to remove it.
Antacid tablets neutralise the excess acid, e.g. Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate in an antacid also neutralises stomach acid: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
Lime is added to acidic lakes to neutralise the acid, so the water becomes less acidic.
Toothpaste neutralises plaque acid, and baking soda is a claimed remedy for a bee sting, which is said to be acidic.
Acid–base reactions produce salts, and the name of a salt comes from the acid and the metal. Knowing this lets you name the product of any acid reaction.
A salt is a compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or an ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, e.g. NaCl, because the chloride ion Cl⁻ is what remains of the acid.
Sulfuric acid gives sulfates; nitric acid gives nitrates; ethanoic acid gives ethanoates; carbonic acid gives carbonates.
Sulfuric acid is diprotic, with two replaceable hydrogens, so one mole of it (a fixed amount of substance) reacts with twice as much sodium hydroxide as one mole of hydrochloric acid does.
General word equation: acid + base → salt + water. A base here includes metal oxides and hydroxides, and ammonia.
With an insoluble metal oxide: 2HCl(aq) + CuO(s) → CuCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l); the black solid dissolves to give a blue solution.
