Work through the chain of ratios one step at a time: permanganate to iodine, then iodine to thiosulfate.
Data: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ KMnO₄ liberates iodine that needs a mean titre of 25.3 cm³ of thiosulfate.
Moles MnO₄⁻ = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0250 L = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Moles I₂ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 5 ÷ 2 = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol, since 2MnO₄⁻ gives 5I₂.
Moles S₂O₃²⁻ = 2 × 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol, since I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻ = 1 : 2.
Concentration of thiosulfate = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0253 L = 0.0988 mol L⁻¹.
Three words describe how solids behave with water from the air. They explain why some substances can't be primary standards.
Efflorescent: a hydrated crystal that loses some of its water of crystallisation to the air on standing, e.g. sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate and washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O).
Hygroscopic: absorbs water vapour from the air without dissolving, e.g. concentrated sulfuric acid and silica gel.
Deliquescent: absorbs so much water from the air that it dissolves in it and forms a solution, e.g. sodium hydroxide pellets.
None of these substances can be a primary standard, because the mass weighed does not correspond to a known amount of substance.
The reagents in these titrations are oxidising, staining or irritant, so protect your eyes, skin and clothes.
Wear goggles: potassium manganate(VII) is an oxidising agent, is harmful, and stains skin and clothes.
Dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant; iodine solution stains and is harmful.
Use a pipette filler, so that no solution is drawn into the mouth.
Iron tablets can be analysed by a redox titration. The iron(II) in a dissolved tablet is titrated with standardised permanganate, which gives the mass of iron per tablet.
Aim: to find the mass of iron in an iron tablet, and the percentage of elemental iron by mass in the tablet, by titration with a standard solution of potassium manganate(VII).
Iron tablets contain iron as iron(II), commonly as iron(II) sulfate (iron(II) fumarate and iron(II) gluconate are also used), and are prescribed to treat iron-deficiency anaemia.
The label usually gives the mass of the iron compound or of iron per tablet, which is the value your result is compared with.
Equation: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 5Fe³⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l), so MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5.
The KMnO₄ solution is first standardised against ammonium iron(II) sulfate, just before use, because its concentration changes on standing.
Hypothesis (example): the tablet contains the mass of iron stated on the label, within a few percent.
The tablets must be turned into a solution of known total volume. Only a measured fraction of it is then titrated.
1. Weigh five tablets together accurately and record the mass; dividing by five gives the mean mass of one tablet.
2. Grind the tablets to a fine powder in a mortar and pestle, adding a little dilute sulfuric acid.
3. Transfer the paste to a beaker with dilute sulfuric acid and deionised water, rinsing the mortar and pestle into the beaker, and stir to dissolve.
4. Transfer the solution, including any insoluble material, through a funnel into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker, glass rod and funnel into the flask with deionised water.
5. Make up to the mark with deionised water, with the bottom of the meniscus on the mark at eye level and the last drops added with a dropper; stopper and invert about 20 times to mix.
Diagram: mortar and pestle holding the tablet powder, labelled with the pestle and the mortar bowl.
Diagram: 250 cm³ volumetric flask with a funnel in its neck, labelled with the graduation mark.
Diagram: beaker with a glass rod stirring the solution, labelled with the glass rod.
A 25.0 cm³ portion of the tablet solution is titrated with standardised permanganate. This is the same method as the standardisation, with the tablet solution in the flask.
1. Rinse the pipette with deionised water and then with the tablet solution; pipette 25.0 cm³ into a conical flask.
2. Add about 20 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid (an excess) to the flask.
3. Rinse the burette with deionised water and then with the standard KMnO₄ solution; fill it and read the top of the meniscus.
4. Titrate, swirling, until one drop gives a permanent pale pink colour; no indicator is added.
5. Do a rough titration, then accurate titrations until two agree within 0.1 cm³; titrate soon after making the solution.
Diagram: burette of purple KMnO₄ above a conical flask of tablet solution on a white tile, labelled with the burette tap and the top of the meniscus.
Each step of the tablet method has a reason. Exams ask for these reasons directly.
Dilute sulfuric acid is used to dissolve the tablets, stopping Fe²⁺ being oxidised to Fe³⁺ by dissolved oxygen; this would make the result too low, because Fe³⁺ does not react with MnO₄⁻.
More dilute sulfuric acid is added before each titration to supply the H⁺ ions needed for MnO₄⁻ to be reduced to Mn²⁺; with too little acid, brown MnO₂ forms and the 1 : 5 ratio no longer holds.

Several tablets are used: the result is an average over tablets that vary slightly in mass and iron content, a larger mass gives a smaller percentage error in weighing, and the solution is concentrated enough to give a reasonable titre.
Grinding increases the surface area so that the tablets dissolve fully and all the iron(II) is extracted.
The solution may be cloudy from the insoluble coating and binder (filler); this does not affect the result, because those substances do not react with the permanganate.
A volumetric flask and pipette are used because the 25.0 cm³ portion must be exactly one-tenth of the total.
No indicator is needed because KMnO₄ is self-indicating: the first excess drop colours the solution pink.
The steps convert the titre into the mass of iron in one tablet, then into a percentage of the tablet's mass.
Data: five tablets have a total mass of 1.80 g, a mean of 0.360 g per tablet; 25.0 cm³ portions of the 250 cm³ tablet solution need a mean titre of 11.6 cm³ of 0.0100 mol L⁻¹ KMnO₄.
Moles MnO₄⁻ = 0.0100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0116 L = 1.16 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Moles Fe²⁺ in 25.0 cm³ = 5 × 1.16 × 10⁻⁴ mol = 5.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol, using the 1 : 5 ratio.
Moles Fe²⁺ in 250 cm³ (five tablets) = 5.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 10 = 5.80 × 10⁻³ mol, since 25.0 cm³ is one-tenth of 250 cm³; per tablet = 5.80 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 5 = 1.16 × 10⁻³ mol.
Mass of iron per tablet = 1.16 × 10⁻³ mol × 56 g mol⁻¹ = 0.06496 g = 65.0 mg.
Percentage of iron by mass = 0.06496 g ÷ 0.360 g × 100 = 18.0%.
If the label gives the iron(II) sulfate content instead: mass of FeSO₄ per tablet = 1.16 × 10⁻³ mol × 152 g mol⁻¹ = 0.176 g = 176 mg; iron is 56 ÷ 152 = 36.8% of the mass of FeSO₄.
Conclusion: compare the result with the label value, calculate the percentage difference, and comment on whether the hypothesis is supported.
Besides the acid and permanganate, the tablets themselves are a hazard.
Wear goggles: dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant, and KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent that stains skin and clothes.
Iron tablets are dangerous if swallowed by young children: keep them secure and do not eat them in the laboratory.
Errors push the result in a known direction, so say whether the result would be too low or too high, and why.
Result too low: Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺ by air before titration, because the solution was not acidified or was left standing too long.
Result too low: tablet material is lost while grinding or transferring, so less iron reaches the titration.
Result too high: overshooting the end point, taking a deep purple colour instead of the first permanent pale pink.
Result too high: tablets that also contain vitamin C or another reducing agent, which also reacts with MnO₄⁻.
Other error: too little acid gives brown MnO₂ and an unclear end point.
Other error: KMnO₄ that has partly decomposed since it was standardised.
Other error: a burette or pipette not rinsed with its own solution, as in acid–base titrations.

A redox titration is one where a measured volume of an oxidising agent (a substance that takes electrons) reacts with a reducing agent (a substance that gives electrons). It is solved with the same mole steps as an acid–base titration; only the source of the mole ratio changes.

Recap: write the balanced equation to get the mole ratio, calculate moles of the known solution with n = c × V (V in litres), convert to moles of the other substance using the mole ratio, divide by its volume, then convert units and allow for dilution.
These are the steps used in acid–base volumetric problems. Allowing for dilution means scaling back up when extra water was added, which lowered the concentration.

The difference in redox problems is that the mole ratio comes from the balanced redox equation (the same number of each atom and the same total charge on both sides), which may need to be balanced first. There is more on this in Balancing redox equations.

The ratio can be checked from electrons: the moles of electrons gained by the oxidising agent equal the moles of electrons lost by the reducing agent, because electrons are only transferred, never created or lost.
Example: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻ and Fe²⁺ loses 1 e⁻, so 1 MnO₄⁻ reacts with 5 Fe²⁺, because five Fe²⁺ are needed to supply the five electrons one MnO₄⁻ takes.

Titration formula for redox: (V_ox × M_ox) ÷ n_ox = (V_red × M_red) ÷ n_red, where V is volume, M is concentration in mol L⁻¹, and n_ox and n_red are the coefficients of the oxidising and reducing agents in the balanced equation.
Volumes can stay in cm³ in this formula because the units cancel, exactly as in acid–base volumetric problems.
Worked example of the formula: 23.8 cm³ of KMnO₄ reacts with 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 M Fe²⁺, with n_ox = 1 and n_red = 5 (sample data).
M_ox = (25.0 × 0.100) ÷ (5 × 23.8) = 0.0210 mol L⁻¹, the concentration of the KMnO₄.
These ratios turn up again and again in redox titrations. Each comes straight from a balanced equation, so learn the equation and the ratio together.
MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5, from MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. Permanganate (MnO₄⁻) is the oxidising agent and iron(II) the reducing agent.
I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻ = 1 : 2, from I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. Here thiosulfate (S₂O₃²⁻) is the reducing agent that uses up iodine.
MnO₄⁻ : I₂ = 2 : 5, from 2MnO₄⁻ + 10I⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5I₂ + 8H₂O, in which permanganate oxidises iodide (I⁻) to iodine.
MnO₄⁻ : S₂O₃²⁻ = 1 : 5 when iodine made from permanganate is titrated with thiosulfate. The combined ratio is 2 : 5 : 10 for MnO₄⁻ : I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻, because 2 MnO₄⁻ make 5 I₂, which use up 10 S₂O₃²⁻.
Ammonium iron(II) sulfate supplies one Fe²⁺ per formula unit, so moles of (NH₄)₂SO₄·FeSO₄·6H₂O = moles of Fe²⁺.
Each Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O supplies one S₂O₃²⁻, so moles of the salt equal moles of thiosulfate ions.
Each I₂ is one mole whether it is written as I₂ or I₃⁻ (the form iodine takes when dissolved in iodide solution).
Some substances can't be titrated directly. Instead they release a product that can be, so the calculation has to run back through two equations.

In an indirect titration, the substance being analysed (the analyte) first reacts with an excess of a reagent (more than enough, so the analyte is completely used up) to release a product in proportion to it.
The product released is then titrated with a solution of known concentration (the titrant). For example, an oxidising agent added to excess iodide releases iodine, which is titrated with thiosulfate.
Work backwards through each equation in turn, starting from the titrant, because the titrant is the only amount you measured directly.
Step 1: divide the moles of thiosulfate by 2 to give the moles of iodine, because I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻ = 1 : 2.
Step 2: use the first equation to convert the moles of iodine to moles of the oxidising agent.
The excess reagent, e.g. KI, doesn't need to be measured accurately, because it is not part of the calculation.
Only the analyte and the titrant must be measured exactly, since the moles you calculate depend only on them.
Titration data rarely give the answer in the form the question wants. You scale up from the small portion titrated, then convert moles into masses and percentages.
Scale from the portion titrated to the whole solution, e.g. × 10 for 25.0 cm³ out of 250 cm³, because only a portion was run against the titrant.
Then divide by the number of tablets if several were dissolved, because the flask holds all of them together.
Mass = moles × molar mass (M, the mass of one mole in g mol⁻¹), and mg = g × 1000.
Percentage by mass of a tablet = mass of the substance ÷ mass of the tablet × 100.
Percentage of the label value = measured mass ÷ stated mass × 100, which shows how close a tablet is to what its label claims.
Concentration in g L⁻¹ = mol L⁻¹ × M.
%w/v (grams of solute per 100 cm³ of solution) = g L⁻¹ ÷ 10. There is more on this in Units of concentration.
A concentration in g L⁻¹ of a hydrated salt (one with water locked into its crystals) uses the molar mass of the hydrate, e.g. Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O for thiosulfate solution.
Use whole-number relative atomic masses (Ar, the mass of an atom relative to carbon-12), as in the SEC Formulae and Tables. Use these values.
Ar: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Mn 55, Fe 56, I 127. Use Ar(Fe) = 56 for iron.
M(FeSO₄) = 152 for iron(II) sulfate, and M(KMnO₄) = 158.
M(Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O) = 248, which includes the five waters of crystallisation.
M((NH₄)₂SO₄·FeSO₄·6H₂O) = 392 for ammonium iron(II) sulfate, and M(I₂) = 254.
Careful technique and a sense check separate a correct answer from one that is slightly off. Redox titrations also have particular errors that push the result in a known direction.
Use the mean of concordant titres (titres that agree closely), because averaging results that agree reduces the effect of random error.
Give answers to three significant figures, with units.
Check the answer is sensible: a tablet usually contains tens of milligrams of iron, not grams.
A percentage cannot exceed 100%, so a result above that signals a mistake.

Taking deep purple as the end point with KMnO₄ (the point where the reaction is complete) makes the titre too high, because extra permanganate has been added. This is a systematic error (one that shifts every result the same way).

Oxidation of Fe²⁺ by air before titration makes the iron result too low, because some Fe²⁺ has already been used up and less permanganate is needed. There is more on random and systematic error in Measurement and error.
At Higher Level a redox titration may use a substance you have not met in class. The chemistry looks new, but the question supplies what you need and the same method applies.
An unfamiliar redox problem may involve a reagent or product not studied before, e.g. hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorite in bleach, vitamin C or sodium oxalate (sodium ethanedioate, Na₂C₂O₄).
The question gives the balanced equation or asks for it, and the same method applies.
1. Identify the oxidising and reducing agents (which substance takes electrons and which gives them).
2. Write or balance the equation, using oxidation numbers (the charge-like numbers that track electron transfer) if needed.
4. Plan the route through moles, including any two-step reaction and dilution, before calculating.
Four reactions show how the ratio changes with the substance. In each case read the ratio from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
MnO₄⁻ : H₂O₂ = 2 : 5, from 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O, where acidified permanganate oxidises hydrogen peroxide to oxygen.
ClO⁻ : I₂ = 1 : 1, from ClO⁻ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → Cl⁻ + I₂ + H₂O, because hypochlorite oxidises iodide to iodine in acid solution.
Vitamin C : I₂ = 1 : 1, from C₆H₈O₆ + I₂ → C₆H₆O₆ + 2H⁺ + 2I⁻.
Vitamin C and sodium oxalate are two substances that exams may use in redox titrations. You need their formulae and one practical detail for each.
Vitamin C is ascorbic acid, C₆H₈O₆, with M = 176 g mol⁻¹; iodine oxidises it to dehydroascorbic acid, C₆H₆O₆.
Sodium oxalate is an alternative primary standard for KMnO₄, meaning a pure, stable solid that can be weighed accurately to make a solution of known concentration for standardising it.
The oxalate titration is done warm, at about 60 °C, because the reaction is slow at room temperature.

Standardising means finding the exact concentration of a solution by titrating it against one of known concentration. Here ammonium iron(II) sulfate, which can be weighed accurately, is used to standardise KMnO₄. The mean titre is the average volume run in from the burette, and all data in these worked problems are sample data.
Data: 9.80 g of ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄·FeSO₄·6H₂O (M = 392), was dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to 250 cm³; 25.0 cm³ portions needed a mean titre of 24.0 cm³ of KMnO₄.
Equation: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, a 1 : 5 ratio. The dilute sulfuric acid supplies the H⁺ in this equation.
Moles of salt = 9.80 g ÷ 392 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0250 mol, in 250 cm³.
Concentration of Fe²⁺ = 0.0250 mol ÷ 0.250 L = 0.100 mol L⁻¹, because each formula unit gives one Fe²⁺.
Moles Fe²⁺ in 25.0 cm³ = 0.100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0250 L = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol.
Moles MnO₄⁻ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 5 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, using the 1 : 5 ratio.
Concentration of KMnO₄ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 0.0240 L = 0.0208 mol L⁻¹.
In g L⁻¹: 0.0208 mol L⁻¹ × 158 g mol⁻¹ = 3.29 g L⁻¹.
Here the titration checks a tablet's label. You work from the titre back to the mass of iron(II) sulfate in one tablet and compare it with the stated value.
Data: five tablets, each labelled “200 mg iron(II) sulfate”, were dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to 250 cm³; 25.0 cm³ portions needed a mean titre of 12.9 cm³ of 0.0100 M KMnO₄.
Moles MnO₄⁻ = 0.0100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0129 L = 1.29 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Moles Fe²⁺ in 25.0 cm³ = 5 × 1.29 × 10⁻⁴ mol = 6.45 × 10⁻⁴ mol, using MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5.
Moles Fe²⁺ in 250 cm³ = 6.45 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 10 = 6.45 × 10⁻³ mol, because 25.0 cm³ is one tenth of the flask.
Moles Fe²⁺ per tablet = 6.45 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 5 = 1.29 × 10⁻³ mol, because five tablets were dissolved.
Mass of FeSO₄ per tablet = 1.29 × 10⁻³ mol × 152 g mol⁻¹ = 0.196 g = 196 mg.
As a percentage of the label value: 196 mg ÷ 200 mg × 100 = 98.0%.
Mass of elemental iron per tablet = 1.29 × 10⁻³ mol × 56 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0722 g = 72.2 mg.
Thiosulfate is standardised in two steps. Permanganate first releases iodine from excess iodide, and the iodine is then titrated with the thiosulfate.

Data: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0200 M KMnO₄ was acidified and excess KI added; the iodine liberated (released) needed a mean titre of 25.0 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution, using starch (an indicator for iodine) near the end point.
Moles MnO₄⁻ = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0250 L = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Moles I₂ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 5 ÷ 2 = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol, using MnO₄⁻ : I₂ = 2 : 5.
Moles S₂O₃²⁻ = 2 × 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol, the same as 5 × the moles of MnO₄⁻.
Concentration of S₂O₃²⁻ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.100 mol L⁻¹.
In g L⁻¹ of Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O: 0.100 mol L⁻¹ × 248 g mol⁻¹ = 24.8 g L⁻¹.
Bleach contains hypochlorite (ClO⁻), which oxidises iodide to iodine. The iodine is then titrated with thiosulfate, and because the bleach was diluted first, the answer must be scaled back up.

Data: 25.0 cm³ of bleach was diluted to 250 cm³; 25.0 cm³ of the diluted bleach was added to excess KI and dilute sulfuric acid, and the iodine liberated needed a mean titre of 18.4 cm³ of 0.100 M sodium thiosulfate.
Equations: ClO⁻ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → Cl⁻ + I₂ + H₂O, so ClO⁻ : I₂ = 1 : 1; and I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.
Moles S₂O₃²⁻ = 0.100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0184 L = 1.84 × 10⁻³ mol.
Moles I₂ = 1.84 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 2 = 9.20 × 10⁻⁴ mol, using I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻ = 1 : 2; this equals the moles of ClO⁻ in 25.0 cm³ of diluted bleach.
Diluted concentration = 9.20 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.0368 mol L⁻¹.
Original bleach = 0.0368 mol L⁻¹ × 10 = 0.368 mol L⁻¹, because the dilution factor is 250 ÷ 25.0 = 10.
As sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl, M = 74.5): 0.368 mol L⁻¹ × 74.5 g mol⁻¹ = 27.4 g L⁻¹.
Here hydrogen peroxide acts as the reducing agent, and the dilution factor is 25 rather than 10.
Data: 10.0 cm³ of a hydrogen peroxide solution was diluted to 250 cm³; 25.0 cm³ portions, acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, needed a mean titre of 20.0 cm³ of 0.0200 M KMnO₄.
Here H₂O₂ is the reducing agent, with oxygen changing from −1 to 0 as it is oxidised to O₂. The permanganate is still the oxidising agent.
Moles MnO₄⁻ = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0200 L = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Moles H₂O₂ = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 5 ÷ 2 = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol in 25.0 cm³.
Diluted concentration = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.0400 mol L⁻¹.
Dilution factor = 250 ÷ 10.0 = 25, so the original concentration = 0.0400 mol L⁻¹ × 25 = 1.00 mol L⁻¹.
In g L⁻¹ (H₂O₂ = 34 g mol⁻¹): 1.00 mol L⁻¹ × 34 g mol⁻¹ = 34.0 g L⁻¹, and as %w/v: 34.0 g L⁻¹ ÷ 10 = 3.40% w/v.
Some reactions finish in a flash and others take years. Rate of reaction is the measure chemists use to say exactly how fast a reaction goes, and it is always a change per unit of time.
Rate of reaction is the change in concentration (the amount of substance per litre of solution) of a reactant (a substance used up) or a product (a substance formed) per unit time.
When concentration is measured, rate is given in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ or mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹, that is, moles per litre changing each second or each minute.
When another quantity is followed, rate is that quantity per unit time, e.g. cm³ of gas per minute (cm³ min⁻¹) or grams of mass lost per second (g s⁻¹).

Rate can be followed by the disappearance of a reactant or the appearance of a product; the two are linked by the mole ratio (the ratio of the numbers in front of the formulas) in the balanced equation.
For example, in 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), H₂O₂ is used up twice as fast, in moles, as O₂ is formed, because the equation shows 2 mol H₂O₂ for every 1 mol O₂.
A fast reaction has a large change in a short time; a slow reaction has a small change over a long time.
For the same amount of change, rate is proportional to 1/time (rate ∝ 1/time), so halving the time taken doubles the rate.

The factors that change the rate are concentration, surface area (particle size), temperature, a catalyst (a substance that changes the rate without being used up) and, for reactions of gases, pressure; the nature of the reactants also matters. There is more on this in “Collision theory”.
To find a rate you need a property that changes as the reaction goes and that you can measure repeatedly. When a reaction gives off a gas, either the gas volume or the mass lost can be tracked.

Measure the volume of gas produced at regular time intervals, collected in a gas syringe (a calibrated syringe that the gas pushes out) or over water in an inverted graduated cylinder, e.g. oxygen from hydrogen peroxide.
When volume is measured, collect the gas in a graduated cylinder or gas syringe, not a gas jar, because a gas jar has no scale to read the volume from.
Diagram: a flask joined by a delivery tube to a gas syringe, or to an inverted graduated cylinder full of water standing in a trough; label the flask, reactants, delivery tube and the gas collector.
Measure the loss in mass as a gas escapes, with the flask on an electronic balance, because the escaping gas carries mass away from the flask.
A cotton-wool plug in the flask neck lets the gas out but stops acid spray being lost, which would give a false mass loss.
Equation for the mass-loss method: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g); the carbon dioxide escapes.
Diagram: a conical flask of calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid, with a cotton-wool plug in its neck, standing on an electronic balance; label the flask, plug, balance and the CO₂ escaping.
Not every reaction gives off a gas. Another way to follow a reaction is to time how long a fixed amount of change takes, or to watch a colour change.
Measure the time for a fixed amount of reaction to happen, e.g. the time for a sulfur precipitate (a solid formed in a solution) to hide a cross under the flask.
Equation for the cross method: Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + SO₂(g) + S(s) + H₂O(l).
The sulfur precipitate is pale yellow; in the cross method, 1/time is used as the rate, because the same amount of sulfur forms to hide the cross in every run, so a shorter time means a faster rate.
Diagram: a conical flask of sodium thiosulfate solution standing on a paper marked with a cross, viewed from above; label the flask, the solution and the cross.
Follow a colour change, by eye or with a light sensor, when a reactant or product is coloured.
The method chosen must measure a property that changes as the reaction proceeds and can be measured quickly without disturbing the reaction.
A reaction does not run at one steady speed. Its rate falls as it goes, and the shape of a graph shows this.
The rate is greatest at the start, when the concentration of reactants is highest, so there are the most particles available to react.
As the reaction proceeds, reactants are used up, their concentration falls, and the rate decreases.
The reaction stops when the limiting reactant (the reactant that runs out first) is used up; the rate is then zero.
On a graph of product volume against time, the curve is steepest at the start, becomes less steep, and levels off to a horizontal line when the reaction is complete.
The gradient (steepness) of the curve at any point is the rate at that time, so a steep curve means fast and a flat line means no reaction.
On a graph of reactant concentration against time, the curve falls steeply at first and levels off; its gradient is negative, but the rate is quoted as a positive number.
The final amount of product depends only on the amount of limiting reactant, not on how fast the reaction went.

Diagram: graph of volume of gas (y-axis) against time (x-axis), a curve rising steeply from the origin, flattening, and becoming horizontal at the final volume; label “reaction fastest”, “slowing down” and “reaction complete”.
Controlling how fast a reaction goes is useful in industry, in the kitchen and in the body.
Industry wants fast reactions, so that products are made quickly and economically.
Slow reactions are also useful: food is kept in a fridge because the reactions that spoil it are slower at low temperature.
The rates of reactions in the body are controlled by enzymes (biological catalysts). There is more on this in “Catalysis and energy profiles”.
Collision theory explains what has to happen at the level of particles for a reaction to take place. It is the idea behind every factor that changes rate.
For a reaction to happen, the reacting particles (atoms, molecules or ions) must collide.
Most collisions do not lead to reaction: the particles just bounce apart.
A collision leads to reaction only if the particles collide with at least a minimum amount of energy, the activation energy, so that bonds can begin to break.
Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
An effective collision is one that results in the formation of products.

The rate of a reaction depends on the number of effective collisions per second: anything that increases the number of collisions per second, or the fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea, increases the rate.
Reactions range from instantaneous to almost undetectable. The syllabus asks for examples of both.
Fast: mixing silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions gives a white precipitate of silver chloride instantly.
Ionic equation (showing only the ions that react) for that reaction: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
Other fast reactions: neutralisation of an acid by an alkali, the explosion of a hydrogen–oxygen mixture when ignited, and burning magnesium.
Slow: rusting of iron takes days to years.
Fermentation of glucose by yeast (the breakdown of glucose by yeast to make ethanol) takes days.
A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen at room temperature, without a spark or catalyst, shows no detectable reaction, even though it explodes when ignited.
Whether a reaction is fast or slow depends on its activation energy, which in turn depends on whether bonds must be broken first.
Reactions between oppositely charged ions in solution are usually very fast: the ions are already free and attract each other, so no bonds need to be broken before they combine.
Because no bonds need to be broken, the activation energy for reactions between oppositely charged ions is very low.
Reactions between covalent molecules are usually slower, because covalent bonds (bonds formed by sharing electrons) must be broken before new bonds can form, so the activation energy is higher.
A reaction with a high activation energy is slow at room temperature because few collisions have enough energy; a reaction with a low activation energy is fast.
Concentration is the first factor that collision theory explains. More particles in the same space means more chances to collide.
Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increases the number of particles per unit volume.
The particles collide more often, so there are more collisions, and more effective collisions, per second, and the rate increases.

In many reactions the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of a reactant: a graph of rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin, as shown by the thiosulfate investigation in “Investigation: factors affecting rate”.
For a solid, only the outside can react. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces exposes more of it without adding any more substance.
Only particles at the surface of a solid can collide with the other reactant, so particles buried inside a lump cannot react until the surface is used up.
Breaking a solid into smaller pieces or a powder increases the surface area exposed for the same mass, so there are more collisions per second and the rate increases.
For example, powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with hydrochloric acid than the same mass of marble chips.
Dust explosions: a very fine combustible powder spread in air has an enormous surface area and can burn so fast that it explodes.
Dust explosions are a risk in flour mills, grain silos and coal mines.
A dust explosion needs a combustible dust, finely divided and dry, dispersed in air (oxygen), in an enclosed space, with a source of ignition such as a spark or flame.
Raising the temperature speeds up most reactions. Collision theory gives two reasons, and one matters far more than the other.
Raising the temperature increases the rate of almost all reactions.
For many reactions near room temperature the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise; this is an approximate rule, not a law.
Reason 1: at a higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy (energy of movement) and move faster, so they collide more often.
Reason 2: a much greater fraction of the collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so a greater fraction of collisions are effective.
Reason 2 is the more important: a 10 °C rise increases the number of collisions per second only slightly, but greatly increases the number of particles with energy at or above Ea.
Raising the temperature does not change the activation energy; it changes how many particles have enough energy to overcome it.
Particles in a sample do not all have the same energy. A graph of how the energies are spread shows why a small temperature rise has such a large effect.
On a graph of number of particles against kinetic energy (a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution), the curve is a skewed hump starting at the origin with a long tail to the right.
The area under the curve to the right of Ea is the number of particles with enough energy to react.
At a higher temperature the curve is flatter, its peak moves to the right, and the area to the right of Ea is much larger, so many more collisions are effective.
Diagram: two energy-distribution curves on the same axes at T₁ and a higher T₂, with Ea marked on the energy axis and the area beyond Ea shaded for each.

Everyday example: food keeps longer in a fridge or freezer, where the reactions that spoil it are slower because fewer particles have energy at or above Ea. There is more on this in “Rate of reaction”.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction without raising the temperature. It does this by changing the route the reaction takes.
A catalyst is a substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction but is itself chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway for the reaction with a lower activation energy, so a greater fraction of collisions have energy at or above Ea and are effective, and the rate increases.
The catalyst is not used up, so a small amount can speed up the reaction again and again. There is more on types of catalysis, enzymes and energy profiles in “Catalysis and energy profiles”.
Pressure is the last factor, and it only matters when gases are reacting.
Increasing the pressure of a gas squeezes the same number of molecules into a smaller volume, which is the same as increasing its concentration.
The molecules collide more often, so the rate increases.
Pressure affects only reactions in which one or more reactants are gases; it has almost no effect on reactions in solution or between solids.
The simple collision theory leaves out some things. Orientation, surfaces that become full, and poisoned catalysts all explain why real reactions can behave differently.
Collisions must be correctly oriented: even with enough energy, a collision is effective only if the reacting parts of the molecules face each other.
Orientation is why only a small fraction of energetic collisions lead to reaction, especially for large molecules.

Concentration may not always affect the rate: when a reaction takes place on a surface (a solid reactant or a solid catalyst) and every site on the surface is occupied, adding more of the other reactant cannot increase the number of reacting collisions, so the rate stays the same.

For example, an enzyme-catalysed reaction speeds up as substrate (the substance the enzyme acts on) concentration rises, but levels off when all the enzyme's active sites (the places where the substrate binds) are occupied; further substrate has no effect.
A catalyst can become saturated: it has a limited number of active sites, and when they are all in use, increasing the reactant concentration no longer increases the rate.
A catalyst can be poisoned: a catalyst poison binds strongly to the active sites and blocks them, so the catalyst stops working.

The catalysts in a car's catalytic converter (platinum, palladium and rhodium) are poisoned by lead compounds, one reason leaded petrol was phased out where converters are used, and by sulfur and phosphorus compounds.

The rate of a reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products appear. You can measure it over a whole stretch of time (average rate) or at the very start (initial rate), and the two give different answers.
Average rate over a time interval is the change in the amount of product or reactant divided by the time taken, for example the total volume of gas divided by the total time.
Initial rate is the rate at the very start (t = 0). It is the greatest rate of the whole reaction because the reactant concentrations are highest then.
The initial rate is the gradient (slope) of the tangent drawn to the curve at the origin. A tangent is a straight line that just touches a curve at one point without cutting it.
A clock reaction is one timed until a fixed amount of product forms, such as the sulfur cross, where you time how long until a mark is hidden. For these, 1/time measures the initial rate.
1/time works as the initial rate because in a clock reaction only a small fraction of the reactants has been used in the time taken, so the rate has hardly changed.
Here one set of results is used to find an average rate, compare two minutes and find an initial rate. Follow the arithmetic step by step so you can repeat it on any graph or table.
Sample data: oxygen from hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide. Time (min) and volume (cm³): 0, 0; 1, 21; 2, 36; 3, 47; 4, 56; 5, 62; 6, 67; 8, 73; 10, 76; 12, 78; 14, 79; 16, 80; 18, 80.
The reaction is complete when the volume stops changing. Here it levels at 80 cm³, at about 16 min.
Average rate over the first 4 min = 56 cm³ ÷ 4 min = 14.0 cm³ min⁻¹.
Average rate in the first minute = 21 cm³ min⁻¹.
Average rate in the second minute = (36 − 21) cm³ ÷ 1 min = 15 cm³ min⁻¹. This is lower than the first minute because the concentration of H₂O₂ has fallen as it is used up.
Initial rate: the tangent at the origin passes through (1.0 min, 24 cm³), so the initial rate = 24 cm³ ÷ 1.0 min = 24.0 cm³ min⁻¹.
To convert a rate in g min⁻¹ to mol min⁻¹, divide by the molar mass (the mass of one mole): M(CO₂) = 44 g mol⁻¹ (C 12, O 16).
If the mass of CO₂ lost is 0.220 g min⁻¹ (sample data), the rate = 0.220 g min⁻¹ ÷ 44 g mol⁻¹ = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CO₂ min⁻¹.
The rate keeps changing as reactants are used up, so sometimes you need the rate at one exact moment. A tangent to the curve gives it.
Instantaneous rate is the rate at one particular moment: the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curve at that time.
To draw the tangent, place a ruler so that it touches the curve at the chosen time without cutting it, and draw a long straight line. A long line makes the gradient more accurate.
Pick two points far apart on the tangent line and calculate gradient = change in y ÷ change in x. Points far apart reduce the error in reading the graph.
The instantaneous rate falls during the reaction because the reactants are used up. The average rate over an interval lies between the instantaneous rates at its start and end.
Instantaneous rate at 2.0 min, from the sample data above: the tangent passes through (0 min, 10 cm³) and (5.0 min, 76 cm³), so the rate = (76 − 10) cm³ ÷ (5.0 − 0) min = 13.2 cm³ min⁻¹.

This reaction gives off carbon dioxide gas, so the mass of the flask falls as the reaction goes. Weighing the flask over time lets you follow the rate and test two factors: particle size and acid concentration.
Aim: to investigate the effect of particle size (and of acid concentration) on the rate of reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid.
1. Place a conical flask (a flask with a flat base and narrow neck) containing a known mass, e.g. 10 g, of large marble chips (calcium carbonate) on an electronic balance.
2. Put a graduated cylinder holding a known volume, e.g. 50 cm³, of 1.0 M hydrochloric acid beside the flask, and record the total mass.
With the flask set up on the balance, you start the reaction and record the falling mass, then repeat with one factor changed.
3. Pour in the acid, put a loose cotton-wool plug in the neck, and start the stopwatch at once.
4. Record the mass every 30 s for about 10 min, until it stops changing. The loss in mass is the mass of CO₂ given off.
5. Repeat with the same mass of small chips or powder, with the same volume and concentration of acid at the same temperature.
6. For concentration, repeat with the same size and mass of chips and the same volume of acid at different concentrations, e.g. 0.5 M, 1.0 M and 2.0 M. (M means mol L⁻¹.)
Alternative: collect the CO₂ in a gas syringe (a calibrated syringe that the gas pushes out) and record its volume every 30 s.
Diagram: conical flask with marble chips and acid, loose cotton-wool plug, on an electronic balance; a graduated cylinder of acid beside it; a stopwatch.
Plotting the results shows which conditions give the faster reaction. Each choice in the method also has a reason, which is what makes the test fair.
Plot mass of CO₂ lost (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for each run on the same axes. The steeper initial curve shows the faster rate.
Smaller chips give a steeper curve, a faster rate, because of their greater surface area: more calcium carbonate is exposed to the acid at once.
More concentrated acid gives a faster rate. There is more on this in Rate of reaction and collision theory.
The chips are in excess (more than enough), so the acid is the limiting reactant (the one that runs out first and so sets the total amount of product).
Because the acid is the limiting reactant, more concentrated acid of the same volume also gives more CO₂ in total.
The cotton-wool plug lets CO₂ escape but stops acid spray being lost, which would otherwise add to the mass loss and give a false result.
The same mass of carbonate and the same acid keep the test fair, so only the factor you chose changes.
In this reaction a solid forms and slowly turns the solution cloudy. Timing how long until a cross under the flask disappears gives a measure of rate without any gas collection.
Aim: to investigate the effect of concentration and of temperature on rate.
The pale yellow sulfur precipitate (an insoluble solid formed in a solution) makes the solution cloudy until it hides the cross.
Draw a dark cross on white paper and place a conical flask on it, so you can look down through the solution at the cross.
Look down through the solution from above and stop the watch when the cross can no longer be seen. Record the time.
To change the concentration you dilute the thiosulfate with water. The total volume must stay the same so that the only thing that changes is the concentration.

Make a series of thiosulfate solutions of the same total volume, e.g. 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 cm³ of 0.20 M Na₂S₂O₃, each made up to 50 cm³ with deionised water (water with dissolved ions removed). This gives 0.20, 0.16, 0.12, 0.08 and 0.04 M.
Dilute with water only, using a burette or graduated pipette (accurate glass tubes for measuring liquid volumes), and keep the total volume constant.
Pour one solution into the flask, add a fixed volume of acid, e.g. 10 cm³ of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid, quickly, swirl, and start the stopwatch at the same moment.
Repeat for each concentration, keeping the acid volume and concentration, total volume, temperature, flask, cross and observer the same. Calculate rate = 1/time.
To test temperature, the concentration is fixed and the starting temperature is changed with a water bath (a container of water held at a set temperature).
Use the same concentration each time, e.g. 0.05 M Na₂S₂O₃, so that temperature is the only factor that changes.
Warm the thiosulfate in a water bath to the chosen temperature, e.g. 20, 30, 40 or 50 °C, add the acid, start timing, and record the temperature of the mixture with a thermometer.
Use the average of the start and end temperatures, because the mixture does not stay at one temperature during the run.
Converting each time into a rate (1/time) lets you plot rate against the factor and draw a conclusion. These results are sample data.
Sample data, concentration: 0.20 M, 20 s; 0.16 M, 25 s; 0.12 M, 34 s; 0.08 M, 50 s; 0.04 M, 102 s.
Rates (1/time) for those concentrations: 0.0500, 0.0400, 0.0294, 0.0200 and 0.0098 s⁻¹.
A graph of rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin, so rate is directly proportional to concentration.
Sample data, temperature: 20 °C, 80 s; 30 °C, 41 s; 40 °C, 21 s; 50 °C, 11 s.
Rates (1/time) for those temperatures: 0.0125, 0.0244, 0.0476 and 0.0909 s⁻¹.
A graph of rate against temperature is a curve rising ever more steeply. The rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise.
The same total volume means the same depth of liquid over the cross, so the same amount of sulfur hides it in each run.
1/time is used as the measure of rate because a shorter time means a faster rate.
Sulfur dioxide is made in this reaction, so there is a safety point to state. The timing relies on judgement, so there are also errors to know.

Safety: sulfur dioxide is a toxic, choking gas that is dangerous for people with asthma. Work in a well-ventilated room, do not heat above about 60 °C, and pour the mixture away promptly when each run ends.
Judging when the cross disappears is subjective (it depends on the person looking), so use the same observer and the same cross.
A delay in starting the stopwatch affects the time recorded, because the clock must start the moment the solutions mix.
The temperature falls during a warm run, which is why the average of the start and end temperatures is used.
Diagram: conical flask standing on white paper marked with a cross, eye looking down from above; thermometer and water bath for the temperature runs.
Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly into water and oxygen. Manganese(IV) oxide speeds this up, and collecting the oxygen lets you follow the rate.

Aim: to measure the rate of decomposition (breaking down) of hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up), and to investigate the effect of one factor: the concentration of H₂O₂, the form of the catalyst, or the temperature.
1. Place a measured volume of dilute hydrogen peroxide, e.g. 5 cm³ of 20-volume H₂O₂ diluted to 25 cm³ with deionised water, in a conical flask.
20-volume hydrogen peroxide gives 20 cm³ of oxygen per cm³ of solution on complete decomposition.
2. Put a small mass, e.g. 0.5 g, of manganese(IV) oxide (manganese dioxide, MnO₂), a black powder, in a small test tube. Lower it into the flask on a thread so that it does not touch the peroxide.
3. Stopper the flask, with a delivery tube leading to an inverted graduated cylinder full of water in a basin, or to a gas syringe.
4. Tilt or shake the flask so the catalyst mixes with the peroxide, and start the stopwatch at the same instant. This starts the reaction without losing any oxygen.
5. Record the volume of oxygen every 30 s or 1 min until no more gas is produced; swirl the flask throughout.
Once the basic run works, you change one factor at a time and compare. A control and a safety check complete the investigation.
Repeat, changing one factor: e.g. half the concentration of H₂O₂ with the same total volume, or granules instead of powder with the same mass, keeping everything else the same.
A control (a run with the factor you are testing left out): hydrogen peroxide without catalyst gives almost no oxygen over the same time. This shows the catalyst is what speeds the reaction.
The catalyst can be filtered off, washed, dried and weighed at the end to show it is unchanged in mass.

Safety: hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising agent (it readily causes other substances to be oxidised) and, in concentrated form, is corrosive to skin and eyes (it damages them on contact). Wear goggles and gloves.
Store hydrogen peroxide in a cool, dark place, because it decomposes in light and heat, building up pressure.
Diagram: conical flask with H₂O₂ and a small test tube of MnO₂ hanging on a thread; stopper and delivery tube to an inverted graduated cylinder of water in a trough, or to a gas syringe.
A graph of gas volume against time changes in predictable ways when you change a condition. The gradient shows the rate, and the final level shows how much product could form.
A faster rate gives a steeper initial curve that levels off sooner. The causes are a higher temperature, a catalyst, powder instead of lumps, or a more concentrated excess reactant.
A faster rate gives the same final volume if the amount of limiting reactant (the reactant that runs out first) is unchanged.
A slower rate, from a lower temperature (e.g. ice-water), larger lumps or no catalyst, gives a less steep curve that takes longer to level off.
A slower rate also gives the same final volume if the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged.
Halving the concentration of the limiting reactant, at the same volume, gives a less steep curve and half the final volume, because there is half as much reactant to form product.
The final volume of gas tells you the amount of limiting reactant; the gradient tells you the rate.

Secondary data (values you are given, not ones you measured) come from a graph or table, such as the volume at a stated time, the time to reach a volume, the time the reaction ended or half the final volume.
Use secondary data to calculate rates as above, and instantaneous rates at Higher Level.
Many reactions are too slow to be useful on their own. A catalyst is a substance that changes the speed of a reaction and comes out of it chemically unchanged, so it is not a reactant.
A catalyst is a substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction (how fast reactants turn into products) but is itself chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
A catalyst works by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (the minimum energy colliding particles need in order to react), so more collisions are successful.
Only a small amount of catalyst is needed, because it is not used up and so can act on reactants over and over.
Catalysts tend to be specific: a catalyst speeds up one reaction or one type of reaction, not every reaction.

A catalyst affects only the speed of a reaction, not its energy change or how much product forms. The decomposition (breaking down) of hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, shows both the speed-up and the recovery of the catalyst.
A catalyst's physical form can change, for example a powder may become finer, but it is chemically unchanged and can be recovered.
Manganese(IV) oxide filtered off after decomposing hydrogen peroxide has the same mass as it had at the start, which shows it was not used up.

A catalyst does not change ΔH (the heat change of the reaction) or the amount of product formed; it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. There is more on this in Le Châtelier's principle.
Without a catalyst, hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly on its own at room temperature.
With manganese(IV) oxide added, hydrogen peroxide decomposes rapidly, with vigorous fizzing of oxygen.
Catalysts are sorted into two types by comparing the phase of the catalyst with the phase of the reactants. The comparison is about phase, not about whether everything is in the same container.
“Phase” means solid, liquid, gas or solution.
Homogeneous catalysis: the catalyst and the reactants are in the same phase, with no boundary between them.
Homogeneous example: iodide ions, from potassium iodide solution, catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution, so catalyst and reactant are both dissolved in one solution.
Heterogeneous catalysis: the catalyst and the reactants are in different phases, with a boundary between them.

Heterogeneous example: solid manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition of aqueous hydrogen peroxide. It is heterogeneous even though both are in one flask, because a solid and a solution are different phases.
Heterogeneous example: solid iron catalyses the Haber process (the industrial manufacture of ammonia), in which the reactants are gases.
A hot platinum wire held above methanol is a heterogeneous catalyst you can watch working, because the wire keeps glowing.
A hot platinum wire held above methanol catalyses its oxidation (reaction with oxygen) by air: 2CH₃OH(g) + O₂(g) → 2HCHO(g) + 2H₂O(g).
The platinum wire keeps glowing red because the reaction on its surface is exothermic (it gives out heat).
The products are methanal and water; methanol and methanal are toxic, and methanol is flammable.
It is heterogeneous catalysis because the solid platinum is in a different phase from the gaseous methanol and air.
Usually a catalyst is added at the start. In autocatalysis the reaction makes its own catalyst.
Autocatalysis: a product of the reaction is a catalyst for it, so the reaction starts slowly (there is little catalyst at first) and speeds up as the product builds up.

Autocatalysis example: Mn²⁺ ions are formed when potassium permanganate reacts with iron(II) or ethanedioate ions, and the Mn²⁺ ions then catalyse the reaction. There is more on this in Redox titrations and iron tablets.
Car exhausts contain harmful gases. A catalytic converter is fitted in the exhaust and uses a solid catalyst to turn them into less harmful gases.
A catalytic converter in a car exhaust uses the metals platinum, palladium and rhodium.
The metals are spread thinly on a ceramic honeycomb (a ceramic support full of small channels), giving a very large surface area for the gases to touch, inside a steel case.
It converts harmful exhaust gases (carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons, which are fuel that did not burn) into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.
It is heterogeneous catalysis: a solid catalyst acting on gaseous reactants, so there is a boundary between the phases.
Environmental benefit: it reduces carbon monoxide, which is toxic, nitrogen oxides, which cause acid rain and smog, and unburnt hydrocarbons in the air.
Poisoning of the catalysts (a substance stopping them from working) is a separate topic. There is more on this in Rate of reaction and collision theory.
Living cells use catalysts too. These are called enzymes, and each of the examples below catalyses one reaction.
An enzyme is a biological catalyst: a protein (a large molecule built from amino acids) produced by living cells that catalyses a reaction in living things.

Catalase, found in liver and potato, catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, a toxic by-product of metabolism (the chemical reactions in cells), into water and oxygen: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g).
Catalase is one of the fastest-acting enzymes known: a piece of liver added to hydrogen peroxide fizzes vigorously.
Amylase, in saliva, catalyses the breakdown of starch into the sugar maltose.
Enzymes in yeast, called zymase, catalyse the fermentation (conversion by yeast into alcohol and gas) of glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g).
An enzyme's action depends on its shape. This explains why each enzyme is so specific and why heat or extreme pH stops it.

Enzymes are very specific: each acts on one substance, its substrate (the substance the enzyme works on), or one type of reaction, because the substrate must fit the enzyme's active site (the region where the substrate binds).
Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature, about 37 °C (body temperature) for human enzymes, and at an optimum pH.
High temperatures and extreme pH denature enzymes by changing the shape of the active site, so the substrate no longer fits and they stop working.
Biological washing powders contain enzymes, such as proteases for protein stains and lipases for fats, that clean at lower wash temperatures, saving energy.
An energy profile diagram shows how the energy of the particles changes as reactants turn into products. It is the way to compare a catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction.
An energy profile diagram plots energy on the y-axis against progress of reaction on the x-axis.

For an exothermic reaction (one that gives out heat) the products are lower than the reactants and ΔH is negative; for an endothermic reaction (one that takes in heat) the products are higher and ΔH is positive.
The curve rises from the reactants to a peak and falls to the products.
The peak is the activated complex (transition state): the high-energy arrangement of atoms in which old bonds are partly broken and new bonds partly formed; it cannot be isolated.
The activated complex is not an intermediate (a species formed in one step and used up in the next): an intermediate sits in a dip between two peaks and can sometimes be detected.
Two heights on the diagram carry the key numbers: how high the peak is above the reactants, and how far apart the reactant and product levels are.
Activation energy (Ea) is the height from the reactant level up to the peak.
ΔH is the difference between the reactant and product levels.
For an endothermic reaction Ea is always greater than ΔH, since the peak is above the products.
The activation energy of the reverse reaction is the height from the product level up to the peak, so Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH.
Sample data: a forward Ea of 100 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH of −60 kJ mol⁻¹ give a reverse Ea of 100 − (−60) = 160 kJ mol⁻¹, because the products start 60 kJ mol⁻¹ lower than the reactants.
To show a catalyst on an energy profile you draw a second pathway on the same axes. Only the peak changes; the start and end levels stay where they were.
On the same axes, the catalysed pathway is drawn as a lower peak between the same reactant and product levels.
The catalyst lowers the activation energy; the reactant and product energy levels, and so ΔH, are unchanged, because the catalyst only changes the route, not the start or end.
Exothermic reaction: both curves start at the reactant level and end at the lower product level; Ea(catalysed) is less than Ea(uncatalysed), and ΔH is negative and the same for both.
Endothermic reaction: both curves start at the reactant level and end at the higher product level; Ea(catalysed) is less than Ea(uncatalysed), and ΔH is positive and the same for both.
The catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction by the same amount as the forward one, which is why it speeds up both directions equally.
The catalysed pathway may show two or more smaller humps with a dip between them when it goes through an intermediate (a species formed in one step and used up in the next).
The lower peak is what makes the reaction faster, and the labelling of the arrows is where marks are easily lost.

With a lower Ea, a much greater fraction of collisions have enough energy to react. On the energy-distribution curve (a graph of how many particles have each energy), the Ea line moves to the left and the area beyond it increases, at the same temperature.
There is more on this in Rate of reaction and collision theory.
Arrows for Ea start at the reactant level, not the axis; the ΔH arrow runs from the reactants to the products.

Diagram: two energy profile diagrams, exothermic and endothermic, each with axes “energy” and “progress of reaction”, reactant and product levels, an uncatalysed curve with a high peak and a catalysed curve with a lower dashed peak, and Ea (uncatalysed), Ea (catalysed) and ΔH marked with arrows.
One way a catalyst works is by taking part in the reaction temporarily. It joins a reactant to make an unstable compound, and is handed back unchanged when that compound reacts on.
In intermediate formation, the catalyst reacts with one reactant to form an unstable intermediate compound.
The intermediate then reacts with the other reactant, or breaks down, to form the products, and the catalyst is regenerated (returned to its original form).
General model: step 1, A + Cat → A–Cat (intermediate); step 2, A–Cat + B → AB + Cat.
Adding the two steps, the catalyst cancels, so it does not appear in the overall equation, giving A + B → AB.
Each step has a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed reaction, so the overall reaction is faster.
The energy profile shows two smaller humps, with the intermediate in the dip between them.
The intermediate is formed and then used up; it is not a product and does not appear in the overall equation.
This mechanism usually explains homogeneous catalysis.
Iodide ions catalysing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is the worked example of intermediate formation. It takes two steps, and the catalyst is used in the first and regenerated in the second.
Step 1: H₂O₂(aq) + I⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + IO⁻(aq); the hypoiodite ion, IO⁻, is the intermediate.
Step 2: H₂O₂(aq) + IO⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + O₂(g) + I⁻(aq); the iodide ion is regenerated.
Adding steps 1 and 2 gives 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), since I⁻ and IO⁻ cancel.
Colour changes in this reaction give visible evidence that a catalyst forms an intermediate. Hydrogen peroxide oxidises (reacts with) potassium sodium tartrate, and a cobalt catalyst makes it fast.
Hydrogen peroxide oxidises potassium sodium tartrate (Rochelle salt) only slowly, even when the solution is warmed to about 70 °C.
A little pink cobalt(II) chloride solution is added as the catalyst.
The solution turns green and fizzes vigorously as gas, oxygen and carbon dioxide, is given off.
When the reaction is over, the solution turns pink again.
The green colour is an intermediate formed from the cobalt catalyst, not a product.
The return of the pink colour shows that the cobalt(II) catalyst is regenerated, unchanged, at the end.
Safety: wear goggles; cobalt compounds are toxic and harmful to the environment; hydrogen peroxide is an oxidiser. The foam can overflow, so use a large beaker.
Diagram: a beaker of warm tartrate solution with H₂O₂ on a hot plate, with a thermometer; show three colour stages: pink on adding cobalt(II) chloride, green and frothing, and pink again at the end.
Surface adsorption is the second mechanism, and it explains most heterogeneous catalysis. The reaction takes place on the surface of a solid catalyst in three stages.
In surface adsorption, reactant molecules are held on the surface of a solid catalyst while they react; this explains most heterogeneous catalysis.
1. Adsorption: reactant molecules diffuse (spread by random movement) to the catalyst surface and form weak temporary bonds with it at active sites (the places on the surface where reactants attach).
2. Reaction: bonds within the adsorbed molecules are weakened or broken, and the molecules are held close together in a suitable orientation, so they react more easily with a lower activation energy.
3. Desorption: the product molecules break away from the surface and diffuse away, freeing the active sites for more reactant molecules.
Adsorption means accumulation on a surface; absorption means taking a substance into the bulk of a material. Catalysts adsorb.
Since reactions happen only at active sites on the surface, a catalyst's surface area matters. The examples show adsorption at work.
The greater the surface area, the more active sites, so catalysts are used as a fine powder, a thin wire or gauze, or a coating spread over a honeycomb support.
A powdered catalyst is more effective than the same mass of pellets, because the powder exposes more surface and so more active sites.
Example: in a catalytic converter, CO and NO are adsorbed on the platinum or rhodium surface, react, and CO₂ and N₂ desorb: 2CO(g) + 2NO(g) → 2CO₂(g) + N₂(g).

Example: hydrogen and oxygen do not react at room temperature, but with powdered platinum the reaction is violently rapid, because H₂ and O₂ are adsorbed and their bonds weakened on the platinum surface.
Diagram: a row of catalyst surface atoms, with reactant molecules arriving and attaching (adsorption), reacting on the surface, and product molecules leaving (desorption).
The two mechanisms explain other features of catalysts, including how they stop working and how enzymes act.
Poisoning explained: a poison is adsorbed so strongly on the active sites that it does not desorb, so those sites are permanently blocked, e.g. lead or sulfur compounds on a catalytic converter.
Saturation explained: when every active site is occupied, a higher reactant concentration cannot speed up the reaction, since molecules must wait for a free site.
Enzymes combine both ideas: the substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, like adsorption on a surface, forming an enzyme–substrate complex, which is an intermediate.
The enzyme–substrate complex breaks down to products and releases the unchanged enzyme: E + S → ES → E + P.
Both mechanisms provide a different pathway with a lower activation energy; neither changes ΔH.
Some reactions run to completion; others reach a balance in which the forward and reverse reactions both continue. Telling the two types apart is the starting point for the whole chapter.
Some reactions go to completion: the reactants are converted completely into products and the reaction cannot easily be reversed, e.g. burning magnesium, 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
A reversible reaction is one in which the products can react to form the reactants again, so both the forward and the reverse reactions take place. It is shown by the sign ⇌, a double arrow.
The forward reaction is the one from left to right as written; the reverse (back) reaction is from right to left. Both are always labelled relative to how the equation is written.
The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. It is named after Fritz Haber (1868–1934); Carl Bosch (1874–1940) developed it industrially.
Hydrogen and iodine react reversibly: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), where HI is hydrogen iodide gas.
Esterification (an acid reacting with an alcohol to make an ester and water) is reversible: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
Nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless, so the colour of the mixture shows how far the reaction has moved.

Weak acids (acids that only partly split into ions in water) and acid–base indicators (dyes that change colour with acidity) are also reversible, e.g. CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) and HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. There is more on this in How indicators work.
In a reversible reaction in a sealed container, the mixture settles into a balance. At chemical equilibrium both reactions continue, and their rates are equal.
Chemical equilibrium is a state of dynamic balance in a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction (how fast reactants turn into products) equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
It is called dynamic because both reactions are still happening: reactant particles are still forming products and product particles are still forming reactants, at the same rate.

Because substances are formed and used up at the same rate, their concentrations (amounts per litre) stay constant at equilibrium, so observable properties such as colour, pressure and density stop changing.
The concentrations are constant but not equal: at equilibrium there may be much more product than reactant, or the reverse. It is the rates that are equal, not the amounts.
Static equilibrium is different: nothing moves at all, e.g. a metre stick balanced at its centre.

Analogy: a person walking up a down-escalator at the same speed it moves stays in the same place, although both movements continue. Likewise nothing seems to change at equilibrium, but both reactions carry on.
Equilibrium only forms if nothing can escape. This is why the container matters.
Equilibrium can be reached only in a closed system, where no reactants or products can enter or leave; energy such as heat can still pass to and from the surroundings.
Heating calcium carbonate in a sealed container, CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g): the CO₂ gas builds up and equilibrium is reached.
Heating calcium carbonate in an open container: the CO₂ escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot happen and the calcium carbonate decomposes completely.
A fizzy drink in a closed bottle contains CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) at equilibrium (gas above the drink and gas dissolved in it); once the bottle is opened the gas escapes and the drink goes flat.
Equilibrium is not instant. The two rates start far apart and move towards each other until they meet.
At the start, when only reactants are present, the forward rate is high and the reverse rate is zero, because there are no products yet to react back.
As reactants are used up the forward rate falls; as products build up the reverse rate rises.
Equilibrium is reached when the two rates become equal; from then on all concentrations are constant. This is why equilibrium is reached some time after the reactants are mixed.

The same equilibrium is reached from either direction: starting with 1 mol of H₂ and 1 mol of I₂, or with 2 mol of HI only, in the same sealed flask at the same temperature, gives the same equilibrium mixture.

Concentration–time graph for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ starting with N₂ and H₂: the reactant curves fall and the product curve rises from zero, each changing quickly at first because the reactants are most concentrated then.

All three curves level off (become horizontal) at the same moment, when equilibrium is reached. H₂ falls three times as fast as N₂, and NH₃ rises twice as fast as N₂ falls, matching the 1 : 3 : 2 ratio in the equation.
Rate–time graph: the forward-rate curve falls and the reverse-rate curve rises from zero until they meet and continue as one horizontal line at equilibrium.

Diagram: draw (a) concentration against time, with the reactant and product curves levelling off and the moment equilibrium is reached marked; and (b) forward and reverse rates against time, meeting at equilibrium.
At equilibrium the concentrations are not random: for a given reaction at a given temperature they always fit one fixed pattern. That pattern is a number, the equilibrium constant Kc.
The equilibrium law: at equilibrium, at a fixed temperature, the concentrations of products and reactants are related by a constant, the equilibrium constant Kc.

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD (where a, b, c and d are the coefficients, the numbers in front of each formula in the balanced equation): Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ. Square brackets mean the concentration in mol L⁻¹ at equilibrium.
Products go on top and reactants on the bottom; each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, and the concentrations are multiplied, not added.
Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) gives Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ [N₂][H₂]³. The 3 in front of H₂ becomes the power 3.
Example: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) gives Kc = [HI]² ÷ [H₂][I₂], with HI squared because its coefficient is 2.
Example: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) gives Kc = [PCl₃][Cl₂] ÷ [PCl₅].
Example: esterification, CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, gives Kc = [CH₃COOC₂H₅][H₂O] ÷ [CH₃COOH][C₂H₅OH]; water is included because it is a product, not the solvent.
Example: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) gives Kc = [FeSCN²⁺] ÷ [Fe³⁺][SCN⁻].
Kc is a ratio of concentrations, so whether it has units depends on how many concentrations are on top and on the bottom.
To find the units, substitute mol L⁻¹ for each concentration in the Kc expression and cancel.
When the total of the powers is the same on top and bottom, as in H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI or esterification, the units cancel and Kc has no units.
For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: (mol L⁻¹)² ÷ (mol L⁻¹)⁴ = (mol L⁻¹)⁻², that is L² mol⁻², because there are fewer powers on top than on the bottom.
For PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂: (mol L⁻¹)² ÷ (mol L⁻¹), so the units of Kc are mol L⁻¹.
Many changes alter the composition of an equilibrium mixture, but the constant itself is much harder to move. Only one factor changes its value.
Kc changes only with temperature, so a value of Kc must always be quoted with its temperature.
Changing a concentration does not change Kc: the system shifts until the ratio in the Kc expression has its original value again.
Changing the pressure of a gas mixture does not change Kc: the concentrations change, but the new equilibrium mixture gives the same value of Kc.

A catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up) does not change Kc: it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner with the same composition.

Exothermic forward reaction (one that gives out heat, ΔH negative): raising the temperature decreases Kc, so less product is present at equilibrium; lowering the temperature increases Kc. Example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, with ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹.

Endothermic forward reaction (one that takes in heat, ΔH positive): raising the temperature increases Kc; lowering it decreases Kc. Example: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂, which is endothermic in the forward direction; PCl₅ decomposes further on heating.
So if Kc rises with temperature the forward reaction is endothermic; if Kc falls with temperature the forward reaction is exothermic.
The size of Kc tells you where the equilibrium lies, and comparing it with the current mixture tells you which way a reaction will go.

A large Kc (much greater than 1) means the equilibrium mixture is mainly products: the equilibrium lies to the right and the reaction goes almost to completion. A small Kc (much less than 1) means mainly reactants: it lies to the left and little product forms.

A Kc near 1 means appreciable amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium. Esterification has Kc ≈ 4 (at room temperature), so starting with 1 mol each of ethanoic acid and ethanol, about two-thirds of a mole of ester forms.
Kc tells how far a reaction goes, not how fast: a reaction with a large Kc may be very slow, e.g. without a catalyst.
The reaction quotient, Q, has the same expression as Kc but uses the concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium.

If Q is less than Kc, the mixture has too little product and the reaction proceeds forward (to the right) until Q = Kc; if Q is greater than Kc, it proceeds in reverse (to the left); if Q = Kc, the mixture is at equilibrium.

Worked prediction (sample data): for esterification with Kc = 4.0, a mixture with 0.50 mol each of acid, ethanol, ester and water has Q = (0.50 × 0.50) ÷ (0.50 × 0.50) = 1.0, which is less than Kc, so more ester forms.

This explains Le Châtelier’s principle (a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change) mathematically: adding a reactant makes the denominator larger, Q falls below Kc, and the reaction proceeds forward until Q = Kc again.
Writing the equation the other way round inverts Kc: for 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂, Kc = [H₂][I₂] ÷ [HI]², which is 1 ÷ Kc for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at the same temperature.
Kc calculations follow the same routine every time. Working through a table of amounts keeps the steps in order and avoids the usual mistakes.
1. Write the balanced equation and the Kc expression.
2. Convert any masses to moles using n = mass ÷ M, where M is the molar mass in g mol⁻¹.
3. Set up a table with rows Initial (moles at the start), Change (moles reacting or forming, in the ratio of the coefficients) and Equilibrium (initial + change) for every species.

4. Divide each equilibrium amount by the volume of the container in litres to get concentrations in mol L⁻¹. When the total number of moles is the same on each side, as in H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI or esterification, the volume cancels, so moles can be used directly.
5. Substitute the concentrations into the Kc expression and calculate; give the answer to 3 significant figures, with units if asked.
To find equilibrium amounts from Kc: let x be the amount that reacts, write each equilibrium amount in terms of x, substitute into the Kc expression and solve for x.
If both sides of the resulting equation are perfect squares, take the square root of both sides. Otherwise rearrange into a quadratic, ax² + bx + c = 0, and use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.
Choose the root that makes physical sense: no equilibrium amount can be negative, so x cannot exceed the starting amount of a reactant.
The simplest type: every equilibrium amount is given, so convert to concentrations and substitute.
Data: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) in a 2.00 L flask at a fixed temperature; at equilibrium there are 0.100 mol H₂, 0.150 mol I₂ and 0.840 mol HI.
[H₂] = 0.100 mol ÷ 2.00 L = 0.0500 mol L⁻¹, because Kc needs concentrations, not moles.
Kc = [HI]² ÷ [H₂][I₂] = (0.420)² ÷ (0.0500 × 0.0750) = 0.1764 ÷ 0.00375 = 47.0 (no units, because the powers on top and bottom match).
Here only one equilibrium amount is given. Use the mole ratio from the equation to work out all the others.
Data: 2.00 mol N₂ and 6.00 mol H₂ are sealed in a 4.00 L vessel; at equilibrium 1.20 mol NH₃ is present, for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Change: forming 1.20 mol NH₃ uses 0.600 mol N₂ and 1.80 mol H₂, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2 from the coefficients.
Equilibrium amounts: N₂ = 2.00 − 0.600 = 1.40 mol; H₂ = 6.00 − 1.80 = 4.20 mol; NH₃ = 1.20 mol.
Concentrations (÷ 4.00 L): [N₂] = 0.350 mol L⁻¹; [H₂] = 1.05 mol L⁻¹; [NH₃] = 0.300 mol L⁻¹.
Here the starting amount is a mass, and the extent of reaction is a percentage dissociated (the percentage of the starting compound that has split up into products).
Data: 41.7 g of PCl₅ is heated in a sealed 5.00 L vessel; at equilibrium 40.0% has dissociated, for PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g).
Moles PCl₅ = 41.7 g ÷ 208.5 g mol⁻¹ = 0.200 mol, using n = mass ÷ M.
Moles dissociated = 40.0% of 0.200 mol = 0.0800 mol, because the percentage applies to the starting amount.
At equilibrium: PCl₅ = 0.120 mol; PCl₃ = 0.0800 mol; Cl₂ = 0.0800 mol, because each PCl₅ that dissociates gives one PCl₃ and one Cl₂.
Concentrations (÷ 5.00 L): [PCl₅] = 0.0240 mol L⁻¹; [PCl₃] = [Cl₂] = 0.0160 mol L⁻¹.
Now Kc is given and you find an amount. When the expression is a perfect square (the same bracket squared on top and bottom), taking a square root avoids a quadratic.
Data: 1.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol are mixed and reach equilibrium; Kc = 4.00 for CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
Let x mol of ester form: at equilibrium the acid and the ethanol are each (1.00 − x) mol, and the ester and the water are each x mol; the volume cancels.
Taking the square root of both sides, which removes the squares, gives x ÷ (1.00 − x) = 2.00.
Rearranging: x = 2.00 − 2.00x, so 3.00x = 2.00 and x = 0.667 mol of ester.
The acid and the ethanol each remain at 1.00 − 0.667 = 0.333 mol, because each mole of ester formed used up one mole of each.
Mass of ester = 0.667 mol × 88 g mol⁻¹ = 58.7 g, using M(CH₃COOC₂H₅) = 88 g mol⁻¹.

When the expression is not a perfect square, it rearranges to a quadratic equation (one containing x²) with two roots, and only one of them is physically possible (the other would need more of a reactant than is present).
Data: 1.00 mol H₂ and 2.00 mol I₂ are placed in a 1.00 L flask; Kc = 49.0 at this temperature, for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
Let x mol of H₂ react: at equilibrium H₂ = (1.00 − x), I₂ = (2.00 − x) and HI = 2x; as the volume is 1.00 L, these amounts are also the concentrations in mol L⁻¹.
Rearranging gives 45.0x² − 147x + 98.0 = 0, which is the form ax² + bx + c = 0 needed for the formula.
x = 2.33 is impossible because it exceeds the 1.00 mol of H₂ present, so x = 0.933.
Equilibrium concentrations: [H₂] = 0.0667 mol L⁻¹; [I₂] = 1.07 mol L⁻¹; [HI] = 1.87 mol L⁻¹.

A reaction at equilibrium (reactants turning into products at exactly the rate products turn back into reactants, so the amounts stay constant) can be disturbed. Le Châtelier’s principle lets you predict how it responds.

Le Châtelier’s principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the system responds so as to oppose the change, and a new equilibrium is set up.
A shift to the right means the forward reaction is favoured, so more products form until equilibrium is restored; a shift to the left means more reactants form.
The principle predicts the direction of the shift, not how fast it happens or how large it is; the change is only partly reversed, so the system never fully cancels the disturbance.

Concentration (the amount of a substance per unit volume of solution) is the easiest disturbance to picture. The equilibrium shifts to use up whatever has been added, or to replace whatever has been taken away.
Adding a reactant (or removing a product) shifts the equilibrium to the right, using up some of the added reactant and forming more product.
Adding a product (or removing a reactant) shifts the equilibrium to the left, because the system opposes the extra product by turning some of it back into reactant.
Kc (the equilibrium constant, the fixed ratio of product to reactant concentrations in the Kc expression) is unchanged: the concentrations adjust until that ratio is back at its old value.
Removing a product as it forms keeps pulling the equilibrium to the right, so the reaction keeps making more product. This is how a yield (the amount of product obtained) is raised.
In esterification (an alcohol reacting with an acid to make an ester), using an excess of ethanol, the cheaper reactant, shifts the equilibrium right and increases the yield of ester.
