In Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) (red), adding either reactant deepens the red colour because more of the red product forms. There is more on this in Investigation: disturbing an equilibrium.

Pressure only affects equilibria that involve gases, because only gases take up very different volumes depending on how many molecules there are. The equilibrium shifts to the side that exerts less pressure when pressure is raised.

Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas, because that side exerts the lower pressure; decreasing the pressure shifts it towards the side with more moles of gas.

Count only the gas molecules, using the coefficients (the numbers in front of each formula): N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) has 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so high pressure shifts it to the right, giving more ammonia.
If both sides have the same number of moles of gas, pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium, e.g. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), with 2 mol on each side.

Compressing H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI makes the purple colour deeper because every concentration, including that of I₂, rises (the same amount of gas is squeezed into a smaller volume); the percentage of each substance is unchanged.
2NO₂(g) (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) (colourless): compressing the mixture in a sealed syringe makes it darker at once, because the concentration of the brown NO₂ rises.
The darkening then fades as the equilibrium shifts to the right, from 2 mol to 1 mol of gas, but the mixture does not become as pale as before.
A change of pressure does not change Kc.

Heat behaves like a reactant or a product: an exothermic reaction (one that releases heat, ΔH negative) gives out heat, and an endothermic one (ΔH positive) absorbs it. Changing the temperature moves the equilibrium to oppose the change in heat.
Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which absorbs heat; lowering it shifts the equilibrium in the exothermic direction, which releases heat.
If the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative), heating shifts the equilibrium to the left and cooling shifts it to the right; the reverse is true if the forward reaction is endothermic.
Example: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), with ΔH about −57 kJ mol⁻¹. Heating shifts the equilibrium to the left, giving a darker brown mixture with more NO₂.
Cooling the same mixture in ice-water shifts the equilibrium to the right, giving a paler mixture because more colourless N₂O₄ forms.
Temperature is the only one of these disturbances that changes Kc: for an exothermic forward reaction Kc falls as temperature rises; for an endothermic one it rises.
Diagram: two sealed tubes of the brown mixture, one in hot water and one in ice-water, each labelled with its colour.
A catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up) is not a disturbance to an equilibrium at all, so it cannot shift one.
A catalyst does not disturb an equilibrium or change its position, because it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally.
A catalyst lets equilibrium be reached more quickly, so the same yield is obtained in less time.
A catalyst does not change Kc.

Le Châtelier’s principle explains familiar things, from the fizz in a drink to the damage that extra carbon dioxide does to sea life. In each case, work out what was disturbed and which way the equilibrium moves.
Fizzy drinks: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq). Opening the bottle lowers the pressure of CO₂ above the drink, so the equilibrium shifts to the left and gas bubbles out.
A cold drink holds more dissolved CO₂.
Oceans: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq); CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq); H₂CO₃(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) ⇌ 2HCO₃⁻(aq). Here H₂CO₃ is carbonic acid and CO₃²⁻ is the carbonate ion.
More CO₂ in the air increases the dissolved CO₂ and carbonic acid; the third equilibrium shifts to the right, using up carbonate ions. This is ocean acidification.
With less carbonate available, shellfish and corals find it harder to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.
Indicators: the colour of an acid–base indicator (a dye that changes colour with acidity) changes because adding acid or base shifts HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. There is more on this in How indicators work.
The Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Le Châtelier’s principle tells you which conditions give the most ammonia at equilibrium, but cost and rate force compromises.
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Ammonia is used mainly to make fertilisers.

Pressure: there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so high pressure increases the yield by Le Châtelier’s principle, and also increases the rate because the concentrations are higher.
In practice a pressure of about 200 atm (range about 150–300 atm) is used as a compromise.
Higher pressures would give more ammonia, but a plant that can withstand them is very expensive to build and run, and the risk of leaks and explosions increases.
Temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher yield at equilibrium. But at low temperature the reaction is too slow to be economic.
In practice a compromise of about 400–500 °C (about 450 °C) gives a reasonable yield at a fast enough rate.
Two more features keep the Haber process economic: a catalyst that makes the reaction fast enough, and the removal of ammonia so that the equilibrium keeps moving right.
The iron catalyst does not change the yield; it lets equilibrium be approached quickly at the compromise temperature.

Ammonia is removed by cooling and liquefying it, which keeps pulling the equilibrium to the right, and unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the catalyst, so the overall conversion is high.

The Contact process makes sulfur trioxide, the step on the way to sulfuric acid. It follows the same pattern as the Haber process: Le Châtelier predicts one set of conditions and practice uses another.
Contact process (sulfuric acid manufacture): 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH about −197 kJ mol⁻¹.
Le Châtelier predicts high pressure (3 mol of gas on the left, 2 mol on the right) and low temperature for the best yield, because the forward reaction is exothermic.
In practice about 450 °C is used as a compromise between yield and rate, with a vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) catalyst.
The pressure is only slightly above atmospheric (1–2 atm), because the yield is already very high and extra pressure would cost more than it gains.
For any equilibrium you can choose conditions the same way. First decide what favours the product, then weigh that against practical limits.

General method for any equilibrium: for the best yield choose the temperature that favours the exothermic or endothermic direction as needed, the pressure that favours the side with fewer (or more) gas moles, and an excess of a cheap reactant or removal of product.
Then weigh these choices against rate, cost, energy use and safety, because the best conditions for yield are rarely the best for the whole process.
Sustainability: lower temperatures and pressures save energy and reduce CO₂ emissions, and a good catalyst lets a process run at a lower temperature.
A reversible reaction that changes colour lets you see the position of equilibrium shift. This investigation tests Le Châtelier’s principle by changing one factor at a time.
Aim: to investigate how changes in concentration and temperature affect the position of an equilibrium, and to test whether the results agree with Le Châtelier’s principle.
Independent variable (the factor you deliberately change): here concentration or temperature.
Dependent variable (what you observe as a result): the colour of the equilibrium mixture, which shows the position of equilibrium; more of the coloured product gives a deeper colour.
Controlled variables (kept the same so the test is fair): the volume of solution, the number of drops added, the observer and the white background.

Set up one equilibrium mixture and divide it into equal portions in identical test tubes; keep one tube untouched as a control (a comparison with no change) and change one factor in each of the others.
Compare each tube with the control and record the colour before and after the change.
This equilibrium is a good test of concentration changes because the product is strongly coloured. Adding or removing a reactant visibly changes the red colour.
Equation: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). Fe³⁺ (from iron(III) chloride) is yellow, SCN⁻ (from potassium thiocyanate) is colourless, and FeSCN²⁺ is blood-red.

Method: add about 1 cm³ of 0.1 M iron(III) chloride and 1 cm³ of 0.1 M potassium thiocyanate to about 100 cm³ of deionised water and stir; a pale red solution forms. Diluting it makes the colour changes easy to see.
Pour equal portions (about 10 cm³) into four test tubes; tube 1 is the control.
Tube 2: add a few drops of iron(III) chloride solution; the red deepens, because [Fe³⁺] (the concentration of Fe³⁺) increases and the equilibrium shifts to the right, forming more FeSCN²⁺.
Tube 3: add a few drops of potassium thiocyanate solution; the red deepens, because [SCN⁻] increases and the equilibrium shifts to the right.
Tube 4: add a few drops of silver nitrate solution; a white precipitate (an insoluble solid formed in a solution) forms and the red colour fades.

Silver ions remove SCN⁻ as insoluble silver thiocyanate, AgSCN, lowering [SCN⁻], so the equilibrium shifts to the left; silver chloride, also white, can form from the chloride ions in the iron(III) chloride.
Conclusion: adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right; removing a reactant shifts it to the left, as Le Châtelier’s principle predicts.
A labelled diagram sums up the four tubes and the colour each one shows.
Diagram: a row of four test tubes in a rack, labelled control, + FeCl₃, + KSCN and + AgNO₃, showing pale red, deep red, deep red, and pale or colourless with a white precipitate.
The cobalt(II) chloride equilibrium shows both concentration and temperature effects, because its two forms are different colours and the forward reaction is endothermic.
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pink and [CoCl₄]²⁻ is blue; the forward reaction is endothermic.
Method: dissolve a little cobalt(II) chloride in water to give a pink solution; add concentrated hydrochloric acid drop by drop until the solution is violet, a mixture of pink and blue.
Divide the violet solution into test tubes, keeping one as a control.
Adding more concentrated hydrochloric acid adds Cl⁻ and turns the solution blue: the equilibrium shifts to the right.
Adding water turns the solution pink: water is a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the left. Dilution also favours the side with more dissolved ions, here the left, with five ions against one.
Because the forward reaction is endothermic, temperature changes move this equilibrium in a predictable direction. The chemicals involved need careful handling.
Heating: a tube placed in a beaker of hot water (about 80 °C) turns blue, because heating favours the endothermic forward reaction.
Cooling: a tube placed in ice-water turns pink, because cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction.
The changes reverse when the tubes return to room temperature, showing that the reaction is reversible and still dynamic.
Because heating shifts this equilibrium to the right, Kc for it increases with temperature.
Safety: concentrated hydrochloric acid is corrosive and gives off choking fumes, so wear goggles and gloves and work in a fume cupboard.
Safety: cobalt(II) chloride is toxic, may cause cancer and skin allergy, and is harmful to aquatic life, so wear gloves and put waste in the residue container, not the sink.

Diagram: three test tubes of the violet mixture, one in a beaker of hot water (blue), one in a beaker of ice-water (pink) and one at room temperature as a control (violet), with a thermometer in each beaker.
This gas equilibrium shows a temperature effect directly, because one form is brown and the other is colourless. The teacher performs it because NO₂ is toxic.
2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), with the forward reaction exothermic; NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless.
Sealed glass tubes containing the same equilibrium mixture are placed in hot water and in ice-water.
The hot tube becomes darker brown, as the equilibrium shifts to the left, the endothermic direction, giving more NO₂.
The cold tube becomes paler, as the equilibrium shifts to the right.
Safety: NO₂ is very toxic; the tubes are sealed and the demonstration is done by the teacher.
Diagram: two sealed tubes, one in hot water and one in ice-water, each labelled with its colour.
Primary data are collected by you in the laboratory; secondary data come from somewhere else, such as a simulation, table or graph. Both can show how an equilibrium responds to a disturbance.

A digital simulation models the particles of a reversible reaction; the user can add reactant or product, or change the temperature, and watch the numbers of each particle and the forward and reverse rates change until a new equilibrium is set up.
Simulations show what cannot be seen in the laboratory: both reactions continuing at equal rates at equilibrium, and concentration–time graphs showing the sudden change and the new constant levels.
Simulations are safe, fast and repeatable and avoid toxic chemicals, but they are models: their results depend on the rules programmed into them, so they are checked against experimental data.
Secondary data, such as a table or graph of the percentage of ammonia at equilibrium at different temperatures and pressures, can be analysed for trends.
The percentage of ammonia rises with pressure and falls with temperature, so the forward reaction reduces the number of moles of gas and is exothermic.
On a concentration–time graph, a sudden vertical jump in one line shows a substance being added; the gradual changes that follow show the shift; new horizontal lines show the new equilibrium.
Judging a colour by eye is not exact, so the method is designed to make the comparison fair and the results reliable.
Judging colour by eye is subjective (it depends on the observer): compare each tube with the control against a white background, use the same volume in identical tubes, and have the same observer.
Add the same number of drops to each tube, and allow time for the new equilibrium to set up (the colour stops changing) before recording.
Concentration changes move the position of equilibrium but do not change Kc; temperature changes both.
Adding a solution also dilutes the mixture a little, so add only a few drops, or add the same volume of water to the control.

Even perfectly pure water contains a very small number of ions, made when water molecules pass protons (hydrogen ions, H⁺) to each other. This is the starting point for understanding pH, because it fixes what 'neutral' means.
Pure water conducts electricity very slightly, so it must contain a small number of ions, since only moving charged particles can carry current through a liquid.

These ions come from the self-ionisation (auto-ionisation) of water, in which one water molecule donates a proton to another. This is a Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction (an acid gives a proton, a base accepts it): H₂O(l) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).

H₃O⁺ is the hydronium ion (a water molecule carrying an extra proton) and OH⁻ is the hydroxide ion. The double arrow shows an equilibrium, a reaction going both ways at the same rate so that amounts stay constant.
In simplified form: H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). This is the same change with the proton written as H⁺ instead of showing it attached to a water molecule.
The equilibrium lies very far to the left, so almost all the water stays as molecules: at 25 °C only about 2 in every 1000 million (1.8 × 10⁻⁹) water molecules are ionised at any moment.
In pure water each ionisation gives one H₃O⁺ and one OH⁻, so [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]. Square brackets mean concentration in mol L⁻¹.
A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], acidic when [H⁺] > [OH⁻], and basic (alkaline) when [H⁺] < [OH⁻]. Even acidic solutions contain some OH⁻ and basic solutions contain some H⁺.
Because water ionises only slightly, its equilibrium constant can be simplified into a single value, the ionic product of water, Kw. Work through it one step at a time.
Step 1: Write the equilibrium constant (Kc, the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentration at equilibrium) for H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻: Kc = [H⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [H₂O].
Step 2: So little water ionises that [H₂O] is effectively constant, because almost every molecule is unchanged: 1000 g of water per litre ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 55.6 mol L⁻¹.
Step 3: Combine the two constants: Kc × [H₂O] = [H⁺][OH⁻]. This new constant is the ionic product of water, Kw.
Definition: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻], or in simplified form Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]; it is the product of the hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion concentrations in water or any dilute aqueous solution.
At 25 °C, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ (units mol² L⁻², often omitted).
Kw links [H⁺] and [OH⁻] in every dilute aqueous solution. It explains why pure water has pH 7 and lets you find one concentration from the other.
So pH = −log₁₀(1.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 7.0, which is why pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C.
Kw applies to every dilute aqueous solution, not just pure water: if [H⁺] rises, [OH⁻] falls so that the product stays 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Example: a solution with [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ (pH 2) has [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² mol L⁻¹.
Taking −log₁₀ of Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] gives pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C, where pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; this is used for bases. There is more on this in pH calculations and dissociation constants.
Kw is an equilibrium constant, so it depends on temperature. The direction of the change follows from whether self-ionisation takes in or gives out heat.
Self-ionisation is endothermic (it takes in heat) in the forward direction, with ΔH about +56 kJ mol⁻¹. It is the reverse of neutralisation, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, which is exothermic (gives out heat).

By Le Châtelier's principle (a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change), raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, the endothermic direction. This produces more H⁺ and OH⁻, so Kw increases; cooling decreases Kw.
Like every equilibrium constant, Kw changes only with temperature; that is why Kw values are quoted with a temperature.
Because Kw rises with temperature, the pH of pure water falls as it gets hotter, yet the water is still neutral. Neutral is defined by [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not by a fixed pH.
Kw at 0 °C is 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, giving a neutral pH of 7.48.
Kw at 25 °C is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving a neutral pH of 7.00.
Kw at 50 °C is 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving a neutral pH of 6.63.
Kw at 100 °C is 5.1 × 10⁻¹³, giving a neutral pH of 6.15.
Hot pure water has a pH below 7 but is still neutral, because [H⁺] and [OH⁻] increase equally and stay equal; neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not pH = 7.
The neutral pH is therefore lower at higher temperatures and higher at lower temperatures, so pH 7 is the neutral point only at 25 °C.
Concentrations of H⁺ in solutions are often tiny numbers such as 0.0000001 mol L⁻¹. The pH scale turns them into easy numbers, usually between 0 and 14.
pH is defined as pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the concentration of hydrogen (hydronium) ions in mol L⁻¹.
The scale was introduced by the Danish chemist Søren Sørensen in 1909, while working at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen, as a convenient way to express very small [H⁺] values.
At 25 °C, pH below 7 is acidic, pH 7 is neutral and pH above 7 is basic (alkaline); the lower the pH, the more acidic the solution.
Where [H⁺] = 10⁻ˣ mol L⁻¹, the pH is x: for example, [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ gives pH 4.

The scale is logarithmic (each step multiplies by a fixed factor): a change of 1 pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. A solution of pH 3 has 10 times the [H⁺] of one of pH 4 and 100 times that of one of pH 5.
Putting numbers on familiar substances helps you judge whether a calculated pH is sensible. These values are approximate.
Stomach acid has a pH of about 1–2; lemon juice about 2–3; vinegar about 3. These are acidic.
Pure water has pH 7, and blood 7.35–7.45.
Baking soda solution has a pH of about 8–9; milk of magnesia about 10.5. These are weakly basic.
Household ammonia has a pH of about 11–12; oven cleaner (sodium hydroxide) about 13–14. These are strongly basic.
Exam questions give you either [H⁺] or the pH and ask for the other. Each direction uses the same relationship, worked here with sample numbers.
From [H⁺] to pH: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. For example, [H⁺] = 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ gives pH = −log₁₀(3.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.46.
For example, [H⁺] = 7.1 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹ gives pH = 6.15, which is slightly acidic at 25 °C because it is below 7.
From pH to [H⁺]: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, the antilog (the reverse of log) of −pH. For example, pH 3.7 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻³·⁷ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹.
For example, pH 8.6 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻⁸·⁶ = 2.51 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹.
On a calculator, use the log key with a minus sign to find pH, and the 10ˣ key (or inverse log) with −pH to find [H⁺]; give pH to two decimal places unless the question asks otherwise.
The pH scale works well for the dilute aqueous solutions met in most experiments, but it breaks down outside them.
It is normally used only between 0 and 14; very concentrated acids and alkalis go outside this range, where pH is not a convenient measure.
For example, 2.0 M HCl has pH −log₁₀(2.0) = −0.30, a negative value.
It is reliable only for dilute solutions; in concentrated solutions (above about 1 mol L⁻¹) the ions interact and the measured pH no longer matches −log₁₀ of the concentration.
It applies only to aqueous solutions (those with water as the solvent).
pH 7 is neutral only at 25 °C, because Kw and so the neutral pH change with temperature.
The simplest way to find a pH is with an indicator, a dye that changes colour with the pH of the solution. Indicators are quick but not precise.

Universal indicator (solution or paper): add a few drops to the solution, or dip in a strip of paper, and compare the colour with the colour chart. It gives the pH only to about the nearest whole unit. There is more on its colours in Acids, bases and their reactions.
Single indicators such as litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein show only whether the pH is above or below their colour-change range, not a pH value.
A pH meter gives a numerical reading, but it must be calibrated (set against known values) and looked after to be accurate.
A pH meter (or pH sensor with a data-logger, a device that records readings automatically) uses a glass electrode probe that responds to [H⁺] and gives a digital reading, usually to 0.01 pH units.
Calibrate the meter before use: place the rinsed probe in buffer solutions of known pH (e.g. pH 4.00 and 7.00, or 7.00 and 10.00) and set the meter to read these values.

A buffer solution resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, so its pH is reliably known. This is why buffers, not water or an acid of supposedly known pH, are used to calibrate.
Rinse the probe with deionised water (water with dissolved ions removed) between solutions and blot it dry gently, so one solution does not contaminate the next; store the bulb wet, as directed.
Exams ask for reasons why a meter is preferred, so know each advantage and what it improves.
A pH meter gives a precise numerical value (e.g. 4.72) rather than an estimate to the nearest whole unit.
A pH meter needs no judgement of colour, which varies from person to person and with lighting.
A pH meter works in coloured or cloudy solutions, where an indicator colour cannot be seen.
A pH meter can record pH continuously, which suits following a reaction over time, as in pH titration curves.
The aim is to compare the pH of several substances by two methods and check that they agree.
Aim: to measure and compare the pH of everyday substances, e.g. vinegar, lemon juice, a soft drink, tap water, toothpaste or an antacid tablet mixed with deionised water, and baking soda solution.
Step 1: Put about 20 cm³ of each sample in a clean, labelled beaker.
Step 2: Test each sample with universal indicator paper and record the pH from the colour chart.
Step 3: Measure each sample with a calibrated pH meter, rinsing the probe between samples.
Use deionised water to dissolve or mix solids, because tap water may contain dissolved substances that change the pH.
Diagram: a pH probe in a beaker of sample, connected to a meter (or data-logger) showing a digital reading.
Diagram: universal indicator paper beside its colour chart.
After the readings, rank the substances, compare the two methods and take care with hazards and errors.
Results: record both sets of readings in a table and rank the substances from most acidic to most basic.
The meter readings are more precise, and the two methods should agree to about one unit, because universal indicator reads only to about the nearest whole unit.
Safety: wear goggles; treat oven cleaner and other strong alkalis as corrosive (use gloves, small volumes, or omit them); do not taste any sample.
Sources of error: a probe that is not calibrated or not rinsed; a temperature different from the calibration temperature; misjudging indicator colours.

The pH depends on the [H⁺] in the solution, which depends on how far the acid dissociates (splits into ions) and on its concentration. A strong acid dissociates almost completely; a weak acid only partly, measured by its Ka (the acid dissociation constant).
Tendency to dissociate: at the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid.
For example, 0.10 M HCl has pH 1.00, but 0.10 M ethanoic acid (Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) has pH 2.87, because the weak acid is only about 1% dissociated.
Concentration: diluting an acid lowers [H⁺] and raises the pH.
Diluting a strong acid ten times raises its pH by 1: 0.10 M HCl has pH 1.00 and 0.010 M HCl has pH 2.00.
Diluting a weak acid ten times raises its pH by only about 0.5: 0.10 M ethanoic acid has pH 2.87 and 0.010 M has pH 3.37.
This is because [H⁺] depends on the square root of the concentration, and dilution makes a weak acid dissociate a larger fraction. There is more on this in pH calculations and dissociation constants.
Temperature changes pH because it changes Kw, Ka and Kb (the dissociation constants of water, weak acids and weak bases).
Temperature: Kw increases with temperature, so the pH of pure water and of neutral solutions falls, to 6.15 at 100 °C.
Ka and Kb also change with temperature, so the pH of weak acids and bases changes; Ka and Kb values are quoted at 25 °C.
For a base, the pH also changes with temperature at fixed [OH⁻], because [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] and Kw changes.
For example, 0.010 M NaOH has pH 12.00 at 25 °C but about 11.3 at 50 °C, because Kw is larger at 50 °C so [H⁺] is larger.
Strength and pH are different ideas. Strength is how far an acid dissociates; pH is the [H⁺] actually present, which also depends on concentration.
pH measures acidity (the [H⁺] in the solution), not the strength of the acid: a very dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid.
For example, 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M HCl has pH 5.00, while 1.0 M ethanoic acid has pH 2.37.

pH is a number that measures how acidic a solution is: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the concentration of hydrogen ions in mol L⁻¹ (M means mol L⁻¹). A strong acid ionises completely, so its [H⁺] can be read straight from the concentration of the acid.

A strong acid is fully dissociated (every molecule splits into ions), so [H⁺] = concentration of the acid × number of H⁺ released per formula unit (its basicity, the number of H⁺ each unit of acid can give).
Monoprotic (monobasic) strong acids, which release one H⁺ each, such as HCl and HNO₃, give [H⁺] = [acid], because each molecule supplies exactly one H⁺.
For example, 0.010 M HCl has [H⁺] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹, so pH = −log₁₀(0.010) = 2.00.
For example, 0.025 M HCl has pH = −log₁₀(0.025) = 1.60.
Sulfuric acid is diprotic (it can release two H⁺) and is treated as fully dissociated: H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻, so [H⁺] = 2 × [H₂SO₄].
For example, 0.050 M H₂SO₄ has [H⁺] = 0.10 mol L⁻¹, so pH = 1.00.
Sometimes a question gives a mass of acid dissolved in a stated volume instead of a concentration. Convert to mol L⁻¹ first, then use the strong acid method one step at a time.
Problem: 5.0 g of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄ = 98 g mol⁻¹, its molar mass) is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. Find the pH.
Step 1: Concentration in g L⁻¹ = 5.0 ÷ 0.250 = 20 g L⁻¹, because 250 cm³ is 0.250 L.
Step 2: Concentration in mol L⁻¹ = 20 ÷ 98 = 0.204 mol L⁻¹, dividing by the molar mass.
Step 3: [H⁺] = 2 × 0.204 = 0.408 mol L⁻¹, because each H₂SO₄ releases 2H⁺.
A strong base is treated like a strong acid, except that it supplies OH⁻ (hydroxide ions) rather than H⁺. So you find [OH⁻] first and then convert it to a pH.
A strong base is fully dissociated, so [OH⁻] = concentration of the base × number of OH⁻ per formula unit: NaOH and KOH give 1 OH⁻, while Ca(OH)₂ gives 2.
Method: find [OH⁻], then pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻] (pOH is the same scale as pH but for OH⁻); pH = 14 − pOH at 25 °C, because pH + pOH = 14 only at that temperature.
Alternative method: [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ [OH⁻] (Kw is the ionic product of water, [H⁺][OH⁻]), then pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; both methods give the same answer.
For example, 0.010 M NaOH has [OH⁻] = 0.010, so pOH = 2.00 and pH = 14 − 2.00 = 12.00.
For example, 0.15 M NaOH has pOH = −log₁₀(0.15) = 0.82, so pH = 13.18.
For example, 0.010 M Ca(OH)₂ dissociates as Ca(OH)₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.020 mol L⁻¹, pOH = 1.70 and pH = 12.30.
Example from a mass: 9.0 g of KOH (56 g mol⁻¹) made up to 500 cm³ gives 18 g L⁻¹ ÷ 56 = 0.321 mol L⁻¹ = [OH⁻].
For the KOH example, pOH = 0.49 and pH = 13.51.

A weak acid dissociates only slightly, so you cannot take [H⁺] equal to its concentration. Instead you use Ka, the acid dissociation constant, a number that measures how far the acid dissociates (the larger the Ka, the stronger the acid).
A weak acid is only slightly dissociated, so [H⁺] is much less than the acid concentration and must be found from Ka.
Formula: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c), where c is the concentration of the acid in mol L⁻¹; this formula must be learned, because it is not in the Formulae and Tables booklet.

It assumes the acid is monoprotic (gives one H⁺ per molecule), that the amount dissociated is very small compared with c (so c − x ≈ c, where x is the amount that dissociates), and that the H⁺ from water is negligible.
The approximation is good: the exact quadratic answer for 0.10 M ethanoic acid is pH 2.88, so the formula is good to about 0.01 pH unit.
Once [H⁺] is found from √(Ka × c), the pH follows with −log₁₀ as for any acid. These examples use Ka values at 25 °C.
For example, 0.10 M ethanoic acid with Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ has [H⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹.
For example, 0.50 M ethanoic acid has [H⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.50) = √(9.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, so pH = 2.52.
For example, 0.10 M methanoic acid with Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ has [H⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.24 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, so pH = 2.37.
Methanoic acid has a lower pH than ethanoic acid at the same concentration, because it is the stronger acid (larger Ka).
Example from a mass: 1.48 g of propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH, 74 g mol⁻¹) in 200 cm³ gives moles = 1.48 ÷ 74 = 0.0200 mol.
Concentration c = 0.0200 ÷ 0.200 = 0.100 mol L⁻¹, with the volume converted to litres.

A weak base reacts only slightly with water to give OH⁻, so it is handled like a weak acid but with Kb, the base dissociation constant (a measure of how far the base dissociates). You find [OH⁻] first.

Formula: [OH⁻] = √(Kb × c), with the same assumptions as for weak acids (the amount dissociated is very small compared with c, and OH⁻ from water is negligible); then pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻] and pH = 14 − pOH.
For example, 0.10 M ammonia with Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ has [OH⁻] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹.
For example, 0.050 M ammonia has [OH⁻] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.050) = 9.49 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹, so pOH = 3.02 and pH = 10.98.
Sometimes the pH is given and you must work backwards to a concentration or to Ka. Undo the log with 10 raised to the power of minus pH.
Concentration of a strong acid from its pH: for a monoprotic acid, [acid] = [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, because pH = −log₁₀[H⁺].
For example, a strong monoprotic acid HX with pH 5.65 has [HX] = 10⁻⁵·⁶⁵ = 2.24 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹.
[OH⁻] from pH: [OH⁻] = Kw ÷ [H⁺], where Kw is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
For example, at pH 5.65, pOH = 14 − 5.65 = 8.35, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁸·³⁵ = 4.47 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹, the same as 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 10⁻⁵·⁶⁵.
Ka of a weak acid from its pH: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, then Ka = [H⁺]² ÷ c, which is the formula [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) rearranged.
For example, a 0.10 M weak monoprotic acid with pH 3.00 has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³, so Ka = (1.0 × 10⁻³)² ÷ 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵.
Concentration of a weak acid from its pH and Ka: c = [H⁺]² ÷ Ka.
For example, ethanoic acid of pH 3.00 has c = (1.0 × 10⁻³)² ÷ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.0556 mol L⁻¹.
Every pH calculation goes wrong if the wrong method is chosen or a conversion is skipped. Work through these checks before and after every pH calculation.
First decide: is the species an acid or a base, and is it strong or weak? For a strong species use the concentration directly; for a weak species use √(Ka × c) or √(Kb × c).
For any base, find [OH⁻] first, then convert to pH; do not put [OH⁻] into −log₁₀ and call the result pH.
Convert masses to mol L⁻¹ first: n = m ÷ M (moles = mass ÷ molar mass), then c = n ÷ V, with V in litres.
Check that the answer is sensible: acids have pH below 7, bases have pH above 7, and a weak acid has a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration.
Give pH answers to two decimal places.

When an acid or base dissolves in water, it splits into ions; this is called dissociation. Writing the equation for it is the starting point for strength and for the dissociation constants that follow.
A general acid is written HA; in water it dissociates by donating a proton (an H⁺ ion) to water: HA(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq), or simply HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq).
For example, ethanoic acid dissociates as CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq); A⁻ is the ethanoate ion.
A general base that contains hydroxide is written BOH: BOH(aq) ⇌ B⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
A base such as ammonia, written B, produces OH⁻ by accepting a proton from water: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
Here B⁺ is the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺ (BH⁺ in some books).

For a strong acid or base the dissociation goes to completion, shown by a single arrow (→); for a weak acid or base it is an equilibrium (⇌, a reaction that runs both ways) that lies well to the left, so most of the molecules stay undissociated.

The acid dissociation constant Ka comes from the equilibrium constant Kc (products over reactants, each concentration in mol L⁻¹) for the acid reacting with water. Water is then left out, for a reason you can state.
Step 1: Write the equilibrium: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻.
Step 2: Write Kc as products over reactants: Kc = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] ÷ ([HA][H₂O]).
Step 3: In a dilute solution [H₂O] is effectively constant (55.6 mol L⁻¹, from 1000 ÷ 18), because so little water reacts; so it is combined with Kc: Ka = Kc × [H₂O].
Result: Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA], or in simplified form Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA]; Ka is the acid dissociation constant.
Example: for ethanoic acid, Ka = [CH₃COO⁻][H⁺] ÷ [CH₃COOH] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 25 °C.
The units of Ka are mol L⁻¹ (concentration² ÷ concentration); they are often omitted.
The base dissociation constant Kb is found by exactly the same steps as Ka, using the equilibrium of a base with water.
For B + H₂O ⇌ B⁺ + OH⁻ (or BOH ⇌ B⁺ + OH⁻), the same steps give the base dissociation constant: Kb = [B⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [B] (or [B⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [BOH]).
[H₂O] is again effectively constant and is absorbed into Kb, so it does not appear in the expression.
Ka and Kb are equilibrium constants, so a large value means the equilibrium lies far to the right and a small value means it lies far to the left. This makes them a direct measure of strength.
Ka measures the strength of an acid, its tendency to donate a proton: the larger Ka, the further the equilibrium lies to the right and the stronger the acid.
Likewise, the larger Kb, the stronger the base.
Weak acids have small Ka values (much less than 1): methanoic acid 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, benzoic acid 6.3 × 10⁻⁵, ethanoic acid 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, propanoic acid 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ (strongest to weakest).
Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) and strong bases (NaOH, KOH) dissociate essentially completely, so their Ka or Kb values are very large and the expressions are not used.
Ka and Kb are used for weak acids and bases.
Like all equilibrium constants, Ka and Kb are constant at a given temperature and do not change with concentration; values are quoted at 25 °C.
The weak acid formula comes from the Ka expression plus one approximation. If you can show these four steps, you can state the formula and the assumption behind it.
Step 1: Start with c mol L⁻¹ of a weak acid HA, of which x mol L⁻¹ dissociates. At equilibrium [HA] = c − x, [H⁺] = x and [A⁻] = x, because each HA that dissociates gives one H⁺ and one A⁻.
Step 2: Ka = x × x ÷ (c − x) = x² ÷ (c − x).
Step 3: A weak acid dissociates so little that x is tiny compared with c, so c − x ≈ c and Ka = x² ÷ c.
Step 4: x² = Ka × c, so [H⁺] = √(Ka × c).
The same steps for a weak base give [OH⁻] = √(Kb × c); the formulas are used in the weak acid and weak base calculations earlier in this subsection.
Strength describes how far an acid or base splits into ions. The degree of dissociation puts a number on this, and it is what separates strong from weak.

The degree of dissociation is the fraction of acid (or base) molecules that have dissociated into ions in solution; as a percentage, % dissociation = (concentration dissociated ÷ initial concentration) × 100.
For an acid HA, % dissociation = ([H⁺] at equilibrium ÷ initial [HA]) × 100; for a base, % dissociation = ([OH⁻] ÷ initial [base]) × 100.
Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) and strong bases (NaOH, KOH) are essentially 100% dissociated in dilute solution, because the reaction goes to completion.
Weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid) and weak bases (e.g. ammonia) are only slightly dissociated, typically a few per cent or less.
For example, 0.10 M ethanoic acid is about 1.3% dissociated, so about 99 out of every 100 molecules remain as CH₃COOH.
So at the same concentration a strong acid gives a much higher [H⁺] than a weak acid, with a lower pH, better conductivity and a faster reaction with magnesium.

In Brønsted–Lowry terms (acids donate protons, bases accept them), a strong acid is a good proton donor whose conjugate base (the ion left after it loses H⁺, e.g. Cl⁻) has almost no tendency to take the proton back, so the equilibrium lies completely to the right.
A weak acid's conjugate base (e.g. CH₃COO⁻) readily takes the proton back, so the equilibrium lies to the left.
Ka and Kb let you rank weak acids and bases and work out their percentage dissociation. Compare them only at the same concentration and temperature.
At the same concentration and temperature, the acid with the larger Ka is dissociated to a greater degree and is the stronger acid; the base with the larger Kb is the stronger base.
For example, methanoic acid (Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁴) is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid (Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵): at 0.10 M, methanoic acid is 4.2% dissociated and ethanoic acid 1.3%.
Formula: degree of dissociation (as a fraction) = [H⁺] ÷ c = √(Ka × c) ÷ c = √(Ka ÷ c); for a weak base, the same form is √(Kb ÷ c).
Worked example: 0.10 M ethanoic acid has [H⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹.
Worked example: 0.10 M ammonia (Kb 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) has [OH⁻] = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, so 1.34% of the ammonia has reacted to form NH₄⁺ and OH⁻.
A very small Ka (or Kb) means a very low degree of dissociation; the Ka values of strong acids are so large that dissociation is complete, which is why Ka is used only to compare weak acids.
Diluting a weak acid does not change Ka, but it does change how much of the acid is dissociated. The percentage dissociation and the [H⁺] move in opposite directions.
Ka is constant at a given temperature, but the degree of dissociation of a weak acid increases as the solution is diluted, because √(Ka ÷ c) gets larger as c gets smaller.
For example, ethanoic acid is 0.42% dissociated at 1.0 M, 1.34% at 0.10 M and 4.2% at 0.010 M.

By Le Châtelier's principle (a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change), dilution lowers the concentration of all species, so the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ shifts to the right, the side with more dissolved particles, to oppose the change.
Even though the degree of dissociation rises, [H⁺] still falls on dilution, so the pH still rises.
A strong acid is fully dissociated at every dilute concentration, so its degree of dissociation does not change on dilution.
An acid and the base left after it loses H⁺ are a conjugate acid–base pair. Their dissociation constants are linked through Kw, the ionic product of water.
For a conjugate acid–base pair in water, Ka (of the acid) × Kb (of its conjugate base) = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
So the larger the Ka of an acid, the smaller the Kb of its conjugate base: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
Example: Kb of the ethanoate ion = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Example: Ka of the ammonium ion = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Carbon moves continuously between stores (places where it is held) through natural processes. The balance between sources and sinks decides how much CO₂ is in the air.

Carbon is stored in the atmosphere (mainly as CO₂), in the oceans (dissolved CO₂, hydrogencarbonate and carbonate ions), in living things (carbohydrates, proteins and fats), in soils and peat, and in rocks (limestone and fossil fuels).

Photosynthesis (the process in which plants build sugar from CO₂ and water) removes CO₂ from the air: 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g). It is powered by sunlight in green plants, algae and phytoplankton (microscopic floating ocean algae).

Respiration, the process in which living things use glucose and oxygen to release energy, returns CO₂ to the air. It happens in plants, animals and microorganisms: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l).
Decay is the breakdown of dead matter by microorganisms. It also releases CO₂, and it releases CH₄ (methane) instead where oxygen is absent.
CO₂ dissolves in the oceans and waterways, so the water is also a store: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq), and then CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq), where H₂CO₃ is carbonic acid.
Marine organisms use carbonate to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons. Over long periods these deposits form limestone, which locks carbon away in rock.
Carbon also returns to the air by burning, and some carbon is held back for very long periods as fuels. This explains how the carbon in fossil fuels reaches the atmosphere.
Combustion (burning) of fuels releases CO₂, for example CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Natural sources also include forest fires and volcanic eruptions.

Peat forms from dead organisms buried over thousands of years, while coal, oil and natural gas form over millions of years. In both cases the material is buried without enough oxygen to decay fully, so they are long-term carbon stores.
Burning coal, oil, natural gas or peat therefore returns carbon, stored for a very long time, to the atmosphere as CO₂.

Diagram: the carbon cycle with atmospheric CO₂ at the centre and labelled arrows for photosynthesis, respiration, decay, combustion, dissolving in the oceans, formation of shells and limestone, and formation of fossil fuels.
Each part of the carbon cycle either adds CO₂ to the air or takes it out. When additions and removals match, the CO₂ level stays steady, and human activity has upset that match.
A carbon source adds more CO₂ to the atmosphere than it removes, for example burning fossil fuels, respiration, decay, volcanoes, and heating limestone in cement-making: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g).

A carbon sink removes more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases, and stores it. Examples are growing forests, the oceans, and undisturbed peatlands and wetlands (peat-forming bogs and marshy land).
Waterlogged conditions in undisturbed peatlands and wetlands stop dead plant material from decaying, so the carbon stays stored.

Before industrialisation (the growth of factories and large-scale fuel burning), natural sources and sinks were roughly in balance, so atmospheric CO₂ stayed fairly steady at about 280 ppm (parts per million by volume).

Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from long-term stores into the air far faster than sinks can absorb it. Deforestation (clearing forests) and draining peatlands both remove sinks and release stored carbon.
As a result, atmospheric CO₂ has risen to about 420 ppm in the mid-2020s.

CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, so a carbon cycle out of balance changes the climate. Natural changes in the cycle over thousands of years have caused past climate changes; the present change is human-influenced and much faster.

Sustainability means using resources so that they are not used up and the environment is not damaged for future generations. For carbon this means keeping emissions in balance with what sinks can absorb, for example by using renewable energy and protecting forests and peatlands.
Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap some of the heat the Earth radiates, keeping the lower atmosphere warm.

Energy from the Sun reaches the Earth mainly as visible light (shorter wavelength), with some ultraviolet and near-infrared. The atmosphere is largely transparent to visible light, so it passes through.
About 30% of incoming solar radiation is reflected back to space by clouds, ice and the surface. The rest is absorbed and warms the land and oceans.
The warmed Earth radiates energy back out as longer-wavelength infrared (IR) radiation, which is heat. Remember that incoming radiation is mainly visible light and outgoing radiation is infrared.
Greenhouse gases absorb some of this IR and re-emit it in all directions, including back down towards the surface, so heat is kept in the lower atmosphere for longer.
This warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere by naturally occurring greenhouse gases is the natural greenhouse effect.
The main natural greenhouse gases are water vapour, the largest contributor, and carbon dioxide, with smaller amounts of methane and dinitrogen oxide (N₂O); ozone also contributes.
The name is an analogy with a glass greenhouse, which lets sunlight in and keeps heat in. The analogy is not exact, because a real greenhouse works mainly by stopping warm air escaping.

Diagram: the Sun, incoming short-wavelength radiation passing through the atmosphere, some reflected, IR emitted from the surface, some absorbed by a layer of greenhouse gases and re-emitted back down, and some escaping to space.
Not every gas in the air is a greenhouse gas. Whether a gas traps heat depends on the structure of its molecules.
Nitrogen (N₂, about 78% of dry air), oxygen (O₂, about 21%) and argon (about 0.9%) do not absorb IR radiation, so they are not greenhouse gases even though they make up about 99% of dry air.
A molecule absorbs IR when the energy makes its bonds vibrate (stretch or bend) in a way that changes how charge is spread across the molecule.
Molecules of two identical atoms (N₂, O₂) cannot do this, while H₂O, CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O, with three or more atoms and polar bonds (bonds where the electrons are shared unequally), can.
Water vapour contributes most to the natural greenhouse effect because it is by far the most abundant greenhouse gas.
The concentration of water vapour is set by temperature, through evaporation (liquid water turning to vapour) and condensation (vapour turning back to liquid), not directly by human emissions.
The natural greenhouse effect is what makes the Earth habitable, and experiments by John Tyndall in the nineteenth century showed which gases absorb heat radiation.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about +15 °C, a difference of about 33 °C.
At −18 °C the oceans would freeze and life as we know it could not exist.
The natural greenhouse effect keeps water liquid over most of the planet and evens out the difference between day and night temperatures.
The natural effect is essential and beneficial. The problem is the extra warming caused by increased greenhouse gas concentrations.

John Tyndall (1820–1893), born in Leighlinbridge, Co. Carlow, used experiments from 1859 at the Royal Institution in London to show which gases absorb heat radiation: water vapour and carbon dioxide do, while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
Tyndall's experiments laid the experimental foundation for understanding the greenhouse effect. The Tyndall National Institute in Cork is named after him.
The natural greenhouse effect is beneficial, but human activity has added greenhouse gases to the air. The extra warming this causes is the enhanced greenhouse effect.
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the extra warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human (anthropogenic) activities.

The main human activities are burning fossil fuels (for power generation, transport, heating and industry), deforestation and land-use change, agriculture (livestock and fertilisers), cement-making and landfill (waste buried in the ground).
The resulting long-term rise in the Earth's average surface temperature is global warming. Together with the other changes it causes, it is called climate change.
Gases differ in how much they warm the Earth for the same mass emitted. To compare them, scientists use a number called the global warming potential.

Gases differ in their greenhouse effect because they differ in how strongly each molecule absorbs infrared radiation, how abundant they are in the atmosphere, and how long they stay there (atmospheric lifetime).

The greenhouse factor of a gas is its global warming potential (GWP): the warming caused by emitting 1 kg (or 1 tonne) of the gas over a set period, usually 100 years, compared with the warming from the same mass of CO₂. The GWP of CO₂ is 1 by definition.
100-year GWPs from the IPCC (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5, 2013) are: CO₂ 1; methane (CH₄) 28; dinitrogen oxide (N₂O) 265.

The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2021) gives slightly different values because the science is refined over time: CH₄ about 27–30, depending on whether the methane is of fossil origin. The AR6 value for N₂O is 273.
Always state which report a GWP comes from, because the values differ between reports.

A high GWP does not make a gas the most important. CO₂ has the lowest GWP of these gases, yet it causes most of the human-caused warming because far more of it is emitted and it stays in the atmosphere for centuries.
Emissions of different gases are compared as CO₂ equivalent, found by multiplying the mass of the gas by its GWP.
Example: 5 tonnes of methane = 5 × 28 = 140 tonnes CO₂ equivalent (AR5 values).
Each greenhouse gas has its own sources and abundance. Abundance is given in ppm, parts per million of the air by volume, and compared with the pre-industrial level.
Carbon dioxide comes from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and cement-making (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂).
CO₂ is about 420 ppm in the mid-2020s, up from about 280 ppm before industrialisation, an increase of about 50%.
Much of the extra CO₂ stays in the atmosphere for centuries, and some for thousands of years, which is why its effect builds up.
Methane comes from ruminant livestock (cattle and sheep, which digest food in the stomach), manure, rice paddies, landfill sites, leaks from natural-gas wells and pipelines, and natural wetlands.
Methane is about 1.9 ppm, more than two and a half times the pre-industrial level of about 0.7 ppm, and its atmospheric lifetime is about 12 years.
Dinitrogen oxide is a long-lived greenhouse gas tied to farming. Ireland's emissions show how these gases link to everyday activities.
Dinitrogen oxide (nitrous oxide, N₂O) comes mainly from nitrogen fertilisers and manure on soils. It is about 0.34 ppm, up from about 0.27 ppm.
N₂O stays in the atmosphere for over 100 years (AR5: about 121 years), which is why it is such a potent, long-lived greenhouse gas.
In Ireland agriculture is the largest single source of greenhouse gas emissions, over a third of the total, mainly methane from cattle and N₂O from fertilisers and manure.
In Ireland energy, transport and heating produce most of the CO₂.
Oxides of nitrogen and sulfur form when fuels burn. They matter in a different way from the main greenhouse gases: one group acts indirectly and the other actually cools the climate.
NOx (nitrogen monoxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO₂) form when nitrogen and oxygen from air combine at the high temperatures in car engines and power stations: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g).
NO then reacts further with oxygen: 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g). Lightning also forms NOx.
NOx are short-lived and are not important direct greenhouse gases. They act indirectly, mainly by helping to form ozone, a greenhouse gas, in the lower atmosphere.
NO₂ also causes acid rain (rain made acidic by dissolved pollutant gases) and harms health.
NOx must not be confused with N₂O, the long-lived greenhouse gas from fertilisers.
Sulfur oxides (SO₂ and SO₃) come from burning coal and oil that contain sulfur, S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), and from volcanoes.
SO₂ forms tiny sulfate particles (aerosols) and droplets in the air that reflect sunlight, so their overall effect on climate is cooling, not warming.
Sulfur oxides also cause acid rain.
Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it behaves differently from the others because temperature, not human emissions, controls how much of it is in the air.
Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas. Its concentration is controlled by temperature, and it stays in the air for only days.
Because of its short stay in the air, human emissions don't change its concentration directly, and water vapour has no GWP.

Water vapour acts as a feedback (a change that reinforces the original change): warming caused by CO₂ and other gases increases evaporation, and the extra water vapour traps more heat, amplifying the warming.
Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour for each °C of warming (Clausius–Clapeyron relation).
Several independent kinds of measurement show that greenhouse gases have risen and that the planet has warmed. Together they support the conclusion that human activity is the cause.
Continuous measurements at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, begun by Charles David Keeling in 1958 (the “Keeling curve”), show CO₂ rising every year, from about 315 ppm in 1958 to about 420 ppm.
Ice cores (long cylinders of ice drilled from ice sheets): air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice show that CO₂ stayed between about 180 and 300 ppm for the 800,000 years before industrialisation.
Today's CO₂ level is far above that range, and the rise matches the growth in fossil-fuel use.
The global average surface temperature in 2011–2020 was about 1.1 °C higher than in 1850–1900 (IPCC AR6), with most of the warming since the 1970s. Recent years have been the warmest on record.
Other observed changes include shrinking glaciers and Arctic sea ice, melting ice sheets and warming oceans.
Sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC AR6), from melting ice and the expansion of warmer water.

Climate models (computer simulations of the climate) that include only natural factors (changes in the Sun and volcanoes) do not reproduce the warming since the mid-twentieth century. Models that also include human greenhouse gas emissions do.
The IPCC (AR6) concludes that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.
Extra warming changes temperature, rainfall, the oceans and living things. The effects are linked: warmer air holds more water vapour, and the oceans absorb extra CO₂.

Global warming brings higher average temperatures, more frequent heatwaves, melting ice and rising sea levels that threaten low-lying coasts and countries, for example Bangladesh, the Netherlands and small island states.
A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour, so the water cycle intensifies: heavier rainfall and more flooding in some regions, and longer droughts in others.
More winter rain is expected in Ireland.
Other effects include changes to ecosystems (species moving or becoming extinct, coral bleaching), threats to food and water supplies, and more extreme weather events.
The oceans take up part of the CO₂ humans emit. This slows warming in the air, but the dissolved CO₂ makes the sea water less alkaline.
The oceans absorb about a quarter of the CO₂ emitted by humans.
CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq). The H⁺ concentration rises as CO₂ dissolves, so the pH falls.
The average surface ocean pH has fallen by about 0.1, from about 8.2 to about 8.1, since pre-industrial times.
Ocean acidification lowers the pH but does not make the sea acidic, because the pH stays above 7.
The extra H⁺ reacts with carbonate ions, H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻, leaving less carbonate for shell-building organisms such as oysters, mussels, corals and some plankton.
Acidified water can also dissolve calcium carbonate: CaCO₃(s) + CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2HCO₃⁻(aq).
Reducing the enhanced greenhouse effect means cutting emissions of greenhouse gases and protecting carbon sinks. Each major source has its own response.
Replace fossil fuels with renewable energy (wind, solar, hydroelectric and tidal), and improve energy efficiency by insulating buildings, using heat pumps and buying efficient appliances.
Transport: use public transport, cycling and walking; use electric vehicles charged from renewable electricity; and use hydrogen fuel cells.
Agriculture: use the right amount of fertiliser at the right time, and use clover and other nitrogen-fixing crops.

Agriculture: breed and feed livestock to produce less methane, and capture methane from manure in anaerobic digesters (tanks where microorganisms break down waste without oxygen, giving biogas) for use as a fuel.
Land use: plant forests, stop deforestation, and protect and rewet peatlands so that they act as carbon sinks again.
Some emissions can be captured or avoided in waste and industry, and governments set targets so that action is shared.
Waste: reduce food waste, recycle, and capture landfill methane and burn it to generate electricity. The CO₂ produced has a much smaller warming effect than the methane would have.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS): CO₂ is captured from power-station or factory flue gases (the waste gases from the chimney), compressed to a liquid, piped away and injected into deep rock formations such as depleted oil and gas fields.
Acid rain can be cut by reducing sulfur and NOx emissions: low-sulfur fuels, removing SO₂ from flue gases, and catalytic converters on cars.
International and national action: the Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep the rise in global temperature well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.
Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 sets a 51% cut in emissions by 2030 (compared with 2018) and climate neutrality by 2050.

A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emissions, as CO₂ equivalent, caused by a person, organisation, product or activity. Individuals can reduce theirs through choices in travel, home heating, diet and consumption.
Water covers most of the planet, yet very little of it can be drunk or used. Contamination (pollution of water by unwanted substances) removes even more of that small share.
About 97.5% of the Earth's water is salt water in the oceans, which is unsuitable for drinking or farming; only about 2.5% is fresh water.

Most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or lies deep underground, so well under 1% is readily available in rivers, lakes and accessible groundwater (water held in rock and soil that can be reached by wells).

Fresh water is constantly recycled by the water cycle (evaporation, rainfall and run-off), but the amount available in a place at a time is limited, and demand rises with population, farming and industry.
Contamination makes some of the available fresh water unusable, so there is even less to share between all these demands.
Making water fit to drink, and cleaning it again after use, takes machinery, chemicals and electricity. Each of these has a cost to the energy supply and to the environment.

Processing water has an energy cost: pumping water from sources to treatment plants and on to homes, running treatment plants (mixing, filtration, UV lamps), and treating waste water before it returns to rivers.

Processing water also has an environmental impact: chemicals such as aluminium sulfate and chlorine are manufactured and transported, and sludge (the solid waste left after treatment) must be disposed of.
Abstraction (taking water out of a river or lake) lowers the level of rivers and lakes, which affects the living things that depend on them.
Leaking pipes waste treated water and the energy used to treat it, because water that is lost has already been pumped and cleaned.
Making fresh water from sea water by desalination (removing the dissolved salts), e.g. by reverse osmosis, is possible but uses far more energy than treating fresh water.
So conserving water, by fixing leaks and using less, also saves energy and reduces emissions.
Fish breathe oxygen that is dissolved in the water, and only a little dissolves. Pollution that feeds bacteria uses that oxygen up, and biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the measure of how much.
Fish and other aquatic life need oxygen dissolved in the water; clean water at 20 °C holds only about 9 mg L⁻¹ (9 p.p.m., parts per million) of dissolved oxygen, and warmer water holds less.

When organic matter (material from living things, such as sewage, slurry, food waste or dead plants) enters water, aerobic bacteria (bacteria that use oxygen) break it down, using up dissolved oxygen.

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the amount of dissolved oxygen used up by biological (biochemical) action when a water sample is kept in the dark at 20 °C for five days. It is measured in mg L⁻¹ (p.p.m.) of oxygen.

A high BOD means a lot of organic pollution: the oxygen is used up and fish die (a fish kill). When the oxygen is gone, anaerobic bacteria (which live without oxygen) take over, producing foul-smelling gases such as hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and methane.
Unpolluted river water has a BOD of only a few mg L⁻¹; raw domestic sewage (sewage that has had no treatment) has a BOD of a few hundred mg L⁻¹ (about 300).

Farm wastes such as silage effluent (the liquid that drains from stored fermented grass) and slurry (liquid animal manure) have a BOD in the thousands to tens of thousands of mg L⁻¹, so a small spill can kill a river.

The BOD test compares the dissolved oxygen in a sample before and after five days of bacterial activity. The conditions are fixed so that the only thing using up oxygen is the bacteria and the results can be compared.
The sample is kept in the dark because this prevents photosynthesis by algae and plants from adding oxygen.
The temperature is fixed at 20 °C because both the solubility of oxygen (how much dissolves in the water) and the rate of bacterial activity depend on temperature.
The time is fixed at five days so that results are comparable.
Step 1: Measure the dissolved oxygen in one bottle of the sample at the start.
Step 2: Fill a second bottle completely and seal it, so no air can add oxygen, then keep it in the dark at 20 °C for five days.
Step 3: Measure the dissolved oxygen in the second bottle after five days.
Step 4: The BOD is the difference between the two dissolved oxygen readings, because that difference is the oxygen the bacteria used.

Diagram: two labelled BOD bottles, one for the initial dissolved oxygen measurement and one completely filled and sealed for incubation (keeping the sample under set conditions) in the dark at 20 °C for five days.
Sewage is waste water from toilets, kitchens and washing. If it is untreated or poorly treated, it harms a river in three different ways.
Untreated or poorly treated sewage contains organic matter, which has a high BOD and causes oxygen depletion (the water losing its dissolved oxygen).
Sewage also contains nitrates and phosphates, which cause eutrophication (an overgrowth of algae caused by too many nutrients).
Sewage contains disease-causing microorganisms, including bacteria such as E. coli and those causing cholera and typhoid, as well as viruses and parasites.

Faecal contamination (contamination with human or animal faeces) of drinking water or bathing water causes gastrointestinal illness (illness of the stomach and gut); this is why sewage must be treated before discharge and drinking water disinfected.
Effluent means liquid waste that flows out into the environment. Farms produce several kinds, and each can reach rivers through spills or run-off (water washing over land into streams).
Agricultural effluent includes animal slurry, silage effluent, milking-parlour washings and run-off of artificial fertilisers.
Slurry and silage effluent have a very high BOD, so they use up the dissolved oxygen and cause fish kills if they reach a river.
Fertiliser and slurry run-off carry nitrates (NO₃⁻) and phosphates (PO₄³⁻) into water, causing eutrophication.
Nitrate in drinking water is a health concern, especially for babies, because it can reduce the blood's ability to carry oxygen.
The EU drinking-water limit for nitrate is 50 mg L⁻¹.
Pesticides (chemicals that kill pests) washed off farmland can contaminate water and are toxic to aquatic life.

Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nutrients, especially nitrates and phosphates, leading to excessive growth of algae and plants. It is a chain of events that starts with added nutrients and can end with the death of fish.
Step 1: Nitrates and phosphates from fertiliser run-off, slurry, sewage and detergents enter a river or lake.
Step 2: Algae and aquatic plants grow rapidly, forming an algal bloom (a thick layer of algae) that covers the surface and blocks light from plants below.

Step 3: The algae die and are decomposed by aerobic bacteria, which use up the dissolved oxygen, so the BOD rises sharply. Living algae growing in light do not use up the oxygen; the bacteria decomposing them after they die do.
Step 4: Dissolved oxygen falls so low that fish and other animals die, and anaerobic bacteria then produce foul-smelling H₂S.
Some algal blooms, e.g. of cyanobacteria ("blue-green algae"), also produce toxins harmful to animals and people.

Prevention: controlled use of fertilisers, meaning the right amount at the right time and not before heavy rain (which would wash it into rivers), and buffer strips (strips of vegetation) along rivers.
Prevention: proper storage of slurry and silage, removing phosphates and nitrates in sewage treatment, and phosphate-free detergents.
Factories and power stations discharge waste water that can harm water in several ways: poisoning it, changing its pH, using up its oxygen or heating it.
Industrial effluent can contain toxic chemicals such as heavy metals, solvents and oils.
Industrial effluent can contain acids or alkalis that change the pH of the water, which harms the organisms living in it.
Organic waste from industries such as breweries and food processing has a high BOD, because bacteria use oxygen to break it down.
Thermal pollution (pollution by heat): warm water from power stations and factories holds less dissolved oxygen.
Warm water also speeds up the metabolism (the chemical reactions of life), and so the oxygen demand, of organisms, so even less oxygen is available.
Oil forms a film on the surface that stops oxygen dissolving and coats birds and animals.
Heavy metals are dense metals whose ions are poisonous to living things. Their danger lies in how they act inside cells and in how they build up over time.
Heavy metal ions such as lead (Pb²⁺), mercury (Hg²⁺) and cadmium (Cd²⁺) are toxic even at very low concentrations, in micrograms per litre.
Heavy metal ions bind to proteins, particularly to sulfur-containing (–SH) groups in enzymes (the proteins that speed up reactions in cells), changing their shape and stopping them working.
Heavy metals damage the nervous system, kidneys and liver.
They are cumulative poisons: the body can't excrete them easily, so they build up in tissues (bioaccumulation).
Their concentration increases up a food chain (biomagnification), so top predators and people who eat fish are most at risk.

Heavy metal ions can be removed from water by precipitation (turning them into a solid that forms in the water) as insoluble compounds, e.g. hydroxides or sulfides, followed by filtration, or by ion exchange (swapping the metal ions for harmless ions).
Each of the three metals reaches water from a different source and harms the body in a particular way. Two Japanese disease outbreaks show what the harm can look like.
Lead comes from old lead pipes in houses built before about 1970, especially where the water is soft and acidic, because such water dissolves lead more readily.
Lead damages the developing brain and nervous system of children, partly because Pb²⁺ takes the place of Ca²⁺.
The EU drinking-water limit for lead is 10 µg L⁻¹ (0.010 mg L⁻¹).
At Minamata, Japan, the Chisso Corporation's chemical factory discharged mercury compounds into the bay.
Methylmercury (an organic mercury compound) built up in fish and shellfish, and people who ate them suffered severe nervous-system damage, birth defects and deaths.
The disease was called Minamata disease and was officially recognised in 1956.
Cadmium comes from mining and some industries and damages the kidneys and bones.
Itai-itai disease in Japan was caused by cadmium from mining, which reached river water used for rice fields.
Plastic that breaks into tiny pieces does not disappear; it spreads through water and into living things. These small pieces are called microplastics.
Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than 5 mm.
Primary microplastics are made small, e.g. microbeads once used in cosmetics and plastic pellets.
Secondary microplastics form when larger plastic items break down, e.g. fibres from synthetic clothing in washing machines, tyre and road wear, packaging and bags.
Plastics are very unreactive and not biodegradable (bacteria cannot break them down), so they persist for hundreds of years. There is more on this in Addition polymers.
Microplastics are swallowed by plankton (tiny drifting organisms), shellfish and fish, blocking feeding and digestion, and they pass up the food chain.
Microplastics can carry adsorbed toxic chemicals (chemicals stuck to their surface).
Microplastics are found in drinking water and food; their long-term effects on human health are still being researched.
Acidification is the lowering of the pH of water. Gases from burning fuels dissolve in rain to make acids, and acidic waste water adds to the effect.
Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃.
Sulfur dioxide and oxygen form sulfuric acid in rain: 2SO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.
Nitrogen dioxide forms nitric acid in rain: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃.
Acidic industrial and mine waste water also lowers the pH of rivers and lakes.
Normal rain is slightly acidic, with a pH of about 5.6, because of dissolved CO₂; acid rain has a lower pH.
Low pH harms water life directly, through enzymes, and indirectly, by dissolving substances from rocks, shells and pipes.
Enzymes work only in a narrow pH range, so low pH disrupts enzyme activity and the balance of ions in organisms' cells.
Fish eggs and young fish are most sensitive, and many fish can't survive below about pH 5.
Acidic water dissolves aluminium compounds from soils and rocks; Al³⁺ ions damage fish gills so that fish can't take in oxygen.
Acidic water dissolves the calcium carbonate shells of snails and shellfish: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂.
In drinking water, acidic water dissolves lead and copper from pipes.
Water taken from rivers, lakes or the ground is not safe to drink as it comes. Treatment is a series of steps, each removing a different problem, so that the water that reaches your tap is safe.
Drinking water must be free of harmful microorganisms (bacteria, viruses and other living things too small to see) and harmful chemicals, and must be clear, colourless and odourless.

In Ireland, public water supplies are treated by Uisce Éireann (Irish Water) and must meet the limits in the EU Drinking Water Directive (the European law that sets the maximum levels of contaminants).

The usual order of treatment is screening, flocculation (coagulation), sedimentation, filtration (sand and, in some plants, microfiltration), disinfection (chlorination and/or UV), fluoridation and pH adjustment.
The exact steps depend on the source water, so a plant treating a clean source needs fewer steps than one treating a muddy river.
The first steps remove suspended solids (tiny solid particles carried along in the water) by physical means; the later steps kill microorganisms and adjust the chemistry of the water.

Diagram: a flow diagram of a treatment plant showing the intake with screen, flocculation tank (aluminium sulfate added), sedimentation tank (sludge removed), sand filter beds, chlorine and/or UV unit, fluoride and pH adjustment, storage reservoir and distribution pipes.
Screening is the first step. It removes the biggest objects before they can block or damage equipment further along.
Water from a river or lake passes through metal screens (mesh) that remove large floating objects such as branches, leaves, plastic and fish.
No chemicals are added at the screening stage, because it is purely a physical straining of the water.

Very fine particles carry charges that keep them apart and suspended, so they cannot simply be left to settle. Flocculation (also called coagulation) is the chemical trick that makes them clump into pieces big enough to sink.
Very small suspended particles (clay, silt and organic matter) don't settle because they are tiny and carry like, usually negative, charges that make them repel each other.

A flocculating agent (coagulant, a chemical that makes particles clump), usually aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃, is added and stirred in; iron salts and polyelectrolytes (long-chain molecules with many charges) are also used.
The positive Al³⁺ ions neutralise the charges on the particles, so the particles no longer repel each other and clump together.
Aluminium hydroxide also forms as a sticky, jelly-like precipitate (an insoluble solid formed in a reaction) that traps the particles: Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3Ca(OH)₂(aq) → 2Al(OH)₃(s) + 3CaSO₄(aq).
The particles join into larger clumps called flocs, which are heavy enough to settle.
Once flocculation has made the particles heavy, gravity can do the work of removing them. This step is called sedimentation (settling).

Water flows slowly through large settling tanks, where the flocs and other heavier particles sink to the bottom under gravity, removing most of the suspended matter. The slow flow gives them time to sink.
The sludge (the thick mud of settled solids) that collects at the bottom is removed and disposed of, and the clearer water flows off the top.
Sedimentation leaves behind the smaller particles that did not sink. Filtration strains these out, using sand and, in some plants, membranes as well.
Sand filtration: water passes down through beds of sand on a layer of gravel, and the remaining small particles and flocs are trapped in the spaces between the sand grains.
The filters are cleaned regularly by backwashing, which pumps clean water up through the bed so that the trapped particles are flushed out and the filter does not clog.

Microfiltration forces water through membranes (thin sheets) with very small pores (about 0.1–10 µm), which remove fine particles, bacteria and protozoan parasites (single-celled organisms that cause disease) such as Cryptosporidium.
Microfiltration does not remove dissolved substances or most viruses, because these are smaller than the pores.
Filtering removes particles, but many microorganisms still get through. Chlorination is the disinfection step: adding chlorine to kill them.
Chlorination kills disease-causing microorganisms (bacteria and viruses) so that the water is safe to drink.
Chlorine gas or sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) is added. Chlorine reacts with water to form hypochlorous acid, the main disinfectant: Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HOCl(aq) + HCl(aq).

Enough chlorine is added to leave a small residual of free chlorine (a few tenths of a mg L⁻¹, that is, a little left over after disinfection), which keeps the water disinfected as it travels through the pipes to the tap.
Some organisms, especially Cryptosporidium, resist chlorine at the levels used, so another barrier (good filtration or UV) is needed.
Too much chlorine gives an unpleasant taste and smell.
Chlorine reacts with organic matter (material from plants and other living things) in the water to form by-products such as trihalomethanes, whose levels are limited by law.
Removing organic matter first, by flocculation and filtration, keeps trihalomethane levels low because there is less for the chlorine to react with.
Ultraviolet (UV) light is an alternative way to disinfect water. It works on organisms that chlorine struggles with, but it cannot protect the water once it is in the pipes.
The water flows past lamps that emit ultraviolet radiation, which damages the DNA (the genetic material) of microorganisms so that they can't reproduce.
UV treatment is effective against Cryptosporidium, which resists chlorine at the levels used.
UV adds no chemicals and does not change the taste or smell of the water.
UV leaves no residual disinfectant in the pipes, so chlorine is still added afterwards to protect the water on its way to the tap.
The water must be clear first, because suspended particles can shield microorganisms from the UV; the lamps also use electricity.
An outbreak of Cryptosporidium infection in Galway in 2007, from the city's water supply, led to UV treatment being installed at the treatment plant there.

Fluoridation is different from the other steps because it is added for dental health, not to make the water safe from germs or particles. A small amount of a fluoride compound is added to public supplies.
A fluoride compound is added to public water supplies: usually hexafluorosilicic acid (H₂SiF₆) in Ireland, and sodium fluoride (NaF) elsewhere.

Fluoride helps prevent tooth decay: it is taken into tooth enamel (the hard outer layer of the tooth), converting some of the hydroxyapatite (the calcium mineral that enamel is made of) into fluorapatite.
Fluorapatite is more resistant to attack by acids made by bacteria than hydroxyapatite is, so the teeth decay less.
Ireland has fluoridated public water supplies since the 1960s, under the Health (Fluoridation of Water Supplies) Act 1960.
The fluoride level is set at 0.6–0.8 mg L⁻¹ (p.p.m., parts per million), with a legal maximum of 0.8 mg L⁻¹ (since 2007).
Too much fluoride causes dental fluorosis, which shows as white flecks or brown staining of the teeth. This is why the level is limited.
Fluoridation is debated, and most European countries do not fluoridate water.
The last chemical step makes sure the water is neither too acidic nor too alkaline. pH is the scale that measures this, with 7 neutral, below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline.
