The pH of drinking water must be kept within legal limits of 6.5–9.5, usually close to neutral or slightly alkaline.

If the water is too acidic (e.g. from peaty, upland areas), lime (calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, or calcium oxide, CaO) or sodium carbonate is added to raise the pH, because these are bases that neutralise acid.
If the water is too alkaline, e.g. after lime has been added in treatment, sulfuric acid or carbon dioxide is added to lower the pH, because these give acidic solutions.
Acidic water corrodes (slowly eats away) metal pipes and dissolves lead and copper from household plumbing, which is a health risk.
Very alkaline water tastes bitter and leaves deposits.
The pH also affects how well flocculation and chlorination work.
Treatment uses energy and chemicals, so it is worth asking what it achieves. Clean water has changed human health and still shapes lives around the world.

Clean drinking water is one of the greatest public health advances: water-borne diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery killed huge numbers of people in cities before treatment and disinfection.
In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in London to a contaminated water pump in Broad Street, an early piece of evidence that disease spreads through water.
Globally, about 2.2 billion people still lacked safely managed drinking water in 2022 (WHO/UNICEF).
Contaminated water and poor sanitation cause many deaths from diarrhoeal disease, mostly of young children.
Clean, safe water and sanitation for all is UN Sustainable Development Goal 6.
Clean water brings benefits beyond health: less time is spent collecting water, often by women and girls; more children attend school; workers are healthier; and economies develop.
Costs: treatment uses energy and chemicals and produces sludge, so treated water should not be wasted. There is more on this in Water contamination.

A lithium-ion cell stores energy in two electrodes (the solid conductors where the reactions happen) that lithium ions can move in and out of. Knowing what each part is made of, and why, lets you explain both discharging and recharging.
A lithium-ion cell is a rechargeable (secondary) cell, meaning its reaction can be reversed by an electrical supply so it can be used again. There is more on this in Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
The negative electrode is graphite, in which lithium atoms are stored between layers of carbon atoms; when the cell is fully charged this is written LiC₆.
The positive electrode is a lithium metal oxide, e.g. lithium cobalt oxide, LiCoO₂; other types use nickel–manganese–cobalt oxides or lithium iron phosphate, LiFePO₄.

The electrolyte (the substance between the electrodes that carries charge as moving ions) is a lithium salt, e.g. LiPF₆, dissolved in an organic (non-aqueous) solvent, which lets Li⁺ ions move between the electrodes.
Water cannot be used as the solvent because lithium reacts with it.
Electrons flow only through the external circuit (the wires and device outside the cell); in the electrolyte the charge is carried by ions.
A porous plastic separator between the electrodes lets Li⁺ ions pass but stops the electrodes touching, which would short-circuit the cell (let current bypass the device).
Li⁺ ions move in and out of the layered structures of both electrodes without destroying them (a process called intercalation), so the cell can be charged and discharged many times.

Diagram: graphite negative electrode (left) and metal oxide positive electrode (right) with a separator between them in the electrolyte, joined by an external circuit with a device; Li⁺ moves through the electrolyte and electrons through the circuit, towards the positive electrode on discharge and towards the graphite on charge.
Discharging is the cell doing its job of powering a device. The cell then behaves as a galvanic cell, and each electrode has its own half-reaction.

When the cell powers a device it acts as a galvanic cell: a spontaneous redox reaction (one with electron transfer, happening by itself) converts chemical energy into electrical energy. There is more on this in Galvanic and electrolytic cells.

At the negative electrode, which is the anode during discharge (the anode is the electrode where oxidation, loss of electrons, happens), lithium is oxidised: LiC₆ → C₆ + Li⁺ + e⁻ (in simplest form, Li → Li⁺ + e⁻).
The electrons flow through the external circuit to the positive electrode, doing electrical work in the device on the way.
The Li⁺ ions move through the electrolyte and separator to the positive electrode, which keeps the charge balanced as electrons leave the negative electrode.

At the positive electrode, which is the cathode during discharge (the electrode where reduction, gain of electrons, happens), the metal oxide is reduced as it takes in Li⁺ ions and electrons: CoO₂ + Li⁺ + e⁻ → LiCoO₂.
Overall discharge reaction: LiC₆ + CoO₂ → C₆ + LiCoO₂.
A typical LiCoO₂–graphite cell gives about 3.6–3.7 V; LiFePO₄ cells give about 3.2 V.
Recharging runs the discharge reaction backwards. Because that reverse reaction does not happen by itself, a charger must force it, and the cell then behaves as an electrolytic cell.

When the cell is connected to a charger it acts as an electrolytic cell: an external electrical supply drives the non-spontaneous reverse reaction, converting electrical energy into chemical energy. There is more on this in Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
At the metal oxide electrode, which is now the anode (where oxidation happens), oxidation releases Li⁺ ions and electrons: LiCoO₂ → CoO₂ + Li⁺ + e⁻.
The charger pushes the electrons through the external circuit to the graphite electrode, and the Li⁺ ions move back through the electrolyte to it.
At the graphite electrode, now the cathode (where reduction happens), Li⁺ ions are reduced and stored between the graphite layers: C₆ + Li⁺ + e⁻ → LiC₆.
Overall charge reaction: C₆ + LiCoO₂ → LiC₆ + CoO₂.
Charging stores energy in the changed electrodes, not as stored electrons; the charge stays balanced throughout.
The anode is always the electrode where oxidation happens, so the graphite electrode is the anode on discharge and the cathode on charge; it remains the negative terminal throughout.
Lithium is chosen because its properties give a battery that is light and delivers a high voltage. Together these make a lot of energy available from a small mass.
Lithium is the least dense metal, with a density of 0.53 g cm⁻³, so batteries are light.

Lithium is at the top of the electrochemical series (the list of species ranked by how readily they gain or lose electrons), with a standard electrode potential of −3.04 V. There is more on this in Balancing redox equations and the electrochemical series.
Lithium loses electrons very easily, so lithium cells have a high voltage.
Together these properties give a high energy density, meaning a large amount of energy stored per kilogram, which suits portable devices and vehicles.
Lithium-ion cells hold their charge well when not in use and have no memory effect (a loss of capacity that some older rechargeable batteries suffer).
The lithium-ion battery was developed by John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino, who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion batteries in 1991.
A battery's life cycle starts with getting its raw materials out of the ground. Mining is the first stage where the battery has environmental and social costs.
A lithium-ion battery needs lithium and, depending on its type, cobalt, nickel, manganese, graphite, copper and aluminium.
Lithium is extracted from hard rock, the mineral spodumene, which is mined mainly in Australia.

Lithium is also extracted from brines (very salty water) pumped from under salt flats in South America, the “lithium triangle” of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia, where the water is evaporated in large ponds.
Brine extraction uses large amounts of water in some of the driest places on Earth, affecting local farmers, Indigenous communities and wildlife.
Hard-rock mining needs energy and produces waste rock, dust and emissions.
About 70% of the world's cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where some is mined by hand in unsafe conditions, including by children.
This has led to responsible-sourcing schemes and to cobalt-free battery types, e.g. lithium iron phosphate.
Refining the raw materials and manufacturing cells uses a lot of energy, so a battery has a large carbon footprint (total greenhouse gas emissions caused) before it is used.
In use, lithium-ion batteries bring real benefits, but they also wear out and carry a safety hazard. A life-cycle answer needs both sides.
Applications include mobile phones, laptops, tablets, cordless tools, e-bikes and e-scooters, electric vehicles, and large batteries that store electricity from wind and solar power for the grid.
Electric vehicles produce no exhaust emissions, which improves air quality in towns.
Over their lifetime, electric vehicles cause lower greenhouse gas emissions than petrol or diesel cars, especially when charged from renewable electricity.
Battery storage helps renewable electricity replace fossil fuels by storing energy when the wind blows or the sun shines.
The capacity falls gradually with each charge–discharge cycle and with age, because of side reactions at the electrodes, so batteries eventually need replacing.
Avoiding very high temperatures and keeping the charge between full and empty extends battery life.
If a cell is damaged, overcharged, short-circuited or overheated, it can undergo thermal runaway: it heats up uncontrollably, and the flammable organic electrolyte can catch fire or explode.
Batteries include a battery management system (electronics that monitor the cell) to prevent overcharging and overheating.
At the end of its life a battery holds both hazardous and valuable materials. Where it ends up decides whether it is a fire risk or a resource.
Used lithium-ion batteries must never go in household bins, because crushed or punctured batteries cause fires in bin lorries and waste facilities.
Used batteries contain toxic and valuable materials, which is why they should be collected separately.
In Ireland, shops that sell batteries take back used batteries free of charge, and used batteries can be left at recycling centres.
Vehicle batteries are returned through the dealers.
Recycling reduces the need for new mining, the waste sent to landfill and the risk of pollution.
Recycling is technically difficult, costly and energy-demanding, and only a fraction of batteries are currently recycled.
The EU Batteries Regulation (2023) sets rising targets for collection, recovery of materials and recycled content.
Used vehicle batteries with reduced capacity can have a “second life” as stationary storage (a fixed battery that stores electricity) before they are recycled, which extends their use.
Recycling works in three steps that turn whole batteries into a powder from which metals can be recovered. Two methods can then be used, with different strengths.
1. The batteries are collected and discharged, which makes them safer to handle.
2. The batteries are dismantled and shredded to a powder called “black mass”.
3. Metals are recovered from the black mass.
Pyrometallurgy is smelting (heating to extract metal) at high temperature; it recovers cobalt, nickel and copper, but uses a lot of energy and loses most of the lithium.
Hydrometallurgy dissolves the metals in acid and separates them by precipitation (making a dissolved metal form a solid so it can be filtered off); it recovers more, including lithium.
Putting the stages together gives a balanced judgement: lithium-ion batteries help the environment in use but cost something at every stage.

Lithium-ion batteries help cut fossil-fuel use, but each stage of the life cycle (mining, usage, disposal and recycling) has environmental and social costs; longer battery life, responsible sourcing and recycling reduce those costs but do not remove them.

The research investigation is a piece of independent work where you take one idea from the course and follow it into the real world. It asks you to use chemistry to explain an issue, not just report on it.
You research one area of the course through one cross-cutting theme (a big topic that links many parts of the course): health, sustainability or technology.
The research must use real chemistry from the course to explain the issue, not just describe it. This means reactions, equations and properties are used to say why something happens.
It should be personal and meaningful: a question you care about, often local or Irish, so that the chemistry connects to something you can see around you.
It shows chemistry as a collaborative, human activity (people working together and building on each other's work) with social and global importance.
Outputs can be a presentation to the class or a short digital report, so you choose the form that suits the audience.
Later research can be more detailed and may include gathering some primary data (data you measure yourself rather than take from a source), for example measuring the pH of local water samples.
The written exam includes questions on applying chemistry to the cross-cutting themes, so the skills and the examples are examinable.

A good investigation follows a fixed path from a question to a justified conclusion. Each step below builds on the one before, so working through them in order stops the research turning into a list of facts.

Step 1: Choose a focused, answerable question that links course chemistry to one theme, for example “Should…?”, “How effective is…?” or “What are the benefits and risks of…?” A focused question keeps the research from becoming too wide to finish.
Step 2: Identify the chemistry involved, such as reactions, equations and properties, so that the research explains why something happens and not only what happens.

Step 3: Find a range of sources: peer-reviewed papers and reviews (articles checked by independent experts before publication), reports from scientific and government bodies (e.g. the IPCC, the EPA, the HSE, WHO and Uisce Éireann), textbooks, and reputable science journalism. Include sources with different viewpoints.
Step 4: Evaluate each source by asking who wrote it and what expertise they have, when it was written (is it current?), and what evidence it gives (data and methods, or just opinion?).
Step 4 also asks whether the source was peer reviewed, and whether the author has a purpose or bias, e.g. funding, selling a product or campaigning.

Step 5: Separate measured data from claims and opinion, compare like with like, and note uncertainties and where scientists disagree. Comparing like with like means the figures you set side by side were measured in the same way.
Step 6: Weigh the evidence on each side, considering benefits, risks, costs and who is affected, locally and globally, now and in the future.
Step 7: Reach a justified conclusion that answers the question, explain the chemistry behind it, state its limitations and suggest further research.
Step 8: Reference all sources consistently, so a reader can find them, and communicate clearly for the audience (a presentation or digital report), using correct chemical terms, equations and units.
This outline shows Steps 1 to 3 applied to a health question. Fluoride is added to Irish public water supplies to protect teeth, and whether that should continue is a real public debate.
Question: “Should Ireland continue to add fluoride to public drinking water?” This is a Step 1 question because it can be answered by weighing evidence.
Chemistry: hexafluorosilicic acid (H₂SiF₆) is added to give 0.6–0.8 mg L⁻¹ of fluoride, a very small concentration. There is more on this in Treating drinking water.

Chemistry: fluoride converts some hydroxyapatite (the mineral that makes up tooth enamel) into fluorapatite, which resists acids made by bacteria in the mouth. This is why fluoride protects teeth from decay.

Sources: Department of Health and HSE information, systematic reviews of the evidence (e.g. Cochrane reviews, which gather and assess many studies together), dental and medical bodies, and the views of groups opposed to fluoridation.

Check the dates of sources, as older studies were done before fluoride toothpaste was common. This matters because the effect of fluoride in water may look different once toothpaste is also supplying it.
Steps 5 to 7 mean setting the evidence for and against side by side and then judging it. For fluoridation, each side has points that must be weighed rather than just listed.
Evidence for: fluoridation reduces tooth decay, with most benefit to people who can't afford dental care, because the fluoride reaches everyone through the water supply.
Evidence for: fluoridation is low cost per person, since one treatment step at the water plant serves a whole population.
Evidence and issues against: dental fluorosis (a change in the appearance of tooth enamel) occurs at higher intakes, so the amount of fluoride matters.
Evidence and issues against: the benefit may be smaller now that fluoride toothpaste is widely used, because teeth already get fluoride from another route.
Evidence and issues against: there are ethical objections to adding a substance to everyone's water without individual consent.
Evidence and issues against: most European countries don't fluoridate water.
Conclusion: a justified judgement weighing the size of the benefit against the risks and ethical issues, based on the most recent reviews.
This outline applies the stages to a sustainability question. The chemistry of what happens to the carbon in an Irish bog depends on whether the peat is wet or drained.
Question: “Is rewetting drained Irish bogs an effective way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions?”

Chemistry: in waterlogged peat (partly decayed plant material), decay is very slow because oxygen is lacking, so carbon builds up in a carbon sink (a store that takes in more carbon than it releases). There is more on this in The natural greenhouse effect and The enhanced greenhouse effect.
Chemistry: when bogs are drained, oxygen gets in and aerobic decay (decay by microorganisms that use oxygen) releases the stored carbon as CO₂.
Chemistry: when the peat is rewetted, the CO₂ release stops, but anaerobic microorganisms (those that live without oxygen) produce some methane (CH₄), which is a stronger greenhouse gas per kg.
Sources: EPA Ireland reports, and Bord na Móna and National Parks and Wildlife Service information.
Sources: peer-reviewed studies of emissions from drained and rewetted bogs, and farming organisations. These groups have different interests, so compare their viewpoints.
Rewetting trades one gas for another, and it also affects people. Weighing it means comparing the climate effects with each other and then with the social ones.

The size of the CO₂ savings is set against the methane emissions. The two are compared using GWPs (global warming potentials, a measure of how strongly each gas warms the atmosphere) and CO₂ equivalent (an amount of any gas expressed as the amount of CO₂ that would warm the same).
Rewetting has benefits for biodiversity and flood control, which are gains beyond the climate effect.
Rewetting affects landowners, jobs and communities that depended on peat, so the people affected must be part of the weighing.
The time scales of the carbon savings and the methane emissions must be considered, because the two may not happen over the same period.
Conclusion: a justified judgement on whether the evidence shows a net climate benefit, and under what conditions.

Public water supplies must be disinfected to kill microorganisms that cause disease. This outline compares two technologies, chemical (chlorine) and physical (UV light), which is a typical technology question.
Question: “Can UV treatment replace chlorine for disinfecting public water supplies?”
Chemistry: chlorine forms hypochlorous acid (Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HOCl + HCl), which kills microorganisms and leaves a residual (disinfectant that stays in the water) in the pipes.
Chemistry: UV (ultraviolet light) damages microbial DNA and works against chlorine-resistant Cryptosporidium (a microorganism that causes water-borne disease), but it leaves no residual.
Chemistry: chlorine can react with organic matter in the water to form disinfection by-products, e.g. trihalomethanes. There is more on this in Treating drinking water.
Sources: Uisce Éireann and EPA drinking-water reports, WHO guidelines, and studies of disinfection by-products.
Case study: the 2007 Galway Cryptosporidium outbreak.
Neither method is best on every measure, so the evaluation sets several issues against each other before reaching a conclusion.
Issue: the effectiveness of each method against different microorganisms, since chlorine and UV do not work equally well on all of them.
Issue: the protection each method gives in the distribution pipes, where a residual disinfectant keeps working after the water leaves the plant.
Issue: the health risks of by-products, set against the much larger risk of water-borne disease.
Issue: the energy use of UV lamps, and cost.
Conclusion: UV is a valuable extra barrier but cannot fully replace chlorine, because a residual disinfectant is needed in the pipes. The reasoning must be shown.
The syllabus asks you to see chemistry as something people do together, with effects well beyond the lab. Personal research is one way to appreciate that.
Modern chemistry is done by teams, often international, and builds on the work of others, so no single scientist works alone.

The lithium-ion battery came from the work of three scientists in different countries over decades. Goodenough (USA), Whittingham (UK-born, USA) and Yoshino (Japan) shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019. There is more on this in The lithium-ion cell.
The IPCC reports are written by hundreds of scientists assessing thousands of studies, which shows collaboration at a global scale.
Chemistry affects society globally through clean water, medicines, energy and materials, and also through pollution and climate change.
Personal research helps students judge claims and take part in public debate, because they can check the chemistry and the evidence behind what they hear.
Thermochemistry rests on one principle: energy is never lost, it only moves between the chemicals and their surroundings. Every energy calculation and explanation in this chapter relies on it.

Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another or transferred. This is why saying energy is 'used up' is wrong: it has gone somewhere else.

In a chemical reaction, chemical energy stored in bonds (the attractions that hold atoms together) is changed into, or comes from, other forms, mainly heat, but also light, sound and electrical energy.
Thermochemistry is the study of the heat changes that take place during chemical reactions and physical changes (changes of state, such as melting or boiling, where no new substance forms).
The system is the reacting chemicals; the surroundings are everything else, such as the solvent (the liquid the chemicals are dissolved in), container, air and thermometer.
Energy lost by the system is gained by the surroundings, and vice versa, so the total stays the same.

This law underpins all of thermochemistry: it is why the heat a reaction gives out can be measured as the heat gained by water, and why Hess's law (the rule for combining enthalpy changes of linked reactions) works. There is more on this in Hess's law.

To compare the heat given out or taken in by different reactions, chemists need a measure of the energy stored in chemicals. That measure is enthalpy, and the quantity you actually use is the change in it.
Enthalpy (H) is the heat content, or stored energy, of a substance. It cannot be measured directly, but changes in it can.
The enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat change in a process carried out at constant pressure (the pressure stays the same throughout): ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
The unit of ΔH is kJ mol⁻¹, meaning kJ per mole (the chemist's unit for an amount of substance) of reaction as written in the equation.

A negative ΔH means heat is given out to the surroundings (exothermic); a positive ΔH means heat is taken in (endothermic). There is more on this in the blocks on exothermic and endothermic reactions below.
Heat of reaction: the heat change when the numbers of moles of reactants shown in the balanced equation react completely.
Every reaction involves breaking bonds, so chemists measure how much energy a bond holds. That measure is bond enthalpy, and it tells you how strong a bond is.
Bond enthalpy: the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond (a bond in which atoms share electrons), with the molecules and the separated atoms all in the gaseous state.
Example: H₂(g) → 2H(g), ΔH = +436 kJ mol⁻¹, so the H–H bond enthalpy is 436 kJ mol⁻¹.
Bond enthalpies are always positive, because energy must always be supplied to break a bond.
The strength of the same type of bond varies slightly from one molecule to another, e.g. a C–H bond in methane and in ethanol, so tables give average bond enthalpies, averaged over many compounds.

The larger the bond enthalpy, the stronger the bond. The triple bond in nitrogen, N≡N (945 kJ mol⁻¹), is very strong, which is why nitrogen gas is so unreactive: a great deal of energy is needed to break it. There is more on this in ΔH from bond enthalpies.

A reaction is a swap of bonds: old ones in the reactants (the starting chemicals) are broken and new ones form in the products (the chemicals made). Whether heat is given out or taken in depends on which side of the swap involves more energy.
In a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds are made in the products.
Bond breaking requires energy, so it is endothermic (it takes energy in).
Bond making releases energy, so it is exothermic (it gives energy out); forming a bond releases the same amount of energy as breaking it requires.
If more energy is released making the new bonds than is used breaking the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall (the net result is heat given out) and ΔH is negative.
If more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making them, the reaction is endothermic overall and ΔH is positive.
Example: in H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), one H–H bond and one Cl–Cl bond are broken and two H–Cl bonds are made.
The energy released forming the two strong H–Cl bonds is greater than the energy needed to break the reactant bonds, so the reaction is exothermic.

Example: in the combustion (burning in oxygen) of methane, the C–H and O=O bonds broken need less energy than is released forming the very strong C=O bonds in CO₂ and O–H bonds in H₂O, so combustion is strongly exothermic.
Even a reaction that gives out heat overall needs a push to get started, and the same bond balance explains the everyday processes the specification names.

Every reaction needs some energy to start breaking bonds, called the activation energy, even if it is exothermic overall. This is why a fuel such as methane does not burn until it is lit. There is more on this in Catalysis and energy profiles.
The processes the specification names all transfer energy as heat because of this balance of bond breaking and making.

They are combustion, neutralisation (an acid reacting with a base), thermal decomposition (breaking a compound down by heating), rusting of iron, photosynthesis (plants making glucose using sunlight) and respiration (cells releasing energy from glucose).
Whether each one gives out or takes in heat depends on whether more energy is released making bonds or needed to break them.
Energy changes are not limited to reactions. When a substance melts, boils or dissolves, no new substance forms, but heat is still taken in or given out.
Changes of state involve enthalpy changes because intermolecular forces (the weak attractions between separate molecules) are overcome or formed. Covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken.
Boiling water breaks the intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between H₂O molecules, not the O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule, so the molecules stay intact as steam.
Melting, boiling and sublimation (solid changing straight to gas) are endothermic: energy is needed to overcome the forces between particles.
Water melting: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔH = +6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ (at 0 °C). Water boiling: H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 100 °C.
Freezing and condensing are exothermic: the same amounts of energy are released as the forces form. This is why steam condensing on skin gives a severe burn.
Dissolving can be exothermic or endothermic. Dissolving sodium hydroxide or concentrated sulfuric acid in water gives out heat.
Dissolving ammonium nitrate takes in heat, which is used in instant cold packs.
Evaporation of sweat cools the body because the water takes in heat from the skin as it evaporates.
Reactions are sorted by the direction of heat flow. The names, the sign of ΔH and the temperature change you can observe all tell the same story.
An exothermic reaction gives out heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative and the products have less enthalpy than the reactants, because the system has lost heat.
An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive and the products have more enthalpy than the reactants, because the system has gained heat.
In an exothermic reaction in solution, the temperature of the mixture rises, so the container feels warm.
In an endothermic reaction in solution, the temperature falls, so the container feels cold, unless heat is being supplied continuously, as in thermal decomposition.

A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation with state symbols ((s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water) and the ΔH value, e.g. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
State symbols matter because changes of state also have enthalpy changes.
Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH: if A → B has ΔH = −x, then B → A has ΔH = +x.

ΔH is proportional to the amounts in the equation, because twice as many moles react: doubling every coefficient (the number in front of each formula) doubles ΔH, e.g. 2CH₃OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), ΔH = −1452 kJ (2 × −726).
Many familiar processes give out heat. Learn the equation and ΔH for each of the named ones, and how to explain why each is exothermic.
Combustion: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹; all combustion reactions are exothermic.
Neutralisation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹. The ionic equation (showing only the ions that react) is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ −2800 kJ mol⁻¹; it releases energy in cells, which keeps warm-blooded animals warm.

Rusting of iron: iron reacts slowly with oxygen and water, which are both needed, to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (an oxide that has water combined with it). The simplified overall equation is 4Fe(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Fe₂O₃(s), ΔH = −1648 kJ.
Rusting is exothermic, but the heat is released so slowly that it isn't noticed. Hand warmers use fast oxidation (reaction with oxygen) of iron powder to give out heat.
Other everyday exothermic processes: reactive metals reacting with acid or water, dissolving sodium hydroxide, condensing and freezing.
Endothermic changes take heat or light in from the surroundings. Some need heat supplied the whole time they run, which is why they only keep going while you keep heating.
Thermal decomposition: breaking down a compound by heating needs a continuous supply of heat, e.g. CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ (making lime).
Sodium hydrogencarbonate also decomposes endothermically: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g), which is the reaction of baking powder in baking.
Photosynthesis: 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g), ΔH ≈ +2800 kJ mol⁻¹; the energy is absorbed from sunlight.
Photosynthesis and respiration are the reverse of each other, so their ΔH values are equal in size and opposite in sign.
Other endothermic processes: melting, boiling, dissolving ammonium nitrate (cold packs), and the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.
A diagram shows at a glance whether a reaction gives out or takes in heat, and how much. There are two ways to draw the transfer.
An enthalpy level diagram has enthalpy (H) on the vertical axis, a horizontal line for the reactants and one for the products, and a vertical arrow between them labelled ΔH.
Exothermic: the products line is below the reactants line, the arrow points down, ΔH is negative, and the energy difference is released to the surroundings as heat.
Endothermic: the products line is above the reactants line, the arrow points up, ΔH is positive, and the energy difference is taken in from the surroundings.

A second way to model the transfer is a box containing the system, with arrows for heat flowing out to the surroundings (exothermic: the surroundings get warmer) or in from them (endothermic: the surroundings get cooler).

Diagram: two enthalpy level diagrams side by side: combustion of methane (CH₄ + 2O₂ above CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, arrow down) and decomposition of calcium carbonate (CaO + CO₂ above CaCO₃, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, arrow up).

Energy profile diagrams, which also show the activation energy (the energy needed to start the reaction) along the reaction pathway, are not needed here. There is more on this in Calculating ΔH and energy profiles.

Neutralisation gives out heat, and that heat can be measured with a thermometer. This experiment turns a temperature rise into an enthalpy change (ΔH, the heat change of a reaction) for hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide.
Aim: to determine the heat of neutralisation (ΔH) of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide, using primary data (results you measure yourself in the experiment).
Heat of neutralisation is the heat change when one mole of water is formed in the reaction between an acid and a base, i.e. one mole of H⁺ ions reacting with one mole of OH⁻ ions.
Equation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l); ionic equation (showing only the ions that actually react): H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
ΔH is the heat change at constant pressure. The cup is open to the atmosphere, so the pressure stays constant during the reaction.

The heat released by the reaction is absorbed by the solution, so the heat produced is found from the temperature rise of the solution: Q = m × c × ΔT (Q is the heat, m the mass of solution, c its specific heat capacity and ΔT the temperature rise).
The method mixes equal amounts of acid and base in an insulated cup and records the highest temperature reached. Each step is there to give an accurate temperature rise.
Step 1: using a graduated cylinder (or, more accurately, a burette or pipette), measure 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M hydrochloric acid into a polystyrene foam cup, which insulates the reaction.
Step 2: measure 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M sodium hydroxide into a second cup or beaker, so the two solutions stay separate until mixed.
Step 3: allow both solutions to reach room temperature, then measure the temperature of each with a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C (or a temperature sensor).
Step 4: rinse and dry the thermometer between the two measurements so no solution is carried across. If the two temperatures differ, take their average as the initial temperature.
Step 5: add the sodium hydroxide to the acid quickly and all at once, put on the lid, and stir gently with the thermometer (or a stirrer).
Step 6: record the highest temperature reached, because the heat produced is worked out from the biggest rise.
Step 7: repeat the experiment and use the mean temperature rise, which reduces the effect of a single poor reading.
Diagram: a polystyrene cup with a lid, a thermometer through the lid into the solution, a stirrer, and the cup standing in a beaker for support.
Every detail of the method has a reason, and the exam asks for these reasons. Most of them are about stopping heat escaping or making a small temperature change easier to read.
Polystyrene foam is a good insulator with a very low heat capacity, so little heat is lost to the surroundings or absorbed by the cup; glass or metal would conduct heat away and absorb heat.
The lid reduces heat loss by convection (heat carried away by moving air) and evaporation.

Moderately concentrated (1.00 M) solutions give a large enough temperature rise (about 7 °C) to measure accurately; with 0.1 M solutions the rise would be under 1 °C, and the percentage error in reading it would be very large.
Equal amounts of acid and base (same volume and concentration) are used so that all of each reacts, so the moles of water formed is known.
Mixing quickly and stirring make the reaction complete at once and spread the heat evenly, so the true maximum temperature is recorded before heat is lost.
A thermometer reading to 0.1 °C is needed because the temperature change is small.
A burette or pipette measures volumes more accurately than a graduated cylinder.
The disadvantage of adding the base slowly from a burette is that heat is lost while it is added.
In the simple method, the mixture starts cooling as soon as it reaches its peak, so the highest reading is a little too low. A temperature–time graph corrects for this.
Record the temperature of the acid every 30 s for a few minutes before mixing, then add the base at a recorded time.
Record the temperature every 30 s for several minutes after mixing, so the whole rise and the cooling that follows are captured.
After the maximum, the temperature falls gradually because heat is lost to the surroundings.

Plot temperature against time and extrapolate (extend) the cooling line back to the time of mixing. The temperature rise read from the graph allows for heat lost while the mixture was warming up, giving a more accurate ΔT.
Diagram: a temperature–time graph with a flat line before mixing, a sharp rise, a gently falling line after the maximum, and the falling line extended back to the time of mixing to give ΔT.
To turn the temperature rise into ΔH, find the heat produced, then divide by the moles of water formed. Each step uses the total mass of the mixture, not the mass of acid alone.
Data: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M HCl and 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M NaOH; initial temperature 18.4 °C; maximum 25.0 °C.
Temperature rise: ΔT = 25.0 − 18.4 = 6.6 °C = 6.6 K; a temperature change is the same in °C and K, so no conversion is needed.
Mass of solution: 100 cm³ × 1.00 g cm⁻³ = 100 g = 0.100 kg, assuming the density and specific heat capacity are those of water.
Heat produced: Q = m × c × ΔT = 0.100 kg × 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 6.6 K = 2.76 kJ.
Moles of water formed = moles of HCl = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol.
Heat per mole: 2.76 kJ ÷ 0.0500 mol = 55.2 kJ mol⁻¹, because ΔH is defined per mole of water formed.
The reaction gives out heat, so ΔH = −55.2 kJ mol⁻¹: Q is the heat gained by the solution, and ΔH is the heat lost by the reaction.

Comparison: the accepted value for a strong acid with a strong base is about −57 kJ mol⁻¹; the experimental value is less negative mainly because some heat was lost to the surroundings and absorbed by the cup and thermometer.
The result does not depend on which strong acid or base you use, but it does change for weak ones. Acids that release two H⁺ ions need extra care when counting moles.

All strong acid–strong base neutralisations have almost the same ΔH, about −57 kJ mol⁻¹, because the acids and bases are fully dissociated (split completely into ions) and the only reaction is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l); the other ions are spectators.
With a weak acid (e.g. ethanoic acid) or a weak base (e.g. ammonia), ΔH is slightly less negative, because some energy is used to complete the dissociation of the weak acid or base as it reacts.
With a diprotic acid (one that can give two H⁺ ions per molecule), count moles of water, not moles of acid: H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).
Sample data: 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 M H₂SO₄ + 50.0 cm³ of 2.00 M NaOH, with ΔT = 17.8 K.
Moles of water = moles of NaOH = 2.00 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol, so ΔH = −55.8 kJ mol⁻¹ per mole of water.
Doubling the volumes of the same solutions gives the same ΔT: twice the moles react and twice the heat is produced, but it heats twice the mass of solution.
The solutions are hazardous, and the experiment always gives a value that differs from the accepted one. Knowing which errors push the value which way lets you suggest improvements.
Safety: 1.00 M hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are corrosive (they damage skin and eyes), sodium hydroxide especially to the eyes; wear safety glasses and gloves and wipe up spills.
Both bottles carry the GHS corrosion pictogram: liquid dripping from two test tubes onto a hand and a surface.

Errors that make the value less negative: heat lost to the air and bench; heat absorbed by the cup and thermometer; not recording the true maximum temperature; solutions starting at different temperatures.
Assumption error: the solution's density and specific heat capacity are taken as those of water.
Improvements: use the temperature–time graph, a lid, two nested cups, a more precise thermometer or temperature sensor, and burettes or pipettes for volumes.
An enthalpy change varies with the conditions it is measured in. So chemists agree one set of conditions, so that values from different reactions can be compared fairly.
Enthalpy changes depend on temperature, pressure and the physical states of the substances, so values are quoted under a standard set of conditions to allow comparison.
Standard conditions for enthalpy changes: a temperature of 25 °C (298 K) and a pressure of 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa).
Solutions have a concentration of 1 mol L⁻¹, and each substance is in its standard state, its normal physical state under these conditions, e.g. water as a liquid and carbon as graphite.
A standard enthalpy change is written ΔH° (ΔH with a superscript ⦵ or °), so the symbol shows the value refers to standard conditions.
IUPAC (the international chemistry body) now uses 100 kPa (1 bar) as standard pressure; the difference from 101.3 kPa has a negligible effect on ΔH values.
Standard conditions are not s.t.p. (standard temperature and pressure: 0 °C, 273 K and 101.3 kPa), which is used for gas volumes. There is more on this in Molar volume and Avogadro's law.

The neutralisation experiment and the zinc and copper(II) sulfate example below both follow the same five steps. The idea is to use the temperature change of a known mass of water or solution to find the heat, then scale to one mole.
Step 1: carry out the reaction in an insulated container (a polystyrene cup) with a known mass of water or solution, and measure the temperature change, ΔT.
Step 2: calculate the heat transferred to the water or solution: Q = m × c × ΔT, where m is the mass of water or solution in kg and ΔT is the temperature change in K or °C.
Here c is the specific heat capacity of the water or solution, 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water.

Step 3: calculate the moles of the reactant that reacted completely (the limiting reactant, the one that runs out first), using n = concentration × V (in L) for solutions or n = m ÷ M for solids and liquids.
Step 4: heat per mole = Q ÷ n, in kJ mol⁻¹, scaled to the moles in the balanced equation if the heat of reaction is asked for.

Step 5: give ΔH a sign: negative if the temperature rose (exothermic, giving out heat), positive if it fell (endothermic, taking in heat). Q is always positive; the sign of ΔH comes only from whether the temperature rose or fell.
Specific heat capacity, c, is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K; for water it is 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (= 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
Dilute solutions are assumed to have the same specific heat capacity as water and a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³, so 1 cm³ of solution is taken as 1 g.
If a heat capacity, C, of the whole mixture is given (in kJ K⁻¹ or J K⁻¹), use Q = C × ΔT instead.
This displacement reaction (a more reactive metal pushing a less reactive one out of solution) is measured in the same way as neutralisation. The key extra step is choosing the limiting reactant.
Data: excess zinc powder was added to 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 M copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup; the temperature rose by 10.0 °C.
Equation: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s); ionic equation: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
Zinc is in excess, so the copper(II) sulfate is the limiting reactant and fixes how much reacts.
Heat per mole = 2.09 ÷ 0.0100 = 209 kJ mol⁻¹; the temperature rose, so ΔH = −209 kJ mol⁻¹.
The value is a little less negative than the accepted value because of heat losses. There is more on errors and improvements in Investigation: heat of neutralisation.
A ΔH value is a heat per mole, so once you know it you can predict the heat for any amount of reactant. Work out the moles, then multiply.
ΔH refers to the moles in the equation as written, so the heat for any amount is found by proportion.
Example: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹; M(CH₄) = 16 g mol⁻¹, so 8.0 g of methane is 8.0 ÷ 16 = 0.50 mol.
Burning 0.50 mol of methane releases 0.50 × 890 = 445 kJ, because half a mole gives half the heat of a full mole.
Example: 0.0500 mol of HCl neutralised released 2.86 kJ, so 1 mol would release 2.86 ÷ 0.0500 = 57.2 kJ and ΔH = −57.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

An energy profile diagram is a graph of how the energy of a reaction changes as it goes from reactants to products. It shows both the overall heat change and the energy barrier the reaction has to climb.

An energy profile diagram shows how the energy (enthalpy) of the reacting system changes during the reaction, with energy on the vertical axis and progress of reaction (reaction pathway) on the horizontal axis.
It shows the reactants' level, a hump rising to a maximum, and the products' level; unlike an enthalpy level diagram (which only compares the two levels), it shows this hump.
The height of the hump above the reactants is the activation energy (Ea), the minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen. There is more on this in Catalysis and energy profiles.
ΔH is the vertical difference between the reactants' and products' levels and does not depend on the height of the hump.
Exothermic profile: products below reactants, ΔH is negative, and the energy released as bonds form is greater than the activation energy taken in.
Endothermic profile: products above reactants, ΔH is positive, and the activation energy is larger than ΔH.

Energy transfer: the energy taken in to climb the hump goes into breaking bonds, and the energy given out on the way down comes from bond making; the net difference is transferred as heat to the surroundings (exothermic) or from them (endothermic).

Diagram: an exothermic profile and an endothermic profile, each with axes labelled, reactants and products named, Ea marked with an arrow from the reactants to the top of the hump, and ΔH marked with an arrow from reactants to products.

Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break a particular covalent bond (a bond where atoms share electrons). Because the same type of bond varies slightly from molecule to molecule, tables give an average value for each, and these are the only values to use in this subsection. There is more on this in “Bond enthalpy and energy change”.
Single bonds (kJ mol⁻¹, kilojoules per mole of bonds broken): C–H 412, C–C 348, O–H 463, H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, C–Cl 338, C–Br 276, C–I 238.
Multiple bonds (double and triple bonds, where atoms share two or three pairs of electrons), in kJ mol⁻¹: C=C 614, C≡C 839, O=O 498.
Bonds in carbon dioxide and nitrogen (kJ mol⁻¹): C=O 799 (in CO₂), N≡N 945.

To predict ΔH (the enthalpy change, the heat energy change of a reaction at constant pressure), picture the reaction as breaking every old bond and then making every new bond. Breaking bonds takes energy in; making bonds gives energy out. The method turns that picture into five steps and a shortcut.
Step 1: write the balanced equation and draw the full structural formula of every reactant and product (a diagram showing every atom and every bond), so that every bond can be seen.
Step 2: list the bonds broken in the reactants, multiplying by the coefficients (the numbers in front of formulae) in the equation, and add up their bond enthalpies (energy taken in).
Step 3: list the bonds formed in the products in the same way and add up their bond enthalpies (energy released).
Step 4: ΔH = Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed), where Σ means “the sum of”. Broken comes first because energy taken in counts as positive.
Step 5: a negative answer predicts an exothermic reaction (one that gives out heat), and a positive answer an endothermic one (one that takes in heat).
Shortcut: bonds that are unchanged, present in both reactants and products, can be left out of both sums; the answer is the same because they cancel.
Combustion (burning in oxygen) of methane, the main gas in natural gas, is a good first example because it breaks and forms several different bond types. Here the water is gaseous (steam).
Equation: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g); CH₄ has four C–H bonds, each O₂ has one O=O, each CO₂ has two C=O, and each H₂O has two O–H.
Bonds broken: 4 × C–H = 4 × 412 = 1648 kJ; 2 × O=O = 2 × 498 = 996 kJ; total 2644 kJ.
Bonds formed: 2 × C=O = 2 × 799 = 1598 kJ; 4 × O–H = 4 × 463 = 1852 kJ; total 3450 kJ.
ΔH = 2644 − 3450 = −806 kJ mol⁻¹: exothermic, because more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them.
Comparison: the measured value for gaseous water is −802 kJ mol⁻¹, so the estimate is close. The standard value (measured with water as a liquid, the usual state at 25 °C) is −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
The extra 88 kJ is released when 2 mol of steam condense (2 × 44 kJ), which is why the standard value is more negative. The bond enthalpy estimate is for gaseous water.
Hydrogenation means adding hydrogen across a double bond. In ethene (a hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond) most bonds don't change, so this example shows the shortcut in use.
Bonds broken: C=C 614 + H–H 436 = 1050 kJ; the four C–H bonds of ethene are unchanged and are left out.
Bonds formed: C–C 348 + 2 × C–H 412 = 348 + 824 = 1172 kJ. The two new C–H bonds are the ones formed when hydrogen adds on, and the C=C becomes a single C–C.

ΔH = 1050 − 1172 = −122 kJ mol⁻¹; the value from heats of formation (calculated from the enthalpy changes of forming each substance from its elements) is −137 kJ mol⁻¹. There is more on this in “Hess's law”.
This reaction involves only diatomic molecules (molecules made of two atoms of the same element), so the calculation is short and the answer can be checked against a measured value.
This is very close to the measured value of about −185 kJ (2 × −92.3), because these diatomic molecules' bond enthalpies are exact values, not averages.
Chlorination means replacing a hydrogen atom in a compound with a chlorine atom. Only one C–H bond is swapped, so only the bonds that change need to be counted.
Bonds broken (only those that change): C–H 412 + Cl–Cl 242 = 654 kJ. The other three C–H bonds in methane are unchanged, so they are left out.
ΔH = 654 − 769 = −115 kJ mol⁻¹, which is negative, so the reaction is predicted to be exothermic.
A bond enthalpy calculation gives a prediction of ΔH, not an exact value. Knowing why it is approximate also lets you explain whether a reaction releases or absorbs energy.
Average bond enthalpies are averages over many different molecules; the actual strength of a bond in a particular molecule is a little different, so the calculated ΔH is only an estimate.

Bond enthalpies apply to substances in the gaseous state; if a reactant or product is a liquid or solid (e.g. liquid water), the enthalpy change of the change of state is not included, so the estimate differs from the standard value.

Values from heats of formation or careful measurement are more accurate; bond enthalpies are useful for predicting ΔH for reactions that haven't been measured and for explaining where the energy comes from.
A reaction is exothermic when the bonds formed are stronger in total than the bonds broken, e.g. combustion forms the very strong C=O and O–H bonds.
The table values follow patterns that can be explained by bond type and atom size. These patterns are used to explain why one bond is stronger than another.
Multiple bonds are stronger and shorter than single bonds between the same atoms: C–C 348 < C=C 614 < C≡C 839 kJ mol⁻¹.
A C=C bond is less than twice as strong as C–C, and C≡C less than three times as strong, because the second and third bonds are pi bonds, which are weaker than the first bond.

The first bond between two atoms is a sigma bond, formed by head-on overlap of orbitals (regions where electrons are found). Pi bonds are weaker because sideways overlap of p orbitals is less effective than head-on overlap.
For bonds from carbon to the halogens (the Group 17 elements), bond enthalpy falls down the group: C–Cl 338 > C–Br 276 > C–I 238 kJ mol⁻¹.
The halogen atom is larger for each step down the group, so the bond is longer and the shared electrons are further from the nuclei, which hold them less tightly.
The N≡N bond (945 kJ mol⁻¹) is one of the strongest, explaining why N₂ is very unreactive: a great deal of energy is needed to break it. There is more on this in “Shapes, bonding and isomerism”.
Some enthalpy changes (ΔH, the heat energy taken in or given out by a reaction) can't be measured directly. Hess's law gets round this by letting us work them out from reactions that can be measured.
Hess's law: if a reaction takes place in a number of stages, the total enthalpy change for the stages is equal to the enthalpy change if the reaction takes place in one stage.
In other words, ΔH depends only on the initial and final states (the reactants you start with and the products you end with), not on the route taken between them.

It follows from the law of conservation of energy (energy can't be created or destroyed). If two routes between the same reactants and products had different ΔH values, energy could be created by going one way and returning the other.
It lets us calculate ΔH for reactions that can't be measured directly, e.g. the formation of methane from carbon and hydrogen, or of carbon monoxide.
Carbon monoxide can't be measured directly because burning carbon in limited oxygen always gives some CO₂ too, so the heat measured would not belong to one reaction only.
Germain Henri Hess (1802–1850), a Swiss-born chemist who worked in St Petersburg, published the law in 1840.
Hess's law can be drawn as a diagram. An energy cycle puts the unknown ΔH on one side and a route of known ΔH values on the other, so the unknown can be found by adding.
An energy cycle (Hess cycle) shows the direct route from reactants to products and an indirect route through intermediate substances, with ΔH on each arrow.
ΔH for the direct route equals the sum of ΔH along the indirect route, because both routes start and end at the same place.
When going along an arrow in the opposite direction, change the sign of its ΔH, because the reverse of a reaction has the opposite enthalpy change.

Methane cycle: the top arrow is C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g) (ΔH = ?), the unknown heat of formation (the ΔH for making a compound from its elements). Both sides lead down to the combustion products CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) (+ O₂).

From the elements to the combustion products: ΔH = ΔHc(C) + 2ΔHc(H₂). ΔHc is the heat of combustion (the ΔH for burning one mole of a substance in oxygen). From methane to the combustion products: ΔH = ΔHc(CH₄).

The same cycle can be modelled as an enthalpy level diagram (a diagram where higher means more enthalpy), with the elements, the compound and the combustion products at different levels and arrows between them.
Diagram: the triangular Hess cycle for methane with all three arrows labelled with their ΔH values, and the same information as an enthalpy level diagram.
Instead of a diagram, you can work with the equations themselves. You adjust the given equations until they add up to the one you want, and adjust their ΔH values in the same way.
Write the target equation first, so you know what the final answer must look like.
Rearrange the given equations so that each substance in the target ends up on the correct side in the correct amount.
Reverse an equation to put a substance on the other side, and change the sign of its ΔH.
Multiply an equation by a number to get the right amount, and multiply its ΔH by the same number.
Add the equations and their ΔH values.
Cancel substances that appear on both sides, then check that the result is the target equation.
Heats of formation give every compound a reference value measured from its elements. With a table of them, you can find the ΔH of any reaction using Hess's law.

Standard heat (enthalpy) of formation, ΔHf°: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states (the usual physical form of each element) under standard conditions.
Formation equations have exactly one mole of product, so fractions may be needed, e.g. ½N₂(g) + 1½H₂(g) → NH₃(g), ΔHf = −46 kJ mol⁻¹.
More formation equations: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔHf = −394 kJ mol⁻¹, and 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l), ΔHf = −278 kJ mol⁻¹.
The heat of formation of an element in its standard state is zero by definition, as nothing is formed, e.g. O₂(g), H₂(g) and C(graphite). CO₂ is a compound, so its ΔHf is not zero.
The heats of formation of CO₂ and H₂O equal the heats of combustion of carbon and hydrogen, which can be measured directly.
Most heats of formation, e.g. of methane, ethanol or ethanoic acid, can't be measured directly and are found by Hess's law from heats of combustion.

From heats of formation: ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants), each multiplied by its coefficient. Σ means the sum of, and the coefficient is the number in front of the substance in the balanced equation.
This follows from Hess's law, going from reactants to elements and then to products.

Methane can't be made cleanly from carbon and hydrogen in a calorimeter (a device that measures heat), but its heat of combustion can be measured. Here the equations are combined to find the heat of formation.
Target: C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g). Given: (a) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394; (b) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286; (c) CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
Keep (a), because it already has C on the left as in the target: ΔH = −394.
Multiply (b) by 2, because the target needs 2H₂: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, ΔH = −572.
Reverse (c), because CH₄ must be a product in the target: CO₂ + 2H₂O → CH₄ + 2O₂, ΔH = +890.
Add the equations: C + 2H₂ + 2O₂ + CO₂ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 2H₂O + CH₄ + 2O₂; cancelling gives C + 2H₂ → CH₄.
ΔHf(CH₄) = −394 − 572 + 890 = −76 kJ mol⁻¹; the data-book value is −75 kJ mol⁻¹, and the difference comes from rounding.
Now the method runs the other way: a heat of combustion (the ΔH for burning one mole of a substance in oxygen) is found from heats of formation using products minus reactants.
Equation: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l); ΔHf: C₂H₅OH(l) −278, CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286, O₂(g) 0 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ is zero because it is an element in its standard state.
ΣΔHf(products) = 2(−394) + 3(−286) = −788 − 858 = −1646 kJ. Each ΔHf is multiplied by its coefficient.
ΔH = −1646 − (−278) = −1368 kJ mol⁻¹; the standard value is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹.
Propane follows the same pattern as ethanol: add up the formation values of the products, subtract those of the reactants, and use the coefficients from the balanced equation.
Equation: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l); ΔHf: C₃H₈ −104, CO₂ −394, H₂O −286 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ is left out of the sum because its ΔHf is zero.

Ethyne (C₂H₂) is a case where the heat of formation comes out positive. The calculation uses the energy cycle result from earlier: elements to combustion products, minus compound to combustion products.
Target: 2C(s) + H₂(g) → C₂H₂(g). Given ΔHc: C −394, H₂ −286, C₂H₂ −1300 kJ mol⁻¹.
The positive value shows ethyne is formed endothermically (heat is taken in): it has more enthalpy than its elements, which helps explain why it releases so much energy when burned.
This problem has no formation or combustion data to lean on. You must reverse and multiply the given equations until they add up to the target.
Target: 2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 3S(s) + 2H₂O(l). Given: (a) H₂(g) + S(s) → H₂S(g), ΔH = −21; (b) S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −297; (c) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ mol⁻¹.
Reverse (a) and multiply by 2, because the target has 2H₂S on the left: 2H₂S → 2H₂ + 2S, ΔH = +42.
Reverse (b), because SO₂ is on the left in the target: SO₂ → S + O₂, ΔH = +297.
Multiply (c) by 2, because the target has 2H₂O on the right: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, ΔH = −572.
Add and cancel 2H₂ and O₂: 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O; ΔH = 42 + 297 − 572 = −233 kJ.

Burning is the everyday reaction that powers fires, cookers and engines. Chemists define it precisely, and then measure how much heat it gives out per mole of fuel, a quantity called the heat of combustion.

Combustion is the reaction of a substance with oxygen, giving out heat (and usually light). It is always exothermic, which means it releases energy to the surroundings, so the temperature around it rises.

Complete combustion happens in plenty of oxygen: all the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen becomes water. For hydrocarbons (compounds of only carbon and hydrogen) and alcohols the only products are CO₂ and H₂O.

Incomplete combustion happens in limited oxygen. It also gives carbon monoxide (a toxic gas) and soot (carbon), and releases less energy because less of the fuel is fully oxidised, e.g. 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l).

Standard heat of combustion, ΔHc°: the enthalpy change (the heat change at constant pressure) when one mole of a substance is completely burned in excess oxygen under standard conditions (25 °C, 101.3 kPa). It is always negative, because combustion is exothermic.

Because it is per mole of the substance burned, the equation for a heat of combustion has 1 mol of fuel, so fractions of O₂ may be needed, e.g. C₂H₆(g) + 3½O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), ΔHc = −1560 kJ mol⁻¹.
The same equation doubled, 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O, has ΔH = −3120 kJ, because twice as many moles of fuel burn and so twice as much heat is released.
Every complete combustion equation can be balanced by the same five steps. The order matters: carbon first, hydrogen second, and oxygen last, because oxygen appears in more than one product.
Step 1: write the formula of the fuel and the products CO₂ and H₂O.
Step 2: balance carbon. The number of CO₂ equals the number of C atoms in the fuel, since each CO₂ holds one carbon.
Step 3: balance hydrogen. The number of H₂O equals half the number of H atoms in the fuel, since each H₂O holds two hydrogens.

Step 4: balance oxygen last. Count the O atoms in the products, subtract any O already in the fuel (one for an alcohol), and divide by two for the number of O₂, since each O₂ molecule holds two O atoms.
Step 5: double everything if you want whole numbers, for example to remove a ½ in front of O₂.

Check: count each type of atom on both sides, and add state symbols (fuel, O₂(g), CO₂(g), H₂O(l) under standard conditions). The (l) for water is because standard heats of combustion are measured with water as a liquid.

Each family of compounds follows a pattern, so one general equation covers every member. Here n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule. The range examined is hydrocarbons with no more than one double or triple bond, and primary alcohols (alcohols with the OH group on a carbon at the end of the chain) up to C6.
Alkanes (hydrocarbons with only single bonds): CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + ((3n + 1)/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O.
Alkenes (one C=C, a carbon-carbon double bond): CₙH₂ₙ + (3n/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + nH₂O.
Alkynes (one C≡C, a carbon-carbon triple bond): CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ + ((3n − 1)/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + (n − 1)H₂O.

These are the complete combustion equations for the alkanes, alkenes and alkyne you may be asked for, with water as a liquid. Where the fuel needs a half-molecule of oxygen, the doubled form gives whole numbers.
Propane: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), because 3 carbons give 3 CO₂ and 8 hydrogens give 4 H₂O.

Each alcohol already contains one oxygen atom in its OH group, so it needs less O₂ from the air than the alkane with the same number of carbons. Step 4 above (subtract the O in the fuel) is what gives these numbers.
Ethanol: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), because the products hold 7 oxygen atoms, one of which comes from the ethanol, so 6 atoms (3 O₂) come from the air.

These are the data values you are given and must be able to use to spot trends. Values are in kJ mol⁻¹ (kilojoules per mole) at 25 °C, with water as a liquid. All are negative because combustion is exothermic.
Alkanes: methane −890; ethane −1560; propane −2220; butane −2877. For example, each is more negative than the one before it.
Primary alcohols: methanol −726; ethanol −1367; propan-1-ol −2021; butan-1-ol −2676; pentan-1-ol −3331; hexan-1-ol −3984.
Two-carbon compounds: ethane −1560; ethene −1411; ethyne −1300; ethanol −1367.

In a homologous series (a family of compounds in which each member differs from the next by one CH₂ group), the heat of combustion changes in a very regular way. The reason lies in the bonds broken and formed for each extra CH₂.
ΔHc becomes more negative as the number of carbon atoms increases, by an almost constant amount for each extra CH₂, so more heat is released per mole of a longer molecule.
For alkanes the increase is about 650–670 kJ mol⁻¹, e.g. 1560 − 890 = 670 and 2877 − 2220 = 657.
For primary alcohols the increase is about 640–655 kJ mol⁻¹, e.g. 1367 − 726 = 641 and 2021 − 1367 = 654.
Each extra CH₂ group adds one C–C and two C–H bonds to break, and needs 1½ more O₂ molecules. It forms one more CO₂ (two C=O bonds) and one more H₂O (two O–H bonds).
More energy is released by the new bonds formed than is needed to break the extra bonds, so each extra CH₂ makes ΔHc more negative.
Because exactly the same extra bonds are broken and formed for every CH₂ added, the increase is nearly constant, so a graph of ΔHc against number of carbon atoms is a straight line.
Bond enthalpies (the energy needed to break one mole of a given bond) let you put a number on the increase per CH₂. The regular straight-line trend also lets you predict a missing value.
Bond enthalpy estimate per CH₂, using C–C 348, C–H 412, O=O 498, C=O 799 and O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹: broken 348 + 2(412) + 1½(498) = 1919 kJ; formed 2(799) + 2(463) = 2524 kJ; difference −605 kJ.
This estimate is for gaseous water. The measured increase is larger because the water formed is liquid, which means extra heat is released when the vapour condenses.
The straight-line trend can be used to predict values, e.g. hexan-1-ol ≈ −3331 − 655 = −3986 kJ mol⁻¹, close to the data value of −3984 kJ mol⁻¹.
An alcohol and the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms give the same CO₂ and H₂O, yet the alcohol releases less heat. The difference comes from the oxygen already inside the alcohol.
A primary alcohol has a less negative ΔHc than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms, e.g. ethanol −1367 against ethane −1560 kJ mol⁻¹, and methanol −726 against methane −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
The alcohol molecule already contains an oxygen atom bonded to carbon and hydrogen (C–O–H), so it is already partly oxidised (it has already combined with some oxygen).
It therefore needs less oxygen (ethanol 3 O₂, ethane 3½ O₂), and less energy is released on complete oxidation, although the same numbers of CO₂ and H₂O are formed.
Comparing compounds with the same number of carbon atoms but different numbers of hydrogens shows a second pattern. Fewer hydrogens means less water formed.
For the same number of carbon atoms, ΔHc becomes less negative in the order alkane, then alkene, then alkyne: ethane −1560, ethene −1411, ethyne −1300 kJ mol⁻¹.
The alkene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane, and the alkyne four fewer, so fewer water molecules (fewer O–H bonds) are formed and less energy is released.
The main reason is the fewer O–H bonds formed, not the C=C bond being harder to break.

You can estimate a heat of combustion in the lab by burning an alcohol under a can of water and measuring how much the water warms up. This investigation uses primary alcohols to test how heat of combustion changes along a series.

Aim: to estimate the heats of combustion of a series of primary alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol) using spirit burners (small lamps that burn liquid alcohol from a wick), and to compare them with standard values.
Heat of combustion: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in excess oxygen.
Principle: the heat released by burning a measured mass of alcohol is absorbed by a known mass of water, so Q = m(water) × c × ΔT.
Here c is the specific heat capacity of water (the heat needed to warm a given mass by one degree) and ΔT is the temperature rise, so Q is the heat the water has gained.
ΔHc = −Q ÷ moles of alcohol burned. The negative sign is there because heat released by the burning alcohol means a negative enthalpy change.
Hypothesis (the prediction being tested): the heat of combustion becomes more negative by a roughly constant amount for each extra CH₂ in the alcohol.
For a fair test, only one thing is changed, one thing is measured, and everything else is kept the same.
Independent variable (the one you change): the alcohol, i.e. the number of carbon atoms.
Dependent variable (the one you measure): the heat released per mole, calculated from the mass of alcohol burned and the temperature rise of the water.
Controlled (kept the same): the same volume (mass) of water, at the same starting temperature, so that the same heat gives the same temperature rise each time.
Controlled: the same copper can, the same distance from wick to can, and the same wick length, so that the share of heat reaching the can is similar for every alcohol.
Controlled: the same temperature rise (e.g. 20 °C), and the draught shield in the same position.
The method is the same for every alcohol: heat a fixed mass of water with the burner, and find out from the change in the burner's mass how much alcohol was burned.
Step 1: measure 100 cm³ (100 g) of water with a graduated cylinder into a copper can (calorimeter, a container used to measure heat changes).
Step 2: clamp the can a fixed distance (about 2–3 cm) above the wick of the spirit burner, and surround both with a draught shield.
Step 3: weigh the spirit burner containing the alcohol, with its cap on, on a balance reading to 0.01 g.
Step 4: record the initial temperature of the water.
Step 5: light the burner and stir the water gently with the thermometer or a stirrer.
Step 6: when the temperature has risen by about 20 °C, put out the flame by replacing the cap, and record the highest temperature reached.
Step 7: reweigh the burner with its cap at once. The mass burned is the initial mass minus the final mass.
Step 8: repeat with each alcohol, using fresh water each time, and repeat each alcohol to check reproducibility (that you get similar results each time).
The apparatus has several parts, and each one has a job in the method, so know every part and where it sits.

Diagram: a copper can of water held by a clamp above a spirit burner, a thermometer and stirrer in the water, a draught shield around the burner and can, the burner on a heat-proof mat, and a balance for weighing the burner.
Every feature of the set-up either gets more of the heat into the water or keeps the measurement of the alcohol burned accurate.
Copper is a good conductor of heat, so heat passes quickly from the flame into the water.
The draught shield reduces heat lost by air currents and keeps the flame steady.

Capping the burner as soon as the flame is out, and weighing immediately, stops the volatile alcohol (one that evaporates easily) evaporating from the wick, which would otherwise be counted as burned.
Stirring spreads the heat evenly, so the thermometer reading represents all the water.
The same temperature rise and set-up for each alcohol make the heat losses similar, so the comparison between alcohols is fair even if the absolute values are low.
A temperature rise of about 20 °C is large enough to measure accurately, but not so large that heat losses, which increase as the water gets hotter, become very large.
The calculation has two parts: the heat absorbed by the water, then that heat divided by the moles of alcohol burned. Here it is for ethanol, using sample data.
For each alcohol: 100 g (0.100 kg) of water heated through 20.0 °C gives Q = 0.100 × 4.18 × 20.0 = 8.36 kJ, using c(water) = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Ethanol (M = 46 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass): mass burned 0.63 g, so moles = 0.63 ÷ 46 = 0.0137 mol.
Heat per mole = 8.36 ÷ (0.63 ÷ 46) = 610 kJ mol⁻¹, so ΔHc(experimental) = −610 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
Percentage error = (standard − experimental) ÷ standard × 100, e.g. ethanol (1367 − 610) ÷ 1367 × 100 = 55%.
Repeating the calculation for all four alcohols gives a set of experimental values to compare with the standard ones.
Methanol (M = 32 g mol⁻¹): 0.82 g burned, giving ΔHc = −326 kJ mol⁻¹.
Propan-1-ol (M = 60 g mol⁻¹): 0.55 g burned, giving ΔHc = −912 kJ mol⁻¹.
Butan-1-ol (M = 74 g mol⁻¹): 0.51 g burned, giving ΔHc = −1210 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
Standard values are −726, −1367, −2021 and −2676 kJ mol⁻¹; each experimental value is about 45% of the standard value.
A graph of experimental ΔHc against number of carbon atoms is a straight line, like the standard values but less steep, so the trend is confirmed even though the values are too low.
The experimental values come out far below the standard ones. A good answer says why each error makes the value too low, not just that it is a problem.
Heat loss: much of the heat from the flame goes to the surrounding air rather than into the water; this is the main reason the values are much less negative than standard values.

Heat absorbed by the copper can, thermometer and clamp is not included in Q, so less heat is measured in the water and the value is too small. It could be added as m(copper) × c(copper) × ΔT, with c(copper) ≈ 0.385 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Incomplete combustion: with limited air at the wick, some carbon forms soot, seen on the base of the can, and carbon monoxide, releasing less energy than complete combustion.
Evaporation of alcohol from the wick: alcohol lost without burning is counted as burned, making the heat per mole too small.
Non-standard conditions: standard values assume products at 25 °C with water as a liquid; in the experiment the water leaves as vapour, so its heat of condensation is not released into the can.
Improvements to reduce heat loss: insulate the can and add a lid, reduce the distance between flame and can, and use a draught shield.
Improvements to reduce other errors: ensure a good air supply for complete combustion, cap and weigh the burner immediately, and include the heat absorbed by the can.
Accurate values are measured in a sealed calorimeter, which is not required here.
Alcohols burn easily and methanol is poisonous, so the main precautions are about fire and fumes.
Alcohols are highly flammable: keep bottles stoppered and away from flames, never refill a burner while it is lit or hot, and refill in a fume cupboard or away from flames.
Methanol is toxic by swallowing, by skin contact and by inhaling its vapour; avoid skin contact and work in a well-ventilated room.
Wear safety glasses, tie back long hair, stand the burner on a heat-proof mat, and let the copper can cool before handling it.

Electrochemistry is the study of the link between chemical reactions and electricity. A redox reaction is one in which one substance loses electrons (oxidation) while another gains them (reduction), and this is the reaction behind every cell below.
Redox reactions can produce electricity, in galvanic cells, and electricity can drive redox reactions, in electrolytic cells (cells that use an electric supply to force a reaction to happen).

A galvanic (voltaic) cell, also called a chemical cell, converts chemical energy into electrical energy using a spontaneous redox reaction, meaning one that happens by itself without any energy being supplied.
A battery is strictly two or more cells joined together, e.g. a 12 V car battery made of six 2 V cells, though the word is also used for a single cell.
An electrode is a solid electrical conductor, a metal or graphite (a form of carbon), through which electrons enter or leave the cell.

Electrons cannot pass through the electrolyte (the conducting liquid or paste in the cell), so they travel through the external circuit, the wires outside the cell, from anode to cathode. Inside the cell the charge is carried by ions.
Every cell has three working parts: two electrodes, where the chemistry happens, and an electrolyte between them. The two electrodes are named by what happens at them.
Anode: the electrode at which oxidation (loss of electrons) happens. In a galvanic cell it is the negative terminal and the source of the electrons that flow out into the external circuit.
Cathode: the electrode at which reduction (gain of electrons) happens. In a galvanic cell it is the positive terminal, where electrons from the external circuit are accepted.
Memory aid: “An Ox, Red Cat” (anode oxidation, reduction cathode), or CROA: Cathode Reduction, Oxidation Anode. This holds in every type of cell; only the signs change in electrolysis.
Electrolyte: a substance that conducts electricity by the movement of ions (charged atoms or groups of atoms), as a solution, a molten compound, a paste or a gel.
The electrolyte carries ions between the electrodes, which completes the circuit inside the cell. Electrons cannot cross it, which is why they are forced round the external circuit.
A primary cell is a galvanic cell that can be used only once. Its chemistry cannot be run backwards, so it is thrown away (and recycled) when it is finished.
Its redox reaction cannot be readily reversed, so when the reactants are used up the cell is “flat” and must be discarded and recycled.
Zinc–carbon cell (1.5 V): the zinc case is the anode (negative), where it is oxidised: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.
Zinc–carbon cell: a central carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by manganese(IV) oxide is the cathode (positive), where MnO₂ is reduced.
Zinc–carbon cell: the electrolyte is a moist paste of ammonium chloride, with zinc chloride.
Alkaline cell (1.5 V): a powdered zinc anode and a manganese(IV) oxide cathode, with potassium hydroxide, an alkali (a soluble base), as the electrolyte.
An alkaline cell lasts longer and gives a steadier voltage than a zinc–carbon cell.
Lithium primary cells (about 3 V) are small button or coin cells used in watches, calculators and car keys, with lithium metal as the anode.
Primary cells suit low-power or occasional devices that must work for a long time without attention, e.g. remote controls, clocks, smoke alarms and torches.
A secondary cell is a galvanic cell that can be recharged. “Secondary” does not mean a different kind of chemistry; it just means the cell is rechargeable.
