Connecting it to an external electrical supply forces its redox reaction to run in reverse, regenerating the reactants, so it can be used many times.
During discharge (when it supplies current) it works as a galvanic cell, converting chemical energy to electrical energy.
During recharging it works as an electrolytic cell, converting electrical energy to chemical energy.
The electrode that is the anode on discharge becomes the cathode on charge, and vice versa, because the reaction at each electrode is reversed.
Recharging is not perfect: side reactions and changes in the electrode structure slowly reduce how much charge a cell can hold.
Secondary cells therefore wear out after many cycles of discharging and recharging, typically hundreds to thousands.
Three secondary cells are worth knowing, each with a different voltage and use. Compare them with the primary cells above, which are used once and discarded.
Lead–acid cell (2 V per cell; six in a 12 V car battery): lead plates (negative) and lead(IV) oxide plates (positive) in sulfuric acid.
On discharge both plates become coated with lead(II) sulfate and the acid becomes more dilute; recharging by the car's alternator (the generator driven by the engine) reverses this.
Nickel–metal hydride (NiMH) cell (1.2 V): rechargeable AA and AAA cells used in place of alkaline cells.
Lithium-ion cell (about 3.6–3.7 V): used in phones, laptops and electric vehicles. There is more on this in The lithium-ion cell.
Both types supply electricity from a redox reaction, but they differ in whether the reaction can be reversed. That one difference drives their cost, waste, storage and uses.
Rechargeable: a primary cell cannot be, because its reaction is not readily reversible; a secondary cell can, because an external current reverses its reaction.
Cost: primary cells are cheap to buy but replaced often; secondary cells are dearer to buy, and need a charger, but cheaper per use over their life.

Waste and resources: primary cells produce far more waste per unit of energy delivered; secondary cells reduce waste and the mining of raw materials, which makes rechargeable batteries a more sustainable use of energy. There is more on this in Fuel cells and sustainability.

Storage: primary cells keep their charge for years on the shelf (low self-discharge, meaning little charge leaks away unused), so they suit emergency and low-drain devices; many secondary cells lose charge more quickly when stored.

Uses: primary cells suit low-drain (small current) or occasional devices; secondary cells suit high-drain devices used daily, such as phones, laptops, power tools, electric vehicles and car starter batteries.
Similarities: both are galvanic cells when supplying electricity, and both have an anode (oxidation), a cathode (reduction) and an electrolyte.
Both should be returned for recycling rather than put in household waste, because they contain metals that can pollute soil and water.
The galvanic cell grew out of Galvani's frog-leg experiments and Volta's disagreement with his explanation of them. Volta's work led to the first battery.
Luigi Galvani, working in Bologna in the 1780s, found that a dissected frog's leg twitched when touched by two different metals at once.
Galvani believed the electricity came from the animal itself, which he called “animal electricity”.
Alessandro Volta showed that the electricity came from two different metals in contact with a conducting liquid, not from the animal.
In 1800 Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile: a stack of zinc and copper (or silver) discs separated by cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water.
Galvanic cells, also called voltaic cells, are named after Galvani and Volta.
A redox reaction moves electrons from one substance to another. If the electrons are made to travel through a wire on the way, the reaction produces a current instead of just heat.
When zinc is put directly into copper(II) sulfate solution, zinc atoms give electrons straight to Cu²⁺ ions: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).

Copper is deposited, the blue colour fades and the energy is released as heat, with no useful current; this is a displacement reaction (a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of solution).
A galvanic cell separates the oxidation and the reduction into two half-cells, so the electrons must travel through an external wire from one to the other.
This flow of electrons is an electric current, which is why separating the half-cells produces useful electricity.
A half-cell is an electrode dipping into a solution of its own ions, e.g. zinc in zinc sulfate solution.
Which metal becomes the anode depends on the electrochemical series, the list that ranks metals by how easily they are oxidised. The positions of the two metals also decide the voltage.

The metal higher in the electrochemical series, the one more easily oxidised, becomes the anode (negative); the lower metal is the cathode (positive). There is more on the series in Balancing redox equations and the electrochemical series.
The further apart the two metals are in the electrochemical series, the greater the voltage of the cell.
Under standard conditions (1 M solutions, where M means mol L⁻¹, at 25 °C) the cell voltages are: magnesium–copper 2.71 V; zinc–copper 1.10 V; iron–copper 0.78 V.
The copper–zinc cell is the standard galvanic cell, with the zinc and copper in separate beakers joined by wires and a salt bridge (a link that lets ions pass between the beakers).
Set-up: a zinc strip in 1 M zinc sulfate solution and a copper strip in 1 M copper(II) sulfate solution, in separate beakers.
The metals are joined by wires through a voltmeter (a meter that measures voltage) or bulb, and the solutions by a salt bridge; the voltage is about 1.1 V.
Zinc electrode (anode, negative, oxidation): Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Zinc atoms lose electrons and go into solution as ions.
Copper electrode (cathode, positive, reduction): Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Copper(II) ions from the solution gain electrons and are deposited as copper.
Overall cell reaction: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), the same redox reaction as the direct displacement described above.
Zinc is the reducing agent (it gives electrons away, so it reduces the other substance) and Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent (it takes electrons, so it oxidises the zinc).
Electrons flow through the external wire from the zinc to the copper, because zinc is the anode and is oxidised.
As the cell runs, the reaction changes both electrodes and the solution. Each change follows directly from the half-equations.
Over time the zinc electrode wears away and loses mass, because zinc atoms become Zn²⁺ ions that dissolve.
The copper electrode gains a fresh pink-brown coating and gains mass, because Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to copper metal on it.
The blue colour of the copper(II) sulfate solution fades as Cu²⁺ is used up, and the voltage slowly falls.
The salt bridge connects the two solutions without letting them mix. Electrons cannot cross it, but ions can, and that is what keeps the cell working.
A salt bridge is a strip of filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate (or potassium chloride) solution, or a U-tube of the salt solution set in agar gel (a jelly that holds the solution in place).
It completes the circuit: ions move through it, carrying charge between the half-cells.
It keeps each solution electrically neutral: as Zn²⁺ ions build up in the zinc half-cell, negative ions (NO₃⁻) move into it.
As Cu²⁺ ions are removed from the copper half-cell, positive ions (K⁺) move into it.
Without it, charge would build up in each beaker and the current would stop at once.
Potassium nitrate is used because its ions do not react with the electrode solutions; it forms no precipitate (an insoluble solid that would appear in the solution).
This investigation builds a copper–zinc cell and tests what it needs in order to work. The aim is to build the cell, measure its voltage, and compare the voltages from different pairs of metals.

Variables: the independent variable (the one you change) is the pair of metals; the dependent variable (the one you measure) is the voltage; the controlled variables are the concentration and volume of the solutions, the temperature, and the size and cleanliness of the strips.
1. Clean strips of zinc and copper with sandpaper (emery paper) to remove the oxide layer, which would otherwise reduce the voltage.
2. Half-fill one beaker with 1 M zinc sulfate solution and another with 1 M copper(II) sulfate solution; stand the zinc strip in the first and the copper strip in the second.
3. Soak a strip of filter paper in potassium nitrate solution and drape it between the two beakers, with each end in a solution.
4. Connect the metals to a voltmeter with leads and crocodile clips, zinc to the negative terminal, and record the voltage.
5. Replace the voltmeter with a small bulb or LED to show that a current flows.
6. Remove the salt bridge and record the voltage again; it falls to zero, showing the bridge is needed.
7. Repeat with other metal pairs, e.g. magnesium–copper and iron–copper, each metal in a solution of its own ions, using a fresh salt bridge each time.
Once the cell is built, the results show how metal choice affects voltage. Safety and sources of error complete the write-up.
Results: the measured voltages are usually a little lower than the standard values, and the larger the gap between the metals in the electrochemical series, the larger the voltage.
A simpler cell: zinc and copper strips pushed into a lemon, or dipped into one beaker of salt solution or dilute acid, also give a voltage, because the juice or solution is an electrolyte.

Safety: wear goggles; copper(II) sulfate is harmful, an irritant and toxic to aquatic life, so do not pour it down the sink and dispose of it as directed; zinc sulfate is an irritant; wash hands afterwards.
Sources of error: an oxide layer left on the metals; solutions not exactly 1 M or not at 25 °C; the salt bridge drying out; the voltmeter drawing some current.

Diagram: two beakers, zinc in zinc sulfate and copper in copper(II) sulfate, joined by a potassium nitrate salt bridge, with wires from each metal to a voltmeter; label the anode (−) and cathode (+) and the direction of electron flow from zinc to copper.
Electrolysis is the use of electricity to bring about a chemical reaction, a redox reaction, that would not happen on its own. It is carried out in an electrolytic cell.
An electrolytic cell has two electrodes dipping into an electrolyte, which is a molten ionic compound or a solution of ions.
The electrodes are connected to an external source of direct current (d.c., current that flows one way only), e.g. a battery or power pack.
The external supply pumps electrons onto one electrode, making it negative, and removes electrons from the other, making it positive.
Positive ions (cations) move to the negative electrode, the cathode, where they gain electrons (reduction).
Negative ions (anions) move to the positive electrode, the anode, where they lose electrons (oxidation).
The current is carried by electrons in the wires and by moving ions in the electrolyte.
Inert electrodes (ones that do not react), platinum or carbon (graphite), conduct electricity but do not take part in the reaction; they ensure the products come only from the electrolyte.
Michael Faraday introduced the words electrolysis, electrode, anode, cathode and ion in 1834; electrolysis means breaking up by electricity.
A galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell are mirror images: one turns a reaction into electricity, the other turns electricity into a reaction.
Energy: a galvanic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy; an electrolytic cell converts electrical energy to chemical energy.
Reaction: a galvanic cell's reaction is spontaneous; an electrolytic cell's reaction is non-spontaneous and driven by the external supply.
Signs: in a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode positive; in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode negative.
In both cells oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode, because the anode is defined by oxidation, not by its sign.
A galvanic cell needs two different electrodes in two half-cells, usually with a salt bridge; an electrolytic cell can use two identical inert electrodes in one electrolyte.
Water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis. Pure water has almost no ions, so it needs help to conduct.
Pure water conducts electricity very poorly, so a little dilute sulfuric acid is added to provide ions and let a current flow.

Apparatus: a Hofmann voltameter (a glass apparatus with graduated tubes that collect the gases), or two inverted test tubes filled with the solution over the electrodes in a beaker, with platinum (or carbon) electrodes connected to a 6–12 V d.c. supply.
Bubbles of gas form at both electrodes; the volume of gas at the negative electrode is twice that at the positive electrode.
Test the gas from the negative electrode (cathode) with a lighted splint: it burns with a squeaky pop, so it is hydrogen.
Test the gas from the positive electrode (anode) with a glowing splint: it relights, so it is oxygen.
Diagram: a Hofmann voltameter with platinum electrodes and a d.c. supply, labelled cathode (−) with hydrogen and anode (+) with oxygen, the hydrogen column twice the height of the oxygen column.
The volumes of gas and the behaviour of the acid are explained by the formula of water and by what is removed from the solution.
The 2 : 1 volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen matches the formula H₂O, showing that water has been split into its elements.
In practice the oxygen volume is often slightly less than half, because oxygen is more soluble in water than hydrogen.
The sulfuric acid is not used up: only water is removed, so its concentration stays the same.

Water can also be split by electrolysing sodium sulfate solution with universal indicator (a dye that changes colour across the pH range) added: the same gases form, and the solution turns blue-purple around the cathode (OH⁻ formed) and red around the anode (H⁺ formed).
In this practical the copper(II) chloride is split into its two elements, copper and chlorine, and each product is identified by what you see or test at its electrode.
Set-up: copper(II) chloride solution in a U-tube or beaker, with two carbon (graphite) electrodes connected to a d.c. supply; carry out in a fume cupboard or for a short time only.
At the negative electrode (cathode) a pink-brown coating of copper metal forms.
At the positive electrode (anode) pale green bubbles of a gas with a sharp smell form; it turns damp blue litmus paper red and then bleaches it, so it is chlorine.
The blue-green colour of the solution fades as copper(II) ions are removed.
Safety: chlorine is toxic, so use a fume cupboard, keep the current on only briefly, and do not sniff the gas directly.
Diagram: a U-tube of copper(II) chloride solution with graphite electrodes and a d.c. supply, labelled copper at the cathode (−) and chlorine at the anode (+), with damp litmus paper at the anode.

Here the two products are identified with indicators: starch for iodine and phenolphthalein (an indicator that is pink in alkali) for hydroxide ions. The surprise is what does not form at the cathode.
Set-up: potassium iodide solution with a few drops of phenolphthalein, in a U-tube with two platinum (or carbon) electrodes connected to a d.c. supply.
At the positive electrode (anode) the solution turns brown (yellow-brown) as iodine forms; a drop of starch solution turns it blue-black, confirming iodine.
At the negative electrode (cathode) bubbles of hydrogen gas form, and the solution turns pink, showing that it has become alkaline because hydroxide ions have formed.
Potassium is not formed at the cathode: potassium is very high in the electrochemical series, so K⁺ ions are very hard to reduce and water is reduced instead.
Safety: wear goggles; iodine stains skin and is harmful.
Diagram: a U-tube of potassium iodide with phenolphthalein and platinum electrodes, labelled brown iodine at the anode (+) and pink colour with hydrogen bubbles at the cathode (−).
Half-equations show what happens to electrons at each electrode. Reduction at the cathode uses electrons and oxidation at the anode releases them.

Acidified water, overall: 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g). The same 4 electrons give 2 H₂ and 1 O₂, which explains the 2 : 1 volume ratio; the H⁺ used at the cathode is replaced at the anode, so the acid is not used up.

Sodium sulfate solution, cathode (reduction): 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq), which turns universal indicator blue-purple; the anode reaction is the same as for acidified water, and turns the indicator red.

The same approach gives the half-equations for the two salt solutions. In each, the oxidation number (a number showing how many electrons an atom has lost or gained) confirms which half is oxidation and which is reduction.
Copper(II) chloride, overall: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → Cu(s) + Cl₂(g).
Potassium iodide, anode (oxidation): 2I⁻(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2e⁻; the iodine dissolves in the iodide solution, colouring it brown.
Potassium iodide, cathode (reduction): 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq); the OH⁻ turns phenolphthalein pink.
Oxidation numbers confirm each half-reaction: the oxidation number of chlorine changes from −1 to 0 (oxidation) and that of copper from +2 to 0 (reduction).
Both kinds of cell turn the energy stored in chemicals into electricity, but they differ in where the reactants are kept. That one difference decides what happens when the reactants run low.

A chemical cell, e.g. a zinc–carbon, alkaline, lead–acid or lithium-ion cell, uses a redox reaction (one substance loses electrons while another gains them) between reactants sealed inside it to convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
A chemical cell stops working when its reactants have been used up, because nothing more can be added to the sealed cell.
When a chemical cell's reactants are used up, a primary cell (a single-use cell) is discarded, while a secondary cell (a rechargeable cell) must be recharged from an external electrical supply.
A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of a fuel, e.g. hydrogen, and an oxidising agent (a substance that takes electrons from the fuel), usually oxygen from the air, into electrical energy.
In a fuel cell the reactants are not stored in the cell but are supplied continuously from outside, and the products, water for hydrogen, are continuously removed.
A fuel cell keeps producing electricity for as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied; it is refuelled, not recharged, and does not run down like a chemical cell.
Despite the difference in how they are supplied, the two types of cell work on the same principle. Seeing that shared principle makes the differences between the two types easier to follow.
Both are galvanic cells: each uses a spontaneous redox reaction (one that happens by itself) to drive electrons through an external circuit, the wires outside the cell.

Both have an anode where the fuel or reducing agent (the substance that gives up electrons) is oxidised (negative), a cathode where the oxidising agent is reduced (positive), and an electrolyte (a liquid or solid that carries ions) that carries ions between them.
In both, oxidation and reduction happen at separate electrodes, so energy is released as electrical energy rather than as heat.

Set side by side, the two types differ in six ways: where the reactants are, where the products go, what happens when the reactants run out, where the energy is stored, what they are used for, and their environmental impact. Learn each as a pair.
Source of reactants: a chemical cell stores its reactants inside and is limited by them; a fuel cell is supplied continuously from external tanks or the air.
Products: in a chemical cell they stay inside the cell; in a fuel cell they are removed continuously, e.g. as water vapour in the exhaust.
When reactants run out: a chemical cell is replaced (primary) or recharged, which can take hours (secondary); a fuel cell is refuelled in minutes.

Energy storage: in a chemical cell the energy is stored in the electrode materials, so more energy needs a bigger, heavier cell; in a fuel cell the energy is stored in the fuel tank, so the range depends on the size of the tank.

Typical uses: chemical cells power portable devices such as phones, laptops and torches, and battery electric vehicles; fuel cells power hydrogen buses, cars and trucks, spacecraft (e.g. the Apollo missions) and backup power supplies.
Environmental impact: a hydrogen fuel cell's only product is water; chemical cells need metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, lead and zinc to be mined, and the cells must be recycled.
A fuel cell needs hydrogen to be produced, stored and transported, so it is only as clean as the way the hydrogen was made.
Hydrogen can release its energy by burning or by reacting in a fuel cell. The overall chemistry is the same, but the way the energy comes out is very different.

In a fuel cell hydrogen and oxygen react by the same overall reaction as when hydrogen burns, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, but without a flame or combustion: the electrons are transferred through the external circuit.

A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy; an engine or power station first converts it to heat, much of which is lost, so a fuel cell is more efficient than burning the fuel.
A fuel cell has no moving parts, so it is quiet.

A hydrogen fuel cell produces no carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide or soot at the point of use and, with no high-temperature flame, no nitrogen oxides (formed when nitrogen and oxygen in air react in a hot flame).
A hydrogen fuel cell is built from two electrodes with a membrane between them. Each part has a job, and exams ask what the membrane and the platinum do.
A hydrogen fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the fuel, hydrogen, is oxidised and the oxidising agent, oxygen from the air, is reduced, producing electricity and water.
Hydrogen gas is fed continuously to the anode (negative electrode); oxygen or air is fed continuously to the cathode (positive electrode).

The electrodes are porous carbon coated with a platinum catalyst: the pores let the gases reach the electrolyte, and the platinum (a catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up) speeds up the electrode reactions.
In the common type the electrolyte is a proton exchange membrane (PEM), a thin sheet of solid polymer between the electrodes.
The membrane lets H⁺ ions (protons) pass from the anode to the cathode, does not conduct electrons, so the electrons must go round the external circuit, and keeps the hydrogen and oxygen apart.

The cell works in five steps, from hydrogen entering at the anode to water leaving at the cathode. The key idea is that the ions and the electrons take different routes to the cathode, and the electrons' route is the electric current.
1. At the anode, hydrogen molecules are oxidised to hydrogen ions, releasing electrons: H₂(g) → 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.
2. The electrons flow through the external circuit to the cathode, powering a motor or other device on the way.
3. The H⁺ ions move through the membrane to the cathode.
4. At the cathode, oxygen is reduced by combining with the H⁺ ions and electrons to form water: O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l).
5. The water is removed from the cathode side, as liquid or vapour, so the reaction can continue.
Overall: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), obtained by doubling the anode equation to balance the electrons: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

Oxidation numbers (the charge an atom would have if its bonds were fully ionic) show which substance is oxidised and which is reduced in the fuel cell. The energy released is the same as when hydrogen burns.
Hydrogen is the reducing agent: its oxidation number rises from 0 in H₂ to +1 in H₂O, an oxidation (loss of electrons) at the anode.
Oxygen is the oxidising agent: its oxidation number falls from 0 in O₂ to −2 in H₂O, a reduction (gain of electrons) at the cathode.

For H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ mol⁻¹, so the reaction is strongly exothermic (it releases a lot of energy); in the fuel cell much of this energy is released as electrical energy rather than heat.
A real hydrogen fuel cell has some limits that affect how it is built and run: its voltage, its heat output and the purity of its fuel.

A single hydrogen fuel cell gives a maximum of about 1.2 V and, in use, about 0.6–0.8 V, so many cells are connected in series in a stack to give a useful voltage; a car's stack contains several hundred cells.
Fuel cells also produce some heat, which can be used, e.g. for heating in buildings or buses.
The hydrogen must be pure: impurities such as carbon monoxide poison the platinum catalyst, meaning they stop it working.
The alkaline fuel cell is a second type of hydrogen fuel cell. It uses a different electrolyte, so the ion that carries charge and the half-equations change, but the overall reaction does not.
In an alkaline fuel cell the electrolyte is potassium hydroxide solution, and OH⁻ ions carry the charge through it.
Overall: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), the same as in the PEM cell.
Alkaline fuel cells powered the Apollo spacecraft and produced drinking water for the astronauts.
Hydrogen fuel cells suit some jobs well, but they have real drawbacks, mostly to do with hydrogen itself. Exams ask for advantages and disadvantages, so learn both sides.
Uses: hydrogen buses, cars and trucks; spacecraft; backup and off-grid power supplies.
Advantages: the only product is water, so there is no CO₂, CO, nitrogen oxides or soot at the point of use; the cell is quiet, is refuelled in minutes, and runs as long as fuel is supplied.
Limitations: hydrogen is highly flammable and forms explosive mixtures with air.
Limitations: hydrogen has a very low density, so it must be stored compressed at high pressure, or liquefied at very low temperature, in strong, heavy tanks.
Limitations: there are few hydrogen refuelling stations, and platinum is scarce and expensive.

Most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide; a fuel cell is only low-carbon overall when the hydrogen is made by electrolysis (splitting water using electricity) using renewable electricity.
Diagram: a PEM fuel cell with hydrogen in at the anode (−) and oxygen or air in at the cathode (+), and the membrane between them with H⁺ moving across.
Diagram: add an external circuit with a load and electrons flowing from anode to cathode, and water leaving from the cathode side; write the half-equations beside each electrode.

Sustainable energy use means getting the energy we need while wasting less and releasing less carbon dioxide. Electrochemical cells (cells that link chemical reactions and electricity) help in several ways, starting with how they use energy.
Electrochemical cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy, without first burning a fuel to make heat, so less energy is wasted than in an engine or a fossil-fuel power station.
Rechargeable (secondary) batteries can be reused hundreds or thousands of times, cutting the waste and raw materials of single-use cells.
Rechargeable batteries let electricity from renewable sources, such as wind and solar, be stored and used later, in devices, electric vehicles and large grid batteries.
This matters because wind and solar power vary with the weather and the time of day, so electricity is not always being made when it is needed.
Electrolysis can make hydrogen, a fuel that stores energy. How clean the hydrogen is depends on how it is made, and the colour names describe the three routes.
Electrolysis can split water into hydrogen and oxygen: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂.
If the electricity comes from renewable sources, the hydrogen is made without releasing carbon dioxide; this is called “green hydrogen”.

Hydrogen stores energy as a fuel: it can be kept, transported and later used in a fuel cell to make electricity again, or used in industry; its only product when used in a fuel cell or burned is water.
Most hydrogen produced today is made from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide; this is called “grey hydrogen”.
“Blue hydrogen” is made the same way but with the carbon dioxide captured and stored.
The syllabus asks you to research one role of electrochemistry in sustainability and technology. The work follows seven steps, from a focused question to an evaluation of your own investigation.
1. Choose one application and write a focused question that can be answered with evidence, e.g. “Are battery electric cars more sustainable than petrol cars in Ireland?”
2. Explain the chemistry involved: the redox reactions, the type of cell (galvanic or electrolytic), and the electrode reactions where known.

3. Gather evidence from a range of sources: textbooks, peer-reviewed articles (checked by other experts before publication), government and public agencies such as the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, the Environmental Protection Agency and the International Energy Agency, manufacturers and news reports.
4. Judge each source by who wrote it and their expertise, and whether it is peer-reviewed or official, because these sources are checked.
4. Also judge how recent it is, as this technology changes quickly, and whether the author gains from the conclusion, e.g. a company selling the product.
4. Finally check whether it gives data and references rather than opinion, and whether other sources agree.
5. Consider the whole life-cycle: raw materials and mining, manufacture, the source of electricity or fuel during use, lifetime, and disposal or recycling.
6. Weigh the evidence on each side (environmental, economic, social and safety) and reach a justified conclusion, stating the conditions under which it holds.
7. Present the findings with references, and evaluate the investigation: gaps in the evidence, conflicting sources, and what further research would help.
This outline applies the seven steps to rechargeable lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles. It starts with the question, the chemistry and the evidence for.
Question: do rechargeable lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles make transport more sustainable?
Chemistry: the lithium-ion cell is a secondary cell, a galvanic cell on discharge and an electrolytic cell on recharging. There is more on this in The lithium-ion cell.
Evidence for: no exhaust emissions at the point of use (no CO₂, CO, nitrogen oxides or particulates from a tailpipe), improving air quality in towns.
Evidence for: electric motors waste less energy than petrol or diesel engines.
Evidence for: batteries can be charged from renewable electricity, and the same batteries can store surplus renewable electricity.
A fair answer weighs the evidence against as well as the evidence for, and then reaches a conclusion that states its conditions.
Evidence against: mining lithium, cobalt and nickel damages land and uses large amounts of water.
Evidence against: most of the world's cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where child labour and unsafe working conditions have been reported.
Evidence against: making the battery releases a lot of CO₂, and the benefit depends on how the electricity is generated.
Evidence against: recycling is not yet widespread, and damaged cells can catch fire.

Justified conclusion (example): electric vehicles reduce emissions over their lifetime where electricity is increasingly renewable, as in Ireland, provided batteries are made responsibly and recycled.
This outline asks whether hydrogen made by electrolysis can be a sustainable fuel. It splits into the question and chemistry, the evidence for, and the evidence against.
Question: can hydrogen produced by electrolysis using wind power be a sustainable fuel?
Chemistry: electrolysis of water, with 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂ at the cathode and 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ at the anode. There is more on this in Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
Evidence for: no CO₂ is released if the electricity is renewable.
Evidence for: it can use surplus wind electricity at times when supply is greater than demand, storing it as a fuel.
Evidence for: hydrogen can power fuel-cell vehicles and replace fossil fuels in industries that are hard to electrify.
Evidence for: the only product when it is used is water.
Making hydrogen and turning it back into electricity costs energy at each stage. This is the main weakness of green hydrogen.
Evidence against: energy is lost at every step, so converting electricity to hydrogen and back to electricity returns well under half of the original energy, much less than a battery.
Evidence against: electrolysers need pure water, and some need scarce metal catalysts such as platinum and iridium.
Evidence against: hydrogen is hard to store, needing high pressure or very low temperature, and it is highly flammable.
Evidence against: green hydrogen currently costs more than grey hydrogen.

Justified conclusion (example): green hydrogen is most useful where batteries are unsuitable, such as heavy transport, industry and long-term storage, but only if it is powered by genuinely renewable electricity.
This outline asks whether hydrogen fuel cells should power public buses. It uses the PEM hydrogen fuel cell described above as its chemistry.
Question: should hydrogen fuel cells power public buses?
Chemistry: a fuel cell is a galvanic cell; at the anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, and at the cathode O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
Evidence for: water is the only product at the point of use, and the cell is quiet and refuelled in minutes.
Evidence for: long range suits buses on long, fixed routes that return to one depot for refuelling.
Evidence against: there are few refuelling stations, and the vehicles are expensive, partly because of the platinum catalyst.
Evidence against: high-pressure storage tanks are needed.
Evidence against: if the hydrogen is grey, the overall CO₂ saving is small or none.
Justified conclusion (example): fuel-cell buses are a good choice only where green hydrogen is available at a competitive price.
Electrochemistry also helps sustainability by making steel last longer. Rusting is a redox reaction, and a more reactive metal can be made to take the damage instead.
Question: how does electrochemistry help steel structures last longer, and why is that sustainable?

Chemistry: rusting is the oxidation of iron. A metal higher in the electrochemical series (the list that ranks metals by how easily they are oxidised), such as zinc or magnesium, is oxidised in preference to iron. There is more on this in Balancing redox equations and the electrochemical series.
Galvanising, a zinc coating, and sacrificial anodes, blocks of zinc or magnesium attached to ship hulls, pipelines and steel piers, both use this protection.
Evidence for: steel lasts much longer, so less steel has to be made to replace it, saving iron ore, energy and the CO₂ released in steelmaking.
Evidence for: it prevents dangerous failures of bridges, pipelines and ships.
Evidence against: sacrificial anodes are used up and must be replaced, and galvanised coatings wear away eventually.
Evidence against: zinc released into seawater can harm marine life.
Justified conclusion (example): corrosion protection is a cheap and effective way of conserving metal resources, though zinc release should be monitored.
Organic chemistry is the study of the compounds of carbon, and hydrocarbons are the simplest of them. Knowing what a hydrocarbon is gives you the starting point for every other organic family.
Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates contain carbon but are classed as inorganic, so they are exceptions to the rule that carbon compounds are organic.

Carbon forms so many compounds because each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds (bonds made by sharing pairs of electrons) and carbon atoms bond strongly to each other. This gives stable chains, straight or branched, and rings of almost any length.

Organic compounds are divided into many groups, or homologous series (families of compounds), each with its own characteristic structure and reactions. There is more on this in Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties.
A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only, which is why hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds.

Other organic families, such as alcohols and carboxylic acids, can be thought of as hydrocarbons with one or more hydrogen atoms replaced by other atoms or groups. So hydrocarbons are the basis for understanding and making other organic compounds.
Crude oil, natural gas and coal are the main sources of hydrocarbons, and all three are fossil fuels. They are the starting point for most of the hydrocarbons that industry and society use.

Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, buried under sediment (layers of mud and sand) and changed by heat and pressure in the absence of air. Crude oil and natural gas formed mainly from tiny marine organisms.
Fossil fuels are finite (non-renewable): they are being used far faster than they form, so they will run out.
Natural gas is mainly methane (CH₄), typically over 80%, with small amounts of ethane, propane and butane.

Crude oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes (hydrocarbons with only single bonds) in chain and ring form. It also holds some aromatic hydrocarbons (ring-shaped hydrocarbons) such as benzene.

Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation (separating a mixture by boiling point) into fractions. Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with a similar range of boiling points and so of similar molecular size.
The smallest molecules, with the lowest boiling points, are collected at the top of the column and the largest at the bottom. There is more on this in Using the kinetic theory: separation techniques.
Fossil fuels are not the only source of hydrocarbons. Living things make some, and industry and laboratories can build others from different starting materials.
Methane forms when bacteria break down plant and animal material in the absence of air, a process called anaerobic decomposition.

This methane is found in landfill sites (refuse dumps), slurry pits (stores of liquid animal waste), marshes and the digestive systems of cattle and sheep. These are sources of methane that are not linked to the oil and gas industry.
Biogas, made deliberately by anaerobic digestion of farm slurry, food waste or crops, is mainly methane and is a renewable fuel because the plant and animal material can be regrown.
Plants also make hydrocarbons, e.g. natural rubber, which is poly(isoprene) (a hydrocarbon polymer, a very long chain molecule) from the rubber tree, and limonene (C₁₀H₁₆) in citrus-fruit peel oil.
Hydrocarbons can be synthesised (made) from other substances, e.g. ethene is made by dehydrating ethanol (removing water from it). There is more on this in Investigation: preparing ethene.
Ethanol made by fermenting sugar cane (using yeast to turn sugar into ethanol) gives a plant-based, or “bio”, ethene.
The Fischer–Tropsch process makes liquid hydrocarbons from carbon monoxide and hydrogen, so synthetic fuels can be made starting from coal, natural gas or biomass (plant and animal material).
Most hydrocarbons are burned for energy, because they release a lot of energy when they burn in oxygen. Different hydrocarbons and fractions suit different fuel jobs.
Complete combustion (burning with plenty of oxygen) of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water. There is more on this in Combustion and heats of combustion.
Methane (natural gas) is used for heating and cooking in homes, and for generating electricity in power stations.
Propane and butane are the main components of LPG (liquefied petroleum gas), sold in cylinders for patio heaters, camping stoves, gas barbecues and some vehicles such as forklift trucks.
Small butane canisters are used in camping stoves and lighters.
Natural gas and LPG have no smell of their own, so a small amount of a strong-smelling sulfur compound, a thiol also called a mercaptan, is added so that leaks can be detected.
Liquid fractions of crude oil are transport fuels: petrol for cars, kerosene for jet aircraft and home heating oil, and diesel (gas oil) for lorries, buses, tractors and cars.
Heavy fuel oil, a thick fraction of crude oil, is used in ships and furnaces.
Ethyne (acetylene) burned in pure oxygen gives a flame above 3000 °C, which is hot enough to be used for cutting and welding metals in the oxyacetylene torch.
A small but important share of hydrocarbons is used as raw materials, or feedstocks (starting materials), for the chemical industry rather than being burned.
Ethene and propene are made into the plastics poly(ethene) and poly(propene). There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.
Ethene is also used to make ethanol and ethane-1,2-diol, the antifreeze, and to ripen fruit, because it is a plant hormone (a chemical that controls plant processes).
Benzene is a feedstock for plastics such as polystyrene, and for detergents, dyes and pharmaceuticals (medicines).
Methane is the main source of hydrogen for making ammonia, which is used to make fertilisers.
Hexane and cyclohexane are used as non-polar solvents (liquids that dissolve non-polar substances such as oils), e.g. hexane to extract vegetable oils from seeds.

The largest molecules give lubricating oils and greases for machinery, paraffin wax for candles, and bitumen, from the residue left at the bottom of the column, for surfacing roads and waterproofing roofs.
The size and bonding of a hydrocarbon decide which use suits it. This links the properties of each group to the uses above.
Small molecules are gases that burn easily, so they make fuels.
Unsaturated alkenes (hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond) react readily, so they make feedstocks for plastics.
Large molecules are viscous (thick and slow-flowing) or solid, so they make lubricants, waxes and bitumen.

The investigation asks for one major impact on society of the continued, extensive use of hydrocarbons, researched from secondary sources (existing reports and data, not your own experiments) and judged on the evidence. You choose one impact and explain the chemistry behind it.
Choose one impact and set a focused question, often about one sector or one country.
Use several reliable sources that agree, judging each for authority (who wrote it), evidence, date and bias, since oil companies and campaign groups may each present one side.

Reliable sources for these topics include peer-reviewed papers (checked by other scientists before publication) and reports of the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change), the WHO (World Health Organization), the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency, Ireland) and the SEAI (Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland).
Explain the chemistry with balanced equations, and consider solutions and their limits.

Set every impact against the benefits: hydrocarbons are cheap, energy-dense (a lot of energy in a small mass) and easily transported fuels and raw materials that made modern transport, heating, electricity, plastics and medicines possible.
Justify the conclusion from the evidence, and acknowledge uncertainty and what the sources could not show.

Research question, e.g. “How does burning hydrocarbons for transport in Ireland contribute to climate change, and how could it be reduced?” The chemistry starts with the fact that every hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide when it burns completely.
Complete combustion of every hydrocarbon releases carbon dioxide, e.g. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
The same happens for octane, a hydrocarbon in petrol: 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l).
Scale for 1.00 kg of methane. Moles of CH₄ = mass ÷ molar mass = 1000 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 62.5 mol.
The equation gives 1 mol CO₂ for each 1 mol CH₄, so 62.5 mol CO₂ forms. Mass = 62.5 mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 2750 g, so 2.75 kg of CO₂ is released.
Scale for 1.00 kg of octane. Moles of C₈H₁₈ = 1000 g ÷ 114 g mol⁻¹ = 8.77 mol.
The equation gives 8 mol CO₂ for each 1 mol C₈H₁₈ (16 for every 2). Mass = 8.77 mol × 8 × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 3088 g, so 3.09 kg of CO₂ is released.

Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the air, and the evidence shows its level and the average temperature rising. The extra carbon dioxide traps heat, and that has effects on the climate and the oceans.

Fossil carbon was locked away for millions of years. Burning it moves that carbon into the atmosphere far faster than the carbon cycle (the natural movement of carbon between air, oceans and living things) removes it, so atmospheric CO₂ rises.
CO₂ and methane are greenhouse gases that absorb infrared radiation (heat radiation) emitted by the Earth and so trap heat. There is more on this in The enhanced greenhouse effect.
Methane escapes from gas wells, pipelines and coal mines, which adds to the greenhouse gases in the air.

Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 ppm today, and global average temperature has risen by more than 1 °C since pre-industrial times.

Consequences include rising sea levels, more extreme weather such as storms, floods and droughts, and ocean acidification (the oceans becoming more acidic) as CO₂ dissolves: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq).
A good investigation does not stop at the problem. It also assesses how emissions could be cut and what holds each solution back.

Solutions include renewable electricity from wind and solar, electric vehicles and heat pumps (devices that heat buildings using electricity efficiently), energy efficiency, biofuels, hydrogen, and carbon capture and storage (trapping CO₂ before it escapes and storing it).

The limits of these solutions include cost, the supply of materials such as those for batteries, the intermittency of renewables (wind and solar supply stops and starts with the weather), and the time needed to change infrastructure.

Research question, e.g. “How has burning solid fuel and road fuels affected air quality and health in Irish towns?” Burning fuels can release pollutants as well as carbon dioxide, depending on the oxygen supply and the fuel.
Incomplete combustion, with too little oxygen, produces carbon monoxide and soot (tiny particles of carbon), e.g. 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l).
Nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine at the high temperatures in engines to form nitrogen oxides: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g); 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g).
Sulfur impurities in coal and heavy oils burn to sulfur dioxide: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g).
Unburned hydrocarbons such as benzene, a carcinogen (a substance that can cause cancer), are released from fuel evaporation and exhausts.
Each pollutant harms the body in a different way, so name the pollutant and its effect together.
Carbon monoxide is toxic: it binds to haemoglobin (the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen) more strongly than oxygen does, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

Particulate matter, such as PM2.5 (particles with a diameter below 2.5 μm), from diesel engines and from burning coal and wood is breathed deep into the lungs, because the particles are so small. It is linked to asthma, lung disease and heart disease.
Nitrogen dioxide irritates the lungs and contributes to acid rain and smog.
Sulfur dioxide irritates the airways and causes acid rain.
Real data show whether action on air pollution works. Ireland's smoky coal ban is the evidence to use.
Dublin banned the sale of smoky (bituminous) coal in 1990. Black smoke fell sharply, and later studies linked the ban to fewer deaths from respiratory and heart disease.
The ban on smoky coal was extended to the whole country in October 2022.
Catalytic converters (devices in exhausts that turn harmful gases into less harmful ones), low-sulfur fuels, particulate filters and electric transport also reduce emissions.
Research question, e.g. “What happens to single-use plastic packaging in Ireland, and how could its impact be reduced?” The chemistry explains why plastic waste lasts so long.

Most plastics are made from hydrocarbon feedstocks: ethene and propene are polymerised (joined into long chains) to poly(ethene) and poly(propene). There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.
Addition polymers are long chains held by strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so microorganisms cannot break them down.
Plastics are therefore non-biodegradable (they cannot be broken down by living organisms) and can persist for hundreds of years.
Because plastics last so long, they build up in the environment and cause harm in several places.
Plastic waste causes litter and fills landfill sites.
Plastic in the sea entangles or is swallowed by marine animals.
Plastics break into microplastics, pieces smaller than 5 mm, which are found in water, food and living things.

Burning plastics recovers energy but releases CO₂, and burning some plastics, such as PVC (poly(chloroethene)), releases toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride unless done in controlled incinerators (furnaces built to burn waste safely).
Solutions work at different points: avoiding waste, reusing material, or changing the plastic itself. Each has limits you should be able to state.
Reducing and reusing plastics avoids the waste altogether.
Recycling involves sorting, washing, shredding, melting and remoulding, but only some plastics can be recycled and only for a limited number of cycles.
Biodegradable and bio-based plastics, deposit-return schemes, bans and levies are other responses; Ireland introduced a plastic bag levy in March 2002.

Research question, e.g. “How does Ireland's dependence on imported oil and gas affect energy prices and security?” Hydrocarbons are built into the economy, so a country that must import them is exposed to events elsewhere.
Modern economies depend on hydrocarbons for transport, heating, electricity generation, farming, where fuel and fertiliser are made from natural gas, and plastics.
Jobs and government revenue depend on the industry.
Fossil fuels are finite and unevenly spread, so countries without their own reserves must import them and are exposed to price shocks (sudden sharp rises in price) and supply cuts.
The 1973 oil crisis was an oil embargo (a ban on supplying oil) by Arab oil-producing countries, and in 2022 gas and electricity prices rose sharply after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Ireland imports most of its energy.
Ireland's own natural gas has come from the Kinsale Head gas field, off Co. Cork, which stopped producing in 2020, and from the Corrib gas field off Co. Mayo.
Getting oil and gas out of the ground and moving it around the world carries risks, and accidents have real economic costs.
Extraction and transport carry risks with economic costs.
Oil spills such as the Exxon Valdez (Alaska, 1989), the Prestige (off Galicia, Spain, 2002) and Deepwater Horizon (Gulf of Mexico, 2010) damaged fisheries, tourism and wildlife.
Ireland can cut its reliance on imported fuel, but the options have costs and trade-offs.
Home-produced renewable energy, energy efficiency and electrification (switching from burning fuels to using electricity) reduce imports.
The transition needs investment and takes time.
Hydrocarbons are still needed as feedstocks for plastics, medicines and fertilisers, so some argue they should be conserved for these uses rather than burned.
The conclusion ties the investigation together. It should answer the question and show that the answer follows from the evidence.
State the answer to the research question in one or two sentences.
Support the answer with the strongest evidence and the chemistry, using equations and data.
Weigh the benefits against the harms, and assess the proposed solutions for cost, practicality and who is affected.
Note the limitations of the sources used and what further research would help.
Ethene is made in the lab by taking the elements of water out of ethanol. The investigation then uses the gas to show what an alkene (a hydrocarbon with a carbon-carbon double bond) is like.
Aim: to prepare ethene by dehydrating ethanol, to observe its physical properties, and to investigate its combustion and show that it is unsaturated (contains a multiple carbon-carbon bond).

Hypothesis: ethene contains a C=C double bond, so it will decolourise bromine water and acidified potassium manganate(VII), while a saturated hydrocarbon (one with only single carbon-carbon bonds) will not.
Ethanol vapour passed over hot aluminium oxide loses a molecule of water: C₂H₅OH(g) → C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g).

This is a dehydration reaction, a type of elimination reaction in which a small molecule, water, is removed from a larger one and a double bond forms. There is more on this in Five types of organic reaction.
Aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, a white powder, is the catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction), so it is not used up in the reaction.
Heat the aluminium oxide, not the ethanol. The method runs in the order below.

1. Push some glass wool (a loose plug of glass fibres that soaks up liquid) into the closed end of a hard-glass boiling tube, which withstands strong heating, and soak it with about 2 cm³ of ethanol, using a dropper.
2. Place a small heap of aluminium oxide about halfway along the tube.
3. Clamp the tube horizontally and fit a stopper with a delivery tube (a bent tube that carries the gas away) that leads under water in a trough.
4. Put an inverted test tube full of water over the end of the delivery tube, standing on a beehive shelf (a perforated support that holds the tube mouth under water).
5. Heat the aluminium oxide strongly with a Bunsen burner; heat conducted along the tube warms the ethanol so that its vapour passes over the hot catalyst.

6. Collect the gas by displacement of water (the gas bubbles up into the water-filled tube and pushes the water out), and discard the first one or two tubes, then collect several tubes of gas, stoppering each under water so that no gas escapes, and storing it mouth down.
7. Before removing the heat, lift the delivery tube out of the water, to prevent suck-back.

Diagram: a horizontal boiling tube, clamped, with ethanol-soaked glass wool at the closed end and aluminium oxide in the middle; a Bunsen flame under the aluminium oxide; a delivery tube to an inverted water-filled test tube on a beehive shelf in a trough of water. Label the ethanol on the glass wool, the aluminium oxide, the heat and the ethene collecting.
Each feature of the set-up solves a practical problem. Knowing the reason for each is what the exam tests.
Glass wool holds the liquid ethanol at the end of the tube, so it doesn't run onto the hot catalyst or the hot glass.

The catalyst is heated rather than the ethanol, because aluminium oxide must be hot to work, and ethanol is flammable with a low boiling point of 78 °C, so gentle conducted heat is enough to vaporise it.
Ethene can be collected over water because it is almost insoluble in water, so very little of it dissolves as it bubbles through.
The first tubes are discarded because they contain mainly air pushed out of the apparatus, not ethene.

Suck-back happens if heating stops while the delivery tube is under water: the gas in the hot tube cools and contracts, cold water is drawn back into the hot boiling tube, and the tube can crack or shatter.
Before testing its chemistry, observe the gas itself. Its properties follow from its small, non-polar molecules.
Ethene is a colourless gas with a boiling point of −104 °C and a faint sweet smell, which should be wafted towards the nose, not sniffed directly.
It is almost insoluble in water, shown by its collection over water, because it is non-polar (its molecules have no charged ends) and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
It dissolves readily in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, because like dissolves like: both have non-polar molecules.
Its density is close to that of air: its relative molecular mass is 28, compared with about 29 for air.
Ethene burns, and the products of burning can be identified. The flame also reveals how much carbon the molecule contains compared with methane.
Remove the stopper and hold the mouth of the tube to a lighted taper or Bunsen flame: ethene burns with a yellow, luminous (bright), slightly smoky flame.

Add limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) to the tube after burning, stopper and shake; it turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms, showing that carbon dioxide was produced: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l).
Droplets of water may condense on the inside of the tube, which is the other product of combustion.
Methane burns with a clean, non-luminous blue flame, whereas ethene's flame is more luminous and smoky, because ethene has a higher percentage of carbon by mass, 85.7% compared with 75.0% in methane.

A C=C double bond can take in extra atoms, which is why alkenes react with bromine and with manganate(VII) while saturated hydrocarbons do not. Each reagent changes colour when it reacts, so the colour change is the evidence.
Bromine water: add a few drops of dilute bromine water to a tube of ethene, stopper and shake; the orange, or red-brown, colour disappears and the solution becomes colourless.
Bromine adds across the double bond in an addition reaction (the two bromine atoms join on and the double bond becomes a single bond): CH₂=CH₂(g) + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br, which is 1,2-dibromoethane.
Acidified potassium manganate(VII): add a few drops of dilute KMnO₄ acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, stopper and shake; the purple colour disappears.
In the manganate(VII) test the alkene is oxidised (it is attacked by the oxidising agent), and MnO₄⁻ is reduced (gains electrons) to almost colourless Mn²⁺, which is why the purple fades.
Both decolourisations are positive tests for unsaturation, meaning a C=C or C≡C bond is present.

Control: repeat both tests with a saturated hydrocarbon, e.g. a few drops of cyclohexane or methane from the gas tap; there is no rapid colour change, so the decolourisation is due to the double bond.

The percentage yield compares the ethene actually collected with the most that the ethanol could give. Sample data: 2.0 cm³ of ethanol, with a density of 0.789 g cm⁻³, was used, and 310 cm³ of ethene was collected, taken as if at s.t.p. (standard temperature and pressure).
Mass of ethanol = volume × density = 2.0 cm³ × 0.789 g cm⁻³ = 1.58 g.
Moles of ethanol = mass ÷ molar mass = 1.58 g ÷ 46 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0343 mol.
The mole ratio of ethanol to ethene is 1 : 1, so the theoretical yield (the most ethene the reaction could give) is 0.0343 mol of ethene.
Theoretical volume = 0.0343 mol × 22.4 L mol⁻¹ = 0.768 L = 768 cm³ at s.t.p.
The yield is low because some ethanol evaporates past the catalyst unreacted and dissolves in the trough water, some ethene is lost in the discarded tubes, and gas is left in the apparatus.
The hazards come from flammable gases, toxic bromine and hot glass. The errors weaken the tests, and the conclusion ties the results back to the aim.
Wear safety glasses; ethanol and ethene are highly flammable, so keep the stock bottle of ethanol away from the flame and add the ethanol before lighting the Bunsen burner.
Bromine water is toxic and corrosive: use small amounts of dilute bromine water in a well-ventilated room or a fume cupboard, and wear gloves.
Potassium manganate(VII) is an oxidiser that stains, and dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant.
Let the apparatus cool before handling it, because the glass is hot, and remove the delivery tube from the water before stopping the heating to avoid suck-back.
Air in the first tubes dilutes the ethene and weakens the tests.
Unreacted ethanol vapour carried over can slowly decolourise acidified manganate(VII) by itself, so the bromine water test and its control are the more convincing evidence.
Bromine water slowly fades in bright light, so the result must be compared with a control.
Conclusion: ethene is a colourless, almost insoluble, flammable gas that decolourises bromine water and acidified manganate(VII), so it is unsaturated.

A hydrocarbon is a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen. Chemists sort hydrocarbons into groups by the kind of carbon–carbon bonds they contain, because the bonding decides how each group behaves.
Hydrocarbons are divided by the type of carbon–carbon bonds present into aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons.
Aliphatic hydrocarbons have open chains of carbon atoms, straight or branched, or rings that behave like chains, such as cyclohexane. They are the alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring (a ring of six carbon atoms with special bonding). Benzene, C₆H₆, is the example given in the specification.
A saturated hydrocarbon (one holding as many hydrogens as it can) has only carbon–carbon single bonds, as in alkanes and cycloalkanes (alkanes whose carbons form a ring).
An unsaturated hydrocarbon contains at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond, as in alkenes and alkynes, so it could take on more atoms by opening that bond.

A homologous series is a family with the same general formula (one formula that fits every member) and similar chemical properties, a gradual change in physical properties, and each member differing from the next by CH₂.
The alkanes are saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with single bonds only. Having no multiple bonds explains why they are so unreactive.
General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is the number of carbons. The first members are methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀, pentane C₅H₁₂ and hexane C₆H₁₄.
Bonding: only single C–C and C–H covalent bonds are present, so the molecule is saturated.
Structure: each carbon is tetrahedral (its four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron), with bond angles of 109.5°. Chains can be branched from butane onwards.
Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, is a ring of six CH₂ groups joined by single bonds; it is saturated and aliphatic.
Cyclohexane has two fewer hydrogens than hexane because the ends of the chain are joined to make the ring. Its ring is not flat because each carbon is tetrahedral.
Alkanes are non-polar (their bonds have no significant positive or negative ends) and insoluble in water, and small members burn with a clean blue flame.
Alkanes are otherwise unreactive: they react with halogens (such as chlorine) only in ultraviolet light, by substitution (one atom replaced by another), e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
The alkenes are unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with one carbon–carbon double bond. That double bond makes them far more reactive than alkanes.
General formula CₙH₂ₙ; the members are ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆, butene C₄H₈, pentene C₅H₁₀ and hexene C₆H₁₂.
Bonding: one C=C double bond is present, so the molecule is unsaturated.
Structure: the two carbons of the double bond and the four atoms attached to them lie in one plane, with angles of about 120°, and there is no rotation about the C=C bond.
Alkenes are, like alkanes, non-polar and insoluble in water, but they are much more reactive.

Alkenes undergo addition (other atoms join on across the double bond, which becomes a single bond) with bromine, which decolourises bromine water (turns it from orange to colourless); with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃; and with hydrogen chloride, e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl.

Alkenes add to one another to form addition polymers (long chains built from many alkene molecules), e.g. ethene forms poly(ethene). There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.
Alkenes burn with a more luminous (brighter), smokier flame than alkanes because of their higher carbon content.
The alkynes are unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with one carbon–carbon triple bond. Like alkenes, they take part in addition reactions.
General formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; the first member is ethyne, C₂H₂, also called acetylene.
Bonding: one C≡C triple bond is present, so the molecule is unsaturated.
Structure: the two carbons of the triple bond and the atoms attached to them lie in a straight line, with an angle of 180°, so ethyne is linear.
Alkynes undergo addition reactions; with excess bromine, ethyne gives 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane: C₂H₂ + 2Br₂ → CHBr₂CHBr₂.
Ethyne burns in air with a very smoky, luminous flame.
Ethyne burns in pure oxygen with a very hot flame, which is used for welding: 2C₂H₂(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
Benzene is the aromatic hydrocarbon on the course. It is unsaturated on paper, yet it behaves very differently from an alkene, and its structure explains why.
Benzene, C₆H₆, is a colourless liquid with a boiling point of 80 °C and a sweet smell.
Its structure is a flat, hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen atom, with bond angles of 120°.
All six carbon–carbon bonds are identical, intermediate in length between single and double bonds, because the electrons beyond the single bonds are delocalised (spread) around the whole ring.
This is why benzene is drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. There is more on this in Shapes, bonding and isomerism.
Although benzene is unsaturated, it is very stable and resists addition: it does not decolourise bromine water or acidified potassium manganate(VII), and it reacts mainly by substitution.
Benzene burns with a very smoky, sooty flame because of its high carbon content, 92.3% by mass, the same as ethyne.
Benzene is toxic and carcinogenic (cancer-causing), causing leukaemia, so it is not used in school laboratories, where safer solvents such as cyclohexane are used instead.
Michael Faraday isolated benzene in 1825, and August Kekulé proposed a ring of alternating single and double bonds in 1865.
The Kekulé structure cannot explain why all the carbon–carbon bonds are the same length, or why benzene does not decolourise bromine water.
Putting the four groups side by side shows a pattern: the type of carbon–carbon bonding decides the shape, the reactivity and the result of the bromine water test.
Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, single C–C bonds, tetrahedral shape with 109.5° angles around each carbon, and methane as the first member; bromine water shows no change.
Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, one double bond, planar (flat) shape with 120° angles, and ethene as the first member; bromine water is decolourised.
Alkynes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, one triple bond, a linear shape with 180° angles, and ethyne as the first member; bromine water is decolourised.
Benzene has the general formula C₆H₆, a delocalised ring, a planar shape with 120° angles, and benzene as the first member; bromine water shows no change.

All four groups are non-polar, with only London dispersion forces (weak attractions between temporary charges in neighbouring molecules) between their molecules, so all are insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar solvents; small members are gases.

Reactivity follows bonding: single bonds only give unreactive alkanes; a localised double or triple bond gives reactive alkenes and alkynes that undergo addition; a delocalised ring gives benzene, which is stable and undergoes substitution rather than addition.
Names follow the systematic IUPAC rules (the internationally agreed system), and only compounds up to C6 need to be named. Start with the stem and then work through the rules for alkanes.
The stem gives the number of carbons in the parent chain (the main chain): 1 meth-, 2 eth-, 3 prop-, 4 but-, 5 pent-, 6 hex-.
The ending is -ane for alkanes, -ene for alkenes and -yne for alkynes.
Find the longest continuous carbon chain, which may bend on paper; this gives the parent name.
Number the chain from the end that gives the side chains (substituents, groups branching off the main chain) the lowest numbers.
Name side chains as alkyl groups: methyl (–CH₃) and ethyl (–C₂H₅); give each a position number, using di- and tri- for repeats.
Separate numbers from one another with commas, and separate numbers from words with hyphens; list different side chains alphabetically.
Applying the rules to branched alkanes shows how the numbering works.
CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ is methylpropane. It needs no number because the methyl group can only be on carbon 2, though 2-methylpropane is also accepted.
CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbutane, not 3-methylbutane, because numbering from the end that gives the lowest number to the side chain puts it on carbon 2.
C(CH₃)₄ is 2,2-dimethylpropane, with di- showing two methyl groups, both on carbon 2.
Alkenes and alkynes follow the same rules, with one addition: the multiple bond decides the numbering and must sit in the main chain.
For alkenes and alkynes the main chain must contain the multiple bond; number from the end nearer to it, and give the number of its first carbon before -ene or -yne.
CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is but-2-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₃ is 2-methylpropene, and CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is hex-1-ene.
HC≡CCH₃ is propyne, and CH₃C≡CCH₃ is but-2-yne.
Ethene, propene, ethyne and propyne need no number, because there is only one position for the multiple bond.
Rings take the prefix cyclo-, as in cyclohexane; benzene keeps its own name.
Three things explain almost every difference in the properties of hydrocarbons: the forces between molecules, the size of the molecules, and the kind of carbon–carbon bond.

Hydrocarbons are non-polar, because C–H bonds have very low polarity (the electrons are shared almost equally), so the only forces between their molecules are London dispersion forces. There is more on this in Bond type and intermolecular forces.

London dispersion forces get stronger as relative molecular mass (Mr, the mass of a molecule compared with the carbon-12 standard) increases, because there are more electrons and larger electron clouds, and as the area of contact between molecules increases.

The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point and the more likely the substance is a liquid or solid at room temperature.
The nature of the carbon–carbon bonds decides chemical reactivity: single bonds only give unreactive compounds, while a C=C double bond gives reactivity through addition reactions.
Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules; it does not break C–C or C–H bonds.
The data show how boiling point depends on carbon number in the straight-chain alkanes (those with no branches).
Boiling points: methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane −1 °C, pentane 36 °C and hexane 69 °C.
Boiling point rises with carbon number because each extra CH₂ increases the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons, and lengthens the molecule, so London dispersion forces get stronger.
The rise for each extra CH₂ gets smaller: the successive differences are 73, 47, 41, 37 and 33 °C, because each CH₂ is a smaller fraction of the molecule.
At room temperature, about 20 °C, methane to butane are gases, while pentane and hexane are liquids.
Larger alkanes up to about C16 are liquids, and beyond that they are waxy solids.
Other properties either follow from the molecules being non-polar or change gradually with chain length. Reactivity does not change at all.
All alkanes are insoluble in water, because they are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
All alkanes dissolve in or mix with non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, following the rule “like dissolves like”.
Liquid alkanes are less dense than water and float on it; hexane has a density of about 0.66 g cm⁻³.
All alkanes burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. C₆H₁₄(l) + 9½O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 7H₂O(l); larger alkanes need more oxygen per mole and release more energy per mole.
Larger alkanes burn with a more luminous, smokier flame and are less volatile (they evaporate less easily), so they are harder to ignite.
The percentage of carbon rises from 75.0% in CH₄ to 83.7% in C₆H₁₄, making incomplete combustion (burning in too little oxygen, giving soot and CO) more likely.
There is no difference in reactivity: all straight-chain alkanes are unreactive, reacting only by combustion or by substitution with halogens in ultraviolet light.

Alkanes with the same carbon number but different structures are structural isomers: they have the same molecular formula and Mr, but a different arrangement of the chain. Their boiling points differ even so.
Butane (−1 °C) and methylpropane (−12 °C) are the isomers of C₄H₁₀.
Pentane (36 °C), 2-methylbutane (28 °C) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (10 °C) are the isomers of C₅H₁₂.
Hexane (69 °C), 3-methylpentane (63 °C), 2-methylpentane (60 °C), 2,3-dimethylbutane (58 °C) and 2,2-dimethylbutane (50 °C) are the isomers of C₆H₁₄.
The more branched the molecule, the more compact, or closer to spherical, it is, so the area of contact between neighbouring molecules is smaller.
Smaller contact gives weaker London dispersion forces and a lower boiling point, since the Mr is the same for all the isomers. Unbranched chains lie alongside each other with a large area of contact.
Branching changes the boiling point enough to change the state at room temperature, but it leaves the chemistry unchanged.
2,2-dimethylpropane, with a boiling point of 10 °C, is a gas at room temperature, although pentane, with the same formula, is a liquid at room temperature because its boiling point is 36 °C.

Isomers show no significant difference in solubility, combustion or reactivity: all are non-polar and insoluble in water, burn to the same products with the same equation, e.g. C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O, and are equally unreactive.
Diagram: two pentane molecules lying side by side with a large area of contact, beside two 2,2-dimethylpropane molecules touching at only a small area.
The monounsaturated straight-chain alkenes (those with one double bond and no branches) show the same boiling point pattern as the alkanes, but a little lower.
Boiling points: ethene −104 °C, propene −48 °C, but-1-ene −6 °C, pent-1-ene 30 °C and hex-1-ene 63 °C.
Boiling point rises with carbon number for the same reason as in alkanes: a larger Mr, more electrons and stronger London dispersion forces.
Ethene to butene are gases at room temperature, while pentene and hexene are liquids.

Each alkene boils a little lower than the alkane with the same number of carbons, e.g. ethene −104 °C against ethane −89 °C and hex-1-ene 63 °C against hexane 69 °C, because it has two fewer hydrogen atoms, so slightly fewer electrons and weaker London forces.
Alkenes resemble alkanes in solubility, but their double bond makes their reactivity and flame different.
All alkenes are insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar solvents, like alkanes.
All alkenes burn to CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. C₃H₆(g) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
Every straight-chain alkene has the same percentage of carbon, 85.7%, since all have the formula CₙH₂ₙ; this is more than in the alkanes, so alkenes burn with smokier flames than alkanes.
All alkenes have one C=C bond, so they all undergo the same addition reactions, e.g. all decolourise bromine water, and they are much more reactive than alkanes.
Changing the chain length or the position of the double bond makes little difference to reactivity.
Use the data tables to predict properties from the trends. Each prediction rests on the three factors: intermolecular forces, Mr and bonding.
To predict a boiling point, use the trend in a table: the value lies between those of the neighbouring members, or of isomers with more and less branching.
Pent-1-ene, with a boiling point of 30 °C, is a liquid at 20 °C but would boil on a warm day or in warm water.
2-Methylpentane boils below hexane, because both are C₆H₁₄ and the branched isomer has a smaller area of contact.
Hex-1-ene will decolourise bromine water and hexane will not, and both will float on water without dissolving.
A mixture of pentane and hexane can be separated by fractional distillation (separating liquids by their different boiling points), because their boiling points differ, at 36 °C and 69 °C.
Of the aliphatic hydrocarbons, alkanes are the most stable. Stable here has a particular meaning, set out below.
Alkanes are the least reactive aliphatic hydrocarbons: at room temperature they do not react with acids, bases, most oxidising agents such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), or bromine water.
Their old name, paraffins, comes from the Latin parum affinis, meaning little affinity, that is, little reactivity.
“Stable” means unreactive under ordinary conditions, not that alkanes can never react: they burn readily once ignited, and they react with halogens in ultraviolet light.
Three features of alkane bonding explain their stability: they are saturated, their bonds are strong, and their bonds are almost non-polar.
Alkanes are saturated: every carbon already has four single bonds, so nothing can add to the molecule, and a bond must be broken before any reaction can occur.
C–C and C–H bonds are strong, so a great deal of energy is needed to break them, which gives a high activation energy (the minimum energy needed to start a reaction).

The electronegativities (a measure of how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons) of carbon, 2.55, and hydrogen, 2.20, differ by only 0.35, so C–H bonds are almost non-polar, and C–C bonds are completely non-polar.
With no significant δ⁺ or δ⁻ sites (slightly positive or negative ends), alkane molecules do not attract ions such as OH⁻ or H⁺, or polar molecules, which react by attacking charged sites.
Alkenes are more reactive because the C=C double bond is an electron-rich site that attracts reagents such as bromine and allows addition.
Alkanes are stable, not inert. They react under two sets of conditions: when ignited, and when exposed to ultraviolet light with a halogen.
Combustion: alkanes burn in oxygen once a flame or spark supplies the activation energy, releasing a lot of energy, e.g. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).

Substitution with chlorine or bromine needs ultraviolet light, or sunlight, to split the halogen molecule into reactive atoms, called free radicals, e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. There is more on this in Reaction mechanisms.
In the dark, an alkane mixed with bromine stays orange; in sunlight the colour slowly fades as substitution happens, which is much slower than the instant decolourisation produced by an alkene.
The unreactivity of alkanes is useful in everyday life, and it also causes an environmental problem.
Alkanes are safe to store and transport as fuels, such as natural gas, LPG and petrol, because they do not react until ignited.
Unreactive liquid alkanes such as hexane and cyclohexane are useful solvents.
Mineral oils and paraffin wax are used as lubricants and protective coatings.

The same chemical stability makes poly(ethene) and other addition polymers, whose chains are alkane-like, slow to break down in the environment. There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.
At Higher Level the stability of alkanes is explained by the type of bond. Single bonds are sigma bonds, while the second bond in an alkene's double bond is a weaker pi bond.
Every bond in an alkane is a sigma (σ) bond, formed by head-on overlap of orbitals (the regions where electrons are found) along the line between the two nuclei.
In a σ bond the shared electron pair is concentrated between the two nuclei, where both nuclei hold it strongly, so σ bonds are strong and their electrons are not exposed to attacking reagents.
