An alkene's double bond is one σ bond plus one pi (π) bond; the π electrons lie above and below the plane of the molecule, further from the nuclei and less tightly held, so they are exposed to attack by electron-seeking reagents.

Typical average bond enthalpies (energies needed to break a bond) are C–C 348 kJ mol⁻¹, C=C 614 kJ mol⁻¹ and C–H 412 kJ mol⁻¹, so the π part of the C=C bond adds only about 266 kJ mol⁻¹ to the σ bond.
So alkenes react by breaking the weaker π bond and keeping the σ bond, which is addition, whereas an alkane would have to break a strong σ bond, which needs much more energy.
Diagram: a C–C σ bond with electron density between the nuclei, beside a C=C bond showing the σ bond and the π electron cloud above and below the bond axis.

There are several ways to write down a hydrocarbon (a compound of only carbon and hydrogen), and each shows a different amount of information. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you what you can and cannot read from it.

A molecular formula gives the number of atoms of each element in one molecule, e.g. C₄H₁₀, but it does not show how the atoms are joined, so it cannot tell two different molecules with the same atoms apart.

An expanded, or displayed, structural formula (a drawing of the structure) shows every atom and every bond as a line, e.g. butane drawn with four carbon atoms in a row, each hydrogen joined by its own line.

A condensed structural formula shows the groups on each carbon in order without drawing the bonds: butane is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ or CH₃(CH₂)₂CH₃, methylpropane is CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃, and but-1-ene is CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃.
Double and triple bonds are always shown in a condensed formula, so you can still see where they are even though single bonds are left out.

A 3D model shows the real spatial arrangement of the atoms (how they sit in space), which a flat expanded formula cannot: the expanded formula draws the bonds of methane at 90°, but in 3D they point to the corners of a tetrahedron (a triangular-based pyramid).
Two flat drawings can show the same molecule: a four-carbon chain drawn bent or straight is still butane, and building the model shows whether two structures are identical.

Building models is the way to see shapes that flat drawings hide, and it is a practical activity you should be able to describe. A molecular model kit is used, and digital models can do the same job on screen.

Use a molecular model kit: black balls with four holes for carbon, white balls with one hole for hydrogen, short rigid links for single bonds, and flexible links, or springs, for double and triple bonds.
Build methane, ethane, propane and butane; each carbon with four single bonds is tetrahedral, so a straight chain (an unbranched chain) is actually a zig-zag, not a straight line of atoms.
Rotate the two ends of ethane about the C–C bond: rotation is free about a single bond, and the different positions, called conformations, are still the same molecule.
Build ethene with two flexible links: the molecule is flat, and the C=C bond cannot be twisted.
Build ethyne with three flexible links: the four atoms lie in a straight line.

Build all the isomers of C₄H₁₀ and C₅H₁₂ (isomers are different molecules with the same molecular formula); try to build another isomer, and check by rotating it whether it is really new or the same as one already made.
Record each model as an expanded and a condensed formula, and give its IUPAC name (the official systematic name).
Digital models, made with molecule-viewing software or apps, can be rotated on screen and show ball-and-stick and space-filling views.

Ball-and-stick models exaggerate the gaps between atoms and are not to scale; space-filling models show size and shape but hide the bonds; no model shows the electrons, and real molecules are constantly vibrating and rotating.
The three model shapes you build are worth drawing, because they show how the number of bonds between carbons changes the geometry.
Diagram: ball-and-stick models of methane (tetrahedral), ethene (planar) and ethyne (linear), labelled with their bond angles.
The type of bond a carbon forms decides the angles around it and whether the groups attached to it can turn. This is why the molecules you built have the shapes they do.
A carbon with four single bonds is tetrahedral, with bond angles of 109.5°, and the groups around it can rotate about each single bond.

A carbon in a C=C double bond is trigonal planar (its three neighbours lie in one flat triangle around it), with bond angles of 120°; the double bond holds the two carbons and the four atoms attached to them in one plane and prevents rotation.
A carbon in a C≡C triple bond is linear, with bond angles of 180°.
In benzene (a ring-shaped hydrocarbon, C₆H₆) all twelve atoms lie in one flat hexagonal ring.

Spatial arrangement helps predict properties: branched isomers are more compact than straight chains, so they have less contact with neighbouring molecules and lower boiling points. There is more on this in Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties.

Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, so the atoms are joined in a different order. Alkanes (hydrocarbons with only single bonds) show this once the chain is long enough to branch.
Isomers can differ in the carbon chain, through branching; in the position of a double bond; or in having a ring instead of a double bond, e.g. cyclohexane and hex-1-ene are both C₆H₁₂.
Methane, ethane and propane have no isomers; isomerism in alkanes starts at C₄, because a chain needs at least four carbons before it can be arranged in more than one way.
C₄H₁₀ has two structural isomers: butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, and methylpropane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.
C₅H₁₂ has three: pentane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃; 2-methylbutane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃; and 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄.
C₆H₁₄ has five. The first three are hexane, CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₃; 2-methylpentane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃; and 3-methylpentane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
The other two isomers of C₆H₁₄ are 2,2-dimethylbutane, CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃, and 2,3-dimethylbutane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃.
Alkenes (hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond) have more isomers than alkanes of the same size, because the double bond can sit in different positions as well as the chain being branched.
Isomers of alkenes also first appear at C₄, and propene's only isomer is the ring compound cyclopropane.
The C₄H₈ alkene isomers are but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃; but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃; and methylpropene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₃.
The C₅H₁₀ alkene isomers are pent-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃; pent-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃; and 2-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
The other two C₅H₁₀ alkene isomers are 3-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃, and 2-methylbut-2-ene, CH₃C(CH₃)=CHCH₃.
The straight-chain alkene isomers of C₆H₁₂ differ in the position of the double bond: hex-1-ene, hex-2-ene and hex-3-ene.
Check for repeats by numbering the chain from the other end or by rotating the model: 1-methylbutane is really pentane, and pent-4-ene is really pent-1-ene.
Ethane is the simplest molecule with a carbon–carbon single bond, and its shape is the pattern for every carbon with four single bonds.
Ethane, C₂H₆, is CH₃–CH₃: each carbon forms four single bonds, three to hydrogen atoms and one to the other carbon.
The four bonds around each carbon point to the corners of a tetrahedron, with bond angles of about 109.5°, so the molecule is three-dimensional and not flat.
The two CH₃ groups can rotate freely about the C–C single bond.
Diagram: ethane drawn in 3D with wedges and dashes, with the 109.5° angle marked.
Ethene has a carbon–carbon double bond, which changes both the shape and whether the molecule can twist.
Ethene, C₂H₄, is CH₂=CH₂: each carbon forms a double bond to the other carbon and single bonds to two hydrogen atoms.
Each carbon is trigonal planar, with bond angles of about 120°, so all six atoms lie in one plane and the molecule is flat.
There is no rotation about the C=C double bond.
Diagram: flat ethene molecule with the 120° angles marked.
Ethyne has a carbon–carbon triple bond, which gives the most extreme shape of the three: a straight line.
Ethyne, C₂H₂, is HC≡CH: each carbon forms a triple bond to the other carbon and a single bond to one hydrogen atom.
The molecule is linear, with a bond angle of 180°, so all four atoms lie in a straight line.
Diagram: H–C≡C–H in a straight line, with 180° marked.
Putting ethane, ethene and ethyne side by side shows a pattern: each extra bond between the carbons changes the shape around them.
As the carbon–carbon bond changes from single to double to triple, the shape around each carbon changes from tetrahedral, 109.5°, to trigonal planar, 120°, to linear, 180°.
This happens because the number of groups of electrons around each carbon falls from four to three to two, and the groups spread as far apart as possible.
The carbon–carbon bond becomes shorter and stronger from single to double to triple: C–C 0.154 nm, C=C 0.134 nm and C≡C 0.120 nm.
Ethane is three-dimensional, ethene is planar, and ethyne is linear.

At Higher Level you explain the shapes using two kinds of covalent bond (a bond made by sharing electrons), σ and π, which differ in how their orbitals overlap. An orbital is the region where an electron is likely to be found.
A σ (sigma) bond is formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the line between the nuclei; a π (pi) bond is formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below that line.
A single bond is σ; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π.

Only the σ bonds and any lone pairs (pairs of electrons not used in bonding) decide the shape: the σ bonds around each carbon spread as far apart as possible (VSEPR theory, electron-pair repulsion), and the π bonds lie over the σ framework without changing the angles.
In ethane each carbon has four σ bonds around it, giving a tetrahedral shape, and rotation about the σ C–C bond does not change the overlap, so rotation is free.

In ethene each carbon has three σ bonds around it, giving a trigonal planar shape; the p orbital left on each carbon, at right angles to the plane, overlaps sideways with the other to form the π bond above and below the plane.
The π bond prevents rotation: twisting one CH₂ group would turn the p orbitals away from each other and break the π overlap, so the molecule is rigid and planar; this is why cis–trans isomers exist.

In ethyne each carbon has two σ bonds around it, giving a linear shape, and the two p orbitals left on each carbon are at right angles to each other. The two π bonds together form a cylinder of electron density around the C–C axis.
Diagram: σ framework of ethene with the π cloud drawn above and below the plane; ethyne with its two π bonds at right angles around the C–C axis.

Benzene is a flat ring of six carbons whose bonding cannot be described with ordinary single and double bonds. Its electrons are spread over the whole ring instead, which is called delocalised bonding.

Benzene, C₆H₆, has each carbon forming three σ bonds, to two neighbouring carbons and to one hydrogen, so each carbon is trigonal planar with 120° angles and the molecule is a flat, regular hexagon. There are twelve σ bonds in total, six C–C and six C–H.
Each carbon has one remaining p orbital, holding one electron, at right angles to the ring.

The six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring, not in three separate pairs, forming a delocalised π system (π electrons shared over the whole ring): one ring of electron density above the plane and one below it, containing six electrons shared by all six carbons.
Delocalisation has measurable effects: the bond lengths are all equal and benzene resists the reactions that alkenes undergo. These are the evidence for the delocalised model.
All six C–C bonds are identical, 0.139 nm long, between a single bond at 0.154 nm and a double bond at 0.134 nm; benzene is drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside to show the delocalised electrons.

Delocalisation makes benzene unusually stable: it does not decolourise bromine water, because addition (joining new atoms on across a double bond) would destroy the delocalised ring, so it reacts by substitution (swapping an atom for another), keeping the ring.
The evidence against the Kekulé structure, with alternating C–C and C=C bonds, is that all the bonds are the same length and benzene does not undergo the addition reactions of alkenes.
Kathleen Lonsdale, born in Newbridge, Co. Kildare, showed in 1929, using hexamethylbenzene, that the benzene ring is flat and a regular hexagon.
Exams ask you to share out the electrons of a benzene molecule between the different kinds of bonding. The total is the starting point, and each group is then counted in turn.
C₆H₆ has 42 electrons in total: 6 × 6 from the carbons and 6 × 1 from the hydrogens.
Of these, 12 electrons are in the six C–H bonds (two per bond), 12 are in the six C–C σ bonds, and 6 are delocalised π electrons.
So 18 electrons are involved in carbon–carbon bonding, and the remaining 12 are the inner (1s) electrons of the carbons, which are not involved in bonding.

Diagram: the planar ring of six C atoms with H atoms, the σ framework, the p orbitals at right angles to the ring, the delocalised π clouds above and below the ring, and the hexagon-with-circle symbol.
Draw a table with one row for each molecule, giving its σ bonds, π bonds, shape and rotation. It pulls the whole section together.
Ethane: 7 σ bonds, no π bonds, tetrahedral with 109.5° angles, and free rotation about the C–C bond.
Ethene: 5 σ bonds, 1 π bond, planar with 120° angles, and no rotation about the C=C bond.
Ethyne: 3 σ bonds, 2 π bonds, and linear with 180° angles.
Benzene: 12 σ bonds and a delocalised π system of 6 electrons, planar with 120° angles, and all C–C bonds equal in length.
There are two ways for molecules to be isomers, and you must be able to tell them apart. The difference is whether the atoms are joined in a different order or only arranged differently in space.
Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, so the atoms are joined in a different order; butane and methylpropane (C₄H₁₀), and but-1-ene and but-2-ene (C₄H₈), are examples.
Geometric, or cis–trans, isomers have the same molecular formula and the same structural formula, so the atoms are joined in the same order, but the atoms are arranged differently in space.
If converting one isomer into the other would mean breaking bonds and joining atoms in a different order, they are structural isomers.
If the order of joining is the same and only the positions in space differ, they are geometric isomers.
Geometric isomerism depends on the rigidity of the C=C double bond. Butene, C₄H₈, is the example, in its but-2-ene form.
Geometric isomerism arises in alkenes because there is no rotation about the C=C double bond, since rotation would break the π bond, so groups are fixed on one side or the other of the double bond.
Each carbon of the double bond must carry two different atoms or groups for geometric isomerism to occur.
In cis-but-2-ene the two CH₃ groups are on the same side of the double bond, and the two H atoms are on the same side.
In trans-but-2-ene the two CH₃ groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.
Not every alkene has cis and trans forms. Apply the condition that each double-bond carbon must carry two different groups to decide.
But-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, has no cis–trans isomers, because one carbon of the double bond carries two identical H atoms.
Methylpropene, CH₂=C(CH₃)₂, has none, because both carbons of the double bond carry identical pairs of groups.
Butene, C₄H₈, therefore has four alkene isomers: but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, trans-but-2-ene and methylpropene (three structural isomers, one of which has cis and trans forms).
Alkanes have no geometric isomers, because groups rotate freely about C–C single bonds.
Other alkenes up to C6 with two different groups on each double-bond carbon, e.g. pent-2-ene, hex-2-ene and hex-3-ene, have cis and trans forms.

In a 3D model of but-2-ene the double bond, made of two flexible links, cannot be twisted, so the cis model cannot be turned into the trans model without taking it apart; digital models show the same when rotated.
Diagram: cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene drawn flat with 120° angles, the CH₃ groups circled on the same and on opposite sides.
Whether isomers react alike depends on whether they have the same types of bond. The same family means the same bonds and so similar chemistry.
Structural isomers of the same family, such as butane and methylpropane, have very similar chemical properties, because they have the same types of bond.

Structural isomers in different families have different chemical properties: hex-1-ene and cyclohexane are both C₆H₁₂, but hex-1-ene, with its C=C bond, decolourises bromine water, and cyclohexane, which is saturated (it has only single bonds), does not.
cis- and trans-but-2-ene have almost the same chemical properties, with the same C=C bond, the same addition reactions and the same combustion: C₄H₈ + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 4H₂O.
Isomers have the same atoms but different shapes, and shape affects the physical property of boiling point.
Branched structural isomers have lower boiling points than unbranched ones, e.g. butane, −1 °C, and methylpropane, −12 °C.

The more compact shape of the branched isomer gives less contact between molecules and weaker London dispersion forces (the weak attractions between all molecules), so less energy is needed to separate them. There is more on this in Polarity and symmetry.
Cis and trans isomers react alike but differ in physical properties such as boiling point and melting point. The cause is the difference in polarity and in how the molecules pack.
cis-but-2-ene boils at 4 °C and trans-but-2-ene at 1 °C.

The cis molecule is slightly polar (it has a side with slightly more negative charge and a side with slightly more positive), because both CH₃ groups lie on one side, so it has dipole–dipole attractions as well as London forces.
The symmetrical trans molecule is non-polar, so it has only London forces; this is why cis boils higher than trans.
The trans isomer has the higher melting point, −106 °C compared with −139 °C for cis, because its more symmetrical, straighter shape packs more closely in the solid.
Cis–trans isomerism has a real consequence for diet, because the shape of a fat molecule affects health.
Cis–trans isomerism matters in food: unsaturated fats (fats with C=C bonds in their chains) in natural oils are mainly cis.
Trans fats are formed when vegetable oils are partly hydrogenated (reacted with hydrogen), and they raise the risk of heart disease.

Carbon is unusual because the same element can exist as very different solids, from the hardest natural substance to a soft slippery one. This is called allotropy, and it comes entirely from how the atoms are bonded together.
Allotropes are different physical forms of the same element in the same state, with the atoms bonded together in different ways. Here every allotrope is made only of carbon atoms.
Carbon's allotropes are diamond, graphite, graphene and the fullerenes (hollow cage or tube molecules of carbon).

Because they are all pure carbon, they have the same chemical properties: each burns in excess oxygen (more than enough oxygen for complete burning) to give only carbon dioxide, C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g).
This burning test is evidence that diamond and graphite are both forms of the same element, because two different elements would not give the same single product.
Their physical properties (such as hardness, conductivity and melting point) differ because their structures differ.

Diamond, graphite and graphene are giant covalent, or macromolecular, structures, in which every atom is joined to its neighbours by covalent bonds (shared pairs of electrons) throughout the whole structure.
Fullerenes are different: they are separate molecules, which are simple molecular, with small groups of atoms bonded inside each molecule and only weak attractions between molecules.
In diamond every carbon uses all four of its outer electrons to bond to other carbon atoms. This gives a rigid network in all three dimensions, and almost every property of diamond follows from it.

Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms arranged tetrahedrally (pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, a four-faced pyramid), with bond angles of 109.5°, forming a rigid, three-dimensional giant covalent network.
Diamond is the hardest natural substance, because a great many strong covalent bonds in all directions must be broken to scratch or deform it.
Its melting point is very high, above 3500 °C, because strong covalent bonds throughout the structure must be broken.
It does not conduct electricity, because all four outer electrons of each carbon are used in bonds, so there are no free electrons or ions to carry charge.
It conducts heat very well, better than copper, because the rigid, strongly bonded lattice (the regular repeating arrangement of atoms) passes on vibrations efficiently.
It is transparent and colourless, and it sparkles because it bends and reflects light strongly.
It is insoluble in water and all solvents, and its density (mass per unit volume) of 3.51 g cm⁻³ reflects the closely packed atoms.
Diagram: a section of the diamond lattice showing one carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others.

Graphite is also pure carbon, but each atom forms only three bonds, so the atoms arrange themselves in flat sheets instead of a 3D network. The strong bonds are inside the sheets and only weak forces hold the sheets together.
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others at 120°, in flat layers of hexagonal rings (six-sided rings), and the layers are stacked on top of one another.
Each carbon uses three of its four outer electrons in bonds; the fourth is delocalised (not held by one atom) and free to move along the layer.

The layers are held together only by weak London dispersion forces (weak attractions between neighbouring layers), about 0.335 nm apart, compared with 0.142 nm between carbons within a layer. So the layers are relatively far apart.
Graphite is soft and slippery, and it marks paper, because the layers slide over each other easily when only weak forces hold them together.
Graphite conducts electricity along the layers, because the delocalised electrons can move and carry charge.
Graphite has a very high melting point, because the strong covalent bonds within the layers must be broken.
Graphite is a grey-black, shiny, opaque solid that is insoluble in water. Its density is about 2.2 g cm⁻³, less than that of diamond, because of the space between the layers.
Diagram: two or three stacked layers of hexagons, labelled strong covalent bonds within layers, weak forces between layers and delocalised electrons.
Graphene is graphite taken to its limit: one single layer. Keeping the same bonding as graphite, it has remarkable properties for something only one atom thick.
Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one carbon atom thick: a flat, two-dimensional sheet of hexagonal rings, with each carbon bonded to three others and one delocalised electron per carbon.
It was first isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at the University of Manchester, who peeled layers off graphite with sticky tape.
Geim and Novoselov won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.
Graphene is extremely strong for its thickness, one of the strongest materials known, because of the strong covalent bonds across the sheet, yet it is very light and flexible.
Graphene conducts electricity extremely well, because its delocalised electrons move freely across the sheet, and it is also an excellent conductor of heat.
A single sheet absorbs only about 2.3% of visible light, so it is almost transparent, and it is impermeable to gases (gases cannot pass through it).
Diagram: a flat honeycomb sheet of hexagons one atom thick.
Fullerenes break the pattern of the other allotropes. Their carbon atoms form closed cages or tubes, which are separate molecules rather than endless networks, and this changes their properties.
Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms joined into closed hollow cages, or tubes, made of hexagonal and pentagonal (five-sided) rings, with each carbon bonded to three others.
Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, has 60 carbon atoms arranged in 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, the shape of a football, and is nicknamed the buckyball.
C₆₀ was discovered in 1985 by Harry Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996. It is named after the architect Buckminster Fuller, whose domes it resembles.
C₆₀ is a simple molecular substance: covalent bonds hold the atoms within each ball, but only weak London dispersion forces (weak attractions between molecules) act between the balls.

So, unlike the giant structures, C₆₀ is soft and has a relatively low sublimation temperature (the temperature at which it turns straight from solid to gas), because little energy is needed to separate the balls.
C₆₀ dissolves in non-polar solvents (liquids made of molecules with no charged ends) such as methylbenzene, giving a purple solution, but not in water.
C₆₀ is a poor conductor of electricity, because its delocalised electrons can move within a molecule but not from one molecule to the next.

Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes, like a sheet of graphene rolled into a tube about a nanometre (one billionth of a metre) across; they are very strong and conduct electricity along the tube.
Diagram: a C₆₀ ball showing its hexagons and pentagons; a short section of a nanotube.
Putting the four allotropes side by side shows that the number of bonds per carbon and the type of structure decide the properties. Comparison questions ask for exactly this.
Bonds per carbon: diamond forms four; graphite, graphene and the fullerenes form three, with one delocalised electron each.

Structure: diamond is a three-dimensional giant covalent network; graphite is giant covalent layers; graphene is a single giant covalent layer; fullerenes are discrete (separate) molecules, and nanotubes are very long tubes.
Hardness: diamond is the hardest; graphite is soft and slippery; graphene is strong and flexible; C₆₀ is soft.
Electrical conductivity: diamond does not conduct; graphite conducts well along its layers; graphene conducts excellently; C₆₀ conducts poorly; nanotubes conduct well.
Melting point: diamond, graphite and graphene are very high, whereas C₆₀ is much lower, because only weak forces act between its molecules.
Solubility: diamond, graphite and graphene are insoluble in all solvents, whereas C₆₀ dissolves in non-polar organic solvents.

The general rule is that properties depend on how many bonds each carbon forms, four giving no free electrons and three giving delocalised electrons, and on whether the structure is a continuous giant network or separate molecules.
Each everyday use of a carbon allotrope depends on one property that comes from its structure. A use is only worth marks when you give the property that explains it.
Diamond is used in jewellery because it is transparent, sparkles and is hard enough not to scratch.

Diamond, mostly synthetic (man-made) industrial diamond, is used on the tips of drill bits, on saw blades for cutting stone and glass, and in grinding and polishing tools, because it is the hardest substance.
Graphite is mixed with clay to make pencil "leads", because its layers slide off and mark the paper.

Graphite is used as a dry lubricant (a slippery solid that reduces friction without oil), e.g. for locks and for machinery that gets hot, because its layers slide over each other and it withstands high temperatures.

Carbon nanotubes and graphene are added to plastics to make strong, light composite materials (materials made by combining two substances) for sports equipment, e.g. tennis rackets and bicycle frames.
Graphite conducts electricity, has a very high melting point and is fairly unreactive, which makes it useful in electrical cells and in electrolysis (using electricity to split a compound).

Graphite is used for electrodes (the conductors that carry current into or out of a solution or cell) because it conducts electricity, has a very high melting point and is fairly unreactive, e.g. in the electrolysis of solutions in laboratories and industry.
In a zinc–carbon dry cell (a battery with a paste instead of a liquid), the positive electrode, or cathode, is a carbon rod made of graphite.

In a lithium-ion cell (a rechargeable battery), the negative electrode is usually graphite: lithium ions fit between its layers when the cell is charged and leave again when it discharges. There is more on this in The lithium-ion cell.
Graphene's very large surface area and high conductivity are being developed for faster-charging batteries and supercapacitors (devices that store and release electrical charge very quickly).
Electronic devices need materials that move electric charge or heat well, and some also need to bend or let light through. Graphene, nanotubes, diamond and graphite each meet part of this need.

Graphene conducts electricity extremely well and is transparent and flexible, so it is being developed for touchscreens, flexible displays, wearable sensors and very fast transistors (the tiny switches inside chips).
Carbon nanotubes conduct electricity and are being developed for transistors and for conductive films and inks.
Diamond conducts heat better than copper but does not conduct electricity, so it is used as a heat sink to carry heat away from powerful electronic components without short-circuiting them.
Graphite and graphene conduct heat well, and they are used in heat-spreading sheets in phones and laptops.
Nanotechnology works with structures so small that single molecules matter. Fullerenes, nanotubes and graphene fit this scale, and their strength and shape suggest uses in medicine and materials.
Nanotechnology is the use of materials and structures on the scale of 1–100 nanometres, where 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m; fullerenes, nanotubes and graphene are nanomaterials.
Fullerene cages and nanotubes are being researched for drug delivery: a drug molecule can be held inside them or attached to the outside, and carried to target cells such as cancer cells.
Nanotubes are among the strongest materials known for their mass, and they are used to reinforce composites.
C₆₀ molecules are tiny, roughly spherical molecules held together by weak forces, so they have been researched as nano-scale lubricants, or "molecular ball bearings".
Graphene-based membranes (thin filtering layers) are being researched for filtering and purifying water, because a graphene sheet is strong and gases and many other substances cannot pass through it.
To discuss the use of carbon allotropes in society, weigh what they offer against what holds them back and what could go wrong. Then tie every use back to structure.

Benefits include lighter, stronger materials that reduce the fuel used by vehicles, better batteries for electric vehicles and for storing renewable energy, new medical treatments, and faster, flexible electronics.
Limits: many graphene and nanotube uses are still at the research stage, because making large, defect-free sheets cheaply is difficult.

Risks: the health effects of nanoparticles are not fully known, and some long, thin nanotubes inhaled as dust may damage the lungs in a similar way to asbestos fibres, so they need careful handling and testing.
Mining natural diamonds has environmental and social costs, and "conflict diamonds" (diamonds sold to pay for wars) have funded wars; synthetic diamonds are an alternative for many uses.
Each use follows from the structure: four bonds per carbon in a three-dimensional network give diamond its hardness and lack of electrical conduction.
Three bonds per carbon with delocalised electrons give conduction in graphite, graphene and nanotubes, and weak forces between layers or molecules give softness and lubrication in graphite and C₆₀.

Organic compounds fall into families, and what decides how a compound behaves is a small group of atoms attached to its carbon skeleton. The members of one family also change gradually from one to the next.

A functional group is an atom or group of atoms, attached to the hydrocarbon part of a molecule (the part made only of carbon and hydrogen), that is responsible for the characteristic chemical properties of a family of organic compounds.
Examples of functional groups are –OH in alcohols and –COOH in carboxylic acids.
The hydrocarbon part, made of C–C and C–H bonds, is fairly unreactive, so reactions take place mainly at the functional group.
Compounds with the same functional group react in the same way; for example, every carboxylic acid fizzes with sodium carbonate.
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula (one formula, written with n carbons, that fits every member) and the same functional group.
Each member of a homologous series differs from the next by CH₂, a mass of 14, so the chain grows one carbon at a time.

Members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties, because they share a functional group, and a gradual change (trend) in physical properties, such as boiling point rising with chain length.
Each family can be written with R standing for the hydrocarbon part, e.g. R–OH for an alcohol, so that attention falls on the functional group.

Each family is listed with its structure, general formula, ending and first member. The first block covers the hydrocarbons, which contain only carbon and hydrogen. There is more on naming alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and benzene in Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties.
Alkanes have C–C single bonds only, so they are saturated, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, ending -ane, and first member methane, CH₄.
Cycloalkanes are limited to cyclohexane, a ring of six carbons with single bonds, C₆H₁₂, and it is named with the prefix cyclo- (a word-beginning that tells you the carbons form a ring).
Cyclohexane is a saturated (single bonds only), non-polar (no charged ends) liquid with a boiling point of 81 °C, used as a solvent (a liquid that dissolves other substances).
Cycloalkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, the same as the alkenes, so a cycloalkane and an alkene with the same number of carbons have the same molecular formula.
Alkenes have a C=C double bond, general formula CₙH₂ₙ, ending -ene, and first member ethene, C₂H₄.
Alkynes have a C≡C triple bond, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, ending -yne, and first member ethyne, C₂H₂.
Aromatics are limited to benzene, C₆H₆, a planar (flat) ring of six carbons with delocalised electrons (electrons shared around the whole ring instead of sitting in one bond).
These families are defined by a functional group that replaces a hydrogen or adds oxygen to the carbon chain. For each, learn the group, the general formula, the ending and the first member.

Haloalkanes have a halogen atom, –X (F, Cl, Br, I, the group 17 elements), in place of H, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X for one halogen, prefixes fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- and iodo-, and first member chloromethane, CH₃Cl.
Alcohols have a hydroxyl group, –OH, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, ending -ol, and first member methanol, CH₃OH.
Aldehydes have a carbonyl group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen) at the end of the chain, –CHO, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁CHO (n = 0, 1, 2 …), i.e. CₙH₂ₙO, ending -al, and first member methanal, HCHO.
Ketones have a carbonyl group, C=O, inside the chain, bonded to two carbons, general formula CₙH₂ₙO (n ≥ 3), ending -one, and first member propanone, CH₃COCH₃.
Aldehydes and ketones share the formula CₙH₂ₙO, so the position of the C=O (end or inside the chain) is what tells the two families apart.
The last two families both contain oxygen in a –COO– arrangement. Together with aldehydes and ketones, they all share one feature, the carbonyl group.
Carboxylic acids (monocarboxylic, meaning one –COOH) have a carboxyl group, –COOH, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH, i.e. CₙH₂ₙO₂, ending -oic acid, and first member methanoic acid, HCOOH.
Esters have an ester group, –COO–, linking two hydrocarbon parts, general formula RCOOR′, CₙH₂ₙO₂ (n ≥ 2), named as alkyl …-oate, and first member methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃.
Carboxylic acids and esters share the formula CₙH₂ₙO₂, so the same molecular formula can belong to an acid or to an ester.
Aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters all contain the carbonyl group, C=O.

IUPAC naming is a set of systematic rules that gives each compound one name, built from a stem for the carbon chain, an ending for the functional group and prefixes for anything attached. Work through the steps in order.
Step 1: find the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the functional group; its number of carbons gives the stem: 1 meth-, 2 eth-, 3 prop-, 4 but-, 5 pent-, 6 hex-.
Step 2: add the ending (suffix) for the functional group (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid or -oate), or the prefix for a halogen (chloro- and so on).
Step 3: number the chain from the end that gives the functional group the lowest number, and put that number before the ending (butan-2-ol) or before the prefix (2-chlorobutane).
Step 4: name and number branches (side chains of carbon, such as methyl- and ethyl-) and halogen substituents as prefixes, in alphabetical order.
Use di-, tri- and tetra- for two, three or four of the same group, giving each a number, e.g. 1,2-dichloroethane and 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol.
Numbers are separated from each other by commas and from words by hyphens.
No number is needed when there is only one possible position: the –CHO and –COOH carbons are always carbon 1, e.g. ethanal and propanoic acid.
There is only one propanone and only one butanone, so no number is needed for them.
A haloalkane is an alkane carrying one or more halogen atoms. They are named with the halogen as a prefix, and several have uses, as solvents, as an early anaesthetic and in making PVC.
A haloalkane is an alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by halogen atoms; a chloroalkane is a haloalkane that contains chlorine.
Chloromethane CH₃Cl, dichloromethane CH₂Cl₂, trichloromethane CHCl₃ and tetrachloromethane CCl₄ are examples, with one, two, three and four chlorine atoms on one carbon.
Further examples, such as chloroethane CH₃CH₂Cl, 1-chloropropane CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and 2-chloropropane CH₃CHClCH₃ are examples.
Other examples, such as 1-bromobutane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (CH₃)₃CBr and 1,2-dichloroethane CH₂ClCH₂Cl are examples.
Naming example: CH₃CH₂CHClCH₃ has a four-carbon chain with Cl on carbon 2, numbered from the nearer end, so it is 2-chlorobutane.
Dichloromethane is a solvent for oils and grease, e.g. in paint strippers.
Trichloromethane (chloroform) was first used as an anaesthetic (a drug that stops a patient feeling pain during surgery) in 1847 by James Young Simpson in Edinburgh, but it is toxic (poisonous).
Chloroethene is the monomer of PVC, meaning the small molecule that joins in long chains to make the plastic.
Alcohols are compounds with an –OH group on a carbon chain. Their names end in -ol, and the number tells you which carbon carries the –OH.
Members, such as methanol CH₃OH, ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH are members.
Other members, such as butan-2-ol CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, 2-methylpropan-1-ol (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (CH₃)₃COH are also members.
Pentan-1-ol and hexan-1-ol are members too, such as with five and six carbons.
Naming: replace the final -e of the alkane by -ol and give the position of the –OH; CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is butan-2-ol.
With more than one –OH, keep the -e and add -diol or -triol, so that the name stays easy to say.
Propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol), CH₂(OH)CH(OH)CH₂OH, has three –OH groups and forms the backbone of fats and oils.
Alcohols are sorted into three classes according to how many other carbon atoms are bonded to the carbon that carries the –OH.
Primary alcohol: the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to at most one other carbon atom (–CH₂OH), e.g. ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
Methanol, with no other carbon attached, is also treated as primary.
Secondary alcohol: the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to two other carbon atoms (>CHOH, a carbon with one H and two carbon neighbours), e.g. propan-2-ol and butan-2-ol.
Tertiary alcohol: the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to three other carbon atoms, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
The class depends on the number of carbons bonded to the carbon with the –OH, not on the number of –OH groups.
Alcohols turn up in drinks, fuels and household products, and one of them is dangerous.
Ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks, and is about 40% v/v (40 cm³ of ethanol in every 100 cm³ of drink) in spirits such as whiskey.
Ethanol is a fuel and a solvent, such as in perfumes, deodorants, hairsprays and varnishes.
Methanol is toxic, so it must not be confused with ethanol.
Propan-2-ol is used in hand sanitisers and as a cleaning solvent, for example.
Both families contain the carbonyl group, C=O. In an aldehyde it is at the end of the chain; in a ketone it is inside the chain, and that difference decides the name.
Aldehydes, for example methanal HCHO, ethanal CH₃CHO, propanal CH₃CH₂CHO, butanal CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO and 2-methylpropanal (CH₃)₂CHCHO.
The –CHO group is always at the end of the chain, and its carbon is carbon 1.
Ketones, for example propanone CH₃COCH₃, butanone CH₃COCH₂CH₃, pentan-2-one CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, pentan-3-one CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ and 3-methylbutan-2-one CH₃COCH(CH₃)₂.
The C=O of a ketone is inside the chain, so the smallest ketone has three carbons.
Naming: replace the -e of the alkane by -al for an aldehyde or by -one for a ketone.
The ketone position is numbered from the nearer end when there is a choice, e.g. pentan-2-one, not pentan-4-one.
Each of these carbonyl compounds has a particular role, from preserving specimens to flavouring.
Methanal in water, called formalin (an aqueous solution of methanal), preserves biological specimens.
Ethanal is the first product formed when the body breaks down ethanol (the first metabolite, meaning the first substance made in the body's chemical breakdown).
Propanone is a solvent, for example in nail varnish remover.
Benzaldehyde gives the flavour of almonds.
Carboxylic acids carry the –COOH group, which is the key to both their names and their behaviour.
Members, for example methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH₃COOH, propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH, butanoic acid CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH and 2-methylpropanoic acid (CH₃)₂CHCOOH.
Pentanoic acid and hexanoic acid are also members.
Naming: replace the -e of the alkane by -oic acid.
The carbon of the –COOH group is counted in the chain as carbon 1, and substituents (atoms or groups added to the chain) are numbered from it.
CH₃CHClCOOH is 2-chloropropanoic acid, and CH₂ClCOOH is chloroethanoic acid, with no number because the Cl can only be on carbon 2.
The carboxyl group contains a C=O and an –OH on the same carbon, but it behaves differently from both an alcohol and a ketone.
Carboxylic acids are acidic, which is how they differ from alcohols and ketones. There is more on this in Physical properties and acidity.
Carboxylic acids occur in nature and in food.
Methanoic acid is in the stings of ants and nettles; its old name, formic acid, comes from the Latin for ant, formica.
Ethanoic acid gives vinegar its sharp taste; vinegar is about 5% ethanoic acid, usually between 4% and 6%.
Ethanoic acid is used as a food flavouring and preservative (a substance that stops food spoiling).
Benzoic acid and sodium benzoate are food preservatives.
An ester is made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, and its name records both parents, alcohol part first. There is more on the reaction in Tests, reaction schemes and preparing an ester.
Esters are formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, with loss of water: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water (⇌ means the reaction is reversible).
Step 1: split the ester at the single-bonded oxygen into the part from the acid, which contains C=O, and the part from the alcohol.
Step 2: name the alcohol part as an alkyl group (a hydrocarbon part named methyl, ethyl, propyl and so on) and write it first.
Step 3: name the acid part by changing -oic acid to -oate; CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, from ethanoic acid and ethanol, is ethyl ethanoate.
The condensed formula is written acid part first, as in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, but the name gives the alcohol part first, as in ethyl ethanoate.
HCOOC₂H₅ and C₂H₅OOCH are the same compound, ethyl methanoate.
Only esters made from monocarboxylic acids (one –COOH) and primary alcohols (–OH on a carbon with at most one other carbon) are required.
Esters of the first few acids and alcohols are the ones to know, and esters have a range of uses, from flavourings and perfumes to solvents.
Esters of methanoic acid, for example, are methyl methanoate HCOOCH₃, ethyl methanoate HCOOCH₂CH₃ and propyl methanoate HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃.
Esters of ethanoic acid, for example, are methyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₃, ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and propyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃.
Esters of propanoic acid, for example, are methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ and ethyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃.
Esters have sweet, fruity smells and give many fruits and flowers their scent.
Esters are used as food flavourings and in perfumes.
Ethyl ethanoate is used as a solvent in glues and in nail varnish remover.
Fats and oils are esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol). There is more on this in Redox and acid–base reactions of organic compounds.
Ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂, is used to show the four ways of representing an organic molecule. Each shows a different amount of information about the same molecule.
Molecular formula: the number of atoms of each element in one molecule, e.g. C₂H₄O₂ for ethanoic acid.
The molecular formula does not show how the atoms are joined.
Condensed structural formula: the atoms bonded to each carbon are written in order along the chain, without drawing bonds, e.g. CH₃COOH.
Branches go in brackets in a condensed formula, e.g. (CH₃)₂CHOH for propan-2-ol.
Expanded (full or displayed) structural formula: every atom and every bond is drawn, e.g. ethanoic acid drawn as H₃C with three C–H bonds, joined to a carbon with a C=O double bond and a C–O–H.
Physical model: a 3D ball-and-stick model, made from a model kit, shows the real spatial arrangement and bond angles.
Model-kit colours are usually carbon black, hydrogen white, oxygen red and chlorine green.
The empirical formula is a fifth way of writing a compound, and ethanol gives a worked example of all the representations side by side.
Empirical formula (the simplest ratio of atoms) may also be asked. There is more on this in Formulae and balancing equations.
Ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂, has empirical formula CH₂O, the same as methanal and glucose.
Diagram: ethanol shown four ways, as C₂H₆O, as CH₃CH₂OH, as the expanded structure with all bonds, and as a ball-and-stick sketch.
The shape around a carbon atom depends on how many groups are bonded to it. Carbon appears in three geometries in this course: tetrahedral, planar and linear.
A carbon with four single bonds has its four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron (a pyramid with four triangular faces), with bond angles of 109.5°; this is tetrahedral geometry.
Every carbon in ethanol and in haloalkanes is tetrahedral.
A carbon with one double bond (C=C or C=O) and two single bonds has its three bonding groups in a flat triangle, with bond angles of 120°; this is planar (trigonal planar) geometry.
The C=O carbon in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters is planar.
Both carbons of ethene are planar, and all six carbons of benzene are planar.
A carbon with a triple bond, as in ethyne, is linear, with a bond angle of 180°; it is neither tetrahedral nor planar in this classification.
An expanded formula drawn on paper shows the tetrahedral angles as 90°; only a 3D model or a wedge drawing shows the true shape.

The shapes follow from electron-pair repulsion: four bonding groups around carbon spread out tetrahedrally, and three groups spread out in a plane, where a double bond counts as one group. There is more on this in Bonding, formulae and shapes.
Classify each carbon atom in the molecule. The oxygen that bridges two parts of an ester is not a carbon, so it is not counted.
Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH has 2 tetrahedral carbons and 0 planar carbons, because each carbon has four single bonds.
Ethanal CH₃CHO and ethanoic acid CH₃COOH each have 1 tetrahedral carbon (the CH₃, with four single bonds) and 1 planar carbon (the C=O carbon).
Propanone CH₃COCH₃ has 2 tetrahedral carbons (both CH₃) and 1 planar carbon, because only the middle carbon has the C=O.
Methyl methanoate HCOOCH₃ has 1 planar carbon (the C=O carbon) and 1 tetrahedral carbon (the CH₃).
Ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ has 1 planar carbon (the C=O carbon) and 3 tetrahedral carbons, because the other three carbons have only single bonds.
Methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ has 1 planar carbon and 3 tetrahedral carbons, because only the C=O carbon is planar.
Ethene CH₂=CH₂ and benzene C₆H₆ have all their carbons planar, because every carbon has a double bond.
Cyclohexane C₆H₁₂ has all six carbons tetrahedral, so its ring is not flat, unlike benzene.
Writing R for the part of a molecule that doesn't matter lets you show a whole family, or a whole type of reaction, in one formula.
R stands for an alkyl group, the hydrocarbon part of a molecule, e.g. CH₃– or C₂H₅–, so the formula highlights the functional group.
R and R′ are used when two hydrocarbon parts may differ.
General structures: haloalkane R–X; alcohol R–OH; aldehyde R–CHO; ketone R–CO–R′; carboxylic acid R–COOH; ester R–COO–R′.
In an aldehyde, a carboxylic acid or the acid part of an ester, R may be a hydrogen atom, as in methanal HCHO, methanoic acid HCOOH and methyl methanoate HCOOCH₃.
In a ketone both R groups must be carbon groups, and in an ester R′ must be a carbon group, because a ketone's C=O is bonded to two carbons.
Alcohol classes written with R: primary R–CH₂OH; secondary R₂CHOH; tertiary R₃COH.
R is used to show a reaction common to a whole family, e.g. RCOOH + NaOH → RCOONa + H₂O.
Isomers are different compounds that share a molecular formula. Structural isomers differ in how the atoms are joined, and the first type differs in the carbon skeleton.
Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, meaning the atoms are joined in a different order.
Chain isomers differ in the carbon skeleton (the chain of carbons), i.e. in branching: butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol (C₄H₁₀O).
Chain isomers also include butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid (C₄H₈O₂).
Two further types of structural isomer: position isomers keep the same functional group but put it in a different place, and functional group isomers belong to different families.
Position isomers have the same functional group in different positions: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol (C₃H₈O).
Position isomers also include 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane (C₃H₇Cl), and pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one (C₅H₁₀O).
Functional group isomers belong to different families: propanal and propanone (C₃H₆O), and butanal and butanone (C₄H₈O).
Further functional group isomers are ethanoic acid and methyl methanoate (C₂H₄O₂), and propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate and ethyl methanoate (C₃H₆O₂).
Cyclohexane and hex-1-ene (C₆H₁₂) are also functional group isomers, since a ring and a C=C double bond give the same formula.
Some formulae have several isomers on the course, and isomers of different types differ in how much their properties change.

The four alcohols of formula C₄H₉OH are two primary alcohols, one secondary alcohol and one tertiary alcohol: butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary, butan-2-ol is secondary, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.
Esters of formula C₄H₈O₂ on the course are ethyl ethanoate, methyl propanoate and propyl methanoate; the acids of the same formula are butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid.
Chain and position isomers have similar chemical properties but slightly different physical properties.

Functional group isomers have very different chemical and physical properties, e.g. ethanoic acid (acidic, boiling point 118 °C) and methyl methanoate (not acidic, boiling point 32 °C). There is more on this in Physical properties and acidity.
Each way of writing a molecule shows something the others hide, so the best choice depends on what you need to show.
The molecular formula is compact but cannot tell isomers apart: C₂H₆O could be ethanol or another compound.
The condensed formula shows the order of atoms and the functional group, so it distinguishes isomers, but it does not show bond angles or shape.
The expanded formula shows every bond, so double bonds and functional groups are clear, but it does not show the 3D shape.
The 3D model shows shape and bond angles, but it is slower to draw, is not to scale, and does not show electron distribution or polarity.
Different representations of the same molecule must contain the same atoms joined in the same way.
In every representation, each carbon must have four bonds, and a double bond counts as two.

When a solid melts or a liquid boils, the molecules move apart from one another but stay intact. So the energy needed depends on the attractions between molecules, and three kinds of attraction matter for organic compounds.

Melting and boiling separate molecules, so they depend on the intermolecular forces (the attractions between separate molecules), not on the covalent bonds (shared electron pairs) inside the molecules.
The stronger the forces, the more energy is needed to pull the molecules apart, so the higher the melting and boiling points.
London dispersion forces are the weak attractions between all molecules, polar or not. They grow stronger as a molecule has more electrons and more surface.

Permanent dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules. A polar bond is one where the shared electrons sit nearer the more electronegative atom (the atom that pulls harder on shared electrons), leaving one end δ+ and the other δ−.

Hydrogen bonding is a strong attraction between an H bonded to O, N or F and a lone pair (a non-bonding pair of outer electrons) on O, N or F of a neighbouring molecule. The order of strength is London forces only, then dipole–dipole, then hydrogen bonding.

Which forces a compound has depends on its family, meaning the functional group (the atom or group that gives a family its properties) and whether that group has polar bonds. None of these families can hydrogen bond to its own molecules.
Alkanes and alkenes (hydrocarbons, made only of C and H) are non-polar, so they have London dispersion forces only.

Haloalkanes (alkanes with a halogen such as Cl in place of an H) have a polar C–Cl bond (Cl 3.16, C 2.55 on the electronegativity scale), so they have permanent dipole–dipole forces as well as London forces.
Haloalkanes cannot hydrogen bond, because they have no H bonded to O, N or F.
Aldehydes and ketones (compounds containing the C=O carbonyl group) have a strongly polar C=O bond (Cδ+=Oδ−), giving dipole–dipole forces.
Aldehydes and ketones cannot hydrogen bond with each other, because their hydrogens are bonded to carbon, not oxygen.
Esters have polar C=O and C–O bonds, giving dipole–dipole forces, but no O–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding between ester molecules.
Alcohols and carboxylic acids both contain an O–H group, so unlike the families above they can hydrogen bond to their own kind.
Alcohols have a very polar O–H bond (O 3.44, H 2.20), so alcohol molecules hydrogen bond to each other as well as having London forces.
Carboxylic acids have both O–H and C=O in the –COOH group, so their molecules hydrogen bond strongly.
In the pure liquid, carboxylic acid molecules pair up as dimers (two molecules joined together) held by two hydrogen bonds, the O–H of each molecule bonding to the C=O of the other.
Diagram: two ethanoic acid molecules facing each other, with dashed hydrogen bonds from each O–H hydrogen to the C=O oxygen of the other molecule, forming a dimer.

Size also affects boiling point, because bigger molecules have stronger London forces. To compare the type of force fairly, you need compounds with about the same relative molecular mass (Mr, the mass of a molecule compared with carbon-12).

At similar relative molecular mass, so with similar London forces, boiling point depends on the type of intermolecular force: London forces only give the lowest boiling point, then dipole–dipole forces, then hydrogen bonding.
Butane (Mr 58) boils at −1 °C, propanal (Mr 58) at 48 °C and propanone (Mr 58) at 56 °C.
Methyl methanoate (Mr 60) boils at 32 °C, propan-1-ol (Mr 60) at 97 °C and ethanoic acid (Mr 60) at 118 °C.
Propanal boils far higher than butane because its polar C=O gives dipole–dipole forces in addition to London forces.
Propan-1-ol boils higher than propanal because its O–H groups form hydrogen bonds between molecules, which are stronger than dipole–dipole forces.

Ethanoic acid boils higher than propan-1-ol because each acid molecule has two oxygens taking part, and pairs of molecules form doubly hydrogen-bonded dimers, so more hydrogen bonding must be overcome.
Two compounds can have the same mass, or even the same formula, and still boil at very different temperatures. The difference comes down to whether hydrogen bonding is possible.
Ethanoic acid (bp 118 °C) and methyl methanoate (bp 32 °C) are isomers (different compounds with the same formula), both C₂H₄O₂, and have the same mass.
The acid hydrogen bonds to other acid molecules, but the ester cannot, as it has no O–H.
Ethanol (bp 78 °C) boils far higher than ethane (bp −89 °C) because ethanol has hydrogen bonding, whereas ethane has London forces only.
Within one family the functional group stays the same, so what changes boiling point is chain length. A homologous series (a family whose members differ by one CH₂ unit) shows this clearly.
Within a homologous series, boiling point rises with chain length, because each extra CH₂ adds electrons and surface area, so London forces get stronger.
Alcohols: methanol 65 °C; ethanol 78 °C; propan-1-ol 97 °C; butan-1-ol 117 °C; pentan-1-ol 138 °C; hexan-1-ol 157 °C, a rise of about 20 °C per CH₂.
Carboxylic acids: methanoic acid 101 °C; ethanoic acid 118 °C; propanoic acid 141 °C; butanoic acid 164 °C.
Aldehydes: methanal −19 °C, a gas; ethanal 20 °C; propanal 48 °C; butanal 75 °C.
Haloalkanes follow the same trend, and adding halogens has its own effect. A longer chain also makes the families more alike.
Chloroalkanes: chloromethane −24 °C and chloroethane 12 °C are gases at room temperature.
Adding more chlorines also raises the boiling point: CH₃Cl −24 °C; CH₂Cl₂ 40 °C; CHCl₃ 61 °C; CCl₄ 77 °C, because more electrons give stronger London forces.
As the chain gets longer, the hydrocarbon part makes up more of the molecule, so the difference between families gets smaller, because the effect of the functional group is diluted.
Molecules with the same formula can have different shapes. A branched molecule is more compact than a straight chain, and that changes how strongly molecules attract one another.

Branched isomers have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers, because they are more compact, with less surface contact between molecules, so London forces are weaker. There is more on this in Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties.
The more compact the molecule, and the more crowded the –OH, the lower the boiling point.
Exams give a table or graph of boiling point against number of carbons and ask for the trend, the reason and a prediction. A fixed three-step method covers all three.
Step 1: from a table or graph of boiling point against number of carbons, describe the trend, for example that boiling point rises as the number of carbons rises.
Step 2: explain the trend in terms of chain length, London forces and the functional group.
Step 3: predict the next member by continuing the trend, e.g. continuing the primary alcohols from butan-1-ol, 117 °C, gives about 138 °C for pentan-1-ol.
Melting also depends on intermolecular forces, but a solid is an ordered packing of molecules. So how neatly the molecules fit together matters too.
Melting points depend on the intermolecular forces and also on how well the molecules pack together in the solid, so they follow trends less regularly than boiling points.
Ethanoic acid melts at 17 °C, high for its size, because of strong hydrogen bonding.
On a cold day, pure ethanoic acid freezes to an ice-like solid, so it is called glacial ethanoic acid.
Compact, symmetrical molecules pack well and melt higher: 2-methylpropan-2-ol melts at about 25 °C, but butan-1-ol melts at −89 °C.
Cyclohexane (a ring of six carbons) melts at 6.5 °C, but hexane (the straight chain) melts at −95 °C, again because the compact ring packs better.
Ionic bonding (attraction between oppositely charged ions) gives far higher melting points: sodium ethanoate, an ionic salt of ethanoic acid, is a solid that melts at about 324 °C.
Whether a compound dissolves depends on whether it can attract the solvent (the liquid doing the dissolving) as strongly as it attracts itself. For water, that means hydrogen bonding.
Like dissolves like: a compound dissolves in water if it can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
Non-polar compounds dissolve in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, where London forces are similar.
Lower alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol) are miscible with water, mixing in all proportions, because their –OH groups hydrogen bond with water.
Lower carboxylic acids, from methanoic acid to butanoic acid, are also miscible with water, for the same reason.
Solubility in water falls as the chain gets longer, because the non-polar hydrocarbon part cannot hydrogen bond and disrupts the hydrogen bonding of the water.
Butan-1-ol is only partly soluble in water, and hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
Longer chains dissolve better in non-polar solvents.
These families cannot hydrogen bond to their own molecules, yet small ones still dissolve in water. The reason is that water can hydrogen bond to them.
Small aldehydes and ketones, methanal, ethanal and propanone, are miscible with water: they have no O–H, but water molecules hydrogen bond to the lone pairs on their C=O oxygen.
Propanone dissolves both polar and non-polar substances, so it is a useful solvent.
Butanone is not fully miscible with water; only the smallest ketone, propanone, is.
Small esters are slightly soluble in water for the same reason, as water hydrogen bonds to their oxygens: about 8 g of ethyl ethanoate dissolves in 100 g of water at room temperature.
Small esters dissolve well in organic solvents.
Compounds with no way to hydrogen bond with water stay out of it, while ionic compounds are pulled in by water's charges. These cases explain common solvents and a purification method.
Alkanes, alkenes, benzene and haloalkanes are insoluble in water, as they cannot hydrogen bond with it, but they dissolve in non-polar solvents.
Haloalkanes are good solvents for grease and oil.

Benzoic acid is only slightly soluble in cold water because of its large non-polar benzene ring, but it is much more soluble in hot water, which allows it to be purified by recrystallisation (dissolving in hot water, then cooling so pure crystals form).
There is more on this in Investigation: synthesising benzoic acid.
Ionic salts of carboxylic acids, sodium ethanoate and sodium benzoate, are much more soluble in water than the acids, because their ions are attracted to water molecules (ion–dipole attraction).
Alcohols and carboxylic acids both contain an O–H group, yet carboxylic acids are far more acidic. To see why, first look at why an O–H hydrogen can be lost at all.
An acid, in the Brønsted–Lowry sense, is a proton donor; both alcohols and carboxylic acids can donate the H⁺ of their O–H group.
The O–H bond is polar because oxygen (3.44) is much more electronegative than hydrogen (2.20), so the shared electrons are pulled towards oxygen.
This leaves the hydrogen δ+, so it can be removed as H⁺ by a base (a proton acceptor).
C–H bonds are almost non-polar (C 2.55, H 2.20), so hydrogens bonded to carbon are not acidic.
In ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, only the hydrogen on oxygen is lost.
How acidic the O–H is depends mainly on how stable the negative ion (the conjugate base, what is left after H⁺ leaves) is.
The more stable the negative ion, the more easily H⁺ is lost and the stronger the acid.
An alcohol can lose H⁺, but the ion it leaves behind is unstable. This is why alcohols are such weak acids.
An alcohol can lose H⁺ to form an alkoxide ion: R–OH ⇌ R–O⁻ + H⁺. Ethanol gives the ethoxide ion, C₂H₅O⁻.
In the alkoxide ion the negative charge is concentrated on one oxygen atom, because it cannot be spread out by resonance (sharing the charge over more than one atom).
The alkoxide ion is therefore unstable and readily takes back H⁺.
The alkyl group (a chain of carbons and hydrogens) is electron-releasing, pushing electron density towards the oxygen, which makes the negative charge on the alkoxide ion even less stable.
Alcohols are therefore weaker acids than water.
Because the alkoxide ion is so unstable, alcohols behave as neutral in water. Their acidic O–H shows up in the reaction with sodium metal.
Alcohols are neutral in water: they do not change the colour of indicators, do not react with sodium carbonate, and do not react to any useful extent with sodium hydroxide.
Alcohols react with sodium metal, giving hydrogen gas and a salt, which is evidence of their acidic O–H.
The reaction of ethanol with sodium is gentler than the reaction of sodium with water, showing that ethanol is a weaker acid than water.
A carboxylic acid loses H⁺ much more easily than an alcohol, and the reason lies in the ion it leaves behind. Its negative charge is not stuck on one atom.
A carboxylic acid loses H⁺ to form a carboxylate ion: RCOOH(aq) ⇌ RCOO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq).
Ethanoic acid gives the ethanoate ion: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.
In the carboxylate ion the negative charge is delocalised (spread out), shared over both oxygen atoms through the O–C–O group.
The carboxylate ion is a resonance hybrid (a blend) of two structures, in each of which a different oxygen carries the negative charge.
Bond lengths show that the charge really is shared, and the sharing is what stabilises the ion. This is why a carboxylic acid is a much stronger acid than an alcohol.
The two C–O bonds in a carboxylate ion are the same length, between the length of a C–O single bond and that of a C=O double bond.
In the acid itself, the C=O bond is shorter than the C–O bond.
Spreading the charge over two oxygens stabilises the carboxylate ion.
So a carboxylic acid loses H⁺ much more readily than an alcohol, whose alkoxide ion has no such stabilisation.

Diagram: the two resonance structures of the ethanoate ion, CH₃–C(=O)–O⁻ ↔ CH₃–C(–O⁻)=O, joined by a double-headed arrow, and the hybrid drawn with a dashed bond over O–C–O and a charge of −½ on each oxygen.
A second effect adds to resonance. Atoms in a molecule pull on electrons along the bonds, and this changes how easily the O–H hydrogen leaves.
The inductive effect is the pulling (or pushing) of electron density along sigma bonds (the single bonds that join atoms) by an atom or group, because of its electronegativity.
In the –COOH group, the electronegative oxygen of the C=O pulls electron density away from the O–H bond.
This makes the O–H more polar and the hydrogen easier to lose than in an alcohol.
Electron-withdrawing groups such as chlorine, attached to the carbon chain, pull electron density towards themselves.
This spreads out the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilises it, so the acid is stronger.
More chlorine atoms, or chlorine nearer the –COOH, give a stronger effect.
Alkyl groups have the opposite effect to chlorine, so they weaken an acid. The Ka values (the acid dissociation constant: the larger the Ka, the stronger the acid) confirm the order.
Alkyl groups are electron-releasing; they push electron density towards the –COO⁻ group, destabilising it, so the acid is weaker.
Methanoic acid, with H on the –COOH, is stronger than ethanoic acid, with CH₃ on the –COOH, which is slightly stronger than propanoic acid.
Ka data at 25 °C: methanoic acid 1.8 × 10⁻⁴; ethanoic acid 1.8 × 10⁻⁵; propanoic acid 1.3 × 10⁻⁵.
Ka data at 25 °C: chloroethanoic acid 1.4 × 10⁻³; trichloroethanoic acid about 0.2.
Order of strength: CCl₃COOH > CH₂ClCOOH > HCOOH > CH₃COOH > CH₃CH₂COOH.

Carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols, but they are still weak acids. A weak acid dissociates (splits into H⁺ and its negative ion) only partly, and a short calculation shows how little.
Carboxylic acids are weak acids, only partly dissociated.

Step 1: the degree of dissociation (the fraction of molecules that lose H⁺) is approximately √(Ka ÷ concentration) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.1) = 0.013, so about 1.3% of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid is dissociated.
Carboxylic acids are still far stronger acids than alcohols, because of the resonance-stabilised carboxylate ion and the inductive effect of the C=O.
Ethanol is a much weaker acid, with Ka of the order of 10⁻¹⁶ (pKa about 16), weaker than water.
The difference in acidity shows up in everyday reactions. Carboxylic acids give the typical reactions of an acid, and alcohols mostly do not.
Carboxylic acids show typical acid properties that alcohols do not: they turn blue litmus red, fizz with sodium carbonate giving carbon dioxide, and react with magnesium giving hydrogen.
Carboxylic acids are neutralised by sodium hydroxide, e.g. CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O. There is more on this in Tests, reaction schemes and preparing an ester.
Sodium metal: an alcohol reacts, giving H₂; an acid reacts, giving H₂.
Sodium hydroxide: an alcohol has no useful reaction; an acid is neutralised.
Sodium carbonate: an alcohol does not react; an acid fizzes, giving CO₂.
Indicator: an alcohol is neutral; an acid is acidic.
Every acidity question has the same logic: the more stable the negative ion left behind, the stronger the acid. A two-step answer follows it.
Step 1 of explaining a difference in acidity: say which anion is more stable and why, referring to resonance and to electron-withdrawing or electron-releasing groups.
Step 2 of explaining a difference in acidity: conclude which acid loses H⁺ more easily.

Almost everything around you, from fuels to medicines to plastics, is built on carbon. Organic chemistry is the study of these carbon compounds, and carbon's bonding explains why there are so many of them.
Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, apart from simple ones such as carbon oxides, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates.
Organic compounds contain carbon, almost always bonded to hydrogen, and often oxygen, nitrogen, halogens (the group 17 elements such as chlorine) or sulfur.
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds (bonds made by sharing pairs of electrons), and carbon atoms bond strongly to each other, so carbon forms chains, branches and rings.
Carbon atoms can be joined by single, double or triple bonds, which adds even more possible structures.
Organic compounds were once thought to come only from living things.
In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound found in urine, from the inorganic salt ammonium cyanate, showing that organic compounds can be made in the laboratory.
Organic compounds have to start from somewhere. Two of the sources are the ground (fossil deposits) and living organisms.
Fossil sources are crude oil, natural gas and coal, formed from the remains of organisms over millions of years.
Fossil sources supply fuels and the feedstocks (starting materials) for most plastics, solvents, dyes, detergents and many medicines. There is more on this in Hydrocarbons: sources, uses and impact.
Fossil sources are finite, or non-renewable, because they take millions of years to form and are used far faster than they are made.
Living things make natural products: plants, animals and micro-organisms (organisms too small to see without a microscope, such as yeast and moulds) make organic compounds that can be extracted.
Oils and fats are extracted from plants and animals, so living things are a direct source.
Essential oils such as clove oil are extracted by steam distillation (passing steam through the plant material and condensing the vapour that carries the oil).
Medicines are extracted from plants, e.g. quinine from cinchona bark.
Micro-organisms can be put to work as tiny chemical factories. This process is called fermentation, and it gives both drinks and drugs.
Fermentation is when micro-organisms convert biomass (plant and other living material) into organic compounds; for example, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Equation: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g), catalysed by enzymes (biological catalysts) in the yeast.
Antibiotics such as penicillin are also made by fermentation.
Fermentation stops at about 12–15% ethanol by volume because the ethanol kills the yeast, so it cannot make a stronger drink.
Spirits (about 40% v/v ethanol, meaning 40% of the volume is ethanol) are made by distilling the fermented liquid, which concentrates the ethanol.
Chemists can also make organic compounds themselves, and they can swap fossil starting materials for plant-based ones.
Synthesis means chemists build more complex molecules from simpler ones, called precursors, in the laboratory and in industry.
Most modern medicines, plastics and pesticides are made by synthesis.
Renewable (bio-based) feedstocks: biomass such as sugar cane, maize and wood can replace fossil feedstocks, because plants can be regrown.
Bioethanol made from biomass can be used as a fuel.
Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) plastic is made from plant starch, e.g. from maize, and is biodegradable (broken down by micro-organisms) under industrial composting conditions.
Organic compounds are the main ingredients of several groups of industrial product. The first three groups are fuels, medicines and plastics.
Fuels are hydrocarbons (compounds of only hydrogen and carbon) such as methane (natural gas), petrol, diesel and kerosene, and alcohols such as ethanol, which release energy when they burn.
Fuels are used for transport, heating and electricity generation, because burning them releases energy as heat.
Pharmaceuticals are medicines that are almost all organic compounds.
Aspirin and paracetamol relieve pain; penicillin is an antibiotic (a medicine that kills bacteria).
Plastics are polymers (very long molecules made by joining many small molecules, called monomers) made mainly from oil-derived monomers.
Poly(ethene), made from ethene, is used for bags, bottles and film.
Poly(chloroethene), known as PVC, is made from chloroethene and used for pipes and window frames.
Plastics are light, cheap, durable, waterproof and insulating, which is why they are so widely used. There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.
The remaining product groups are pesticides, synthetic materials and a range of everyday organic chemicals such as solvents, flavourings and preservatives.
Pesticides are compounds that kill or control pests.
Insecticides kill insects, herbicides kill weeds and fungicides kill fungi, so each is chosen to match the pest.
Natural pesticides include neem oil, from the neem tree, and pyrethrins, from chrysanthemum flowers.
Synthetic pesticides include malathion, an insecticide, and glyphosate, a herbicide.
Synthetics are man-made materials that replace or improve on natural ones.
Synthetic fibres such as nylon and polyester are made from monomers that link into polymers, and are used for clothing, ropes and carpets.
Synthetic dyes, detergents and synthetic rubber are further synthetic products.
Ethanol is used as a solvent (a liquid that dissolves other substances) in perfumes and deodorants, and propanone is a solvent used in nail varnish remover.
Several smaller organic products appear in food, cosmetics and cleaning.
Esters are used as flavourings and fragrances, for example as flavourings and fragrances in products.
Ethanoic acid is used as a food preservative in vinegar, and sodium benzoate is also a food preservative.
Soaps and detergents are organic products. There is more on this in Surfactants and soap.
Organic products have changed how people live, which is why they are made in such quantity. Any evaluation starts with these benefits.
Fuels give energy for transport and heating.
Medicines and sanitation give longer, healthier lives.
Pesticides give higher crop yields and less food lost to pests.
Plastics are cheap, light, durable materials, so they suit packaging and pipes.
Synthetic fibres and other products supply clothing and goods for large populations.
The same products that bring benefits also cause environmental problems. Fuels, plastics and the use of fossil resources each have their own impact.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas linked to climate change.
Burning fossil fuels also releases pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and soot. There is more on this in Hydrocarbons: sources, uses and impact.
Most plastics are not biodegradable, so they persist for decades or longer as litter, in landfill and in the oceans.
In the oceans, plastics harm wildlife and break into microplastics (tiny fragments of plastic).
Burning plastics can release toxic gases.
Fossil feedstocks are finite, so they will eventually run out.
Extracting and processing fossil feedstocks uses energy and can cause spills and pollution.
Pesticides and medicines are designed to act on living things, so they can harm the wrong organisms or have unwanted effects.
Some pesticides are toxic to non-target organisms (living things the pesticide was not meant to kill) such as bees, birds and fish.
Persistent pesticides (ones that do not break down) such as DDT build up in food chains, which is called bioaccumulation.
DDT was banned for agricultural use in most countries, and the Stockholm Convention (2001) restricts it to disease-vector control.
The EU restricted outdoor use of three neonicotinoid insecticides in 2018 because of harm to bees.
Pesticide run-off (rain washing pesticide off fields) can contaminate water.
Medicines can cause side effects and addiction, for example addiction to opiates.
Overuse of antibiotics leads to antibiotic resistance, and drug residues reach waterways.
To decide whether a product is a good idea, you weigh its benefits against its impacts over its whole life, and look at ways to reduce those impacts.
A product's impact is assessed across its whole life, from raw material and manufacture to use and disposal; this is a life-cycle view.
Ways to reduce impact include recycling and reuse.
Renewable feedstocks and biodegradable alternatives reduce impact.
Designing safer molecules that break down after use reduces impact.
Using less, e.g. targeted pesticide use, reduces impact.
A natural source is not automatically safer or more sustainable, because natural compounds can be toxic.
Growing biomass uses land, water and fertiliser, so bio-based feedstocks have costs of their own.
A balanced answer names a benefit and an impact, and says how the impact can be reduced.
