These six words are used throughout the study of pharmaceuticals, so each needs a clear definition.
A pharmaceutical is a substance used to prevent, diagnose, treat or relieve the symptoms of disease; almost all are organic compounds.
A natural product is an organic compound made by a living organism such as a plant, animal or micro-organism, e.g. quinine in cinchona bark, morphine in the opium poppy and penicillin from a mould.
A narcotic is a drug that dulls pain and causes drowsiness or sleep; many, e.g. morphine and heroin, are addictive and are legally controlled.
A precursor is a starting compound from which another compound is made; salicylic acid is the precursor of aspirin.
The active ingredient is the compound in a medicine that produces its effect; the rest of a tablet, such as fillers, binders and coatings, is inactive.
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or biological systems to make useful products, e.g. making penicillin by fermentation.
Long before laboratories, people used plants as medicines. Many of these plants contain a single active compound that explains their effect.
Willow bark has been used to relieve pain and fever since ancient times; its use in ancient Greek medicine is traditionally credited to Hippocrates, about 400 BC.
Willow (Salix) bark contains salicin, which the body converts into salicylic acid, the active compound.
Cinchona bark, from trees native to the Andes of South America, contains quinine, which has been used to treat malaria (a disease spread by mosquitoes) since the 1600s.
Quinine is also the bitter flavour in tonic water.
The dried latex (sap) from unripe seed pods of the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) is opium, which contains morphine, a powerful painkiller.
Opium also contains codeine, a milder painkiller and cough suppressant.
Morphine was one of the first active compounds to be isolated pure from a plant, by Friedrich Sertürner in about 1804.

The coca plant gives cocaine, an addictive, illegal stimulant once used as a local anaesthetic. Sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) gives artemisinin, a modern anti-malarial; Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in 2015.
Plants can supply a medicine, but harvesting them is rarely a dependable way to meet demand.
Natural products often occur in tiny amounts, so huge amounts of plant material are needed.
Their amounts vary with season, weather and location.
They may come from rare or slow-growing organisms, so extraction alone is often not enough.
Aspirin is the classic example of improving on a natural product. Chemists started from the active compound in willow bark and modified it.
Salicylic acid, C₇H₆O₃ (M 138), relieves pain but irritates the mouth and stomach.
In 1897 Felix Hoffmann, a chemist at the German company Bayer, made acetylsalicylic acid from salicylic acid.
The product was sold from 1899 as Aspirin.

Aspirin is made by converting the –OH group on the benzene ring of salicylic acid into an ester group, by reacting it with ethanoic anhydride, a derivative of ethanoic acid. Salicylic acid is the precursor.
Aspirin, C₉H₈O₄ (M = 180), contains three functional groups (the parts of a molecule that decide how it reacts): a benzene ring, a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) and an ester group (–OCOCH₃).
Aspirin has several medical uses, but it is not risk-free.
Aspirin relieves pain and reduces fever and inflammation.
Low daily doses of aspirin reduce blood clotting and are prescribed to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Aspirin irritates the stomach less than salicylic acid, which is a reason chemists modified the natural compound, but it can still cause stomach irritation and bleeding.
Aspirin is not given to children under 16 because of the risk of Reye's syndrome.
Penicillin is an antibiotic. Its discovery came from a mould, and it works by attacking bacteria specifically.
Alexander Fleming discovered in 1928 that the mould Penicillium killed bacteria.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain purified penicillin and showed around 1940 that it worked in patients.
Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Penicillin is an antibiotic: it kills bacteria by stopping them building their cell walls.
Penicillin has no effect on viruses, because it works by stopping cell wall building.
Penicillin has a key structural feature, the β-lactam ring, and it is made by growing a mould rather than by building it from scratch.
Its key structural feature is a four-membered ring containing nitrogen and a C=O, the β-lactam ring, joined to a ring containing sulfur.
Penicillin G is C₁₆H₁₈N₂O₄S and also contains a carboxylic acid group.
Penicillin is made on a large scale by fermentation (biotechnology): the mould is grown in large tanks of nutrient broth.
This fermentation process was scaled up during the Second World War.
Semi-synthetic penicillins, such as amoxicillin, are made by chemically changing the side chain of the penicillin made by fermentation.
Semi-synthetic penicillins work against more types of bacteria or are better absorbed.
Antibiotics lose their power when bacteria adapt, which changes how penicillin can be used.
Overuse and misuse of antibiotics has led to antibiotic-resistant bacteria (bacteria that are no longer killed by the drug).
Some bacteria make enzymes that break the β-lactam ring, so the penicillin is destroyed before it can stop cell wall building.
Taxol is an anti-cancer drug that comes from a tree. It is a very large molecule, which makes it hard to obtain.
Taxol (paclitaxel) is an anti-cancer drug, used for example for ovarian, breast and lung cancers.
Taxol was found in the bark of the Pacific yew tree (Taxus brevifolia) in a US plant-screening programme in the 1960s, and its structure was published in 1971.
Taxol is a very large, complex molecule, C₄₇H₅₁NO₁₄, with many functional groups.
Its functional groups include several ester groups, hydroxyl (–OH) groups, a ketone, an amide and three benzene rings.
Getting taxol from the bark was a problem for the tree, so chemists found other routes.
Stripping the bark kills the slow-growing tree and gives very little taxol, so this was not sustainable.
Taxol is now made semi-synthetically from a precursor extracted from the needles of the European yew (Taxus baccata), which regrow, so the tree is not killed.
Taxol can also be made by growing yew cells in fermentation tanks.
Complete laboratory synthesis, first achieved in 1994, needs too many steps to be economic.
Opiates show how a small change to a molecule can change its effect completely. They are vital medicines and also dangerous drugs.
Opiates are the natural compounds of opium, morphine and codeine, and drugs made directly from them, such as heroin.
Opioids is the wider term that also includes fully synthetic drugs, e.g. fentanyl.
Morphine, C₁₇H₁₉NO₃, has several rings and functional groups, including two –OH groups, an ether link, a C=C double bond and an amine nitrogen.
Small changes to a functional group change the effect of the drug.
Codeine is morphine with one –OH converted to –OCH₃, giving a milder effect.
Heroin (diamorphine) is morphine with both –OH groups converted to ester groups, giving a stronger and more addictive effect.
Opiates are essential for severe pain, e.g. after surgery and in cancer care.
Opiates cause addiction and tolerance (needing larger doses for the same effect) and, in overdose, fatal slowing of breathing, so they are tightly controlled.
Most modern medicines are built by chemists, step by step, from simpler starting compounds.
Most modern pharmaceuticals are large, complex organic molecules with several functional groups, each of which may be needed for the drug to bind to its target in the body.
They are built in a sequence of reactions from simpler organic precursors, many derived from crude oil or from natural sources.
Each step changes or adds a functional group.
Every step loses some product, so long syntheses have low overall yields, which raises cost and waste. There is more on this in Theoretical, actual and percentage yield.
If a plant already makes a medicine, it is fair to ask why chemists bother. There are four reasons, and the examples show them at work.
Synthesising or modifying gives a reliable supply that does not depend on harvests or rare organisms.
Synthesis or modification gives pure products of consistent strength.
Changing the structure can improve a drug, with fewer side effects, a stronger effect or better absorption, e.g. aspirin from salicylic acid and amoxicillin from penicillin.
Two other organic medicines are very widely used, and all new medicines must pass safety checks.
Paracetamol, C₈H₉NO₂, is used for pain and fever relief.
Ibuprofen is used for pain and inflammation.
New drugs must be tested for safety and effectiveness in clinical trials and approved by a regulator before use.
In Ireland the regulator is the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA); in the EU it is the European Medicines Agency (EMA).
This topic is a research-based investigation, so you must be able to plan and present research about a pharmaceutical.

The specification expects you to research a use of organic compounds in pharmaceuticals, using evaluated sources, and to present the chemistry involved, the benefits and the issues, with a justified conclusion.
Example question: "Should medicines that come from plants be extracted from the plant or made in the laboratory?", taking taxol and aspirin as case studies.
Other possible questions: how chemists turned willow bark into aspirin; how antibiotic resistance has changed the use of penicillin; how opiates can be used safely.
A good investigation uses reliable sources and checks them before trusting them.

Sources include textbooks; peer-reviewed journals (where experts check papers before publication) and review articles; official bodies such as the HPRA, the EMA, the World Health Organization and the HSE.
PubChem gives structures and formulae, and museum and university websites give history.
Judge a source by who wrote it and their expertise, whether it is peer reviewed, and how recent it is.
Judge a source also by any commercial or other bias, e.g. a drug company's advertising, and by whether other reliable sources agree.
The write-up should cover the chemistry, weigh the issues on both sides, and end with a conclusion that answers the question.
Include the structure and functional groups of the compound, and its natural source.
Explain how the compound is extracted or made from precursors, e.g. ester formation in aspirin or semi-synthesis of taxol.
Explain why the structural change improves the drug.
Weigh health benefits against side effects and addiction.
Weigh the sustainability of natural sources, such as taxol from the Pacific yew, against protecting biodiversity, where future medicines may be found.
Weigh antibiotic resistance, cost and access to medicines worldwide, and drug residues in the environment.

Conclude by answering the question with evidence from both sides, e.g. semi-synthesis of taxol from renewable yew needles combines a natural precursor with laboratory chemistry and is more sustainable than either bark extraction or full synthesis.

Organic reactions fall into five types, and the first is addition. It is the characteristic reaction of compounds with a carbon-carbon double bond, because the double bond can open up to take on new atoms.
An addition reaction is one in which two or more molecules react to form a single molecule.
Atoms add across a double (or triple) bond, so an unsaturated compound (one with a C=C or C≡C bond) becomes saturated (only single bonds) and there is only one product.
Ethene and bromine: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br, giving 1,2-dibromoethane. Bromine water changes from orange (red-brown) to colourless, which is the test for unsaturation.
Ethene and chlorine: CH₂=CH₂ + Cl₂ → CH₂ClCH₂Cl, giving 1,2-dichloroethane.
Ethene and hydrogen chloride: CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl, giving chloroethane.
Ethene and water: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH, giving ethanol; this is the industrial route to ethanol.
Ethene and hydrogen with a nickel catalyst (a substance that speeds up the reaction without being used up): CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃, giving ethane; this is hydrogenation.

Addition polymerisation, e.g. ethene to poly(ethene), is a series of addition reactions, because each monomer (small molecule) adds on to the growing chain. It is taught in full later in this subsection.
In a substitution reaction one atom or group is swapped for another, so two reactants give two products. Alkanes, which have no double bond to add across, react this way.
A substitution reaction is one in which an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group of atoms; two reactants give two products.
Chlorination of an alkane in ultraviolet light: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, where a hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom.
Ethane gives chloroethane in the same way: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl.
Esterification: a carboxylic acid (contains –COOH) and an alcohol (contains –OH) give an ester and water, catalysed by H⁺ from concentrated sulfuric acid, e.g. CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
In esterification the –OH of the acid is replaced by the –OC₂H₅ group of the alcohol, which is why it counts as substitution.
Esterification is classed as substitution; it is also called a condensation reaction, because water is lost as two molecules join.
Hydrolysis of an ester (splitting it using water or a base) is also a substitution: the –OR group is replaced by –OH (or by –O⁻ in base), e.g. CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH.
Alkanes (saturated hydrocarbons) react by substitution, not addition, because they have no double bond to add across.
Elimination is the reverse of addition. A small molecule is stripped out of a larger one, and the larger molecule is left with a double bond.
An elimination reaction is one in which a small molecule is removed from a larger molecule, leaving a double bond in the larger molecule.
Dehydration of ethanol over heated aluminium oxide (a white solid, used as the catalyst): CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O.
Water is the small molecule removed, so this elimination is also called a dehydration.
Propan-2-ol gives propene and water: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O.
A haloalkane (an alkane with a halogen atom such as Cl) can lose a hydrogen halide: CH₃CH₂Cl → CH₂=CH₂ + HCl.
1,2-dichloroethane loses HCl to give chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl), the monomer of PVC (the small molecule that is later joined into the polymer PVC).
Elimination is the reverse of addition: one reactant gives two products, and a saturated compound becomes unsaturated.
Redox means reduction and oxidation happening together. In organic chemistry you can usually spot them by counting oxygen and hydrogen atoms.
In organic chemistry, oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of hydrogen.
Reduction is the gain of hydrogen or the loss of oxygen.
Oxidation is also the loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation number (the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic). There is more on this in Oxidation and reduction.
Ethanol is oxidised to ethanal, which loses two H atoms, and then to ethanoic acid, which gains one O atom, using acidified potassium permanganate as the oxidising agent.
Ethanal is reduced to ethanol by hydrogen with a nickel catalyst: CH₃CHO + H₂ → CH₃CH₂OH. This is reduction because the molecule gains hydrogen.
Combustion (burning in oxygen) is a redox reaction in which the carbon and hydrogen are oxidised, e.g. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
An acid–base reaction is about a proton moving from one species to another. Carboxylic acids show this clearly, while alcohols are barely acidic.
An acid–base reaction is a transfer of a proton (H⁺) from an acid to a base, as defined by Brønsted–Lowry.
Carboxylic acids react with bases: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
Carboxylic acids react with carbonates: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.

Base hydrolysis of esters, including the saponification of fats to make soap, is classed by the specification as an acid–base reaction: the hydroxide ion is the base, and the carboxylic acid formed ends up as its salt.
Alcohols are only very weakly acidic: ethanol is neutral to indicator and does not react with sodium carbonate.
Ethanol does release hydrogen with sodium, forming sodium ethoxide: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂; there is more on this in Physical properties and acidity.
At Higher Level you must be able to look at an unfamiliar reaction and say which type or types it is. Work through the checks in a fixed order.

Compare the molecules before and after: two reactants giving one product across a C=C bond is addition; one reactant giving two products with a new C=C bond is elimination; two reactants giving two products with one group swapped for another is substitution.

Then check for redox, by asking whether the organic compound has gained or lost O or H (whether an oxidation number has changed), and for acid–base, by asking whether a proton has moved from an acid to a base.
One reaction can be of more than one type, so give every type that fits: hydrogenation of ethene is addition and reduction.
Esterification is substitution and condensation, and base hydrolysis of an ester is substitution and acid–base.
Higher Level questions also ask which bonds break and form. A pi bond is the second, weaker bond of a C=C double bond, added to the stronger C–C sigma bond that is already there.
Dehydration of ethanol: a C–H bond and a C–O bond are broken and an O–H bond forms in the water; a C=C double bond forms, with a pi bond added to the existing C–C sigma bond.
Addition of water to ethene: the pi bond of C=C and an O–H bond of water are broken; a C–H bond and a C–O bond are formed.
Ethanol to ethanal is oxidation: an O–H bond and a C–H bond are broken and a C=O pi bond forms.
Ethanal to ethanoic acid is oxidation by gain of an O atom: a C–H bond is replaced by C–OH.
Reaction of a carboxylic acid with magnesium shows acidic behaviour but is a redox reaction: Mg is oxidised to Mg²⁺ and H⁺ is reduced to H₂.
The reaction of sodium with ethanol is likewise a redox reaction.
Many everyday plastics are built by joining huge numbers of small molecules into one very long molecule. The words polymer, monomer and repeating unit describe this.
A polymer is a very large molecule, a macromolecule, made of many small units called monomers joined by covalent bonds in a long chain.
A monomer is a small molecule that joins with many others to form a polymer; polymerisation is the reaction in which monomers join to form a polymer.
The repeating unit is the part of the polymer whose repetition makes up the whole chain, apart from the ends.
Polymer chains contain thousands of repeating units, so their relative molecular masses (Mr, the mass of a molecule compared with the carbon-12 standard) are very large and vary from chain to chain.
Example: a poly(ethene) chain of Mr 28 000 contains about 28 000 ÷ 28 = 1000 ethene units, because the Mr of ethene is 28.
Many plastics are polymers, and most addition polymers are made from monomers obtained from crude oil.
Monomers with a C=C double bond can join end to end because each double bond opens up, just as in an ordinary addition reaction. Repeating this thousands of times builds the chain.
An addition polymer is formed when monomers containing a C=C double bond join by addition reactions; usually only one type of monomer is used.

In each addition the pi bond of C=C (the weaker, second bond of the double bond) breaks, and the electrons form new C–C single bonds to neighbouring monomers, giving a long chain of carbon atoms, the backbone.
No other product is formed, so the polymer has the same empirical formula (simplest whole-number ratio of atoms) as the monomer.
General equation: n CH₂=CHX → –(CH₂–CHX)ₙ–, where X is H, Cl or C₆H₅.
The polymer is saturated, with no C=C left, so unlike its monomer it does not decolourise bromine water.
Drawing: show the monomer with its C=C; show the repeating unit with single bonds and a bond sticking out at each end.
To draw two repeating units, show four backbone carbons in a row, with the side groups on alternate carbons and an open bond at each end; do not write atoms at the ends of the open bonds.
Poly(ethene) is the simplest addition polymer. How closely its chains pack decides whether it is soft and flexible or strong and rigid.
The monomer is ethene, CH₂=CH₂, and the repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–; poly(ethene) is also called polythene or polyethylene.
Low-density poly(ethene), LDPE, has branched chains that cannot pack closely, so it is soft and flexible.
LDPE is used for plastic bags, food-wrapping film and squeezy bottles.
High-density poly(ethene), HDPE, has unbranched chains that pack closely, so it is stronger and more rigid, with a higher melting point.
HDPE is used for milk crates, bottles, buckets, bowls, toys, pipes and car fuel tanks.
Diagram: two repeating units of poly(ethene), –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–, with open end bonds.
PVC is ethene with one hydrogen replaced by chlorine. The polar C–Cl bond gives it very different properties from poly(ethene).
The monomer is chloroethene, also called vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl; the repeating unit is –CH₂–CHCl–.
Poly(chloroethene) is also called polyvinyl chloride, PVC.
The polar C–Cl bonds (the shared electrons sit nearer the chlorine) give permanent dipole–dipole attractions between the chains, so rigid PVC is strong and rigid.
Rigid PVC is used for window frames, doors, gutters, drainpipes, water pipes and bank cards.
Adding plasticisers, small molecules that let the chains slide past each other, makes flexible PVC.
Flexible PVC is used for electrical cable insulation, flooring and raincoats.
Diagram: two repeating units of PVC, –CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CHCl–, with open end bonds.
Polystyrene is ethene with one hydrogen replaced by a large benzene ring (a ring of six carbon atoms). The bulk of that ring controls the properties.
The monomer is phenylethene, also called styrene, C₆H₅CH=CH₂, which is ethene with one hydrogen replaced by a benzene ring; the repeating unit is –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–.
The bulky benzene rings stop the chains moving past each other, so solid polystyrene is rigid and brittle.
Solid polystyrene is used for yoghurt cartons, disposable cups and cutlery, CD cases and ballpoint pen cases.
Expanded polystyrene is blown with gas into a foam, which makes it very light and a good thermal insulator.
Expanded polystyrene is used for packaging, takeaway food boxes, ceiling tiles and building insulation.
Diagram: two repeating units of polystyrene, with a benzene ring on alternate carbon atoms.
Addition polymers are used everywhere because their properties suit the job. The same few polymers turn up in fuel systems, farming, food packaging and the home.
Fuels: HDPE fuel tanks in cars are light, tough and do not corrode; plastic fuel cans and pipes are also used.
Waste plastics can be burned for energy, or broken down by heating (pyrolysis) into liquid fuels.
Food production: poly(ethene) film is used for polytunnels and greenhouses, silage wrap and mulch film on farms.
PVC and poly(ethene) pipes are used for irrigation and water supply.
Food packaging: poly(ethene) film and bags and polystyrene trays keep food clean and moist and keep air out, so food lasts longer and less is wasted.
Household products: buckets, bowls, bottles, bags, toys and containers are made from poly(ethene); pipes, gutters and window frames from PVC; insulation and packaging from polystyrene.
These polymers suit their uses because they are cheap, light, waterproof, durable, easily moulded and unreactive, so they do not react with food, water, fuels or most chemicals.
Biodegradability depends on whether living things can break a substance down. Addition polymers resist this because of their bonding.
A substance is biodegradable if microorganisms, bacteria and fungi, can break it down into simple substances such as carbon dioxide and water.
The backbone of an addition polymer is a long chain of strong, non-polar C–C single bonds with C–H bonds around it.

Like an alkane, an addition polymer has no pi bonds and no polar functional group (a reactive atom or group) for a reagent to attack, so it is chemically stable and unreactive. There is more on this in Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties.
Microorganisms break down natural polymers, such as starch and proteins, with enzymes (biological catalysts) that attack specific polar linkages.
Addition polymers have no such linkages, so microorganisms have no enzymes able to break them down.
The stability that makes addition polymers so useful is the same property that makes plastic waste a problem.
The same stability that makes addition polymers useful, being durable, waterproof and resistant to chemicals and decay, means they persist in the environment for hundreds of years.
Consequences: plastic litter on land and in oceans, harm to wildlife that eats or becomes tangled in it, and filling of landfill sites.
Sunlight and wear break plastics into small fragments, called microplastics, rather than breaking them down chemically.
Because plastics do not break down, society has to manage them: use less, recycle, burn for energy, or switch to polymers that can degrade.
Responses include reducing use, reusing, and recycling.
Plastics are sorted for recycling by resin identification code, e.g. 2 for HDPE, 3 for PVC, 4 for LDPE and 6 for polystyrene.
Incineration gives energy but releases CO₂, and burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride.

Biodegradable polymers with ester linkages, which microorganisms can hydrolyse (split using water), are being developed. These can break down because the ester linkage gives microorganisms something to attack.
Poly(lactic acid), PLA, is one example: it is made from plant starch and breaks down in industrial composting.

Aldehydes and ketones both contain the carbonyl group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, C=O), so they look alike. The difference is one hydrogen atom, and that hydrogen decides whether the compound can be oxidised (have oxygen added or hydrogen removed) by a mild reagent.
An aldehyde has the –CHO group: the carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen atom, e.g. ethanal, CH₃CHO.
A ketone has the C=O group joined to two carbon atoms, so its carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen, e.g. propanone, CH₃COCH₃.

An aldehyde is easily oxidised to a carboxylic acid, because the hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon can be replaced by –OH. This makes aldehydes good reducing agents (substances that get oxidised themselves while reducing something else).
A ketone is not oxidised by mild oxidising agents, because its carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen; oxidising a ketone would mean breaking a C–C bond, which a mild reagent cannot do.
A mild oxidising agent that changes colour on reaction therefore tells them apart: an aldehyde gives a colour change, while a ketone gives none.
Fehling's reagent is the mild oxidising agent the specification uses to test for aldehydes. It is made from two solutions that are kept apart and mixed only when needed.
Fehling's reagent is made fresh by mixing equal volumes of Fehling's A (copper(II) sulfate solution, blue) and Fehling's B (potassium sodium tartrate and sodium hydroxide solution, colourless).
The mixture is a clear deep-blue solution containing Cu²⁺ ions, which are the part that reacts with an aldehyde.
The tartrate keeps the Cu²⁺ ions in solution in the alkaline mixture; without it, copper(II) hydroxide would precipitate (form as an insoluble solid).
The aim is to show which of two unlabelled liquids is the aldehyde (ethanal) and which is the ketone (propanone). Both are tested in the same way so the results can be compared.
Method: put about 2 cm³ of Fehling's reagent into each of two test tubes, so that one can be tested with each liquid for comparison.
Method: add a few drops of ethanal to one test tube and a few drops of propanone to the other.
Method: warm both test tubes in a beaker of hot water (a water bath) for a few minutes; do not heat them with a naked flame, because the liquids are flammable.
With ethanal, the blue solution gives a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O.
With propanone there is no change: the solution stays blue.
An unknown carbonyl compound that gives a brick-red precipitate is an aldehyde, because only aldehydes reduce the Cu²⁺; one that leaves the reagent blue is a ketone.
Both the reagent and the liquids being tested carry hazards, which is why the heating is done in a water bath.
Wear goggles, because Fehling's B contains sodium hydroxide, which is corrosive.
Ethanal (boiling point about 21 °C) and propanone (boiling point 56 °C) are volatile (they evaporate easily) and flammable, so keep them away from flames and use a water bath.
Diagram: two test tubes standing in a beaker of hot water, labelled Fehling's reagent + ethanal (brick-red precipitate) and Fehling's reagent + propanone (blue).
The colour change is a redox reaction (one where electrons are transferred). The copper ions in the reagent are reduced while the aldehyde is oxidised.
Fehling's reagent is a mild oxidising agent: the Cu²⁺ ions oxidise the aldehyde and are themselves reduced to copper(I).
The aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylic acid; in the alkaline reagent the acid is present as its salt, so ethanal forms ethanoate ions.
Reduction half-equation: Cu²⁺ + e⁻ → Cu⁺, so the oxidation number of copper falls from +2 to +1.
Full ionic equation for the reduction in alkaline solution: 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu₂O(s) + H₂O(l).
Fehling's reagent is a weak oxidising agent, so ethanal reducing it shows that aldehydes are very easily oxidised; the reagent is too weak to oxidise a ketone.

Carboxylic acids such as ethanoic acid show the usual properties of an acid. Three reactions (with a metal, a carbonate and a base) and an indicator (a dye that changes colour with acidity) are used to show this.
Aim: to show that ethanoic acid behaves as an acid, by its reactions with a metal, a carbonate and a base, and by its effect on an indicator.
Dilute ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red and has a pH below 7 (about 3, on universal indicator or a pH meter).

Control: repeat the tests with ethanol in place of ethanoic acid; ethanol gives no fizzing with magnesium or sodium carbonate and is neutral to indicator, which shows that the –COOH group, not the –OH group alone, is acidic.
An acid reacts with a reactive metal to give a salt and hydrogen gas, and the gas is identified with a lighted taper.
Add a clean piece of magnesium ribbon to dilute ethanoic acid; bubbles of gas form slowly and the magnesium dissolves.
The gas burns with a pop when a lighted taper is held at the mouth of the tube, so it is hydrogen.

Ethanoic acid reacts more slowly with magnesium than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration does, because it is a weak acid that is only partly dissociated (split into ions), so its H⁺ concentration is lower.
Diagram: a test tube of dilute ethanoic acid with magnesium ribbon, and a lighted taper held at the mouth of the tube.
Acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide, which gives a clear visible sign of reaction.
Add a little solid sodium carbonate to ethanoic acid; the mixture effervesces (fizzes).
The gas turns limewater milky, so it is carbon dioxide.
Diagram: a test tube of ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate, and a delivery tube bubbling the gas into limewater.
A base neutralises an acid, giving a salt and water. Because this gives no gas, a different way of seeing the reaction is needed.
Sodium hydroxide neutralises ethanoic acid, forming the salt sodium ethanoate and water: CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l).

There is no visible change in this reaction, so add phenolphthalein (an indicator that is pink in alkali) to the acid and add sodium hydroxide until the solution just turns pink; alternatively follow the pH or note the temperature rise.
Concentrated ethanoic acid and the hydrogen test both need care.
Wear goggles, because concentrated (glacial) ethanoic acid is corrosive, so use the dilute acid.
Keep flames away from any flammable liquid when testing for hydrogen, because hydrogen burns with a pop.
A reaction scheme is a map of organic chemistry. Reading one means working out, arrow by arrow, what has changed and what caused the change.
A reaction scheme is a diagram that links organic compounds by arrows, each arrow labelled with the reagent (and sometimes the reaction type) that converts one compound into the next.
A scheme shows how compounds of different families are related, and how a target compound can be made from a simpler starting material in several steps; this is organic synthesis.
To read a scheme, name each compound and its functional group (the atom or group that gives a family its reactions), then for each arrow compare the formulae before and after.
Decide what has been added, removed or swapped at each arrow, then name the reaction type and the reagent.
A formula change of +H₂ across C=C or C=O is addition (two molecules joining with no atoms lost) or reduction; a change of −2H is oxidation; a change of +O is oxidation.
A change of −H₂O or −HCl with a new C=C bond is elimination (a small molecule removed, leaving a double bond); one atom swapped for another is substitution.
A carboxylic acid converted to its sodium salt is an acid–base reaction.
Ethene, the two-carbon alkene (a hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond), sits at the centre of the scheme. Most of its conversions are additions across the double bond.
Ethane to chloroethane: chlorine in ultraviolet light (substitution, because a chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom).
Ethene to ethane: hydrogen with a nickel catalyst (addition, because H₂ adds across the C=C; also reduction).
Ethanol to ethene: heated aluminium oxide (elimination, because water is removed and a C=C forms).
Chloroethane to ethene: loss of HCl (elimination, because a hydrogen and a chlorine are removed and a C=C forms).
Ethanol links to the oxidation sequence and to the ester. Here the carbon skeleton stays the same except where two molecules join or split.
Ethanol to ethanal to ethanoic acid: acidified potassium permanganate, as two oxidation steps.
Ethanal to ethanol: hydrogen with a nickel catalyst (reduction, because H₂ adds across the C=O).
Ethanoic acid and ethanol give ethyl ethanoate and water, with concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst (substitution, esterification).
Ethyl ethanoate and sodium hydroxide give sodium ethanoate and ethanol (base hydrolysis, splitting the ester with the help of water and base).
Ethanoic acid to sodium ethanoate: sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate (acid–base).
Ethene and its chlorinated relative can also be joined into long chains, giving plastics.
Ethene to poly(ethene) by addition polymerisation (many ethene molecules adding together into a chain).
1,2-dichloroethane to chloroethene by elimination of HCl, then polymerisation to poly(chloroethene), PVC.

Diagram: the two-carbon scheme as a map, with ethene at the centre and arrows to ethane, chloroethane, 1,2-dichloroethane, ethanol and poly(ethene); ethanol linked to ethanal, ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate; each arrow labelled with its reagent and reaction type.
The same reactions apply to longer chains. Whether the alcohol is primary or secondary decides whether oxidation gives an aldehyde and acid or a ketone.
Propan-1-ol (a primary alcohol, with the –OH on an end carbon) to propanal to propanoic acid: acidified potassium permanganate (oxidation).
Propan-2-ol (a secondary alcohol, with the –OH on a middle carbon) to propanone: acidified potassium permanganate (oxidation).
Propanone to propan-2-ol: hydrogen with nickel (reduction).
Propene to propane: hydrogen with nickel (addition, because H₂ adds across the C=C).
Phenylmethanol to benzoic acid: potassium permanganate under basic conditions (oxidation). There is more on this in Investigation: synthesising benzoic acid.
When a scheme is incomplete, the product tells you what must have come before it, and counting carbon atoms checks your answer.
A scheme that ends in an aldehyde probably began with a primary alcohol; a ketone comes from a secondary alcohol.
An alkene can come from an alcohol by elimination, or go to an alcohol by addition of water.
Carbon atoms are neither gained nor lost in these steps, except in esterification, which joins two molecules, and hydrolysis, which splits them, so the carbon skeleton checks each answer.
To predict a product, recognise the functional group and recall its typical reaction. Multi-step syntheses just chain these together.
To predict a product, identify the functional group and apply its typical reaction.
An alkene with X₂, HX, H₂O or H₂ gives an addition product.
A primary alcohol with an oxidising agent gives an aldehyde, then a carboxylic acid; a carboxylic acid with an alcohol gives an ester; an ester with NaOH gives a salt and an alcohol.
Example: ethene to ethanoic acid in two steps, by adding water to give ethanol (addition), then oxidising with excess acidified potassium permanganate (oxidation).

Example: ethanal to ethyl ethanoate, by reducing part of the ethanal to ethanol with H₂ and nickel, oxidising another part to ethanoic acid with acidified KMnO₄, then esterifying the two with concentrated H₂SO₄.
Example: chloroethane to ethanol in two steps, by eliminating HCl to give ethene, then adding water.
Example: heating propan-1-ol with methanoic acid gives propyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃; the alcohol supplies the propyl part and the acid supplies the methanoate part.

The shape around a carbon atom depends on its bonds. Tracking whether a carbon is tetrahedral (four bonds pointing to the corners of a pyramid-like shape) or planar (flat) shows what a reaction does to a molecule.
A carbon atom with four single bonds is tetrahedral, with bond angles of about 109.5°.
A carbon atom in a C=C or C=O double bond is planar (trigonal planar), with bond angles of about 120°.
Ethene has no tetrahedral carbon atom; ethanal and ethanoic acid each have one planar carbon (the C=O carbon) and one tetrahedral carbon.
Ethanol and ethane have only tetrahedral carbon atoms.
A reaction that adds to or removes a double bond changes the carbons involved between planar and tetrahedral. Reactions that leave the C=O in place change nothing.
Addition to C=C, as in ethene to ethane, ethene to ethanol or polymerisation, changes the two carbon atoms from planar to tetrahedral.
Elimination, as in ethanol to ethene, changes the two carbon atoms from tetrahedral to planar.
Oxidising an alcohol to an aldehyde or ketone changes the carbon bearing the oxygen from tetrahedral to planar.
Reducing an aldehyde or ketone to an alcohol changes that carbon from planar to tetrahedral.
Aldehyde to carboxylic acid, and acid to ester, leave the carbonyl carbon planar, so there is no change in geometry.
Each reaction needs a particular feature in the molecule. Where it is missing, the reaction cannot happen, and the reason always comes back to that feature.
Tertiary alcohols (alcohols with the –OH on a carbon bonded to three other carbons), such as 2-methylpropan-2-ol, are not oxidised by acidified potassium permanganate.
The carbon bearing the –OH group of a tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen atom to lose, and oxidation would mean breaking a C–C bond.
Ketones are not oxidised by Fehling's reagent or potassium permanganate, for the same reason: there is no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon.
Alkanes and poly(ethene) cannot undergo addition, because they are saturated (they have only single bonds) and have no pi bond, so they do not decolourise bromine water.
Methanol cannot be dehydrated to an alkene, because it has only one carbon atom and a C=C bond needs two.

Benzene does not decolourise bromine water as an alkene does: its delocalised pi electrons (shared around the whole ring) make the ring unusually stable, so it resists addition. There is more on this in Shapes, bonding and isomerism.
Ethanoic acid is not oxidised further by potassium permanganate; it is the end product of oxidising a primary alcohol.
An ester is the compound formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol. In this investigation methyl propanoate is made from propanoic acid and methanol.
Aim: to prepare a sample of an ester, methyl propanoate, from propanoic acid and methanol by heating under reflux (boiling with a condenser that returns the vapour to the flask).
Equation: CH₃CH₂COOH(l) + CH₃OH(l) ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOCH₃(l) + H₂O(l), with propanoic acid and methanol giving methyl propanoate and water in a mole ratio of 1 : 1 : 1.
Molar masses: propanoic acid 74 g mol⁻¹, methanol 32 g mol⁻¹ and methyl propanoate 88 g mol⁻¹.
The alternative preparation is ethanoic acid with ethanol: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, giving ethyl ethanoate.
The specification needs only esters made from monocarboxylic acids and primary alcohols.
Esterification does not go to completion, which shapes the whole purification. Isotope labelling shows exactly which bond forms.
Esterification is slow and reversible: it reaches an equilibrium (the forward and reverse reactions balance) with only part of the acid and alcohol converted.
The product mixture therefore also contains unreacted acid and alcohol, water and the sulfuric acid catalyst.
Isotope evidence: when the alcohol is labelled with oxygen-18 (a heavier form of oxygen used as a tracer), the ¹⁸O is found in the ester, not in the water.
So the –OH lost as water comes from the acid, the H comes from the alcohol, and the bond formed is the C–O bond between the acid's carbonyl carbon and the alcohol's oxygen.
The reactants are mixed with a catalyst and boiled gently for a while. A condenser fitted vertically stops the volatile liquids escaping.
In a fume cupboard, put measured volumes of propanoic acid and methanol (about 10 cm³ of each) into a round-bottomed flask.
Add about 1 cm³ of concentrated sulfuric acid a drop at a time, swirling and cooling the flask under the tap, because mixing is exothermic (gives out heat).
Add a few anti-bumping granules, so that the mixture boils smoothly.
Fit a Liebig condenser vertically on the flask, with cold water entering at the bottom and leaving at the top, and leave the top of the condenser open.
Heat the flask in a water bath, or with a heating mantle, so that the mixture boils gently under reflux for about 20–30 minutes.
Diagram: reflux apparatus, with a round-bottomed flask holding the mixture and granules in a water bath, a vertical Liebig condenser with water in at the bottom and out at the top, and an open top.
After reflux the flask holds a mixture. The ester is separated from the other substances by washing, drying and then distilling.
Cool the flask, then pour the mixture into a separating funnel (a tapped funnel for separating two liquids that do not mix) with some water and shake.

The ester forms the upper layer, because it is less dense than water and only slightly soluble in it; run off and discard the lower aqueous layer, which holds most of the acid, methanol and sulfuric acid.
Add sodium carbonate solution to the ester in the funnel and shake gently, opening the tap often (inverted) to release the carbon dioxide formed; this neutralises the remaining acid.
Run off the lower aqueous layer, which now holds the sodium salt of the acid and the water, so the ester is left on its own.

Run the ester into a dry conical flask and add a few lumps of anhydrous calcium chloride (a drying agent that removes water) to remove water; swirl until the liquid is clear, then decant (pour off) or filter it.
Distil the dry ester and collect the fraction boiling at about 80 °C: methyl propanoate boils at 79.8 °C and ethyl ethanoate at 77 °C.
Identify the product by its boiling point and its pleasant, fruity smell, wafting the vapour towards the nose rather than sniffing directly.
Diagram: separating funnel with the upper ester layer, the lower aqueous layer, the stopper and the tap.
Every choice in the method has a purpose. Exams ask for these reasons directly.
Reflux lets the mixture boil for a long time without losing the volatile reactants and product: vapour rises into the condenser, condenses and drips back into the flask.
Concentrated sulfuric acid is the catalyst, providing H⁺ ions; it also absorbs water, which helps shift the equilibrium towards the ester.
A water bath or heating mantle is used rather than a Bunsen burner, because methanol and the ester are flammable; it also gives gentle, even heating.
Anti-bumping granules give smooth boiling by providing sites for small bubbles to form, which prevents sudden violent boiling (bumping).
The condenser is never stoppered, because heating a closed system would build up pressure.
Sodium carbonate removes acid without destroying the ester: Na₂CO₃ + 2H⁺ → 2Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂.
The pressure in the separating funnel must be released because carbon dioxide is produced.
Distillation separates the ester from remaining alcohol and other impurities by their boiling points, giving a purer product.
The hazards are corrosive and flammable chemicals. The yield is low because of the equilibrium and because product is lost in handling.
Concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive: wear goggles and gloves, and add it slowly.
Methanol is toxic and flammable, and propanoic acid is corrosive and has a strong smell; work in a fume cupboard and keep naked flames away.
The yield is well below 100%, because the reaction is an equilibrium.
Some ester dissolves in the aqueous layers and is lost in transfers, and some evaporates.
Percentage yield = actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100. There is more on this in Theoretical, actual and percentage yield.
Sources of error include not drying the ester fully, which gives a cloudy product and a low boiling point reading.
Not releasing the pressure in the separating funnel can blow out the stopper and lose product.
Heating too strongly lets vapour escape from the top of the condenser.

This experiment makes benzoic acid from an alcohol by oxidation (adding oxygen or removing hydrogen), then purifies and tests it. Knowing the chemistry first explains every colour change and step in the method.

Aim: to prepare benzoic acid by oxidising phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol, C₆H₅CH₂OH) with potassium permanganate under basic conditions, to purify it by recrystallisation (re-dissolving and crystallising again), and to find its melting point and percentage yield.

Phenylmethanol is a primary alcohol (the OH is on a carbon bonded to only one other carbon), so it is oxidised all the way to the carboxylic acid. In the basic solution the acid is present as the benzoate ion, C₆H₅COO⁻.
The permanganate is reduced (gains electrons) to manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂, a brown solid, so the purple solution turns brown. This colour change shows the oxidation is happening.
The mole ratio of phenylmethanol to benzoic acid is 1 : 1 (3 : 3 in the equation), so each mole of alcohol can give at most one mole of acid. This ratio is used in the yield calculation.
Phenylmethanol is a colourless liquid; benzoic acid is a white crystalline solid.
Benzoic acid (E210) and sodium benzoate (E211) are used as food preservatives.
The first stage mixes the alcohol with an excess of oxidising agent in basic solution and heats it. Excess permanganate makes sure all the alcohol reacts.
1. Measure 2.0 cm³ of phenylmethanol with a graduated pipette (or burette), which gives small volumes accurately, into a flask.
Its mass is volume × density, using a density of 1.04 g cm⁻³. You need this mass later to find the moles for the yield.
2. Add potassium permanganate solution in excess (more than the equation needs), together with sodium carbonate solution, which makes the mixture basic.

3. Heat under reflux (boiling with a condenser fitted so vapour returns to the flask), or in a boiling water bath, for about 20 minutes, swirling. The purple colour fades and a brown precipitate of MnO₂ forms.
Diagram: a flask with a condenser attached above it for reflux, or a flask standing in a beaker of boiling water.
After oxidation the benzoic acid is dissolved as benzoate and mixed with brown MnO₂. Acid turns it into solid benzoic acid and clears the brown solid, so the acid can be filtered off.
2. In a fume cupboard, add concentrated hydrochloric acid and sodium sulfite solution with swirling until the brown precipitate has dissolved and the mixture is acidic.
The mixture becomes colourless and white crystals of benzoic acid appear.
3. Cool the flask in an ice-water bath so that as much benzoic acid as possible crystallises, because it is less soluble in cold water.
4. Collect the crystals by suction (vacuum) filtration with a Büchner funnel and flask, and wash them with a little ice-cold water.
Diagram: a Büchner funnel on a Büchner (side-arm) flask connected to a vacuum pump, with filter paper and crystals.
Adding hydrochloric acid and sodium sulfite does three separate jobs. Each one removes a problem from the mixture.

The hydrochloric acid converts the soluble benzoate into benzoic acid, which is only slightly soluble in cold water and so precipitates (comes out of solution as a solid): C₆H₅COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → C₆H₅COOH(s).
The hydrochloric acid also neutralises the excess sodium carbonate, the base added earlier.
In acid, sodium sulfite reduces the brown MnO₂ to soluble, almost colourless Mn²⁺ ions, so the white benzoic acid is not mixed with brown solid: MnO₂ + SO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + H₂O.
The fume cupboard is needed because concentrated hydrochloric acid gives off HCl fumes, and sulfite in acid can release sulfur dioxide.

The crude crystals still contain impurities. Recrystallisation purifies them by dissolving them in hot solvent and letting pure crystals form again on cooling, so each step is designed to keep benzoic acid in or out of solution at the right moment.
Recrystallisation removes impurities from the crude benzoic acid: soluble salts such as KCl, NaCl and MnCl₂, and any insoluble matter.
Water is a suitable solvent because benzoic acid is very soluble in hot water but only slightly soluble in cold water, while the salt impurities are soluble in both hot and cold water.
1. Dissolve the crude crystals in the minimum volume of boiling water, so that the solution is saturated (holds as much solute as it can) and as much as possible crystallises on cooling.

2. Filter the hot solution quickly through fluted filter paper (folded into pleats) in a warmed stemless funnel, to remove insoluble impurities: fluted paper filters fast, and the warm funnel stops benzoic acid crystallising in it.
3. Leave the filtrate (the liquid that passes through the filter) to cool slowly to room temperature, then cool it in ice; pure benzoic acid crystallises and the soluble impurities stay in solution.
Wait until cooling is complete before filtering, or crystals that are still dissolved will be lost.
4. Collect the crystals by suction filtration and wash them with a little ice-cold water, because warm water would dissolve them.
5. Dry the crystals on a clock glass in air, in a desiccator (a sealed container with a drying agent) or in a low oven, then weigh them.
A pure solid melts at one sharp temperature, but impurities change this. Measuring the melting point of the recrystallised crystals therefore tells you how pure they are.
Seal one end of a capillary tube (a very thin glass tube), push the open end into the dry crystals, and tap the tube so the solid packs at the sealed end.
Place the tube in a melting-point apparatus, an electrically heated metal block with a thermometer; a water bath cannot be used because benzoic acid melts above 100 °C.
Heat slowly near the expected melting point, and record the temperature at which melting starts and the temperature at which it is complete, the melting range.
Pure benzoic acid melts sharply at about 122 °C, over a narrow range of 1–2 °C.
Impurities lower the melting point and widen the range: crude crystals may melt over 116–119 °C.
A sharp melting point close to 122 °C therefore shows that the recrystallised sample is pure.
Diagram: a capillary tube of benzoic acid in a heated melting-point block, with a thermometer or digital probe beside it.
Percentage yield compares the mass of benzoic acid you actually made with the most the equation says you could make (the theoretical yield). The worked example below uses sample data.
Sample data: 2.0 cm³ of phenylmethanol (density 1.04 g cm⁻³) gave 1.65 g of dry recrystallised benzoic acid.
Mass of phenylmethanol = 2.00 × 1.04 = 2.08 g; M(C₆H₅CH₂OH) = 108 g mol⁻¹, so moles = 2.08 ÷ 108 = 0.0193 mol.
Moles of benzoic acid expected = 0.0193 mol, from the 1 : 1 ratio; M(C₆H₅COOH) = 122 g mol⁻¹, so the theoretical yield = 0.0193 × 122 = 2.35 g.

The yield is below 100% because some benzoic acid stays dissolved in the cold filtrates, crystals are lost in transfers and on filter papers, too much water may have been used in recrystallisation, and the oxidation may be incomplete.

The yield calculation assumes phenylmethanol is the reagent that runs out. At Higher Level you check this by calculating how much permanganate the reaction needs and comparing it with the amount used.
From the equation, 3 mol of phenylmethanol need 4 mol of KMnO₄, so for 0.0193 mol of phenylmethanol the KMnO₄ needed = 0.0193 × 4 ÷ 3 = 0.0257 mol.
M(KMnO₄) = 158 g mol⁻¹, so 0.0257 mol = 4.06 g.

Using 5.00 g (0.0316 mol) means KMnO₄ is in excess and phenylmethanol is the limiting reagent (the one that runs out first), so the yield is calculated from the phenylmethanol. There is more on this in Limiting reagents.
Several chemicals in this preparation can harm skin or lungs, so protection and a fume cupboard are part of the method.
Wear goggles and gloves: concentrated hydrochloric acid is corrosive.
Potassium permanganate is an oxidising agent and stains skin, and phenylmethanol is harmful.
An equation only shows what you start with and what you end with. A mechanism shows what happens in between, and it needs a few terms and an arrow notation that the rest of this subsection uses.

A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step description of how a reaction happens: which bonds break, which form, and how the electrons (the negatively charged particles that make up a covalent bond) move.
Homolytic fission: a covalent bond (a shared pair of electrons) breaks so that each atom keeps one of the two bonding electrons, forming two free radicals, e.g. Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•.
Heterolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks so that one atom takes both bonding electrons, forming a positive and a negative ion (a charged atom or group of atoms), e.g. Cl–Cl → Cl⁺ + Cl⁻.
A free radical is an atom or group of atoms with an unpaired electron (an electron not part of a pair), shown by a dot, e.g. Cl• or •CH₃. Free radicals are very reactive and short-lived.

A curved arrow with a full arrowhead shows the movement of a pair of electrons. It is drawn from where the pair starts (a bond or a lone pair, which is a pair on one atom not shared in a bond) to where it ends up.
A fishhook arrow, with a half arrowhead, shows the movement of a single electron. Two fishhooks from one bond show homolytic fission, one electron going to each atom.
A carbocation (carbonium ion) is an ion with a positive charge on a carbon atom, e.g. CH₃CH₂⁺ or CH₂ClCH₂⁺.
A chain reaction is one in which a product of one step is a reactant in another step, so the reaction keeps itself going.

Methane reacts with chlorine only in ultraviolet (UV) light, and the reaction runs as a chain of radical steps. Substitution means a chlorine atom replaces a hydrogen atom in the molecule. The chain has three stages: initiation (it starts), propagation (it carries on) and termination (it stops).
Overall: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, in ultraviolet light. Replacing just one hydrogen is called monochlorination.
Initiation: UV light causes homolytic fission of chlorine molecules, Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Draw two fishhooks from the Cl–Cl bond, one to each chlorine atom.
Propagation step 1: a chlorine radical takes a hydrogen atom from methane, Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, forming a methyl radical.
Propagation step 2: the methyl radical takes a chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule, •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.
The Cl• formed in step 2 starts step 1 again, so the two propagation steps form a chain reaction: each radical used is replaced by a new one.
Termination: two radicals combine, removing radicals and ending a chain: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆ (ethane).
With more chlorine, further substitution gives dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane, so a mixture of products is formed.
Ethane follows exactly the same three stages as methane, with an ethyl radical, •C₂H₅, taking the place of the methyl radical.
Overall: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl, giving chloroethane, in ultraviolet light.
Initiation: UV light splits chlorine into radicals, Cl₂ → 2Cl•.
Propagation: first Cl• + C₂H₆ → HCl + •C₂H₅, forming an ethyl radical; then •C₂H₅ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + Cl•, which makes a new chlorine radical to repeat the cycle.
Termination: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •C₂H₅ + Cl• → C₂H₅Cl; •C₂H₅ + •C₂H₅ → C₄H₁₀ (butane). Each removes two radicals and ends a chain.
Radicals are too short-lived to see directly, so the mechanism is supported by indirect evidence. Each observation below is explained by radicals and chains.
The reaction does not happen in the dark at room temperature but starts in UV light, which supplies the energy to split Cl₂ into radicals in initiation.
Thousands of molecules of product form for every photon (packet of light energy) absorbed, because one radical starts a long chain of propagation steps.

Traces of ethane form in the chlorination of methane, and traces of butane in the chlorination of ethane. These can only come from two methyl or two ethyl radicals joining in termination, so the radicals must exist.

Termination is rare, because radicals are present at very low concentration. A radical is far more likely to collide with a CH₄ or Cl₂ molecule than with another radical, so the ethane or butane is only a trace.
Adding a substance that produces free radicals, such as tetramethyl lead, Pb(CH₃)₄ (a source of methyl radicals), speeds up the reaction, which shows that radicals are involved.
Adding oxygen, which combines with free radicals, slows the reaction, which shows that a radical chain is being broken.

Ethene has a C=C double bond, which is rich in electrons and so attracts electron-poor species. Addition means the two chlorine atoms join across the double bond, and the reaction goes in four steps through ions, not radicals.
Step 1, polarisation: the C=C double bond is a region of high electron density from its pi electrons (the electrons of the second bond in the double bond).
As a Cl₂ molecule approaches, these pi electrons repel the electrons of the Cl–Cl bond, inducing a dipole (one end slightly positive, one slightly negative) Clδ⁺–Clδ⁻.
Step 2, heterolytic fission: the Cl–Cl bond breaks with both electrons going to the further chlorine atom, giving Cl⁺ and Cl⁻. Draw a curved arrow from the Cl–Cl bond to the Clδ⁻ atom.

Step 3, carbocation formation: the pair of pi electrons forms a bond to Cl⁺, so one carbon bonds to Cl while the other, having lost its share of the pi pair, carries a positive charge, giving CH₂ClCH₂⁺. Draw a curved arrow from the C=C pi bond to Cl⁺.
Step 4, attack by the negative ion: Cl⁻ uses a lone pair to bond to the positive carbon, giving 1,2-dichloroethane. Draw a curved arrow from a lone pair on Cl⁻ to the C⁺.
It is called ionic addition because the two parts add as ions, one after the other.
Hydrogen chloride adds to ethene by the same ionic route as chlorine, but it is shorter because HCl is already polar and needs no induced dipole.
Overall: CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl, giving chloroethane.
The H–Cl bond is already polar, Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻, because chlorine is more electronegative (it pulls the shared electrons towards itself), so no dipole needs to be induced.

Step 1: the pi electrons of C=C form a bond to the Hδ⁺ atom, and the H–Cl bond breaks heterolytically, giving Cl⁻ and the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺. Draw a curved arrow from the pi bond to H, and one from the H–Cl bond to Cl.
Step 2: Cl⁻ bonds to the positive carbon, giving chloroethane. Draw a curved arrow from a lone pair on Cl⁻ to C⁺.
Evidence that the H–X bond breaks in the mechanism: the rate of addition to ethene increases in the order HF < HCl < HBr < HI, the order in which the H–X bond gets weaker.
If chlorine added to ethene in one move, only 1,2-dichloroethane could form. Mixed products show that the reaction goes in steps through a carbocation, which other species in the mixture can attack.
When ethene reacts with chlorine water (chlorine dissolved in water), the products include 2-chloroethanol, CH₂ClCH₂OH, as well as 1,2-dichloroethane.
2-chloroethanol forms because a water molecule, using a lone pair on its oxygen, attacks the carbocation instead of Cl⁻, and then loses H⁺.

This shows the reaction happens in steps through a positively charged intermediate (a short-lived species formed between reactants and products): if both chlorine atoms added at the same moment, no 2-chloroethanol could form.
With bromine water containing sodium chloride, ethene gives 1-bromo-2-chloroethane, CH₂BrCH₂Cl, as well as 1,2-dibromoethane.
The Cl⁻ ions attack the carbocation, but no 1,2-dichloroethane forms, because the first atom to add is always from Br₂.
The two mechanisms differ in the type of hydrocarbon, how bonds break, the conditions and the intermediate. Comparing them side by side helps keep the arrows and conditions straight.
Free radical substitution is shown by alkanes (hydrocarbons with only single bonds), involves homolytic fission, needs UV light, has radical intermediates and uses fishhook arrows.
Ionic addition is shown by alkenes (hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond), involves heterolytic fission, needs no light, has a carbocation intermediate and uses curved arrows.
Diagram: the four steps of ionic addition of Cl₂ to ethene, with the δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges, the carbocation and every curved arrow, and the initiation step of chlorination with its two fishhooks.
Organic chemists track redox (electron-transfer) changes by watching oxygen and hydrogen, because carbon compounds rarely show ions. This gives a simple ladder from alcohols up to carboxylic acids.
An organic compound is oxidised when it gains oxygen or loses hydrogen, and reduced when it gains hydrogen or loses oxygen. These are the quick tests to apply to any organic change.
The oxidation number of the carbon involved (the charge it would have if the bonds were fully ionic) rises on oxidation and falls on reduction, which matches the oxygen and hydrogen rule.

The oxidation ladder: primary alcohol (OH on a carbon with one other carbon attached) to aldehyde (–CHO) to carboxylic acid (–COOH); secondary alcohol (OH on a carbon with two other carbons attached) to ketone (C=O inside the chain).
Each step up the ladder is an oxidation, and the reverse of each step is a reduction.

Equations may be written with [O] for oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent (the substance that removes electrons or hydrogen), so the organic change is shown without the reagent: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O, and CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH.

Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidising agent that shows its own progress by colour. In acid it removes hydrogen or adds oxygen to alcohols, so it carries organic compounds up the oxidation ladder.
Acidified potassium permanganate, KMnO₄ with dilute sulfuric acid, is a strong oxidising agent. It is reduced from purple MnO₄⁻ to almost colourless Mn²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

It oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids: ethanol to ethanal to ethanoic acid, and propan-1-ol to propanal to propanoic acid. The purple colour fades as the permanganate is used up.

Balanced example: 5C₂H₅OH + 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ → 5CH₃CHO + 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O, built from the organic half-equation (the electron-losing half) C₂H₅OH → CH₃CHO + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ and the permanganate half-equation, so that the electrons cancel.
To stop at the aldehyde, distil it off as it forms (heating so it boils out of the mixture) and do not use the oxidising agent in excess.
This works because ethanal boils at about 21 °C, well below ethanol at 78 °C, so it leaves before it can be oxidised further.
Whether acidified permanganate reacts depends on how many hydrogens sit on the carbon bearing the oxygen. This decides how far each type of alcohol gets.

To make the acid, use an excess of oxidising agent and heat under reflux (boiling with a condenser that returns the vapours to the flask), so the aldehyde stays in the mixture until it is oxidised to the acid.
It oxidises secondary alcohols to ketones: propan-2-ol to propanone, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O.

It does not oxidise tertiary alcohols (OH on a carbon with three other carbons attached), such as 2-methylpropan-2-ol, or ketones. Neither has a hydrogen on the carbon bearing the oxygen, and oxidation would need a C–C bond to break.
Carboxylic acids are not oxidised further.
Permanganate behaves differently in alkaline conditions: it is reduced less far, so a different product and colour result. The alcohol is still oxidised up the ladder.
In basic (alkaline) solution, e.g. with sodium carbonate, permanganate is reduced to brown manganese(IV) oxide instead of Mn²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻.
The colour change is from purple to a brown precipitate (an insoluble solid that forms in the solution).

It oxidises a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid, which is present as its salt in the basic solution because the base neutralises it: phenylmethanol gives benzoate ions, which give benzoic acid on acidifying. There is more on this in Investigation: synthesising benzoic acid.
Fehling's solution is a gentler oxidising agent than permanganate. Because it only oxidises aldehydes, it can tell an aldehyde from a ketone or an alcohol.
Fehling's solution is a mild oxidising agent containing Cu²⁺ ions.
It oxidises aldehydes to carboxylic acids, present as carboxylate salts (the acid's anion) in the alkaline reagent, and is itself reduced to brick-red copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O.
It does not oxidise ketones, and, being mild, it does not oxidise alcohols, so it is used to identify aldehydes. There is more on this in Tests, reaction schemes and preparing an ester.

Reduction is the reverse of the oxidation ladder: hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst (a solid that speeds up the reaction without being used up) adds hydrogen to a double bond. It turns carbonyl compounds back into alcohols.
Hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst is the reducing agent: it adds hydrogen across a C=O or C=C double bond.
Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols: CH₃CHO + H₂ → CH₃CH₂OH (ethanal to ethanol).
Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols: CH₃COCH₃ + H₂ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (propanone to propan-2-ol).
Alkenes (hydrocarbons with a C=C bond) are reduced to alkanes: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃; this is also an addition reaction, because two molecules join to form one product.

Hydrogenation of vegetable oils: oils contain many C=C bonds (they are polyunsaturated), and adding hydrogen over nickel converts some C=C to C–C. This raises the melting point, so the liquid oil becomes a soft solid fat used in margarine.
The degree of hydrogenation (how many C=C bonds are converted) sets how hard the product is.
Carboxylic acids can give away a proton (H⁺), so they react like other acids with bases. Alcohols hold on to their proton much more tightly.
Carboxylic acids are weak acids (only partly ionised in water) that transfer a proton to bases: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
With carbonates they give carbon dioxide: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
With hydrogencarbonates they also give carbon dioxide: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.

Alcohols are far weaker acids than carboxylic acids, about as weak as water itself, so they do not react with sodium carbonate or usefully with sodium hydroxide. There is more on this in Physical properties and acidity.

An ester (the compound formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid) can be split again by water. With a base the hydroxide ion acts as a base, so this is an acid–base reaction, and it goes all the way to completion.
Hydrolysis is the breaking of a compound by reaction with water.
Esters can be hydrolysed by acid, which is reversible and is the reverse of esterification (making an ester from an acid and an alcohol), or by base.

Base hydrolysis: heating an ester with sodium hydroxide gives the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid and the alcohol: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH (ethyl ethanoate to sodium ethanoate and ethanol).
It is an acid–base reaction because the hydroxide ion acts as a base and the carboxylic acid formed is converted to its carboxylate ion (the acid minus its H⁺).
This is why base hydrolysis goes to completion, while acid hydrolysis reaches an equilibrium (a balance in which reactants and products are both present).
Acidifying the product mixture (adding H⁺) converts the carboxylate salt back into the free carboxylic acid: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH.
Fats and oils are esters with three ester links, made from one glycerol and three fatty acids. Their structure explains why one is solid and the other liquid.

Fats and oils are tri-esters, or triglycerides, of glycerol, propane-1,2,3-triol, HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH (an alcohol with three –OH groups), with three long-chain carboxylic acids called fatty acids. Stearic acid, octadecanoic acid, C₁₇H₃₅COOH, is an example.
Fats, mostly from animals, are solid at room temperature and contain mainly saturated chains (chains with only C–C single bonds).
Oils, mostly from plants, are liquid and contain more unsaturated chains with C=C bonds.

Diagram: a triglyceride, with a three-carbon glycerol backbone, each carbon joined through an ester group (–O–CO–) to a long hydrocarbon chain R; and the products, glycerol with three –OH groups and three RCOO⁻Na⁺ ions.
Heating a fat or oil with sodium hydroxide is base hydrolysis of all three ester links at once. It makes soap and glycerol.
Base hydrolysis of a fat or oil is called saponification, the process of soap-making: fat + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3 sodium salts of fatty acids (soap).
Example: glyceryl tristearate reacts with sodium hydroxide: (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₃C₃H₅ + 3NaOH → 3C₁₇H₃₅COONa + C₃H₅(OH)₃, giving sodium stearate and glycerol.
The mole ratio of fat : NaOH : soap : glycerol is 1 : 3 : 3 : 1, because each fat has three ester links and each needs one NaOH.
Molar masses: glyceryl tristearate 890 g mol⁻¹, sodium stearate 306 g mol⁻¹ and glycerol 92 g mol⁻¹.
Glycerol, the co-product (the second product made alongside the soap), is soluble in water and is used in cosmetics and medicines.
Water on its own is poor at cleaning greasy things, because water and oil do not mix. A surfactant is the kind of substance that fixes this, and soap is the best-known example.

A surfactant (surface-active agent) is a substance whose molecules or ions have a water-attracting (hydrophilic) part and a water-repelling (hydrophobic) part, so one particle can interact with both water and oil.
Dissolved in water, a surfactant lowers the surface tension (the pull between surface water molecules that makes water bead up), which helps water wet surfaces and mix with oil and grease.
Soap is a surfactant: the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid, called a fatty acid (an acid with a long hydrocarbon chain ending in –COOH).
Sodium stearate, C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻Na⁺, is sodium octadecanoate, a typical soap.
Potassium soaps are softer and are used in liquid soaps.
A soap ion has two ends with opposite attitudes to water. This split personality is what lets soap clean, and it is the basis of any question on how soap works.

The head, the carboxylate group –COO⁻, is ionic and hydrophilic: it is attracted to polar water molecules (molecules with slightly positive and negative ends) by ion–dipole attraction, and so dissolves in water.

The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain of about 12–18 carbon atoms; it is non-polar and hydrophobic, so it does not mix with water but dissolves in grease and oil through London dispersion forces (weak attractions between non-polar molecules).
This dual nature lets one soap ion interact with both water and grease.
Soap can dissolve the non-polar oils on skin, and through its ionic heads and the water it also removes the salts in sweat.
Diagram: a soap ion drawn as a long zig-zag tail, with a circled –COO⁻ head and a separate Na⁺ ion, labelled hydrophobic tail and hydrophilic head.
Grease holds dirt to skin and fabric, and plain water cannot lift it. Soap works in a fixed sequence, ending with the grease trapped in tiny spheres that rinse away.
1. In water, soap lowers the surface tension, so the water spreads over and wets the greasy surface or fabric instead of beading up.
2. The hydrophobic tails dissolve in the grease or oil, while the hydrophilic heads stay in the water at the surface of the grease.
3. Rubbing or agitation breaks the grease into tiny droplets, each surrounded by soap ions.
4. Each droplet becomes a micelle: a sphere with the grease and the tails inside, and the negatively charged heads facing out into the water.

5. The negative surfaces of the micelles repel one another, so the droplets do not join up again and stay dispersed in the water as an emulsion (tiny droplets of one liquid spread through another); this is emulsification.
6. Rinsing carries the micelles away, with the dirt and microorganisms trapped in the grease.
Diagram: a micelle, with an oil droplet in the centre, soap tails pointing inward into it, and heads (–COO⁻) on the outside in water.
Soap does not work equally well in all water. In hard water it is partly wasted, because ions in the water react with it.
Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, for example water from limestone regions.
These ions react with soap ions to form an insoluble scum (a solid that does not dissolve): 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻(aq) + Ca²⁺(aq) → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca(s).
In hard water, soap forms scum and lathers poorly until all the hardness ions have been precipitated (removed as solid), which wastes soap.
In deionised, soft water (water with the ions removed), soap lathers easily.
Chemists solved the scum problem by changing the head of the surfactant. Surfactants can then be sorted into groups by the charge on that head.
Synthetic detergents, also called soapless detergents, have a similar head-and-tail structure but a different head, e.g. a sulfonate group (–SO₃⁻) in alkylbenzene sulfonates.
Their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble, so synthetic detergents work well in hard water and form no scum.
Surfactants are grouped by their head: anionic (negative head), e.g. soaps and sulfonates in washing-up liquid and laundry detergent.
Cationic surfactants have a positive head, e.g. quaternary ammonium compounds in fabric conditioners and some disinfectants.
Non-ionic surfactants have an uncharged head and are used in many cleaning products.
Any job that needs oil and water to mix, or a liquid to spread over a surface, uses a surfactant. The uses fall into four groups.
Cleaning: bar and liquid soaps, hand wash, shower gel, shampoo, washing-up liquid, laundry detergent, and household and industrial surface cleaners.
Personal care: toothpaste, where sodium lauryl sulfate is the foaming agent; shampoo; and cosmetics and creams, where surfactants act as emulsifiers (substances that keep oil and water mixed).
Food: emulsifiers such as lecithin, a natural emulsifier from soya or egg yolk, keep oil and water mixed in mayonnaise, chocolate and margarine.

Other uses: fabric conditioners; wetting agents (substances that help a liquid spread over a surface) in paints, inks and agricultural sprays, so that the spray spreads over leaves; firefighting foams; and dispersants that break up oil spills at sea.
Surfactants have made a major contribution to public health, because they remove microorganisms and the grease that shelters them.
Handwashing with soap removes microorganisms from the skin, trapping them in micelles that are rinsed away.
Handwashing is one of the most effective ways of preventing the spread of infectious diseases such as diarrhoeal diseases, respiratory infections and influenza.

Soap destroys enveloped viruses (viruses with a fatty outer layer), such as influenza viruses and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19: the hydrophobic tails insert into the virus's fatty lipid outer membrane and break it apart.
Public-health advice during the COVID-19 pandemic was to wash hands with soap and water, scrubbing for at least 20 seconds.
Detergents used in laundry, dishwashing, hospitals and food processing remove the grease that shelters bacteria, improving hygiene in homes, hospitals and the food industry.
Surfactants also caused pollution problems, and the solutions show how detergent design changed. These facts belong here only as impacts of surfactant use.

Early synthetic detergents with branched hydrocarbon chains were not biodegradable (microorganisms could not break them down), so they caused foam on rivers in the 1950s and 1960s; they were replaced by biodegradable linear-chain detergents.

Phosphates added to some detergents as builders (additives that improve cleaning) can cause eutrophication (over-enrichment with nutrients) of lakes and rivers, so their use has been restricted, e.g. in laundry detergents in the EU.
The EU restricted phosphates in household laundry detergents from 2013 and in household dishwasher detergents from 2017.
Soap can be made at small scale from kitchen materials. The reaction splits a fat or oil into soap and glycerol using sodium hydroxide.

Aim: to make soap on a small scale from household reactants, by base hydrolysis (saponification, the splitting of a fat or oil by an alkali) with sodium hydroxide, and to compare the product when sodium hydroxide is limiting with when it is in excess.
Word equation: fat or oil + sodium hydroxide gives soap (the sodium salts of fatty acids) + glycerol.
One mole of fat reacts with 3 moles of NaOH, because each fat molecule has three ester links to break.
Household reactants: a vegetable oil or fat, e.g. olive, sunflower or coconut oil, or lard; sodium hydroxide, sold as caustic soda; water; and table salt for brine (concentrated salt solution).
A reflux method (boiling with a condenser fitted to return the vapour) is not required: the mixture is heated gently in an open container in a water bath.
The method has two halves: making the soap by heating, then separating it from the other products with brine and washing.
1. Weigh a known mass of oil, e.g. 10 g, into a beaker or evaporating basin.

2. Add a measured volume of sodium hydroxide solution of known concentration; a little ethanol, if available, can be added as a solvent in which both the oil and the sodium hydroxide dissolve, so that they mix and react faster.
3. Heat gently in a water bath, stirring continuously, for about 20–30 minutes, adding a little water if the mixture dries out; the mixture becomes thick and creamy as soap forms.

4. Pour the mixture into a beaker of saturated salt solution (brine) and stir; the soap separates as solid curds, because soap is much less soluble in concentrated salt solution than in water; this is salting out.
5. Collect the soap by filtration or by skimming it off, and wash it with a little ice-cold water, because warm water would dissolve the soap.
6. Press the soap dry between filter papers, leave it to dry and weigh it.
